en: Preface to the *Sifen jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts), following the words of the commentary:
What, then, is this *śīla-sūtra*? It is the standard for bhikṣus and the essential gateway to Nirvāṇa. If the standard is lost, the mind will lack order;
if the gateway is lost, it will be difficult to reach the other shore. Therefore, from the Deer Park at the beginning until [the final teaching], the Tathāgata...
At the Śāla trees, he earnestly instructed and exhorted us, commanding that we take the Prātimokṣa as our teacher and regard it as identical to the Buddha.

For those today to turn their backs on his final testament and disparage the Vinaya—how is this different from a rebellious son defying his compassionate father, or like the heretic Sunakṣatra insulting the holy words?
To turn one's back on the final instructions is to be no Buddha; to revile the *vinaya* is to be no Dharma; to see those who uphold the precepts and mock them is to be no Saṃgha.
Since one thus fails to honor and instead destroys the Triple Gem, how can such a person be called a son of the Śākyas?

Indeed, the dharma of the precepts is the *amṛta* (essence) that counteracts the seeds of karma born of ignorance, and it is the sublime art for cultivating and realizing the fivefold Dharma-body. These seeds of karma...
If one does not sever [these bonds], the causal flows will overflow, the Dharma-body will remain incomplete, and there will be no day of liberation.

To practice in opposition to this, even if one attains wondrous awakening and meditative concentration manifests before them, it is ultimately the work of Māra. The sūtras contain explicit statements; these are not the speculative words of men.

In the present age, those who practice falsely and attain erroneous realizations cast the *vinaya* (liberation) outside of their speech, taking their own views as their personal standard of measurement. Being unable themselves...
I maintain that those who desire others to be as they themselves are biased will destroy the Dharma and extinguish the Vinaya; one cannot bear even to look upon them.

Observing this, I have constantly exhorted beginners to apply their eyes to the *Vinaya*, so that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) may have a foundation and the True Dharma may endure for a long time. However, the meaning of the Vinaya texts is profound and abstruse;

regarding the categories of "abiding" and "maintaining," or "acting" and "transgressing," as well as their names, types, natures, and characteristics, there is no one among readers who does not become bewildered. Therefore, I, Man, [have composed this work].
I have diligently extracted the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and explained it according to the Vinaya; hence, it is said to be "explained as [in the Vinaya].

Although this explanation is not exhaustive, I have supplemented it with other schools to complete it. This work serves as the primary key to the Vinaya, enabling students to kneel at the threshold and traverse the pathways.
Though the phrasing may be concise, the stages of its meaning are truly comprehensive. Those who wish to ascend the pavilions and galleries of Śamatha should step upon this very work.
One foot. In the winter of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era, the Bhikṣu Pútíxīn of Xīláishān wrote this preface at Xiàngwánggé Hall.
General Principles, Section Thirteen:
Regarding this *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, there are two versions in the Tibetan canon (*bKa' 'gyur*). One is the translation by the Venerable Buddhayaśas of the Later Qin dynasty;
the other was compiled and extracted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka* by the Vinaya Master Huaisu of the Tang dynasty. As for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*:

One section, comprising sixty fascicles, was also translated by the Venerable Guṇavarman. It has been revered and practiced by all the eminent virtuous ones of this land from the Qin to the Tang dynasties;
yet, it is regrettable that the commentaries produced by many scholars have not survived. Since the Song dynasty, those who have composed works on it have been few.
Nowadays, beginners studying the Vinaya often find the ritual details (dharmas) difficult, and most simply abandon the scrolls as being too lofty.

Consequently, the study of the Vinaya gradually declined; practitioners became ignorant of both the observance and violation of precepts, and the essential dharma of the Śākyaputrīyas became nothing more than ancient texts.

Observing this, I feared that the True Dharma would perish before long. Therefore, I have selected the most profound Sanskrit and Chinese phrases from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), annotated and explained them, and titled this work the *Explanatory Glossary of Terms and Meanings in the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

This work comprises twenty-eight fascicles; it serves merely as a general guide to the Vinaya and is intended to facilitate the understanding of subsequent commentaries so that one is not hindered by the literal text.
However, the labor involved in such a commentary is vast and cannot be completed in a single day.

Desiring to enable beginners to quickly understand the rules of observance and violation, I have therefore extracted the *Prātimokṣa* and explained it according to the Vinaya. Yet, because the Vinaya text is so extensive and detailed, it was impossible to follow it in its entirety.

This original collection has had its redundancies excised and its essentials highlighted, yet the meaning remains entirely intact. As for the rules of opening and closing, maintaining and violating the precepts, not even a hair’s breadth has been added or omitted.
The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, knows the karmic dispositions and natures of all sentient beings and bestows upon them the precepts accordingly.
This is beyond the capacity of even Bodhisattvas or Arhats; how much less could ordinary, ignorant people possibly add to or subtract from it?

Since the principle is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), it is said to be "explained according to suchness. Nevertheless, the basis of this explanation still relies upon the Vinaya-piṭaka and the collections compiled by Master Sū.

Within these, there are passages that are concise and plain, which I fear beginners may find difficult to follow; therefore, I have taken one or two characters from the translated versions [to clarify].

It is easy to clarify this. However, beneath each precept, I have appended the Vinaya texts of other schools along with various treatises and biographies, intending to mutually elucidate their underlying principles and to supplement what was incomplete.
This is by no means intended to substitute the heavy for the light or to replace prohibitions with ease.
Each Vinaya has its own specific intent; they cannot be conflated or superimposed. If the thieving mind is not severed, how can one be said to possess faith and precepts? As for practice:
One should simply maintain [the teachings] within one's own school; there is no need for the trouble of engaging in forced interpretation.

As for those matters and principles that are universally applicable, whose textual meanings are thorough and detailed, there is no fault in employing them. If one wishes to explain them extensively, it is necessary to consult the entire Tripiṭaka before doing so.

If one is to serve as a preceptor, it is essential to study extensively and investigate deeply, delighting in simplicity and detesting complexity; for the Vinaya teachings contain severe condemnations.

The Buddha ordained that a *bhikṣu* must have completed ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*), be proficient in the Tripiṭaka, and possess a correspondence between his practice and understanding before he is permitted to act as a preceptor, bestow the full ordination upon others, and maintain *śrāmaṇeras*. Should one be unable to master all three collections, [the Vinaya scriptures...]
One must be clearly aware of this. If one does not know what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts, one is like a white sheep.

How can one who wishes to hastily act as a teacher for others provide guidance? Since one has already contravened the Buddha’s explicit regulations while wishing to cause others to follow them, how could that ever be possible?
To harm oneself and harm others—what kind of teacher’s dharma is that?

When a bhikṣu violates the seven groups of precepts (*sapta-varga*), with the exception of the first category which requires irreversible penance (*āpattipratideśana*), the remaining categories must be confessed and extinguished before another person.
This may be done by repenting within the assembly or by confessing face-to-face (*pratyekapratideśana*). Thus, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*) is restored to its original purity.

In the present day, people do not distinguish between black and white; they know nothing of the gravity or lightness of offenses. For serious transgressions, they merely require the recitation of mantras for a certain number of times, while for minor ones...
Most [monks] ignore this entirely. This greatly violates the Buddha’s regulations and completely contradicts the intent of the Vinaya.
The Buddha ordained that one should not eat after midday; this brings great benefit to both body and mind, providing relief for oneself and others alike.
Thus, the Venerable Kāśyapa was the first to transmit the seal of the mind, observing the dhūta practices until the end of his life, taking only a single meal at noon and nothing more.
The rest is consumed. Among the bhikṣus, they receive food before midday; after midday, they are again permitted to drink thin gruel. This too is sufficient.

Since you have already left the home life out of right faith, abandoning all worldly affairs of body and mind as if discarding excrement, why do you, for the sake of this meager amount of food and drink, violate your own original faith and destroy the Buddha’s clear regulations? Or perhaps you say, "I have no..."
Attachment! Alas! To deviate so one-sidedly from the Vinaya teachings—is this not a great attachment?
The Vinaya takes liberation as its primary aim; it does not indulge in worldly flavors. The Teachings enjoin the renunciation of the five desires, as if discarding nasal mucus or spittle.
Yet today, people hoard goods in chests and bags, more than a yak cherishes its tail. This not only contravenes the intent of the Vinaya, but is in fact...
This further binds one to the burdens of birth and death; deeply submerged in the river of craving, one sinks into the ford of delusion from which rescue is difficult. Some may say:
"I keep these for the sake of others and have no personal attachment. If this is so, why not present them as offerings to the Triple Gem to relieve all living beings?
If you say they are accumulated for the sake of others, then to use them privately constitutes the offense of theft.

The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus must possess three robes and may not be separated from them for even a single night; to be separated from them results in the forfeiture of the robes and incurs guilt.
Nowadays, people do not follow the Dharma and willfully separate themselves from them; they receive the robes but do not maintain them.
How can they avoid having the present *kāṣāya* depart from their bodies and, in the future, having their bodies bound by iron plates? Beyond these three robes, whatever surplus...

Regarding long-term possessions, the Buddha permitted monks to declare them "pure" (*śuddhi*) by forming the intention of entrusting them to others, thereby allowing them to maintain and store such items.
This was intended to manifest freedom from attachment and the burden of claiming things as one's own. Now that this method has entirely fallen into disuse, the bhikṣus are all utterly bewildered.
Although the Mahāyāna permits Bodhisattvas to possess items for the sake of sentient beings, they must still declare them pure; if one does not follow these instructions, [one incurs fault].
This is called an offense.
According to the Vinaya regulations, the five groups of the ordained must all wear the *kāṣāya*. The *kāṣāya* refers to a garment of "deteriorated color" (*prakṛti-varṇa-vipariṇata*).

By means of three colors that accord with the Dharma, one alters the five primary colors. In recent times, those who respond to worldly affairs have come to designate the five-colored garments as [the true *kāṣāya*].
To wear the *kāṣāya* [in this manner] is a great error. The Buddha previously predicted that in the final dharma age (*mofa*), the *kāṣāya* would change into five colors.
To don it now is truly a sign of the decline of the final dharma age; sons of the Śākya should take note of this.
At present, śrāmaṇeras wear the three robes (tricīvara) of a bhikṣu; however, this is nowhere to be found in the Vinaya texts of the five schools.
The *Ekottarakarman* strictly admonishes that it is not permitted, stipulating instead that they should wear only the seamless robe (*saṃkakṣikā*) without any features such as pleats or partitions.
In recent times, teachers who do not master the Vinaya scriptures have recklessly conferred the precepts upon others.

This erroneous custom has been passed down in succession and treated as the orthodox standard, leading even laymen and laywomen to don the five-strip *kāṣāya* robes of a bhikṣu; such is the extent of this delusion.

How truly laughable! Having been corrupted by long-standing habit, it cannot be restored in a single evening. Nevertheless, we who have inherited and flourished [in this tradition] should together support and propagate the correct path, ensuring that such [corruptions] do not gain further traction—this would be our greatest fortune.
The precepts of a bhikṣu are most sublime; they can serve as a virtuous field of merit and a source of auspicious protection for both humans and devas.
They are not merely for one’s own emergence from birth and death. Now that you have received them, you shall employ them to respond to the affairs of the human world.
How deeply regrettable! Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, throughout kalpas sacrificed his head, eyes, marrow, and brain to attain this Dharma.
To now trade it for the meager, defiled profits of the world—is this not truly heart-rending? Moreover, the practice of responding to invitations for rituals originated in this land;
it is entirely absent in the Western Country (India). It is profoundly contrary to the monastic law and was never taught by the Buddha during his appearance in the world.
You, my guest, should quickly recognize this and reform.

Precepts are the substance of concentration (*samādhi*); wisdom (*prajñā*) is the function of concentration. If the substance is not established, there is no basis from which the function can be applied.
Therefore, all sages and worthies have achieved perfection through precepts, and all members of the sevenfold assembly of disciples are established by means of the precepts. Thus, the South...
Even after one has attained the Dharma through the lineage, it is still necessary to ascend the altar and receive formal transmission.

National Teacher Qingliang was himself an Avatamsaka Bodhisattva who personally disciplined his body according to the ten precepts; how could the patriarchs of successive generations have ordained others while remaining in lay dress?
The Tathāgatas of the three periods all take the precepts as their primary restraint; thus, when our Śākyamuni Buddha first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he immediately...

Together with the various bodhisattvas, he established the *prātimokṣa*. Upon examining the sūtras and vinayas of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, there is not one that does not praise those who uphold the precepts;
nor has a single Buddha ever been seen to extol those who violate the prohibitions. Let the wise examine this closely:
in ten thousand cases, there is never an instance of self-deception.
When the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted us with the instruction to rely upon the *prātimokṣa* as our teacher.
Now, people abandon the *vinaya* and do not study it; this is not only to turn their backs on the Buddha’s final exhortation, but is already to have discarded their own teacher.

When they see someone upholding the precepts, they immediately mock and revile them. Unless one’s wisdom surpasses that of the Tathāgata, such a person is effectively contending with the Buddha himself. I—
This means that one who disparages others is, in fact, slandering the Buddha. Please examine yourself; should you not be afraid?

In the Western regions, the method of studying the Dharma begins with the study of the Hīnayāna, followed by the reading of the Mahāyāna teachings. Once the general principles are mastered, every single dharma...
This is not Madhyamaka. Thus, one knows that "Great" and "Small" [vehicles] depend upon the mind; the Dharma itself possesses neither expansion nor inferiority.

How could one possibly give rise to grasping or rejecting, or praise or disparagement, toward it? If one does not begin with the elementary studies and first practice the Great Canon, there will surely be many who sit idly and falsely boast of Prajñāpāramitā while repudiating cause and effect.
The Buddhas of the three periods all preach the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

While both the Sūtra and Abhidharma Piṭakas are accessible to both laypeople and monastics, only the Vinaya Piṭaka is maintained exclusively by Bhikṣus. It is like a king’s secret treasury, not under the jurisdiction of external officials;
therefore, if a layperson or a Śrāmaṇera should peruse it first, they shall never thereafter be permitted to receive the full precepts. This is a transgression.
This is categorized as being on the same footing as the five heinous crimes. Any who act as a preceptor must be most cautious and prudent.

[The following is] the General Diagram of the Two Hundred and Fifty Rules of Full Ordination (*Upasampadā*), including the characteristics of the full precepts, dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), and minute conduct. Regarding the practice of walking, standing, sitting, and...
Each of the four postures (*īryāpatha*) has two hundred and fifty [subdivisions], totaling one thousand.
Following these through the three periods of past, future, and present constitutes three thousand postures.
These three thousand are then applied to the seven [modes] of body and speech.
These constitute twenty-one thousand [teachings].

These twenty-one thousand, in turn, serve as antidotes to the four types of afflictions—namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and those of equal proportion—thereby forming eighty-four thousand subtle practices. This is the eighty-four [thousandfold dharma].
There are four thousand rules of discipline (*vinaya*). As for the statement regarding the eighty thousand minor precepts (*anuśīla*), this is merely an abbreviated enumeration.
If one were to discuss their origination, then the *pārājika* offenses constitute the roots; the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses constitute the stumps;
the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses constitute the branches; and the *pāyattika* offenses constitute the stalks. The *prātideśanīya* [offenses]... [the text continues].
Training is the leaves; repentance of faults is the flowers; the settling of disputes is the fruit.
The indeterminate states are the skin, sinews, and joints. If one upholds them, the seven factors of enlightenment are the flowers and the four noble truths are the fruit;
if one violates them, there are the seven branches of bodily and vocal conduct.
The flowers are the four evil destinies;
the fruits are the fourfold Prātimokṣa Sūtra.

Commentary on the *Sifen jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts), Fascicle One.
Written by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Jiqi.
Regarding the exegesis of this code of precepts, the major outline is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the main text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title:
The *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Code of Precepts) is named after its place of origin; it originally emerged from the Dharmaguptaka school.

The Vinaya is divided into four parts. The first part clarifies the rules for bhikṣus; the second clarifies the rules for bhikṣuṇīs, as well as the methods for receiving the precepts and the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha);
the third clarifies the rules for the rainy season retreat (varṣā) and the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā), among others; and the fourth clarifies the rules concerning dwellings and other matters.
This present *Śīlaskandhaka* (Sūtra of the Precepts) is that very first part, namely the Sūtra of the Two Hundred and Fifty Bhikṣu Precepts.
Furthermore, as for the Vinaya regulations: they began at the Deer Park and concluded beneath the Śāla trees. The Tathāgata’s silent proclamations were continued and proclaimed by Upāli.
Reciting the words of the Tathāgata, the text comprises eighty sections, hence it is called the *Aṣṭaka-bhāṣita-vinaya*.
First, Mahākāśyapa received it upon his head; next, Ānanda bore and maintained it; third was Madhyāntika; and fourth was Śāṇakavāsin.
Ti. The fifth was Upagupta. Thus these five masters transmitted and upheld [the teaching] in succession for over one hundred and ten years;
the transmission from teacher to disciple remained unchanged. Later, King Aśoka ruled the world, revering the Triple Gem and convening a vast assembly of the Sangha.
When the Tripitaka was recompiled, the bhikṣus each clung to their own views and experiences, editing and arranging the Sūtras and Vinaya according to the teachings of their respective teachers.
Because their citations and tenets differed, two schools eventually emerged. They disputed right and wrong with one another and sought a royal adjudication.

White and black voting sticks were distributed to indicate which version was new and which was old; at that time, the older version received the majority of votes, and thus it was named "The Majority" (Mahāsāṃghika).
They were called the Mahāsāṃghika. Because they adopted few [new] points, while the Sthavira was named after its leader, it was called the Sthavira-vāda.
From these two schools, eighteen schools further emerged within the course of two hundred years.
Among the eighteen schools, five serve as the primary pillars: First is the Dharmaguptaka (translated as "Dharma-Secret"; a personal name; its Vinaya is the *Four-Part* [Caturvarga]).

Second is the Sarvāstivāda (translated as "Proponents of All Existence"; the root school; this refers to the *Ten Recitations* [Daśabhāṇavāra]). Third is the Kāśyapīya (translated as "Reverent Contemplation of Emptiness"; its Vinaya is the *Vimukti*;

it contains only one fascicle of the precept manual, which arrived here at this time). Fourth is the Mahīśāsaka (translated as "Contemplation of Neither Attachment to Existence nor Non-existence"; its Vinaya is the *Five-Part* [Pañcavargika]).

The fifth is the Vātsīputrīya (translated here as "Child of the Goat"; the original Vinaya text has not yet arrived). Regarding the compositions of these five schools, their textual expressions vary in breadth and their accounts differ in detail.
As for the gravity of offenses and the permissions or prohibitions regarding them, although there is no great difference, there are minor discrepancies.

Nevertheless, they were all proclaimed by the One Buddha; it is simply because what was heard and received was not extensive, and what was transmitted and recited is incomplete, that each school relies upon its own [version].
On one hand, they have come to form many distinct divisions. As the Tathāgata predicted in the past:

"After my parinirvāṇa, the Sūtras and Vinaya shall be divided into five schools, eventually reaching eighteen. Although their names differ, none of them will obstruct the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas or the Great Nirvāṇa.
By practicing in reliance upon them, all shall attain liberation. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Not yet..."
Come, my disciples! There are twenty schools that are able to cause all dharmas to abide. These twenty schools have all attained the four fruits;
the Tripitaka is equal for them, without inferior, middling, or superior distinctions. It is like the water of the ocean, whose taste is no different.
It is as if a man had twenty sons; this is what the Tathāgata has truly taught.
The two fundamental divisions emerge from the Mahāyāna; they emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā. Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas—all emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse: "The eighteen and the two divisions All emerge from the Mahāyāna; There is no such thing [that does not]."
Nor is it non-existent; I say that it arises in the future. As for the statement regarding the two fundamental divisions, these are the Mahāsāṃghika and Sthavira divisions.
From the Mahāsāṃghika division, seven sub-sects branched out; from the Sthavira division, eleven sub-sects branched out.
Together with the two root [vinayas], they constitute twenty schools in total. Of these, that which has been transmitted here in China exists only in four schools:
namely, the Mahāsāṃghika, the Dharmaguptaka, the Sarvāstivāda, and the Mūlasarvāstivāda. Regarding the causal origins of the precepts, the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* is an ancillary work of the Vinaya;
as are the remaining texts such as the *Samantapāsādikā*, the *Vinayamātṛkā*, the *Mātṛkā*, and the *Sarvāstivādavinaya-mātṛkā*.
The *Vinayavibhāṣā*, the *Prakaraṇapāda*, and other such texts are all concise expositions on the names and meanings of the Vinaya.
Since these categories have been personally certified by the Buddha himself, there is no need for doubt;

knowing that they are neither right nor wrong, what further deliberation is necessary? They are like ships, rafts, and life-preserving bags: though their names differ, when it comes to [crossing over], they are the same.
The shore is no different. Therefore, throughout the various kingdoms of the Five Indias, each adhering to a single teaching, all have attained the fruits of the Path.
In China, meanwhile, all four schools have been practiced, and all have ascended to the realization of the sages.

If it were not for the Tathāgata’s skillful response to the capacities of diverse beings, by what cause could such superior benefits have been obtained? Thus, one should carefully protect the life-preserving bag; there shall be none who do not reach the other shore.

Three: The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion with three proclamations);
Four: Reciting the Preface to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. I. Exposition of the Verses of Praise (twelve verses in total, divided into nine exegeses):
I prostrate my head in worship to all Buddhas, And to the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; Now I shall expound the Vinaya-dharma.

Regarding the phrase "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time," the commentary states: the first half-verse is an act of taking refuge in and paying homage to the Triple Gem; the second half-verse reveals that the precepts shall now be explained so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Whenever one performs a ritual act, it is essential to first pay homage to the Triple Gem in order to seek their empowerment, so as to [ensure] the internal...
Obstacles are subtly eliminated; external demons cause no disturbance, and religious rites are successfully accomplished.

As for "prostrating" (*kai-shou*), it originates from the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou) among the nine types of bows. It refers to lowering the head to the ground, pausing with the head held there for a short duration before rising.
"Ritual" (*li*) means "to tread upon. It signifies the principle that one's advancing and retreating must have measure, and that there must be a distinction between the honorable and the humble.
However, as customs differ across regions, ritual is not uniform. In Western lands, one pays homage by prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground;
in this land, one shows the utmost respect by bowing the head to the ground. Now, we shall adopt the practice of the Sui dynasty as the rite for expressing devotion.

The term "all" (*zhū*) refers collectively to the ten directions and the three periods of time. "Buddha" (*fó*), in its full form, is *buddha*, a title for Great Enlightenment that exhausts all principles and perfects all natures.
This enlightenment possesses three meanings: first, self-enlightenment, which is the realization that one's own nature is truly eternal.
First, awakening to the delusions as being empty and false. Second, awakening others by exercising unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) to deliver the realm of sentient beings.

Third, the perfection of awakening and practice, which means reaching the source and the ultimate depth, such that practice is fulfilled and the fruit is perfected. As for "Dharma," it refers to the essential points of the pure Dharma taught by the Tathāgata according to the capacities of beings;
it is definitively able to cause sentient beings to attain freedom from feverish affliction and to proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.
This is the holy teaching of one who has internally realized the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and whose wisdom is perfected. To explain it according to its meaning:

*Dharma* carries the sense of being a "normative guide" (*gati*) and a "sustainer" (*dhṛti*). As a guide, it gives rise to understanding in beings; as a sustainer, it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Sustaining" refers to the essence of the Dharma, while "guiding" refers to the function of the Dharma.
To maintain without abandoning means each remains steadfast in its own nature, just as water flows downward and fire rises upward—such is their nature.

Each is determined; this is the essence (*dharmatā*) of the dharma. "Norm" (*vinaya*) refers to a model that can produce understanding in sentient beings, such as fire for cooking food or water for floating a boat;
each takes its respective standard—this is the function (*prayojana*) of the dharma. Regarding the "Bhikṣu-saṃgha": a bhikṣu...
This is called "Bhikṣu" (the Beggar). "Begging" (*bhikṣā*) is a term for seeking; "sage" (*śi*) is an appellation for elegance and purity.

It means that internally one cultivates elegant and pure virtue, while externally one remains free from the four types of wrong livelihood, seeking only the necessities of life to benefit sentient beings and thereby perfect that elegant and pure virtue.

It is also called "The One Who Removes Famine" (*kṣapaṇaka*). This means that sentient beings lack the means to sustain themselves and suffer greatly from want and scarcity; [the Bhikṣu] emerges [to relieve them].
The observance of the precepts within the household is a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). It is capable of producing the goodness of sentient beings;

for this reason, people of the world take refuge in it with faith, making offerings and planting seeds of merit. It is like a rich, well-tilled field that can produce excellent crops and eliminate their hunger and deprivation.
Regarding the term *bhikṣu*, there are five distinct meanings as is commonly known. As for *saṃgha*, the full term is *saṃgha*; this word means "assembly."

This is a designation for those consisting of four bhikṣus or more; it is the general term for the assembly of those who purely uphold the precepts, as well as those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
"Now" (*jin*) refers precisely to the time when the precepts are being proclaimed. *Vinaya* is translated here as "extinction" (*mie*), meaning the extinction of greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is also called "subduing" (*zhefu*), meaning the taming of all afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it is called "discipline" (*lü*).

This refers to the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha, which adjudicates matters of light and heavy offenses, and prescribes what is permitted and what is prohibited, as well as what constitutes observance and transgression, thereby causing all evils to cease and manifold virtues to arise.
Regarding "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time": the True Dharma refers to the supramundane, untainted Noble Path.
Because the performance of *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts ensure that the True Dharma does not perish from the world, it is called the *Vinayapiṭaka*.
This is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma; as long as the Vinaya-piṭaka endures, the Buddha-dharma also endures.
For all wholesome dharmas—sublime concentration and supreme wisdom—are all produced by means of the precepts.

The precepts are like the ocean, boundless; Like jewels, they are sought without satiety. Desiring to protect the wealth of the noble Dharma, listen as I speak. *Explanation:* The first half of the verse clarifies the supreme virtues of the precepts; the second half exhorts the listeners to receive the benefits. As for "the boundless": the precepts refer to the two hundred and fifty *pratimokṣa* rules, together with all the various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Within each individual precept, ten kinds of merit for upholding the Saṃgha arise; within each of these merits...
Ten kinds of right dharmas arise: namely, the five faculties such as faith; the three wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
and the two restraints of body and speech. Because these bring about an ocean of merit that is without limit, it is said to be "boundless.
As for the phrase "like one who never tires of seeking jewels," "jewels" refers to the sovereign wish-fulfilling gem within the ocean, which accords with whatever sentient beings desire.
Because it can provide all manner of instruments of happiness, the world seeks it without ever wearying. Within the ocean of the Buddha-dharma, ethical discipline (śīla) is pure and bright;
it gives rise to the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and all other supreme wholesome qualities, which are obtained upon mere thought, just like that king of jewels.

Those who seek [these treasures] never grow weary. The "wealth of the noble Dharma" refers to the various superior and wholesome qualities such as those of the highest faculties, as well as faith, ethical discipline (*śīla*), learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame. These riches of the Dharma cannot be guarded without ethical discipline;

therefore, ethical discipline possesses the function of preventing what is improper and ceasing evil, just as brave soldiers and fierce generals can subdue enemies and prevent them from committing acts of aggression.
If you wish to protect this wealth, you should gather together in one place to listen and reflect, and act according to what is taught.

"The assembly" refers to those who have attained the perfect precepts in accordance with the Dharma. "Gathering" means that the faculty of the body assembles in one place; "listening" belongs to the auditory consciousness.
Regarding the words and meanings spoken there, one receives them through the auditory consciousness and understands them with a decisive mind. This is what I say.
This means that the words and their meanings are not in conflict; it is spoken in accordance with the Vinaya.

Desiring to eliminate the four *pārājika* dharmas and to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas, as well as the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas, I shall speak before the assembled community. Please listen.
The commentary states: This verse clarifies the faults avoided by listening to the precepts.
Regarding the four *pārājikas*—namely, sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying—if one commits even one of them, all meritorious qualities, the path, and its fruits are entirely abandoned.

Furthermore, one is forever cast out from the pure assembly and may no longer dwell together with the *bhikṣus*. It is like the great ocean, which does not accept a corpse but casts it adrift and abandons it.

On the shore, within the ocean of the precepts and Dharma, those who have broken the precepts are not admitted; therefore, they are forever cast outside the assembly of the pure and neither questioned nor disciplined.

Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension from the community), there are thirteen matters in total. This means that if one commits such an offense, there still remains a small residue that can be remedied;
by performing repentance according to the Dharma before a community of twenty monks, it may be removed.
It is extinguished; it is not like the previous four [categories], as there remains nothing further that can be remedied. Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture):

there are thirty such matters in total. These offenses arise from the fault of hoarding wealth and goods. One who commits such an offense must first forfeit the object in the midst of the community, and subsequently confess the *pāyattika* offense.
As for why the offense is termed "falling" (*pāyattika*), it means that if this offense is not confessed and removed, one immediately falls [into a lower state].

In the three miserable realms, one undergoes the suffering of being burned and boiled. Desiring to eliminate the four *pārājika* offenses, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the obstructive *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, you should all assemble together and listen with a single mind.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni— To these World-Honored Ones of Great Virtue, I speak this matter for you;
I now wish to explain it well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
The commentary states: The first verse summarizes the seven Buddhas; the latter verse describes the entrustment and requests for attention.
Vipaśyin is also called Vīra; this is translated as "Victorious Vision" (勝觀). Śikhin is also called Śikhin; this is translated as "Fire" (火). Viśvabhū...
In full, he is called Viśvabhū; this means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. (These three Tathāgatas appeared in the world at the end of the past Adornment Eon.)

Krakucchanda: translated as "That Which Should Be Severed" (*kṛta-vighna*) or "Adorned with Activity. He appeared in this ninth minor kalpa of the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan had decreased to sixty thousand years;
he was the first of the thousand Buddhas. Kanaka-muni: translated as "Golden Silence" (*kanaka-mauneya*) or "Golden Sage. He appeared in the world when the human lifespan was forty thousand years.
Kāśyapa: the full name is Kāśyapa. Translated as "Drinker of Light" (*jyotir-āśin*). [He appeared] when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.

He appeared in the world during an age when the human lifespan was one hundred years. Śākyamuni means "Able Sage" (Nengru); he is also called Śākyamuni, which means "Able Benevolent One" (Nengren) and "Silent Sage" (Jimo).
He appeared in the world during an age when the human lifespan was one hundred years. These four Tathāgatas appeared in succession in this world at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa.

The term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) refers to one who is endowed with the ten titles, for whom gods, humans, ordinary beings, and sages, as well as those of the mundane and supramundane worlds, all pay respect. The term "Virtuous One" (Mahābhāga) refers to one who possesses merit.
"Wisdom is his two feet; he possesses the virtues of the ten titles, peerless in the world. These two lines refer collectively to the aforementioned seven Buddhas.
"He who has spoken these matters for me" clarifies the transmission between teacher and disciple, demonstrating that it was not something to be spoken of casually. "Me" [refers to myself].

"Pointing to the person present who is able to recite the precepts" refers to the one currently speaking. "This matter" refers to everything from the *Nidāna* (the introduction) up to the verses of the Seven Buddhas.
"I now wish to explain it well" means to explain it skillfully; that is, to speak in accordance with the Dharma so that the words are free from error or confusion.

"May all you venerable ones listen together" refers to "all you venerable ones," meaning those who have received the precepts from their first ordination—whether they have no seniority (*anvaya*) or even up to a hundred years of seniority.
"Listen all together" means that everyone should gather in one place and listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
For example, if a person's feet are destroyed, they are unable to travel anywhere; likewise, one who has violated the precepts cannot be reborn among gods or humans.
If one wishes to be born in the heavens or, if born among humans, [to enjoy such states], [one must maintain the precepts].
"One should always protect the feet of the precepts, lest they be damaged or destroyed.

The commentary states: The first verse consists of two parts; the first half provides a metaphor, while the second half clarifies that obstacles arise regarding the wholesome paths. The subsequent verse [is as follows].

The first half [of the verse] indicates birth in the happy realms; the second half exhorts one to protect the causes of goodness. "For example" (*tadyathā*) is a term used for a hypothetical illustration.

"To destroy" (*dhvamsa*) means to ruin. "To tread upon" (*vilaṅghana*) means to step over or violate. "To destroy the precepts" refers to the act of breaking the precepts. "Heaven" (*deva*) here refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The twenty-eight heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Humans" refers to the inhabitants of the four great continents (*caturdvīpa*), the eight intermediate continents (*antaradvīpa*), and the various minor islands.
"One should always guard the feet of morality" means that one must not violate the precepts even for a moment.
"To damage" means to wound; it is not merely a warning against major violations, but even minor transgressions are impermissible.
This is a point of regret. As for the statement that one is reborn among devas and humans, this is merely a provisional teaching (upāya) adapted to the capacities and worldly conditions of the time.

This is because the people of the Western Regions generally delight in being born in the heavens; thus, when the Buddha first appeared in the world, he preached the Dharma according to their inclinations.

However, this was not the Sage’s ultimate intention, nor was it the fundamental purport of the Vinaya. The Vinaya takes liberation as its primary goal; how could it ever point toward the outflows (āsrava) of the realms of humans and devas?
Furthermore, the heavenly realm is originally a perilous path. There are two such perilous paths: first, rebirth in the heavens; second, the evil destinies.
Although one experiences superior bliss upon being born in the heavens, when merit is exhausted, one falls back into the evil realms.

Using this as proof, it is clear that [the heavenly realm] is not the ultimate goal of the Vinaya. If one were to destroy the precepts, one would not even be able to ascend to the perilous path, let alone reach Nirvana.
This is the path of delighting in *nirvāṇa*. That it does not explicitly say "nirvāṇa" here is for the sake of brevity. As the *Mahāvibhaṅga* states:
"Whether seeking heaven or *nirvāṇa*, one should guard the precepts through skillful means. If they remain thus unimpaired, one will surely be able to cross the perilous path. It further says:
"By thus mindfully cultivating the precepts, one can avoid all evil conduct, eliminate the afflictions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and enter *nirvāṇa* in peace and security."
[The Śrāvaka] originally, out of weariness with the fruits of suffering in the three realms, abandons the accumulation [of karma], cultivates the path, and realizes cessation.

How could he ever again expect the retributive fruits of humans or devas? The Bodhisattva does not crave worldly pleasures; fearing and wearying of the afflictions of birth and death, he deeply delights in Nirvāṇa.
The Śrāvaka’s fear and weariness of the afflictions and his deep delight in Nirvāṇa do not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of that of the Bodhisattva.
If one possesses even a single fraction [of virtue], how could one hope for the sensual pleasures of humans or devas?
Just as a charioteer entering a perilous path feels anxiety when the axle-pin is lost or the axle breaks, so too is it with one who has violated the precepts;
at the time of death, they harbor fear and dread.
The commentary states: The first half of the verse establishes a metaphor; the second half of the verse demonstrates the recognition of its faults.
"Axle" refers to the pivot within a wheel; "pin" is the iron bolt at the head of the axle.

It is like a charioteer traveling along a perilous road who, midway, loses the pin and breaks the axle, harboring grief and distress and giving rise to great terror. The destruction of the precepts is like that loss of the pin.
The broken axle: at the time of death, it is as if one were in the middle of a perilous road.

Having realized for oneself that the precepts have been violated and that one will inevitably fall into the evil realms, one harbors terror and dread, like the anxiety and fear of entering a dangerous path where the axle-pin has been lost and the axle has broken.
Just as when a person looks into a mirror, Joy or sorrow arises from what is beautiful or ugly, So it is with the recitation of the precepts:
From their being complete or destroyed, joy or grief arises.
Commentary: The first half-verse establishes the analogy; the second half-verse reveals the integrity or deficiency of the precepts. Just as a person [looks] into a mirror...
When one looks upon their own face, if the countenance is upright, joy arises; if the appearance is coarse, one harbors grief and sorrow.
Now, at the time for the recitation of the precepts, one should examine oneself by means of those precepts: if they are complete, one harbors joy within and feels no shame before others;
if they are violated, grief and sorrow arise within and one feels ashamed before others.
Just as when two armies engage in battle, The brave advance while the timid retreat; So too it is with the recitation of the precepts:
From purity comes peace, and from defilement, fear. Commentary:
The first half of the verse establishes a metaphor; the second half clarifies the gain and loss regarding the precepts. It is like two military arrays...

In combat, the brave advance with composure, while the cowardly retreat in fear. Now, as the assembly gathers for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), we are truly engaged in battle against the demonic armies of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one’s precepts are pure like those of a hero, both body and mind will be at peace.

If one’s precepts are defiled like those of a coward, one will naturally shrink from the objects of desire and emotion, eventually sinking into the ranks of the afflictions and being overpowered by Māra.
Among those in the world, the king is supreme; Among all streams, the ocean is supreme; Among all stars, the moon is supreme;
Among all noble ones, the Buddha is supreme. Among all the various codes of discipline, The Sūtra of Precepts is the highest and most supreme.
The Tathāgata established these prohibitions and precepts, To be recited every half-month.
The commentary states: Regarding the first verse, the first line is preeminent by virtue of its nobility; the second line is preeminent by virtue of its profundity and vastness;
the third line is preeminent by virtue of its clarity and purity; and the fourth line is preeminent by virtue of the excellence of its fruition.

This means that while the fruition of the practice of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas is not yet perfected, the Tathāgata’s practice is fulfilled and his fruition is complete; thus, among all the noble ones, he alone is [supreme].

"Most excellent. This also serves as a metaphor for the bhikṣu. He is a prince of the Golden Wheel, a noble descendant of the Dharma King, whose virtue and wisdom are profound and vast, and whose essence of precepts is perfect and luminous.
Among those in heaven and among men, none can equal him; thus he is the most honored among all assemblies.
Regarding the first two lines of the final verse, they explicitly reveal that the Sūtra of Precepts is the most excellent. "Sūtra of Precepts" refers to the [Prātimokṣa]...
This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* of the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya. Regarding "Prātimokṣa" (individual liberation):

it means that by practicing according to this sūtra, one gradually eliminates the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the nine grades—beginning with the lowest of the low—and thereby attains liberation from all defilements.
Furthermore, since the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are each numerous, they are categorized into their respective distinct grades.
Because it is able to relinquish and abandon [defilements], it is called "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation).
Sentient beings are bound by the fetters of afflictions and delusions, sinking into the three realms; this sutra can cause them to attain liberation and proceed toward Nirvana.

Therefore, this sutra is regarded as the most supreme among all codes of discipline (*vinaya*), including the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, and even the ten wholesome actions of a Wheel-Turning King—these being mundane dharmas.

[This refers to] the Vinaya and the heterodox prohibitions of various non-Buddhist paths. The Mahāvinaya states: "Among the hundreds of thousands of millions of sūtras, the precepts are the foremost and most supreme.
This means that not only are other teachings inferior, but even within the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the precepts are considered the most important.
Thus, the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya says: "The Buddha taught the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, with the Vinaya as the head. The Buddha...
Wandering through the world, they preach the Dharma wherever they go; yet the teachings of the Vinaya are not like this. Therefore, know that it is difficult to encounter:
the Buddhas who realize Bodhi, the Pratyekabuddhas whose body and mind are tranquil, and the Arhats—all have achieved their state through the practice of the Vinaya.
All the sages and saints of the three periods of time, having distanced themselves from the bonds of conditioned existence, take the Vinaya as their foundation; thus they are able to reach peace.
In its hidden depths, it is like the earth supporting all living beings and enabling the growth of all plants and trees; the Vinaya teachings are likewise able to give birth to all merit and wisdom.
The Vinaya is the king among dharmas and the foremost guide of all Buddhas. The bhikṣu is likened to a merchant, for whom this [Vinaya] is a priceless treasure.
According to what is taught in the Vinaya, if one does not practice in accordance with it, one will ultimately achieve nothing. Even if...

To have anything to gain is entirely the work of Māra. Thus, a sutra says: "Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not uphold the precepts, they will inevitably fall into the path of Māra.
That the Tathāgata established the prohibitive precepts demonstrates that these were personally ordained by the Tathāgata himself.

It was not something arrogantly fabricated by other sages, nor does it differ from the sutras and śāstras; while others might have offered their own teachings, these were presented for the Buddha’s approval.
This is because the Tathāgata’s wisdom pervades the entire dharma-realm and exhaustively understands the nature of all things;

he knows the distinctions among the faculties and karmic actions of sentient beings and what is appropriate for them as precepts—something that neither śrāvakas nor bodhisattvas are capable of accomplishing. It is like the rites and music of the world, which do not originate with anyone other than the Son of Heaven.

It was not established by anyone; it is the grand, world-transcending rule that no one but a Buddha could institute. As for the instruction to recite the precepts every half-month, this refers to the two months of the waxing and waning phases.
It serves to represent the two types of karma—black and white—with the intent that the black be exhausted and the white be perfected.

Therefore, the precepts are recited every half-month so that the bhikṣus may recall their transgressions, repent and eliminate them according to the Dharma, and thereby cause evil to be utterly exhausted.
This concludes the section on "Excellence" (*sucarita*). The twelve verses above were arranged by the various Arhats at the time of the council.
According to the original Vinaya text, there are a total of forty-six verses.
II. Performing the Preliminary Preparations (divided into seven explanations).
"Has the Sangha assembled?
The commentary states: Whenever performing a *karmavācanā* or a *poṣadha*, all bhikṣus within the same boundary must be gathered together. This is the assembly.
In one place, in order to prevent a separate group from causing a schism in the Saṃgha, it is necessary to ask first.
There are four kinds of Saṃghas: namely, those consisting of four, five, ten, or twenty persons. Regarding a Saṃgha of four persons:

with the exception of the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the invitation for self-reflection (*pravāraṇā*), and the resolution of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, all other *karmans* (formal acts) should be performed. Regarding a Saṃgha of five persons: with the exception of [the formal acts] in the Central Land...

The full ordination (*upasampadā*), the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*), and all other *karmavācanā* procedures should be performed. Regarding the assembly of twenty monks: all *karmas* should be performed by such an assembly.
Within these four types of assemblies, if even one person is missing, the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is not accomplished. If there are more than required, it is according to the Dharma;
if fewer, it is contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, resulting in an offense. With the exception of the *poṣadha*, for other essential matters requiring *karmavācanā*, the assembly...

It is often difficult to assemble [the community] due to various obstacles or hindrances. It is permitted to perform the ritual on the boundary of the *sīmā* (the ordination platform); there is no fault in not assembling [the full assembly].
Regarding "is it harmonious?":
the commentary states that for a single *karmavācanā* (formal act), those assembled in one place must have no conflict in thought or speech. As for those who do not come...

Regarding the granting of consent (*chandadāna*): if there are those present who ought to be censured, one does not censure them. This is because, in order to prevent the causes and conditions for strife and contention, which would obstruct the performance of the Dharma-affairs, it is necessary to inquire in succession.
"One who has not received the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) should depart.

The commentary explains: "One who has not received the full ordination" refers to one who has not yet obtained the complete precepts through a formal rite of motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma.
"Should depart" means to be sent outside the assembly, away from a place where they can be seen or heard. The Buddha said: "One should not [remain] among those who have not received..."

When performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) before those who have received the Great Precepts (*mahāśrāmaṇera*), the monks who do not attend must declare their consent (*chanda*) and their purity (*pāriśuddhi*).
The commentary explains: "Those who do not attend" refers to those who do not come to the assembly. This applies to all ritual procedures involving the *karmavācanā*.
It is essential that both body and mind be assembled together for a true *saṃgha* (congregation) to be formed.

Should there be matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, or matters regarding illness, or circumstances such as tending to the sick, one may open the mind to assemble [the community]. Therefore, it is permitted to transmit the intention through speech;

provided the matter before the Saṃgha is properly addressed, both parties’ objectives will be accomplished without hindering the religious rites, and no fault of being apart from the assembly (*pṛthag-varga-doṣa*) will arise. To "express the desire" (*chanda-vāda*) means to express...
"Intention" means that one finds joy in and consents to the Dharma-accordant monastic business (*saṃghakarma*) performed by others.
"Purity" (*pariśuddhi*) refers to being free from transgressions oneself; this is the offering of purity during the *poṣadha*.
Furthermore, since the Saṃgha performs various formal procedures (*karmas*) at the time of the *poṣadha*, both consent and purity must be offered together; they cannot be offered separately.
If one says "I am pure" when it actually obstructs the affairs of the Saṃgha, nor may one say "I give my *chanda* (consent) for such-and-such a matter.
One should instead say: "I give my *chanda* and am pure regarding the *dharmic* affairs of the Saṃgha. In this way, there will be no delay and no affliction of the Saṃgha’s *karmavācanā*.
There are five ways of giving *chanda*: saying "I give you my *chanda*"; saying "I speak my *chanda*"; saying "For me, speak my *chanda*"; or... [if the text continues].

If one is ill and unable to speak, one should communicate through physical gestures. If the formal act of granting consent (*chanda*) is performed extensively, it constitutes a valid grant of consent;
if it is not done in this manner, it does not constitute a valid grant of consent, and one must grant consent to another person.

In this context, the grant of consent must be given by one who is physically present within the boundary (*sīmā*). Furthermore, one may not grant consent for today on behalf of tomorrow. If a sick bhikṣu has already granted his consent...

If one hears the Dharma or the Vinaya being preached within the Saṃgha and goes there personally to listen, but becomes weary from sitting for a long time and thus silently leaves their seat using the previously granted *chanda* (consent), this is not considered a valid granting of *chanda*. Because the prior consent has already been broken, one must grant *chanda* once again.

Other circumstances should be understood according to this principle. If a sick bhikṣu is unable to give his consent through body or speech as described above, he should be supported and carried to the midst of the Saṃgha.
If it is feared that supporting and carrying him would increase his illness, the entire Saṃgha should go to the sick person's location, surround him, and perform the *karmavācanā*.
If there are many sick persons, it is best if they can be assembled in one place; if they cannot, [the procedure should be performed for each].
The Saṃgha should go outside the boundary to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Poṣadha*. There is no other expedient by which one may perform a *karmavācanā* for a separate assembly.
If one wishes to give a formal consent (*chanda*) extensively, one should approach a person capable of transmitting the consent and compose one’s demeanor.
He speaks as follows:

"Venerable sirs, please attend to me with one mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], regarding this matter of the Saṃgha conducted in accordance with the Dharma, grant my consent and declare my purity" (stated once).
If it is during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one should say, "I give my consent for the *pravāraṇā*. For all other *karmas*, one simply says, "I give my consent.

The monk who has received the consent should carry that consent to the midst of the Saṃgha. Once the presiding officer of the *karman* has asked as above, he should immediately assume the proper deportment and reply:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, [Name], a bhikṣu, have received from him the formal consent (*chanda*) and purity (*viśuddhi*).

He has thus granted his consent and purity for the legal matters of the Saṃgha (this is stated once). [Alternative version: Listen, O separate assembly; let the one who holds the consent speak it to his neighbor seat, rather than announcing it to the entire great assembly."
To prevent procrastination and because it would give rise to various faults such as fatigue for the Saṃgha,
once the person holding the *chanda* has received the *chanda*, if they pass away, go elsewhere, abandon the path (leave the order), enter among the followers of other paths, join another faction,

arrive at the boundary of the ordination platform (*sīmā*), see the first light of dawn, or themselves declare that they have committed one of the ten offenses such as the "borderline sins" (*antaryāpatti*), [the *chanda* is no longer valid].

Third, regarding those who raise objections: if one has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), or has been expelled (*pabbājaniya-kamma*), or is subject to expulsion; or if one possesses supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and is in the air;
or if one is beyond the range of sight or hearing—in all such cases, the granting of consent for purity (*chanda-suci*) is not valid.

One must grant the consent to another person. The same applies if one is on the road or has arrived at the assembly. As for the person receiving the consent, if they are asleep or have entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [the consent is likewise invalid].
If one forgets, or if it was not done intentionally, it is considered that the *chanda* (consent) has been granted. If one intentionally fails to communicate it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, this does not apply if one encounters an obstructed road, or if there are bandits, wild beasts, rising river waters, or any threat to life.
The holy life is difficult; one cannot attain it. When someone comes from outside the boundary into the midst of the Saṃgha, they do not lose their *chanda* (consent) in this manner.
Furthermore, it is permitted for one person to receive the *chanda* of two, three, four, or even many people.

If one is able to fully remember and recognize the names [of those giving consent], they may receive the *chanda* according to however many they can recall. If one cannot remember the names, they should state the family name (*gotra*). If they cannot... [the sentence continues].
One should record their names and clans, and state their physical characteristics. If one cannot record their characteristics, one may simply say "many bhikṣus.
Regarding the formal monastic affairs (*dharmasaṃghakārya*), they grant their consent (*chanda*) and purity (*viśuddhi*).

If the person who has received the consent encounters an urgent matter and is unable to go into the midst of the Saṃgha, they may authorize the transfer of that consent to another bhikṣu by saying: "Venerable One, with a single mind..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], together with [Name] and the many other bhikṣus, have received the *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purity).
They and I shall grant our *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* for the Dharma and Vinaya matters of the Saṃgha.

If a bhikṣu, having granted his *chanda* due to some business, finds that matter has ceased, he should go to the place where the *poṣadha* is being recited. If there are four bhikṣus or more at a single residence, they should assemble together.
Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*):
it is not appropriate to announce one's consent (*chanda*). [Question: Who sent the bhikṣuṇī to come and request instruction?

[Answer: The commentary states: Because bhikṣuṇīs possess a defiled physical nature and are heavily constrained by their bodily form, they lack the necessary means for traveling to various regions to seek the Way. At dawn...

The benefit of instruction during the twilight hours is profound. Out of compassion for this, the Tathāgata established the rule that every half-month one must go to the Saṃgha to request formal instruction.
The Saṃgha then dispatches those endowed with virtue to instruct them with subtle words and encourage them toward the ultimate Way.

However, as the time since the Sage has long passed, monks and nuns have grown negligent toward the teachings. Since they no longer follow or uphold them, this Dharma is gradually being lost; those who even hear of it are still few, let alone those who practice it.
Such instances are extremely rare. Desiring to restore this tradition, I have therefore provided a detailed commentary.

On the day of the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, the community of *bhikṣuṇīs* shall assemble and perform a formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint one *bhikṣuṇī* to go to the monastery of the monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) and request instruction.
If she travels alone without protection, two or three others should be appointed as companions. Having arrived at the monastery, she shall proceed to...
Having paid homage to a resident bhikṣu (the principle being that the Saṃgha should appoint a person to receive the entrustment from that bhikṣuṇī), she bows her body, lowers her head,
joins her palms, and says:
"Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. The community of bhikṣuṇīs is in harmony; they prostrate at the feet of the community of bhikṣus and request instruction.
(Recite this three times). When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, the one who recites the precepts asks: "Who has sent the bhikṣuṇī to request instruction? (The Buddha said:

"When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, the Elder asks: 'Whom has the community of bhikṣuṇīs sent? Now, one should simply take the person who was present at the time of the recitation and ask them"). First, she receives [the instruction] from the bhikṣuṇīs...
The one who is to give the formal instruction should immediately rise, assume the full dignified posture, and announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. The community of bhikṣuṇīs at [place name] is in harmony.

They have appointed the bhikṣuṇī [name] to pay homage at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and to request a person to provide instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs. Having spoken thus three times, according to the principle, she should proceed.
The Elder asked: "Venerable one, are you compassionate and able to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?
If he replies that he is incapable, then [the questioner] must ask each person down to those with twenty years of seniority (*varṣa*).
That person presiding over the *poṣadha* should further ask: "Who will instruct the bhikṣuṇīs? If there is anyone [capable], they should be appointed. As for that instructor...
One who possesses ten qualities: first, being fully endowed with the precepts; second, being learned; third, having mastered the recitation of the two sets of precepts;
fourth, possessing decisive judgment free from doubt; fifth, being skilled in preaching the Dharma; sixth, having left the household life from a noble family;

seventh, having a handsome appearance such that the community of nuns rejoices upon seeing him; eighth, being capable of preaching the Dharma to the nuns and encouraging them to rejoice; ninth, not... [text incomplete]
Having gone forth as a monk under the Buddha and donned the Dharma robes, one who has committed a grave offense— if they have completed twenty years of residence (varṣa),
or more than twenty years— should be appointed in this manner.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Which elders consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak. The Sangha has approved the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

Because the Sangha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. (If there are many instructors, one should ask the bhikṣuṇīs whom they request; according to their words, one should appoint them.
If they say, "We follow the Sangha’s disposition," then one should appoint them in the order of those regularly assigned to teach. That bhikṣuṇī shall go again on the sixteenth day.
The monk sent from the monastery asked whether it would be acceptable. That appointed monk took another monk as his companion and went at the designated time;

the nun also came to meet them at the appointed hour. Once the instructor for nuns had observed that the assembly of nuns was gathered, he preached the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) for them, and thereafter taught the Dharma according to their capacities to guide them.
If there were no one to instruct the nuns, they should make a general request [to find one].
[It is] so. That bhikṣu who has received the entrustment returns to the place of the Elder and reports: "I have inquired among the entire community of monks, but there is no one capable.
At that time, the Elder should briefly provide instruction on the Dharma and say to the person who received the entrustment:
"There is no teacher capable of instructing and admonishing in this assembly. Tomorrow the nuns will come to request [instruction]; it may not be the proper time. He should reply: "Yesterday, for..."
The community of nuns sent out invitations everywhere, yet there was no one to provide instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs.

However, the Elder had issued a decree commanding the assembly of nuns to practice the Path with diligence and to be prudent, not being negligent. On the sixteenth day, the nuns arrived; having been informed according to the decree, they returned to their residence and assembled the community.
They fully proclaimed the Sangha’s decree, and all the nuns joined their palms at their crowns to receive it in reverence.
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it perform? The commentary explains:
This refers to whatever *dharmakārya* (religious rites) the Saṃgha, having already assembled in harmony, intends to perform. Furthermore, such matters do not exceed three types:

first, matters concerning sentient beings, such as receiving confessions (*pratideśanā*); second, matters concerning non-sentient things, such as [the formal act of] establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*).
Regarding the various elements (*dhātu*) and so forth—the three matters concerning sentient and non-sentient objects—as well as the rules for being separated from one's robes and the like:

since these matters to be performed must be deliberated upon by the Saṃgha according to what is appropriate, it is necessary to question the person performing the act before the assembly. One individual shall respond to the matter accordingly.
The *Poṣadha-karman* (if it is not the time for the *poṣadha*, refer to the specific matter; in response, say "such-and-such *karman*").
The commentary states: In the Sanskrit language, *karman* means "matter" (*vastu*) or "the performance of a matter," referring to various ritual affairs by which they are accomplished.

However, in terms of their essential form, there are only three types of *karman*: the *jñapti* (motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion followed by one proclamation), and the *jñapti-caturtha* (motion followed by three proclamations), according to the specific matter at hand.

[The procedure] is performed according to the measure [of the offense]. For light matters, a *jñapti* (single motion) should be made; for middling matters, a *jñapti-dvitīya* (motion with one proclamation);

for grave matters, a *jñapti-caturtha* (motion with three proclamations). These three types of *karmavācanā* encompass all *karmas*. Briefly stated, there are one hundred and twenty-one such procedures:
twenty-seven are *jñaptis*, fifty-seven are *jñapti-dvitīyas*, and thirty are *jñapti-caturthas*.
Eight. As for the other schools, their numbers either increase or decrease; within the fundamental school, there are one hundred and one items in total.

For all *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), it is necessary to perform the preliminary procedures (*pūrvakaraṇīya*). However, at the time of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, one adds the inquiry regarding whether a *bhikṣuṇī* has come to request instruction.
Aside from this, the remaining six methods apply universally to all *karmas*, with the sole exception of the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*).

If there is an absence [of a necessary participant], the rite is not accomplished; this is because the characteristics of the *dhātu* (the assembly) must be mutually understood. One does not permit the omission of the announcement; rather, all matters must be fully assembled.
○ Third, the performance of the *jñapti-karman* (a formal motion consisting of a single announcement).

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon. The community of monks shall recite the Prātimokṣa. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let us recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony. This is the formal motion.

The commentary states: “Venerable Saṃgha, listen” means to cause the auditory consciousness of all bhikṣus to refrain from taking other objects as its focus, so that they may concentrate their minds on a single object and correctly remember and maintain what is heard.
“On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight” refers to the first half of the month; the latter half of the month is the dark fortnight. Months vary in length, being sometimes...

On the fourteenth day, or the fifteenth day, one should recite it according to the proper time. That "the assembly of monks recites the precepts" (*poṣadha*) indicates that this is not for any other purpose.
According to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* translated by Yaśas, it is called "the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts. That it is not mentioned here is an abbreviation. Why is this?
The "recitation of the precepts" (*śīla-vyākhyāna*) directly states the matter itself but does not yet manifest its underlying meaning; whereas the *poṣadha*...

"Sa" (Sangha) has the meaning of "nurturing" and "purifying. This means that by means of the assembly reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), one is able to nurture merit and purify afflictions and all unwholesome dharmas.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha" (*saṃghasya samayaḥ prāptaḥ*): "time" refers to the time for reciting the precepts;
"arrived" means that the Saṃgha has assembled at that time. "May the Saṃgha listen with patience": this refers to the great assembly present before them. When...
"May we together accept, permit, and harmoniously recite the Prātimokṣa precepts. "The motion is thus" means that one informs others by means of this matter.

Whenever the day for the Poṣadha arrives, the junior bhikṣu should first go to the hall where the precepts are recited, sweep and sprinkle it, arrange the seats, prepare water, light lamps, and provide the voting sticks (śalākā). If he does not know how to do so—
The Elder shall instruct; if he does not instruct, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If [the others] do not follow the instruction, there is likewise a *dukkaṭa* offense.

When the recitation of the precepts is finished, they should be collected and returned to their original place; otherwise, one incurs the aforementioned offense. Regarding "providing tally-sticks" (*śalākā*):
this means causing the number of people to be known. These tally-sticks should be made of copper, iron, bamboo, or wood and kept in a box or tube. Thus it is compared.
Those present shall examine one another to ascertain who has arrived and who has not. Having first announced this, they should then recite the precepts.
If the assembly is large and it is impossible for all to hear during the recitation, they should prepare a high seat that is as lofty and well-crafted as possible;
the precepts should be recited from atop it. Should the reciter forget or err while chanting, the bhikṣu seated next to him must provide the correct words. If...
Therefore, as for the one who forgets: the second bhikṣu in order should recite in his place, and he shall do so according to that sequence; he must not repeat what has already been said.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu who recites the precepts should first practice reciting them from memory until they are proficient, so as not to commit errors when speaking in the midst of the assembly.
If, at the time of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, eight kinds of obstacles arise or other circumstances occur, it is permitted to recite the precepts in an abbreviated form. The eight obstacles are:
a king, bandits, water, fire, illness, harmful insects, humans, and non-humans. Other circumstances include: when the great assembly has gathered but there are few seats;
when many members of the assembly are ill; when the covering over the seats is incomplete; when it rains; or when there is quarreling and strife.

Regarding the matter: if it has already been a long time since the Dharma was preached at night, and the listening has continued until the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodgama*), one should perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

There is no other expedient means available for receiving the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śuddhi*) overnight. For the *karmavācanā* recitation of the precepts, the preliminary formalities (*pūrvakalpa*) are abbreviated.
Just as with the extensive version of the Dharma, the measure [of the recitation] is difficult to determine as being either long or short.

If there are no obstacles, one must not give an abbreviated recitation. If, after reciting the introduction to the *Prātimokṣa* and asking whether the assembly is pure, an obstacle arises, one should announce:
"Venerable sirs, these four *pārājika* dharmas are constantly heard by the Saṃgha; likewise, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and so on, up to the *śaikṣa* dharmas. If...
If an obstacle suddenly arises, one should state it as it occurs, saying, "It has already been stated that we have reached such-and-such a place; the remainder is as the Saṃgha regularly hears.

If the circumstances of the obstacle are so imminent that there is no time to recite the introduction, as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "Venerable sirs, today is the fifteenth day of the uposatha.
Each of you should rectify your body, speech, and mind, and do not be negligent. Having said this, each may then proceed according to their own inclination.
If a single bhikṣu is living alone, on the day of the poṣadha, he should go to the hall for the recitation of the precepts, sweep it, and arrange it as previously described.
If visiting bhikṣus arrive—whether there be four or more—he should first announce this.
Thereafter, the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) is performed. If there are only three persons, or if there are two, they should each face one another and speak as follows:
"O two elders, remember: today is the fifteenth day of the month for the *saṃgha* to recite the precepts. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure" (this is to be said three times).
If there is only one person alone, he should mentally reflect and say aloud: "Today is the fifteenth day of the month for the *saṃgha* to recite the precepts."
