"I, [Name], a bhikṣu, am pure" (recite this three times). If there be one who has committed an offense, he shall not recite the precepts, nor shall he hear the precepts;
he shall not confess his offense before another who has committed one, nor shall the one who has committed the offense receive confession from another.
He should go to a pure bhikṣu, bare his right shoulder, remove his sandals, place his right knee on the ground, and join his palms. If he is a senior...
Having sat down, one should prostrate at his feet, state the name of the offense committed, and perform repentance according to the Dharma.
If one has doubts regarding an offense, one should likewise go to a pure bhikṣu as described above, state the name of the offense, and say:
"I, [name], have developed doubts concerning an offense committed; I now declare it to you, O Virtuous One. When I am later free from doubt, I shall..."
One should perform the confession according to the Dharma. Having done so, one may listen to the recitation of the precepts.

If, while a bhikṣu is correctly reciting the precepts, he remembers having committed an offense or has doubts in his mind, and if he speaks of it to the assembly, fearing it will cause a disturbance, he should speak to his neighbor or reflect upon it mentally.
Once the session has concluded, he must confess according to the Dharma. One who acts in this manner is permitted to hear [the precepts].

Regarding the precepts: if the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense or harbors doubts, they should confess their transgressions and resolve their doubts before a pure visiting bhikṣu, and only then recite the precepts.

If no visitor arrives, two or three persons should be dispatched to a nearby community of pure monks to resolve their doubts and perform confession; having returned to their own residence, the bhikṣus should then [proceed] toward this...
The bhikṣus should first confess their offenses and then recite the precepts. If there are no pure monks nearby, they should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and then perform the confession.
The announcement is made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This entire assembly of monks has committed an offense.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. This entire assembly of monks now confesses. Having made this announcement in this manner, [they should proceed].

Thereafter, the precepts are recited. (This particular method of repentance refers to cases where one recognizes the name, category, and characteristics of the offense committed, yet there is no pure bhikṣu before whom to perform a formal confession;

therefore, this "white" (jñapti) confession is permitted. It is not for those who are ignorant of their offenses or who act with reckless indifference; rather, it is by performing this *karman* that the offense is eliminated.
If the entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding the offense, they should perform the *jñapti* and then declare the offense. The *jñapti* should be made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen."
This entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.

This assembly of monks shall themselves declare their offenses. Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, the precepts are then recited. (In this case, one merely reveals the offense and is permitted to hear the recitation of the precepts.

As for the original offense, one must wait until there is no longer any doubt; at that time, one must still confess it by declaring it to another. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is permitted to repent before a monk who has committed the same offense, but one must not repent before someone who has committed the same offense as oneself. However, in the case of a sick monk, it is permitted to repent together with one who has committed the same offense).
If one does not recognize the name or the characteristics of an offense, one should wait for a visiting bhikṣu who is an upholder of the Vinaya to arrive and inquire of him;

then, one should perform confession according to the Dharma. If, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the resident bhikṣus have assembled and have already finished reciting the introduction to the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), and there arrive a few visiting bhikṣus, the visitors should announce their purity (*pāriśuddhi*) by speaking as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen to me..."
"Such-and-such a person is pure. Having made this announcement, the others should listen in succession.
Whether the recitation of the precepts is finished and the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, one should likewise announce their purity.

If the introduction to the precepts is finished, or if the recitation of the precepts is finished, and visiting bhikṣus arrive—whether they are equal in number or more numerous—one should repeat the recitation from the beginning.
Regarding the Precepts: If visiting bhikṣus recite the precepts first and resident bhikṣus arrive later, it is to be handled as previously described.
If a bhikṣu’s mind is distracted, deranged, or insane, one should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the deranged and insane for him. There are three types of such derangement:
(1) at the time of the recitation of the precepts, he may or may not remember [the rules], and he may or may not attend; (2) he may remember and attend; or (3) he may...

If one does not remember [the offense] and it has not occurred, the latter two types among these should not be performed. For the first type, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) should be performed.
If the insanity ceases, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* should be performed to revoke the suspension.

A bhikṣu with five years of seniority should recite the precepts and the *karman* procedures until they are mastered. One should not allow many ignorant bhikṣus to assemble in one place; since this is already...
One knows the precepts, yet does not know how to recite them; one does not know the *poṣadha*, nor does one know the *poṣadha-karman*.
Such a person should rely upon a monk who can recite the precepts for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

If, during the retreat, the person upon whom they rely passes away, travels far away, renounces the path, or falls into any of the thirteen grounds of defeat (*antarāyika-dharma*), and the date for the later retreat has not yet arrived, they should go to...
One should observe the later *anvāraka* (rainy-season retreat) in a nearby location; or one should invite someone capable of reciting the *Prātimokṣa* to come and stay for the retreat.
If the later *anvāraka* has already passed, the monks should go to a nearby place where there is someone who knows how to recite the *Nidāna*.
If one recites the four matters, the thirteen matters, or even up to the ninety matters, or if one recites the remaining rules (śeṣa-dharma),
each having finished their recitation, shall return to their original dwelling place and teach another person to recite them.
If that one person is unable to recite them all, they shall each recite according to what they previously mastered, following the proper sequence, and must not recite anything redundantly.

If this is so, it is well; if not, then after merely preaching the Dharma and reciting the sutras, one should rise from one's seat and depart (meaning that on the day of the *poṣadha*, the precepts must necessarily be recited;

since no one is capable of reciting them, it is permitted to preach the Dharma and recite the sutras instead, but this is not intended as a permanent rule). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the entire assembly is unable to perform [the ceremony], the *sthavira* should be sent outside the boundary to perform the *poṣadha* through mental recollection and verbal declaration.

The remaining three persons within the boundary shall perform the *poṣadha* by means of the 'three-fold speech' (*tri-vākya*). This is a penalty for the *sthavira*. One should not perform the *poṣadha* prematurely. If there is only one bhikṣu residing there, he should wait for visiting monks to arrive and perform it together with them."

One should perform the *poṣadha*. If no guests arrive and there are those with offenses, one should form this thought: "If I obtain a pure bhikṣu, this matter shall be removed according to the Dharma. Having formed this thought, one should perform the *poṣadha* by reciting it three times mentally and verbally.

If the *poṣadha* is finished and a guest arrives, the guest should express approval, saying: "Venerable sir, the *poṣadha* has already been performed; I, [Name], approve. If one does not express approval, one should perform the *poṣadha* outside the world [of that community]. In a single residence, one must not perform the *poṣadha* twice.

If a bhikṣu is traveling on a journey and arrives at a bhikṣu’s residence on the day of the *poṣadha*, after performing the *poṣadha*, he should not depart in silence; he should entrust his affairs to a *śrāmaṇera*, a village guard, or a herdsman, [instructing them]: "If another bhikṣu comes..."

One should inform them [of this]. Within this [area], the *poṣadha* has already been performed. If there are no people present, one should write on a pillar or a door-panel, or else mark the boundaries by scattering [grain] or similar means. Those who arrive later should ask about it and seek out these signs; they must not perform the *poṣadha* arbitrarily.

If traveling together with merchants, and on the day of the *poṣadha* there is danger or difficulty such that the merchant caravan cannot wait, one may go and perform the *poṣadha*. First, one should deliberate on how far it is possible to recite the *Prātimokṣa* before completing it. Whether it be a mountain or a rock, one should establish a boundary for the *poṣadha* through a formal act (*karmavācanā*) using a visible landmark, such as a distance where one can reach out and touch another. Only after this has been done should the *poṣadha* be performed.

According to the specific school (*nikāya*), if one is traveling through a village-less wilderness on the day of the *poṣadha*, one should establish a small boundary (*sīmā*) and recite the precepts. In such cases, there are no external landmarks. Thus...

The place where one sits constitutes the substance of the boundary (*sīmā*). Therefore, the *karmavācanā* text states: "Now, so many bhikṣus have assembled to establish a small boundary (*khuḍḍaka-sīmā*). From this, it is known that there is no requirement for a large number of people; rather, those residing in such a location should gather together in one place and recite the *Prātimokṣa* in harmony.

If the Saṃgha cannot achieve such harmony, then according to their respective teachers or virtuous friends, they should assemble in one place at a lower path (or a secondary location) and, through a formal act of two announcements (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), establish a small boundary to recite the precepts.

This is permitted only in the event of difficult circumstances; it is not allowed when there are no such reasons. Once the recitation of the precepts is finished, they should again perform a formal act of two announcements to dissolve the boundary before departing. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "One should not recite the precepts using a singing tone. One should instead recite them with a loud and clear voice. There are five faults incurred by using a singing tone. First..."

The mind becomes stained by attachment to these sounds. Second, one is despised by the world. Third, one is no different from worldly people. Fourth, it obstructs and causes the abandonment of the practice of the Path. Fifth, it hinders entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* does not permit preaching the Dharma with singing, yet it does not prohibit the recitation of the precepts;

this is likely an error of omission. According to the *Dharmapada-vidhi*, at first one may listen, but later, if there are faults or transgressions, one must not listen. There are five kinds of such faults (which are largely the same as those described in the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*).
IV. The Preface to the Recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra (Divided into Two Parts): First, the Proper Exposition of the Preface; Second, the Concluding Inquiry.
△ First, the Proper Exposition of the Preface:
"Venerable sirs, I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts. Listen attentively and reflect well upon them."
If you know for yourself that you have committed an offense, you should immediately confess it; if you have committed no offense, remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that the Venerable Ones are pure. If someone else asks you, you should answer in the same way.

Thus, when a bhikṣu is in the midst of the assembly, if he remembers having committed an offense and does not confess it after being questioned up to three times, he incurs the offense of intentional lying. Therefore...
Regarding false speech: the Buddha has taught that it is a dharma which obstructs the path. If a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purity, he should confess it;
through confession, one attains peace and happiness.
The commentary states: "Venerable sirs, I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts.

This is an announcement to inform the assembly that the time for the recitation of the precepts is approaching; each person should maintain their dignified deportment and rectify the three types of action (body, speech, and mind).
Do not be distracted. *Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "individual liberation" (*bie jie tuo*), the meaning of which has been explained previously.
It is also translated as "preserving liberation," meaning that it enables the practitioner to preserve themselves from being born into the ocean of birth and death.

"You all, listen attentively" is an admonition to focus the mind and listen with careful scrutiny and detail; through this, one establishes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) regarding the meaning of what is spoken.
"Reflect upon it well" means that one should contemplate the meaning as it was heard, recollecting it without forgetting in order to accomplish the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
"If you know for yourself that you have committed an offense," etc., means that once you have heard and reflected upon the meaning, the beautiful and the evil will manifest within your own mind;
you should then abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome in order to accomplish the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Cultivation...

If wisdom is perfected, then the stream of the Dharma will flow constantly into the mind. Regarding "having committed an offense," this refers to an act of transgression that has not yet been confessed and repented before another;
one must now personally confess and reveal that fault, for only then is one fit to hear the precepts. Do not wait for another to report it, lest you commit further offenses.
Regarding "no offense," this means either that no offense was committed, or that having committed one, it has already been confessed and repented. Regarding "remaining silent," this means...
Since there is nothing for which you have committed an offense, you should listen to the precepts with single-minded silence. Regarding the phrase "because of being silent":
it is because of this silence that one knows oneself to be pure and without fault. If someone else questions you, you should answer in the same manner;
as at other times when another raises a question and you answer according to the truth, here too you should answer in accordance with reality. It is to be understood in this way.

"When the Blessed One was among the assembly, he asked three times," [the Buddha said]. "Bhikṣus, 'among the assembly' refers to the community of monks present before whom the precepts are being heard.
Asking three times is intended to ensure that the words are complete, avoiding the faults of being either too brief or too prolix.

If it were too brief, those who are dull-witted would find it difficult to suddenly perceive [the offense], and those lacking a sense of shame would not yet feel remorse. If it were too prolix, the listeners..."

"Arising of affliction" means that weariness arises in the mind. Regarding "recollection and so forth," it refers to the case where, due to three questions posed by another, one recalls and recognizes the offense committed but fails to disclose it;
thus, one incurs the offense of lying. Although one remains silent and does not speak, because one expresses the verbal action through bodily gestures, the act is completed.
Even if an offense was previously committed, if one does not now recall or recognize it, there is no offense of lying for each individual question.
One incurs an offense according to what one recalls. If one is asked three times and recalls it three times, one incurs three offenses.

Regarding the "dharmas that obstruct the path," this refers to the Buddha’s teaching that intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the path. What path does it obstruct? It means it obstructs the various dhyānas, samādhis, and the four fruits [of the śrāvaka].
Regarding the path to *nirvāṇa*: one who seeks purity means one who seeks to be pure and free from transgression, and thus performs self-confession (*pratideśanā*).
This confession is not performed out of fear of being interrogated or punished by others, but for the sake of purification itself.

There are two kinds of purity: first, the cause of purity; second, the fruit of purity. The cause refers to pure precepts (*śīla*); the fruit refers to *nirvāṇa*. If one wishes to attain *nirvāṇa*, one should...
Maintain the pure precepts. Should even a hair’s breadth of flaw sprout within the heart and mind, one must immediately disclose its root;
do not allow it to remain hidden so that its branches and trunk may grow day by day, resulting in foul blossoms and the loss of the fruit of purity.
That repentance brings peace and happiness is because through disclosure and confession, body and mind become tranquil and settled, whereby one immediately attains the various dhyānas and samādhis.
Until one attains the blissful fruit of Nirvāṇa.

△ Next, the summary and inquiry to the Venerable Ones: "I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this regard? (Recite three times.)
"Venerable sirs, herein we are pure, for we remain silent; thus shall this matter be upheld. The commentary states:
"The introduction to the *Śīla-sūtra* refers to this as the preamble to the two hundred and fifty *Prātimokṣa* rules.
'Thus shall this matter be upheld' means to maintain it with full understanding. Having thus questioned the assembly three times, all remained silent.
It is pure. Because it is pure, there is silence. By this silence, I now understand this matter thus:
it is fit to recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
*Commentary on the Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, Fascicle One, Phonetic Glossary:
The "Four Perversities" refer to the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). First is "food taken by mouth," which refers to compounding medicines, sowing grains, and planting trees.

1. Impure livelihood by means of downward-facing practice (*adhomukha-ājīva*); 2. Impure livelihood by means of upward-facing practice (*ūrdhvamukha-ājīva*), which refers to observing the stars, the sun, the moon, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and hail;

3. Impure livelihood by means of horizontal-facing practice (*tiryagmukha-ājīva*), which refers to fawning upon those of high status and power, acting as a messenger in all four directions, and seeking much through clever speech;
4. Impure livelihood by means of intermediate-facing practice (*vidig-mukha-ājīva*), which refers to studying various incantations, arts, and divinations.
One who makes a living through omens, fortune-telling, or impure means is not a bhikṣu.
A bhikṣu possesses five qualities: first, his nature is soft and supple; second, he spreads out like a creeping vine;
third, his fragrance is known afar; fourth, he can cure pain; and fifth, he does not turn his back on the sun.
The *Vinaya* is the same as the *Vini*.
[From] the second fascicle of the *Explanation of the Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra*,
elucidated by the Śramaṇa of Guangzhou, Shi Hongzan, at Ziqi.
● General Enumeration of the Characteristics of the Precepts (divided into eight): 1. The Rules for Renunciation;
2. The Saṃghāvaśeṣa Rules; 3. The Aniyata Rules; 4. The Naiḥsargika-pāyattika Rules; 5. The Pāyattika Rules; 6.
The Pratideśanīya Rules; 7. The Śaikṣa Rules; 8. The Adhikaraṇa-śamatha Rules.
○ First: The Rules on Expulsion (Opening in three parts): 1. General Statement; 2. Specific Enumeration; 3. Concluding Inquiry.
△ 1. General Statement:
"Venerable sirs, these four rules of expulsion (*pārājika*) are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra."
The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "derived from the Sūtra on the Precepts," these four dharmas originate from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and were spoken directly by the Buddha;
they do not originate from other scriptures or from the teachings of others. As for *pārājika*, it inherently contains many meanings, and therefore its translations are not uniform.
Here, it is translated as "abandonment" (*qi*), or "defeat by another" (*tasheng*), or "that which leaves no remainder. This means:
There is no other dharma that can cure it, because it cannot be purified through confession and repentance.
Alternatively, it is said to have the meaning of "extreme evil," for there is no matter more grave than this. Or it is said to have the meaning of "severed head," for it will not arise again.

Some say this refers to the meaning of "points of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*). That is to say, when a bhikṣu receives the precepts, he seeks to transcend birth and death and engages in battle against the four māras.
If he violates these precepts, he immediately falls into a point of defeat. It is like a scorched seed:
even if planted in fertile soil and diligently watered, it will not produce sprouts or fruit. Violating these precepts is likewise; even if one exerts diligent effort, in the end—
It cannot produce the sprouts and fruits of the path’s realization. Furthermore, at the very moment of transgression, one is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya;
one loses the nature of a bhikṣu, deviates from the practice of nirvāṇa, and falls into ruin and collapse, being utterly defeated by those who practice purity.
Moreover, as a bhikṣu is a son of the Dharma King, he has been conquered by the invading armies of unrighteousness.
One is defeated by another; having lost what is most honored, it is called "defeat by another" (*parājika*). Because one is no longer honored, one is forever cast out from the pure assembly.
One may no longer participate with the community in the recitation of the precepts, *karmavācanā*, the *poṣadha*, or the *pravāraṇa*. All merits are completely abandoned;
hence it is said to be "cast out. This is a brief explanation.
△ Detailed Enumeration of the Individual Precepts ○ First: The Precept Against Impure Conduct.
If a bhikṣu shares the same precepts as other bhikṣus, yet does not return his vows, nor confess his weakness in observing them, he commits an offense of impurity.
[Engaging in] sexual intercourse, even with animals; this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and may not dwell in communion.
The commentary states: When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, for the first twelve years, the assembly was entirely pure and no tainted dharmas had arisen;
he recited the Sūtra of Precepts briefly for the community free from legal issues. Upon reaching the thirteenth year, tainted dharmas gradually arose. At that time, the Buddha...
In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, at the village of Kalandaka, the son of an elder named Sudinna left the household life to follow the path with firm faith.
Later, following his mother’s instruction to ensure that the lineage would not be severed, he provided for his wife and settled her in a son.
He then committed the three types of impure acts with his wife. Filled with remorse, his fellow students questioned him and learned the reason; he then related the matter to them in full detail.
“World-Honored One, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and, using countless skillful means, rebuked them, saying:
‘What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not that of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not conduct in accordance with the Dharma, and something that should not have been done.
How can you, within this pure Dharma leading even to the extinction of craving and nirvāṇa, engage in impure sexual intercourse with a former wife?’”
Yes. It would be better to place the male organ into the mouth of a venomous snake than to place it within the female organ. Why is this?
Because one does not fall into the evil realms on account of that; however, if one violates a woman, at the end of life one will fall into the three evil realms.
I have taught the Dharma for severing desire through countless skillful means—to sever the thought of desire, to extinguish the mindfulness of desire, and to dispel the fever of desire.
Having transcended the fetter of craving, I have taught through countless skillful means that desire is like fire,
like a torch of grass, like the fruit of a tree, like a borrowed object, like a skeleton, like a piece of meat, like what is seen in a dream, like treading upon a sharp blade,
like a new earthen vessel filled with water placed in the sun, like the head of a venomous snake, and like a wheel.
The whirling blade is like a sharp spearhead or a piercing trident; it is utterly loathsome and has been censured by the Buddha.
Having so censured it, he assembled the ten points of meaning and established the precept for the bhikṣus. At that time, there was a Bhadrayānīya bhikṣu.
Distressed and finding no joy in the pure life, he returned home to engage in sexual desire with his wife. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You foolish men!
You have committed a pārājika offense and may not remain in the community. "If a bhikṣu finds no joy in the pure life, I permit him to relinquish the precepts and return home.
If he later wishes to leave the household life again to cultivate the pure life, he should be ordained, allowed to go forth, and receive full ordination (upasampadā)."
For this reason, he again took the vow of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), using the words: "My precepts have become weak, yet I do not repent.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who lived in a forest grove; he engaged in unchaste conduct with a female macaque. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had rebuked him, he further established the rule regarding the keeping [of animals] together with livestock. As for the ten points of meaning:

first, "gathering the Saṃgha. This means that there are virtuous men and women in the world who, having conceived deep reverence and faith within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), thereby gathering them to constitute the pure assembly.

Therefore, there are two [factors]: first, causing the Saṃgha to rejoice; that is, by practicing the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*) within the true Dharma and Vinaya, one causes wholesome qualities to increase and always maintains a state of joy.
Second, causing the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; that is, because of such joy, one attains the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and cessation (*nirvāṇa*);
furthermore, by purifying the holy life, one repays the debt of the faithful laity’s offerings, whereby the mind attains peace and happiness.

Fourth, to cause those who have not yet developed faith to believe: this means that when persons who have not yet believed behold such pure and holy conduct (*brahmacarya*), they immediately give rise to pure faith.
Fifth, to cause those who already have faith to increase it: this means that for those in whom faith has already arisen, one should skillfully protect that faith so that it may expand and broaden.
Sixth, to cause those who are difficult to discipline to become disciplined and compliant: this refers to those who are shameless and violate the precepts.
Such persons are disciplined by means of this Vinaya. Those who should be punished are punished; those who should be expelled are expelled.

This brings peace and happiness to the seven types of conscientious individuals—namely, those practitioners of the holy life who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame—so that they may dwell in security, free from doubt and regret, and without dispute. Eighth, the abandonment of the present...

1. Regarding the presence of outflows (*sāsrava*): this means that the manifest fetters (*paryavasthāna*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not function. 2. Severing nine future outflows:
this means causing unarisen afflictions not to arise and ensuring that the seeds of already arisen afflictions are forever severed.

3. The long endurance of the True Dharma (*saddharma*): this means that through the maintenance of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and the Tathāgata’s true teaching, the Dharma remains long in the world.
These ten benefits and merits are present within each and every precept. Therefore, within each individual precept, one is able to produce ten kinds of merits, such as the gathering of the Saṃgha.
Within each of these merits, one is able to produce ten kinds of true dharmas, namely:
the five faculties beginning with faith; the three roots of goodness beginning with non-attachment; and the two [faculties] of body and speech.
Guarding these two hundred and fifty precepts together forms twenty-five thousand rivers of merit.

Furthermore, among the various *khandakas*, each of the precepts established by the Tathāgata can give rise to ten kinds of meritorious qualities of the True Dharma, thereby forming immeasurable rivers of merit.
Because these rivers of merit flow constantly, they perpetually wash away and cleanse all the fetters of affliction.
Because it purifies defilements, it enables the practitioner to attain liberation from birth and death and to bring the perfections of merit and wisdom to fulfillment.

Regarding "if there is a bhikṣu," there are eight kinds of bhikṣus: first, the bhikṣu by name (referring to worldly people who have been given the name "bhikṣu" but do not belong to the community of those who have left the household life);

second, the bhikṣu in appearance (referring to someone who has shaved off their hair and beard but has not received the Buddha’s precepts, yet whose physical appearance, deportment, and movements resemble those of a bhikṣu; this too is not [a true bhikṣu]).

1) The *dharma-saṃgha*. 2) One who has received the full ordination through the formal motion and proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). 3) One who claims to be a bhikṣu for oneself (that is, one who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, and among the Saṃgha claims for himself, "I am a bhikṣu"—this is called a person who dwells as a thief;

he should be expelled and barred from the community, and one must not confer the precepts upon him). 4) The "Welcome, O Bhikṣu" (*svāgata-bhikṣu*) (that is, when the Buddha was in the world, there were those who attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) in the presence of the Buddha;

they came before the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata addressed them, saying, "Welcome, O bhikṣu! You may practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to bring an end to the source of suffering. At that moment, their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, the *kāṣāya* clothed their bodies, and they attained the nature of a bhikṣu. These obtained the precepts directly from the golden mouth [of the Buddha]; it is not otherwise that they are obtained).

5) The bhikṣu who begs (the term *bhikṣu* carries the meaning of "one who begs. Just as various non-Buddhists and laypeople say, "I am a bhikṣu" when begging from others, such individuals are called bhikṣus who beg;

they belong to the assembly of those who do not follow the Dharma). 6) The bhikṣu who wears cut-and-sewn robes (originally, the three robes of a bhikṣu are to be dyed and worn in cut-and-sewn fashion.

If various non-Buddhists or laypeople wear these, they are also called bhikṣus, yet they belong to the assembly of those who do not follow the Dharma). 7) The bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) (all afflictions are termed "fetters," meaning they are able to bind and constrain).

Sentient beings are driven to wander through the three realms. If a person leaves the household life—whether they are twenty years of age or not—they can destroy and sever these afflictions and realize arhatship; this is called attaining full ordination (*upasampadā*). Eighth, receiving the great precepts (*mahāśīla*) through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations):

when accomplished according to the Dharma, one obtains the status of a bhikṣu. That is to say, there is a son of good family who seeks the full precepts and generates a superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*).

He requests them before the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha then performs one motion and three proclamations. When the matter to be performed is accomplished according to the Dharma, reaching its ultimate completion, he becomes established in the nature of a bhikṣu; this is called receiving the great precepts.

A bhikṣu who has attained his status through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* according to the Dharma abides within the dharma of a bhikṣu; this is the meaning of "bhikṣu. Herein, we take the bhikṣu established by the eighth *jñapti-caturtha-karman* as the subject for the formulation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*).

As for those who have come forth by the "Come, Bhikṣu" formula, those who have destroyed the fetters, and those who possess spontaneous morality—because they are eternally free from the faults of violating prohibitions, their afflictions (*kleśa*) have been severed, and their holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established—they are excluded. The remaining five types are merely nominal designations.
The same applies here. However, because they are not members of the *saṃgha*, they are not subject to the prohibitions. Regarding "sharing the same precepts as the bhikṣus":

just as other bhikṣus receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* and thereby obtain the status and abide within the dharma of bhikṣus—this is the meaning of "sharing with the bhikṣus.
What is meant by "same precepts"? It means that one observes and maintains them identically together with the other bhikṣus, even at the cost of death.
There is no offense. Whether old or young, they study together as equals with no distinction.
Even that which one who has previously received the full precepts for a hundred years ought to learn is no different from what a newly ordained person learns;

and that which a newly ordained person ought to learn is no different from what a bhikṣu of a hundred years studies. This refers to the rules regarding the observance and transgression of all the precepts.
The ritual procedures are entirely identical; therefore, it is called "identical precepts. If one does not return the precepts, this constitutes not relinquishing them.
That is to say, if a bhikṣu finds no joy in the holy life (brahmacarya), he is permitted to relinquish the precepts and return to lay life.

Should he later wish to leave home again to cultivate the holy life, he is permitted to be ordained once more, granted the going-forth, and receive the full precepts (upasaṃpadā). However, within this process, there are cases where the relinquishment is valid and cases where it is not.
What is meant by "not constituting the relinquishment of the precepts"? It refers to cases where one has a deranged mind, is mentally disturbed, or is overwhelmed by intense suffering;
or if one is mute, or deaf; or if one relinquishes the precepts in the presence of someone who is deranged, or even someone who is mute or deaf;

or if a person from a central land relinquishes them before a person from a borderland, or a person from a borderland relinquishes them before a person from a central land, because their speech is not mutually intelligible; or...

If one who is not tranquil forms the perception of being tranquil (this is not [the case]; it refers to one's own person), or if one who is tranquil forms the perception of being untranquil; or if one acts with frivolity or laughter;
or if one speaks in the presence of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, sleeping persons, the dead, or the ignorant; or if one does not speak oneself;

or if one speaks but the person before them does not understand—such cases as these are all not termed "abandoning the precepts" (*śīla-tyāga*). What, then, constitutes the completion of abandoning the precepts? If a bhikṣu...
Feeling weary of the life of a bhikṣu, he then approaches those who are not as described above—such as the mute, the deaf, and so forth—and speaks these words:
"I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dharma; I renounce the Saṃgha; I renounce my upādhyāya; I renounce my ācārya; I renounce my fellow upādhyāyas and fellow ācāryas;

I renounce all fellow practitioners of the holy life; I renounce the Vinaya; I renounce the training rules. I accept the way of a householder; I shall become a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure-provider). I...
"I am an upāsaka; I am a śrāmaṇera; I am a follower of an external path; I am a disciple of an external path;
I am not a śramaṇa; I am not a son of the Śākya. Or if one further speaks thus: "I stop; I have no need for the Buddha;
what benefit does the Buddha provide me?"—to depart from the presence of the Buddha, and so on, even regarding the matters of training, it is likewise. If one makes other such statements:
To disparage the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, even down to the matters of training;

or to praise household affairs, even down to saying, "He is not a śramaṇa, he is not a son of the Śākya"—if one utters any such word and speaks it clearly, it is called the abandonment of the precepts (*śīla-tyāga*).
Regarding "the weakening of the precepts without repentance": this refers to being powerless to uphold the Tathāgata’s system of precepts and feeling weariness in one's heart; this is what is meant.
One whose precepts have weakened harbors inner grief and anxiety, yet does not confess or repent; this is what is meant by "not repenting.

Within this context, there are those whose precepts have weakened but do not relinquish them, and those whose precepts have weakened and do relinquish them. What is it to have one's precepts weakened yet not relinquish them?

If a bhikṣu is sorrowful and finds no joy in the holy life (brahmacarya), grows weary of the dharma of a bhikṣu, and his mind longs for the household life—even to the point of desiring to abandon the status of a śramaṇa and the dharma of a son of the Śākya—he speaks thus:
"I think of my father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, children, villages, towns, gardens, fields, and so forth; I wish to abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. And so on.

Regarding the matter of returning to secular life: if one intends to take up the affairs of a household, even to the point of adopting practices that are neither those of a śramaṇa nor those of a son of the Śākya, and merely utters various such words, yet has not yet reached a firm decision to declare it to others—this is called "weakening of the precepts without relinquishing them.
What is meant by "weakening the precepts and relinquishing them"? It is when a bhikṣu is distressed and finds no joy.
Regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*), a bhikṣu who becomes weary of the monastic discipline may think, "I wish to renounce the precepts," and then renounce them;

this is called "renouncing the precepts due to the weakening of one's resolve. (According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, at the time of renouncing the precepts, there need not be other renunciants present.

Whether it be a layperson, a follower of the Buddha, or even one who is not a follower of the Buddha, provided that their voices can be heard and they understand human speech, the renunciation of the precepts is accomplished. It is effected by a single declaration; three declarations are not required. This is because when receiving the precepts, it is like entering the ocean to gather jewels—it is obtained only through countless skillful means, and thus requires the three masters and seven witnesses.)

When relinquishing the precepts, it is like losing a treasure; it may be scattered and lost in an instant by thieves, fire, or water. It is also like falling from a great height; for this reason, one may relinquish them even before a single person.

According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, it is not permitted to relinquish the precepts in the presence of śrāmaṇeras, non-Buddhists, or laypeople, as such an act does not constitute a valid relinquishment. Regarding the commission of impure conduct, "commission" refers to acting with intentional thought;

it does not apply to cases of being coerced by force where there is no mind of seeking pleasure, nor to matters occurring in dreams. Among these, a transgression is a non-virtue produced by bodily action.
Pure conduct: this refers to the practice of sexual desire. Because of such conduct, the mind-ground is defiled; it opposes the Noble Path and deviates from Nirvāṇa.
"Even down to [associating] with animals" means from humans, devas, ghosts, and spirits, down to associating with animals.
Regarding base and evil deeds, if one merely engages in sexual intercourse, the offense is established.
That which is called *pārājika* is like severing a person's head; they cannot be restored to life. A bhikṣu who commits this dharma no longer remains a bhikṣu.

Therefore it is called a *pārājika*. The remaining meanings are as explained previously. "Not living together" means that one should be expelled and not permitted to dwell with the community of monks (*saṃgha*).
There are two types of communal living: performing the same ritual acts (*kamma*) and reciting the precepts together.
Because one is not permitted to abide in these two matters, it is called "not living together. Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein:

What is it? It means that if a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, approaches any person, non-human being, or animal—whether male, female, hermaphrodite, or eunuch—and inserts [the organ] even as much as a hair’s tip into the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth, he immediately incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If he employs the preparatory effort but does not insert it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (here translated as "grave offense"). If, regarding those aforementioned [beings], he is capable of performing [the act]...

Regarding the object of sexual misconduct: if one enters with something wrapped as a barrier; if one enters while there is already a barrier present; if one enters from a state with a barrier into a state without a barrier; if one enters from a state without a barrier into a state with a barrier;
or if one enters from a state without a barrier into a state without a barrier—in all these cases, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense. This also applies if one is forcibly compelled by an enemy.

When one inserts the male organ into the three orifices—whether at the moment of initial entry, during the act, or upon withdrawal—if at any one of these three times a feeling of pleasure arises in the mind, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).

If an enemy forcibly commits an impure act within a bhikṣu’s anus, and [the bhikṣu] experiences pleasure at any one of the three times, he incurs the fundamental offense. If [this occurs] while sleeping with the male organ...

It arises. If another person engages in sexual intercourse with it while one is unaware, there is no offense. For a person who has not yet abandoned desire, there are five causes and conditions that cause the male organ to arise:
first, urgency of feces; second, urgency of urine; third, a wind disorder; fourth, being bitten by insects; [and fifth, contact with a woman].

Regarding the mind of the five desires: if one who is free from desire lacks the last of these types [of intent], yet takes another's organ or his own organ and places it in his own mouth, experiencing pleasure, he incurs the full offense (mūlāpatti).
If he instructs another bhikṣu to do so, the instructor incurs a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).

The one who receives the instruction incurs the root offense. If the instructor does not perform the act themselves but instructs another to do so, the instructor incurs a *duṣkṛta* (translated here as "evil deed").
If, being coerced by an enemy, one causes a corpse that is not yet decomposed, or many such corpses, to enter [the vagina] and experiences pleasure, one incurs the root offense.
This applies equally if the corpse is half-decomposed, mostly decomposed, or if it is a bone, or if it is inserted into the space between images of women made of clay or paint, or into the ground.
Regarding orifices: a mud hole, the mouth of a jar, or any other bodily orifice—engaging in these all constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

If it is a [sexual] path and one perceives it as such, or if one entertains doubt, or perceives it as a non-path, one incurs the full offense (*pārājika*). If it is a non-path but one perceives it as a path, or if one entertains doubt, [one incurs a grave offense].

One incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). It should be known that if a bhikṣu employs skillful means with the intent to perform what is unlawful, if it is accomplished, he incurs the fundamental offense;

if it is not accomplished, he incurs the preparatory *sthūlātyaya*. From the initial arousal of the skillful means and the adjusting of his robes, up until the point before touching the body, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If a bhikṣu possesses faith and a sense of moral restraint, as well as a sense of dread...
Pressed by afflictions, he committed unrighteous acts; yet, without a single thought of concealment, he wept with flowing tears, unwilling to cast off his dharma robes.
He requested three times before the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to grant him the training rules (*śikṣamāṇā*).
For as long as life lasts, he must practice thirty-five matters in accordance with the rule. Whether it be the recitation of the precepts or the *karman* of the Saṃgha...
Whether they come or do not come, the community of monks is without fault. If a bhikṣuṇī violates this precept, she also incurs a pārājika offense.
A śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī incurs a duṣkṛta offense and is subject to expulsion. (Regarding the final three precepts, the offenses incurred by the four assemblies are the same as this;
they are not separately specified. One does not incur an offense if one does not experience pleasure in the mind and has no lust whatsoever.
[This applies to] one who is insane, whose mind is deranged, or who is overwhelmed by intense pain.
"Initial" refers to the period before the Buddha had yet formulated the precepts, such as in the case of Sudinna and others.

"Insane" means being driven mad due to the death of a relative, the loss of wealth, the affliction of the four great elements (physical illness), or the ripening of karmic retribution from previous lives. "Deranged in mind" means... [or]...
If one is afflicted by non-human spirits, or by diseases of the four elements, or by the retribution of past karma;

or if one suffers from ailments such as wind, cold, or heat that cause the heart to be tormented and oppressed—such diseases as these cause one to lose their natural composure, such that they cannot distinguish between east and west, or purity and impurity, and no longer perceive themselves as being a bhikṣu. Therefore, there is no offense.
All the precepts listed below likewise possess these four factors; thus, they do not constitute an offense. This should be understood accordingly, and therefore they will not be repeated here.

However, for this particular precept to be fully established as an offense, four conditions must be met: first, one must be a true bhikṣu (meaning one who has received the precepts in accordance with the Dharma);

second, the object must be a complete sentient being (meaning a human whose faculties are intact, or a non-human, or an animal); third, one must enter [the private parts] by even a hair’s breadth; fourth, the mind...

Experiencing pleasure (wherein "experiencing pleasure" means like obtaining food when hungry or obtaining drink when thirsty; "not experiencing pleasure" means like eating foul excrement or being burned by a red-hot iron). If one possesses these four conditions, one incurs an *anāpatti-pārājika* (a *pārājika* offense for which there is no rescue).
If, however, one possesses a mind of faith and precepts, a mind of dread, and a mind free from concealment, one incurs a *pārājika* that is subject to confession (*sappatikamma-pārājika*).
This refers to those who are under training (*śikṣamāṇā*). Once they have been granted the training, if they commit the offense again, [they incur a further penalty].

One should immediately expel [the offender] (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: having committed one precept for the first time, one has already destroyed the vessel for receiving the Path; this is called a *pārājika*. If he subsequently kills another person, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

Although the actual offense is grave, it does not bear the name of *pārājika*, because there is no longer a vessel of the Path to be destroyed). The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* says: "Having been granted the training, he is called one who maintains pure precepts; however, with this single body, he cannot transcend birth and death, though he is obstructed from entering hell.

According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, even the three lower assemblies are granted the training. Regarding the "thirty-five matters": one may not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, one may not provide dependence (*niśraya*) to others, and one may not keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*). If appointed to instruct and admonish...

A bhikṣuṇī must not accept [the appointment]. Even if she is appointed, she should not go to provide instruction. She should not recite the precepts for the saṃgha. She should not engage in questions and answers regarding the Vinaya within the saṃgha. She should not accept an appointment from the saṃgha to serve as an administrator (karmadāna). She should not accept an appointment from the saṃgha to adjudicate legal cases.

She should not accept an appointment from the saṃgha for a mission. She should not enter a village early and return at sunset. She should associate with bhikṣus; she must not associate with non-Buddhists or laypeople. She should comply with the rules of the bhikṣus and must not speak of other worldly matters.

She must not recite the Vinaya in the midst of the assembly, unless there is no one else capable of reciting it. She must not commit this offense again. Nor should she commit others that are similar, or those arising from this, or those more serious than this.

This person may not invalidate a *saṃgha-karman*, nor may they perform a *karman*. They may not receive from a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu a seat, have their feet washed, have their leather sandals wiped, have their body massaged, or receive his prostrations, welcoming, and inquiries after his well-being.

They should not accept a pure bhikṣu’s taking hold of their robe or bowl. They may not raise a pure bhikṣu for the purpose of performing a formal act of remembrance (*smṛti-vinaya*) or a formal act of confession (*pratijñā-kāraka*). They should not testify in matters concerning a person of integrity. They may not obstruct a pure bhikṣu’s recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or his invitation at the end of the retreat (*pravāraṇā*).

They may not engage in dispute with a pure bhikṣu. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One must observe and practice all the precepts established by the Buddha. One should sit on a lower seat than the great bhikṣus. One may not stay together with the great *saṃgha* for more than three nights. One may not [stay] with those who have not yet received [the full ordination]."

One who has completed more than two nights among the community may perform the two types of *karmavācanā*—the *pravāraṇā* and the *poṣadha*—with the Saṃgha, but he cannot count toward the quorum. He may not perform other communal legal acts (*saṃghakarma*). He may, however, receive the *varṣā* (formal end of the rains retreat).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu’s food is impure, that [food] is also impure; if that food is impure, the bhikṣu’s [possession of it] is also impure. One may accept food from a śrāmaṇera, except for food that has been purified by fire, the five kinds of living seeds, gold, silver, and food received directly from a śrāmaṇera.
The Second Precept: Abstaining from Taking What Is Not Given.

If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind, according to the nature of taking what is not given, he may be seized by a king or a king’s minister, or he may be executed, bound, or driven out of the country, being accused: "You are a thief!"
"You are deluded; you have no understanding. This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and may not dwell in communion.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, the bhikṣu Cunda had his thatched hut destroyed by wood-gatherers.
He then mixed mud and used firewood to burn it into a completely finished tile-roofed house. The Buddha then established this precept.
He did not permit it. The King commanded that the monks break it open. Thereupon, they went and deceived the men guarding the king’s timber, taking the essential materials reserved by King Bimbisāra.
A minister informed the King, who thought: "One cannot deprive a renunciant of his life for the sake of a small amount of material.
He then rebuked them and released them. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha asked the bhikṣus: "According to the laws of the kingdom, how much constitutes theft?"

Regarding the object permitted [to be stolen]: one should be put to death. He addressed [the Buddha], saying: "If one takes five *kārsāpaṇas*, or an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, one should be put to death.
The Buddha then established the precept according to the royal law: "If one steals an amount reaching five *kārsāpaṇas*, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
As for the term "in a village," it refers to a place where people reside, within the bounds of a city's moats, fences, or walls. As for "in a secluded place," it refers to a village... [text ends].
"Outside the fence or wall" refers to open space. "Taking what is not given" means taking without it being granted; that is, it was not bestowed by another.

"Taking with a thieving mind" means knowing the object belongs to another and, with the intent to steal, taking it for oneself—not with the thought of temporary use, nor with the thought that it is taken from a consenting friend.
"According to the law of taking what is not given" refers to the value reaching five *māsakas*.

If it exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas*, or if it is an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas*—according to the law of the kingdom of Rājagṛha, stealing more than five *kārsāpaṇas* constitutes a capital offense—the Buddha, based on this law, established a general regulation for the region of Jambudvīpa where the Buddha-dharma currently exists:

one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) upon stealing five *kārsāpaṇas*. If a country does not use coinage, the offense is completed according to an object equivalent in value to five *kārsāpaṇas*.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one copper *kārsāpaṇa* is worth sixteen small copper coins; thus, stealing a full eighty small coins constitutes a grave offense. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one incurs a grave offense upon reaching five *māṣakas*. *Māṣaka* is a numerical term; one *māṣaka* consists of eighty cowrie shells, and five *māṣakas* [total one hundred and sixty cowries].

If four hundred cowrie shells (*kapardaka*) are separated from their place at once, it is then called a grave offense. Cowrie shells are also called cowrie seeds; they are colloquially referred to as "conch shells for warding off fright" (*ya-jing-luo*) and also known as "sea-pa" (*hai-ba*), which are small conchs found in the sea.
In ancient times, they were prized as precious currency. Even now, in some places, they are still used as coins. "King" refers to the sovereign of the state.

"Minister" refers to those who preside over state affairs; they are the regents of the kingdom. "To seize" means to take hold of. "To kill" means to sever [life] by means of weapons such as swords or staves.
"His life. "Bound" refers to being shackled with cangues, fetters, stocks, and chains. "Expelled from the country" means banishing him beyond the borders of the kingdom.
These punishments are all administered by kings and ministers who lack faith; because their mental capacity is narrow and they harbor feelings of intolerance, they inflict such penalties.
If the king and his ministers were respectful and faithful, they would merely utter words of reprimand such as: "You..."
Regarding "those who are like thieves": this refers to those who, having departed from wholesome and neutral states of mind, harbor evil thoughts; therefore, they are called thieves.
Because of their delusion and lack of discernment, they commit these evil deeds.

Within this context, an offense occurs if one takes [the object] oneself, or instructs another to take it, or instructs another to seek it out, provided there is the intent to steal, the application of effort, and that the object belongs to an owner. If one acts... [in this manner].

There is the perception that it has an owner; it is a valuable object worth five *māṣaka* coins or more; one lifts it and moves it from its original place; and one forms the thought that it belongs to oneself.

At the very moment it is moved from its place, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. If one employs means to lift it but fails to do so, or even when touching the object, shaking it, or turning it over, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense.
If, after moving it from its original place with the thought that it belongs to oneself, one subsequently regrets it and returns it, [the offense is mitigated].

If one returns it to its original place, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). If one sees an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas* and thinks, "I shall steal it," but later develops a mind of regret and does not take it, one incurs a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) states: "Regarding 'taking what is not given' (*adattādāna*): there are cases where one takes what is not given but it is not theft; for example, taking an object belonging to another while believing it belongs to no one.

Conversely, there are cases of theft that do not constitute 'taking what is not given': for example, when three portions of cake are being distributed among the Saṃgha, one takes four with a thieving mind; or when one takes an ownerless object while perceiving it as having an owner—this constitutes theft, not merely 'taking what is not given.'"

Taking [what is not given] occurs in two ways: first, because one takes what has been entrusted to oneself; second, because there is no owner. This may be "taking what is not given" by a thief, such as taking the property of an owner with a thieving mind; or it may not be "taking what is not given" by a thief, such as taking the property of no owner without a thieving mind.

Regarding "locations": whether it be a location on the ground (meaning objects such as the seven treasures buried within the earth); a location above the ground; a location on a vehicle (meaning vehicles such as elephants, horses, chariots, or foot-soldiers);
a location on a load (meaning loads carried on the head, shoulders, back, or in the arms, upon which there are objects such as the seven treasures);

a location in the air (meaning objects blown by the wind into the sky, or birds and other creatures that have owners); a location above (meaning on trees, walls, fences, stakes, clothing racks, beds, mattresses, pillows, or spreadings); or a location in a village. Or...
An araṇya (a forest hermitage) refers to an unoccupied plot of land outside a village that belongs to an owner, where there are the seven precious gems or other necessary items.

Whether by means of a stratagem to destroy another's land, by relying on intimacy or force, or by deceiving through eloquent speech, if one takes [them], one incurs a pārājika offense upon first obtaining them. A field site refers to fields such as those for rice, wheat, or sugarcane, where there are the seven precious gems or other items; whether by means of a stratagem to destroy another's field...

...up to and including deceiving others to take [it]. Whether at a location (meaning a domestic location, a marketplace location, or a garden, pond, courtyard, front of a house, back of a house, and other such locations), or at a boat location.
If one takes things from a watery place (meaning items belonging to others placed in the water, such as fish, turtles, or lotuses—items that have an owner);

or if one privately crosses a frontier or barrier without paying tax (monks have no obligation to pay taxes; if a layperson has goods subject to taxation and a monk, with a thieving mind, causes them to pass through for another, whether by throwing them beyond the barrier, burying them to retrieve them later, deceiving them through eloquent speech, or passing them by means of incantations—if it is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*);
or if one takes another’s entrusted property (meaning receiving an item entrusted by another and carrying it away with a thieving mind). [The text continues: ...the head...

He moves it upward onto his shoulder; from the shoulder, he moves it onto his head. He moves it from the right shoulder to the left, and so on, shifting it back and forth between the two. Whether he carries it in his arms or places it on the ground—according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, if one receives an object entrusted to him and the owner comes to reclaim it, and the recipient replies, "I did not receive your entrustment," he incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If he causes the owner to fall into doubt, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If the owner says, "I have not recovered this object," it is a *pārājika* (defeat).

If he takes water—meaning jars large or small, or various water vessels, whether it be scented water or medicinal water—even down to stealing the irrigation water of another's field, or for another's sake stealing or diverting the water from a field, or if he has a grudge against someone and diverts or discards the water from that person's field—if the value reaches five *māsaka* coins [or more], it constitutes an offense.

[This constitutes] the fundamental offense). Whether it be tooth-sticks (whether one, two, or even a bundle or a load), or a garden site (meaning all grasses, trees, thickets, flowers, and fruits that belong to an owner), or footless beings, or two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed beings, or shared property (meaning wealth obtained through theft that ought to be held in common).

If one makes an agreement with another (meaning instructing the other to go steal property and bring it so that they may share it); or if one waits in ambush (meaning going oneself to observe and wait for them to obtain the object so that they may share it);

or if one acts as a guardian (meaning when property is obtained from outside, saying "I shall guard it, and the object obtained shall be shared"); or if one watches the path (saying "I shall watch the road;

if anyone comes, I shall inform you, and the object obtained shall be shared")—in such places as these, if there are the seven treasures or other necessary items belonging to an owner, [one who takes them]...

If one takes with a thieving mind an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). If one employs the means to take it but does not obtain it, one incurs a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

If one employs the means to seek an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more but obtains less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, one incurs a gross offense. If one seeks an object worth less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, [one incurs a light offense].

If one obtains five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense. If one seeks less than five *kārsāpaṇas* and obtains them, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one does not obtain them, it is an *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one instructs another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas* or more and they obtain them, both are guilty of the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*); if they do not obtain them, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If one instructs another to seek less than five *kārsāpaṇas* and [the other] obtains five *kārsāpaṇas*, the one who takes them is guilty of the fundamental offense, while the instructor is guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If they do not obtain [them], [the instructor is guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense].

In both cases, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one instructs [another] to seek five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, and the one who receives the instruction takes a different object or takes the object from a different location, the one who takes it incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*), while the instructor incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If the one who receives the instruction lacks the intent to steal, there is no offense;
the instructor incurs an offense based on the value of the object. If one instructs another to take an object without the intent to steal, and the one who receives the instruction...
This refers to instigating theft. The one who takes incurs the offense; the one who instigates is not guilty.
If many bhikṣus send a single person to take another's property, and the value reaches five coins or more, all are guilty of pārājika. This applies even if there is doubt among the assembly.

He immediately forbade it, yet the other went anyway to take it. If he obtained five *kārsāpaṇa* or more, the one who forbade him incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), while the one who did not forbid him incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If they obtain five *kārsāpaṇa* and divide them equally, even though each receives less than five *kārsāpaṇa*, all incur the fundamental offense.
If one obtains goods worth five *māṣakas* at that location, but upon arriving here their value has decreased to less than five *māṣakas*, one still incurs the fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*).
If one obtains goods worth less than five *māṣakas* at that location, but upon arriving here their value exceeds five *māṣakas*, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

If one first consents to another’s going to steal an object, but later regrets it and does not go, one also incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If one intends to steal another’s property but makes a mistake...

If one takes an object belonging to oneself, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If another person has stolen an object and one seizes that stolen object back from the thief, one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If, with the intent to steal, one swaps the counting-sticks (*śalākā*) belonging to another's portion, one incurs the root offense as soon as the stick is picked up.

If one takes [the objects] before and after such that they total five coins (*paṇa*), this is also the root offense. If, with the intention to cause loss, one destroys, burns, or buries another's property...

Regarding objects worth five *kārsāpaṇas*: one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). If dividing land, and with a thieving mind shifting another's boundary markers, worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a fundamental offense.
If taking food belonging to birds or rats from within their nests or burrows, the offense is established according to its value.

If gold or silk that the owner has no use for, there is no offense. Regarding property belonging to an owner, if one perceives it as such and steals it to the extent of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, [it constitutes an offense].

One incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*). If one takes less than five *kārsāpaṇas* when there is doubt regarding an owner, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more when there is doubt regarding an owner, it is a grave offense;

if one takes less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If there is no owner, yet one perceives one as having an owner, or again gives rise to doubt, and takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more— [the same applies].

A grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). A reduction of five *kārsāpaṇas* constitutes a transgression of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). There is no offense in the following cases: when one has the perception that it was given by another; the perception that it is one's own property;

the perception that it is refuse-rag (*pāṃśukūla*) belonging to no owner; the perception that it is taken temporarily; or the perception that it belongs to a close friend or relative, and so forth. In this context, the offense is fully established only when six conditions are met:
first, the person is a genuine bhikṣu; second, there is the intention to steal; third, either acting for oneself or instructing another; fourth, [the object is]... (text truncated).
[It concerns] another's property. (1) One perceives it as belonging to an owner; (2) the value reaches five *māṣaka* coins; (3) one removes it from its original place;

(4) one perceives it as one's own property. If these conditions are met, one incurs the full offense (*pārājika*). If the conditions are not complete, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:

"When an object belongs to another and is protected by another, to take it without it being given is called 'the intent to steal. Furthermore, taking another's property with a deceitful mind, a crooked mind, a mind of anger, or a mind of fear is also called 'the intent to steal. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Briefly, there are five types of acts of stealing: first, taking by force in the presence [of the owner]; second..."

1. Taking by theft; 2. Taking by means of trickery; 3. Taking by means of deception; 4. Taking what was entrusted; 5. Taking back what was given. These five types are all considered the acts of a thief. If a bhikṣu, speaking falsely, requests [an item] from that wife and obtains whatever object [he seeks], [he commits an offense].

At that time, regarding the gravity of the offense: stealing scriptures all constitutes an offense according to their value. Stealing relics—if they are guarded by someone who intends to make offerings to them with the thought of regarding them as the Great Teacher—one commits a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one steals them with the intention of selling them for profit, one incurs a *pārājika* (defeat) offense. If the ornaments within a celestial shrine or a stūpa/monastery are guarded by a person, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; if guarded by a non-human being, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

if there is no guardian of a non-human being, yet one has the thought that they are guarded by various devas or yakṣas, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. If one steals a person, the offense of theft is committed upon reaching the agreed-upon place and time. If a disciple is stolen away by another—whether they have already become the property of that other person or not—the offense is established or not according to the preceding sequence.

If a bhikṣu is forcibly abducted by others to become a slave and flees on his own initiative, there is no offense. If a sentient being is bound by a net, or if a thief steals an ox and ties it to a pillar, when one releases it with the intent to steal, the act is completed as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) once it leaves its place;

if one releases it out of compassion, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If a hunter pursues a deer into a monastery, whether or not the deer is wounded, there is no offense in not returning it; however, if the deer dies, it should be returned. If another person’s fields, gardens, shops, or the like, one may speak improperly for the sake of the Saṃgha and contend over them.

If the official has passed judgment at the time [of the offense], yet the person’s mind has not yet relinquished [the intent], they incur a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If the mind does relinquish it at that time, they incur the full primary offense (*mūlāpatti*). If the official does not pass judgment, they incur a grave offense. If they go before the king for judgment and judgment is passed, they incur a heavy offense;

it is not necessary to wait for the other's mind to cease before the offense is committed. If one takes their own property to a tax station and causes another to pass it through, they incur the full primary offense. Even if it is truly their own wealth, if they resolve in their heart to divert it to their parents or others and tell the tax collector, "This is not my property; I will not give you the tax," [they are free from offense].

Whether traveling through the air, holding the object in the mouth, wrapping it in one's robes, or taking a detour—doing any of these constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If a merchant places taxable goods inside a bhikṣu’s robe-bag and the bhikṣu, unaware of their presence, carries them across the frontier, there is no offense.

If one carries such items across a customs post for the sake of one’s parents or for the Three Jewels, one should preach various Dharma teachings to the tax official, extol the Three Jewels, and speak of the kindness of one’s parents. If they do not take the tax, there is no offense. If they still demand it, one should give it.

Regarding the property of the Three Jewels, one should set aside one portion to pay the tax value; subsequently, this should be shared equally so that no one receives less than their due. If a gift arrives and one knows it does not belong to oneself, yet says, "I deserve to receive this," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one accepts the item, [the offense remains].

An offense is established according to the value of the object. If one holds an item for another person intending to provide relief for a sick person, but hears that the person has died, the object should be returned to the original owner. If the person was still alive when the object was received and only dies later, this constitutes an "abandoned object" (*mṛtadravya*). If a thief steals another's property and gives it to a bhikṣu out of fear, it should not be accepted.

However, if one accepts it with the intention of returning it to the original owner, there is no offense. If the leader of the thieves brings an object to give as a gift, it may be accepted at will. If an item was initially borrowed with the intent not to return it, the full offense is incurred at the moment of that final decision.

In the case of gambling or stealing a piece from a game, an offense is established according to the value of the object. Regarding all objects staked in gambling, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If an object stolen by a thief has already been relinquished [by the original owner], it belongs to the thief; it should not be taken back.

[The object] is recovered. The recovery constitutes an offense according to the number [of items taken]. When one's property has been stolen by another, one should not hastily form the intention to abandon it; if it is later seen, it should be reclaimed. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu is robbed by bandits and, having already formed the thought that he has lost the items, recovers them, he is as if robbing the bandits once again.

If the bandits have gone to a village and are about to divide the goods, and he recovers them by begging from them, there is no offense. If he uses force or intimidation to make them return them, there is no offense. If he informs the village headman and uses skillful means to persuade him to return them, there is no offense.

However, if he knows that doing so will cause the person to be killed or bound, he should not inform him. The *Sudarśana-vinaya* says: If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, takes back the property of a thief and separates it from the thief’s possession, and if that person is capable [of retaliation], he must return it.

[If one] takes it away, even if the bhikṣu does not actually obtain the object, it is still a *pārājika* offense, because he has definitively obtained it through the act of stealing and the mind [of theft] has moved the object from its original place. If a donor gives a fruit tree to the Saṃgha—whether intended for clothing or for medicinal decoctions—the Saṃgha may not consume the fruit.

If the fruit tree was given as an offering for the four requisites, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, consumes more than his share, he incurs an offense according to the value of the amount. If it was given for the construction of a dwelling for the Saṃgha, and he diverts it for food, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense; he must repay the value.

If clothing is offered as a gift, it should be made into robes. If there is famine or danger, and the Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā* in harmony, there is no offense in consuming [the gift]. It is the same if clothing offered for the purpose of building a dwelling is used for food and drink, or if a dwelling offered for the purpose of making food and drink is used for other purposes.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu serves as the master of a monastery (*vihārasvāmin*) and the stūpa has no property while the Saṃgha does, he might think: "The reason devas and humans make offerings to the Saṃgha is that they all receive the grace of the Buddha; to offer to the Saṃgha is to offer to the Buddha.

If he then takes property belonging to the Saṃgha to repair the stūpa, this master of the monastery commits a *pārājika* offense. Conversely, if the stūpa has property and the Saṃgha has none, he might think: "In making offerings to the Saṃgha, the Buddha is also included therein. If he then takes property belonging to the stūpa to provide for the Saṃgha, the master of the monastery [commits an offense].

If one uses [the property], it is a *pārājika* offense. If the stūpa has no property but the Saṃgha does, one may borrow and use it according to the Dharma, provided one clearly records in writing that it was borrowed at a certain time and must be returned at a certain time. If the Saṃgha has no property but the stūpa does, [the same applies].
