It is also like this. When there is a handover [of property], one should read the formal statement (*śāstra*) clearly within the Saṃgha and perform the transfer. If one does not read the formal statement, it is an offense against the Vinaya. If two bhikṣus have shared property that ought to be divided, and one bhikṣu takes it alone with a thieving mind, [it is likewise an offense].

Excluding one's own portion; if another's portion is taken in full, it is a *pārājika*. If one takes it with consent, or if one thinks, "I will use this now and return it later," there is no offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: When a donor invites the Saṃgha and the turn for a certain monk has not yet arrived, that monk says of himself, "I should leave."

*Pāyattika*. When obtaining food, one incurs an offense according to its value. Destroying a bird’s nest or taking a bird’s nest constitutes *duṣkṛta*. To destroy game out of a desire for pleasure is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); to destroy it out of compassion is *duṣkṛta*. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:

"If a monastery is empty and deserted with no one present, and a bhikṣu comes and sees fruit on a tree, he should strike the *ghanṭā* or, at the very least, clap his hands three times before eating; there is no offense. Otherwise, he commits the offense of theft. If the resident monks have fled to avoid danger and a visiting bhikṣu comes and sees food, drink, or fruit, and takes it with a thieving mind, the offense is determined according to the circumstances.

If a bhikṣu steals a person or their clothing, and the person runs away, leaving the clothes on the ground, and the bhikṣu continues to pursue them but turns back before catching up, yet takes the clothes once they are off the ground, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a person steals and the victim runs away, leaving their clothes behind and casting them aside, and the thief pursues but cannot catch up and returns; seeing the clothes on the ground, he thinks, "This person has cast them aside; I shall pick them up," and there is no offense. However, he incurs the grave offense of *thullaccaya* (a serious transgression) due to the preparatory act of intending to steal the person's property.

If that person turns his head and speaks from afar, saying, "Monk, do not take my clothes," and the monk nevertheless takes them, he incurs the fundamental offense (*pārājika*) once they have left the ground. If it is another’s slave, and the monk says to him, "You are suffering here; why do you not run away? and [the slave] reaches... [the text ends].

"In another place, you may find satisfaction. If he follows the monk’s words and departs from the two-footed [master], he incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). If a slave rebels and the monk shows him the way, urging him to leave, the monk incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) according to the instructions given.

If the slave departs slowly and the monk says, "The master will surely catch you if you go at a leisurely pace," and the slave runs swiftly in accordance with those words, the monk incurs a grave offense. If the monk says, "Such-and-such a region is extremely pleasant and has abundant food; who could refuse to go there?

and the slave, upon hearing this, pursues the monk and leaves of his own accord, there is no offense. Furthermore, it is said: "When four people steal together, three incur offenses while one escapes. Why is this? It is like four monks: one is the teacher and three are disciples. They wish to steal six *kārsāpaṇas*. The teacher says..."

The disciple said, "Each of you stole one coin; I stole three. The first disciple said, "The teacher stole two; I stole one. You two each stole one coin. The other two disciples likewise instructed one another in turn in the same manner. That teacher, having stolen three coins himself, incurred a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

For instructing the three disciples to steal, he also incurred a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Why is this? Stealing by oneself is one thing; instructing others to steal is another. Therefore, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses. How is it that the three [disciples] incur a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*)?
It is because they were instructed to steal five coins in total.
The Third Precept: Taking Human Life.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, provides a weapon to another, praises death, encourages death by saying, "O man, what is the use of this wretched life?
It is better to die than to live," or if he forms such a thought and employs various means [to bring about death].
He then praised death, exclaiming how pleasant it was to die. This bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and shall not dwell in communion.

The commentary states: While the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī, he stayed in the lecture hall by the side of the Monkey River and taught the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus immediately practiced this meditation on impurity; having emerged from their meditative absorption, they became weary of [the world].

Afflicted by his own body and life, he was filled with grief and found no joy; he then sought a blade, intending to take his own life. He sighed for death, praised death, and exhorted others toward death.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Mṛgāra-nandi (translated as "Deer-Joy" [Lùxǐ]; other vinayas refer to him as the "Deer-Staff Heretic").
Carrying a sharp blade in his hand, he entered the Pārileyyaka Garden. There was another bhikṣu who was weary of his own body and life, to whom [Mṛgāra-nandi] said: "You may cut me."
"Life! I give my robe and bowl to you. He accepted the employment and immediately took his life. In this manner, he killed as many as sixty people.
Ānanda informed the Buddha, whereupon the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and taught them the *ānāpāna-samādhi*, which is tranquil and blissful.
"Whenever unwholesome states arise, one should immediately extinguish them, ensuring they never arise again. Thus he spoke.
Having finished [this discourse], he then established a precept for the bhikṣus: "One who intentionally takes human life. "Intentionally" means with focused intent;

it does not refer to an error or mistake. "With one's own hand" means performing the act personally. "Taking life" means causing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) to cease its continuity and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to disperse.
"Human" specifically refers to the human realm (*manuṣyagati*), indicating that this does not apply to other destinies. Why is this so?
It is for the sake of life. All sentient beings take consciousness as their basis. This consciousness is of six kinds, arising from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Because they are able to produce consciousness, they are called "roots. From these six roots, six kinds of consciousness arise;
this is termed "life. Why is this so? It is because these six roots and six consciousnesses are able to arise in continuous succession.
The cessation of this continuity is called death; therefore, this [continuity] is termed life. This life is of two kinds:
first, from the initial entry into the mother’s womb until there are only the three faculties of body, life, and mind;
second, from the forty-ninth day onward, when the six faculties are fully complete. Both of these are termed human life. If one kills either of these two...
All these are termed "taking life. As for "giving a knife to another," this refers to inciting murder;
that is, handing over weapons such as knives or clubs to another person, thereby causing them to take their own life.

Alternatively, knowing that a person is weary of their own body and life, one gives them a knife or similar instrument and praises or exhorts them to commit suicide. This includes praising the dead—that is, commending those who desire death.
They praise and extol his virtuous qualities, saying: "You have performed many good deeds; you have cultivated merit; you have provided protection.
You have experienced manifold sufferings while alive; if you die, you shall be reborn in the heavens.
By various means they laud him and encourage him to die. Thus, they skillfully exhort those who would find pleasure in death, urging them on.
He says: "The evil you have committed is devoid of compassion; you harbor a poisonous mind and have performed no virtuous deeds.
You have provided no protection. Since you were born, you have incurred much guilt; it would be better for you to die than to live.
Thus, before both the virtuous and the wicked, he encourages them to take their own lives, whether by speaking with his voice, manifesting signs through his body or speech, or otherwise.
He sends someone to speak [of it], or he sends someone with a letter to that person to cause them to die.
"Ho! Man!"—this is a word used for calling out. "What is the use of this wretched life? It would be better to die than to live" means:
"Why do you maintain this unwholesome, sinful way of life? If you live, your sins will increase day by day; it would be better to face death. Not... [to live].

If [the victim] is born, their merit will be great. Because he previously exhorted and praised [him], yet [the victim] did not comply, he uttered these words of reproach and disparagement to cause him to seek death.

"One who conceives such thoughts" refers to one who, if [the victim] does not comply with the reproach, further seeks another method with such a murderous intent. "Various means" and so forth refers to employing various...
One employs various skillful means of exhortation and praise to ensure that the person dies. In this context, there are three general types of such expedients:

first, physical; second, both physical and vocal; and third, vocal. If one carries out the killing with one's own hand, or with materials such as tiles, stones, knives, or clubs, this is called physical [killing].
If one hands a knife to another and instructs them to carry out the killing, or hands a knife to them and exhorts and encourages them to do so...
Suicide is termed [an offense of] body and speech. To revile, urge, or praise [someone] so as to cause them to die is termed [an offense of] speech.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the transgression? If one causes death by means of the three aforementioned methods, one incurs a *pārājika* offense in every case.
If they do not die, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense. Furthermore, if one employs other expedients—such as digging a pit to cause them to fall, or...
One triggers the mechanism to cause a fall; or one gives non-medicinal substances; or one causes another’s fetus to miscarry.
If the mother dies but the child lives, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), because it was not one's original intention [to kill the child].

If a group of many bhikṣus sends one person to take another's life, and among them there is one who has doubts and immediately restrains him, yet that person nevertheless goes and takes the life, the one who restrained him incurs a *sthūlātyaya*, while the others who did not restrain him do not.
In all such cases, it is a *pārājika*. If a bhikṣu attempts suicide through various means, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one kills a deva, nāga, yakṣa, or ghost, or an animal that understands human speech and can assume human form, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if it does not die, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

If one kills an actual human being while perceiving them as a human, it is a *pārājika*. If one kills an actual human being while harboring doubt about their status, or while perceiving them as a non-human, [it is likewise a *pārājika*].
In all such cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If it is a non-human being, yet one perceives it as a human, or if there is doubt [regarding its identity], it is still a *sthūlātyaya*.

There is no offense in cases of accidental killing where there is no intent to harm whatsoever. In this context, the offense is fully established only when five conditions are met: first, the perpetrator is a bhikṣu;

second, the object is a human being (meaning a male, female, eunuch, or from the moment of entering the mother’s womb thereafter); third, there is intentional killing; and fourth, there is the perception of the object as a human.

Fifth, regarding the severance of life: if there is a deficiency in the causal conditions, one does not incur the fundamental offense (*pārājika*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu takes up a knife for the purpose of killing a person, he incurs a *vyatikrama-vinayātikrama* (offense of transgression).

If he touches the person's body, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If the person dies, it is a *pārājika*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are three ways of severing a person's life: first, by means of internal form (*rūpa*), such as a bhikṣu striking another with his hand or foot."

Whether it be the head or other parts of the body—these two involve the use of non-internal matter, namely by hurling wood, tiles, stones, swords, arrows, and so forth at another person from a distance. Thirdly, there is the use of internal and non-internal matter, namely by grasping wood, tiles, stones, swords, arrows, and so forth with one's own hand to strike another.

Furthermore, there are cases where one does not employ these three types of matter, but instead uses poison, constructs pits, sets snares, lays traps, employs mechanical devices, or raises zombies through incantations. If a bhikṣu constructs such pits, stocks, snares, traps, or mechanical devices for the sake of others...

...and so forth. If a person dies because of this [act], one incurs a *pārājika* offense. If they do not die immediately, but later die because of it, one also incurs a *pārājika* offense. If they do not die because of it later, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a non-human (*amanuṣya*) or an animal dies because of it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* in all cases. If one makes a pit or the like for a non-human, and that non-human dies, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if a human or an animal dies, it is also a *duṣkṛta*. If one makes a pit or the like for an animal, and that animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*; if a human or a non-human dies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If the intention is indefinite—making [a trap] for a single purpose with the intent that whoever comes along shall die—if a human dies, it is a *pārājika*; if a non-human dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*. If there is no [intention at all], [there is no offense].

If [the victim] dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one cuts off one's own penis, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one cuts off one's own finger, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "When a bhikṣu strikes his own generative organ, the Buddha said: 'One should strike this;

to strike something else instead is the act of one who lacks wisdom,' and he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If a person who is carrying an animal fetus causes an abortion, it does not constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*). If an animal carrying a human fetus causes an abortion, it constitutes a grave offense. If one intends to kill an ordinary person but kills an arhat, or intends to kill... [text ends].

If one kills an ordinary person who is an Arhat, or intends to kill one's father but mistakenly kills one's mother—or the reverse—in all such cases, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), but does not incur the crime of parricide (*ānantarya*). If one has already performed the preliminary means (*prayoga*) for killing one's mother and then dies first, while the mother dies later, it constitutes a grave parricide.

If one dies first and the mother dies later, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The same applies to the case of a father who is an Arhat. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If, by the words of a bhikṣu, one leads an army to invade a foreign country and thereby acquires both territory and wealth, one incurs both the *pārājika* offenses of killing and stealing."
The Fourth Pārājika: The Precept Against Grave Falsehood.
If a bhikṣu, while lacking any actual realization, claims of himself: "I have attained the state of a superior person;
I have entered the sublime Dharma of noble wisdom; such am I; I have seen this," and at a later time—whether questioned or unasked—he desires to clear himself...
Because it is pure, he speaks thus: "I truly did not know or see, yet I said I knew and I saw; this was a false, deceptive, and lying speech.
With the exception of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
The commentary states: At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through Vaiśālī and resided in the High-Roofed Lecture Hall on the bank of the Monkey River.

At that time, grain was expensive and alms were difficult to obtain. In the monastery by the Vālukā River, various bhikṣus spoke to the lay devotees, saying, "I have attained the state of a superior person," and they further praised a certain bhikṣu, saying that he too had attained it.

Regarding the status of a superior person (*uttamapudgala*): the various householders, believing his words, immediately provided him with food and drink as offerings. He was not troubled by these provisions for food and drink.

When the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) had concluded, he went to see the World-Honored One. After the Buddha had greeted him with words of comfort, he reported all the aforementioned matters to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said, "You fools, you should not speak even of what is real to others, let alone what is unreal.
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu of overweening pride who told people, "I have attained the Way. Later, at another time, he applied himself with diligence and without slackening, earnestly seeking the method.

He then realized the supreme and most excellent Dharma, yet he feared the offense of lying and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Except for those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), there is no offense.

That bhikṣu was practicing in an araṇya; having briefly attained *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* and subdued his afflictions (*kleśa*), he later traveled among people in the world. Failing to restrain his sense faculties, his afflictions then arose.

He felt great shame and remorse, applied himself with diligent skillful means, and attained arhatship. "Having nothing to know" means that regarding the states of superior persons (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), he had no realization or awakening.
"To claim for oneself" means to claim and declare for oneself what one has attained. "The states of superior persons" refers to the dharmas cultivated and realized by the noble ones (*ārya*).

These dharmas, in contrast to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), six sense bases (*ṣad-āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) of all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), [are the qualities of the noble ones].

The elements (*dhātu*), up to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), the ten fetters (*daśa-saṃyojana*), and all phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*)—because these are surpassed by what is most supreme, namely mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the samādhis, and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Furthermore, that which can eliminate those phenomena associated with outflows is also called the "Dharma of the Superior Person" (*uttara-puruṣadharma*). As for my statement, "I have entered the supreme Dharma of noble wisdom," it means that I have already...
"Entry" means one's own realization and entry [into the path]. "Noble" refers to the Buddhas and the śrāvakas.
"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—as well as other various forms of wisdom.

This wisdom is the most supreme and excellent dharma, capable of realizing the noble fruits of the three vehicles. "I know this" means knowing those four: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

The Noble Truths. As for "I see these," it means seeing the principle of those Four Noble Truths and attaining the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to observe all sentient beings as they are born here and die there according to the retribution of their wholesome or unwholesome karma. Furthermore, one sees devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits coming to my presence;
moreover, one knows that which belongs to the faculty of mind (*manendriya*), attains purity of the mental faculty, and realizes entry into noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
"Seeing" refers to the faculty of the eye. One attains the purity of the eye-faculty and clearly perceives all phenomena without error or omission.
"At another time" means that "he" refers to the person who gave false testimony; "another time" refers to a subsequent occasion distinct from the time of the false statement.
"Being questioned" means being interrogated by another: "By what method did you obtain it? From whom did you obtain it?
Where did you obtain it? How was it obtained? It is only when questioned in this manner that one speaks.
"Not being questioned" means that although another does not ask, one confesses of one's own accord because remorse has arisen within oneself. "Desiring to be pure" means seeking the precepts.
Śuddha then addressed others, saying: "I truly did not know or see the dharmas such as the Four Noble Truths;
it was only that I claimed to know and claim to see. This was merely empty, deceptive, and false speech. 'Empty' means that what one has spoken lacks reality.
'Deceptive' means that it was originally intended to delude others. 'False speech' means that one speaks of oneself based on a deluded mind. Why is this so?"
Regarding the precepts, if there are expressions such as "whether asked or unasked" and "seeking purification," does one only incur the offense once another person has made it known?
This is because one first confesses to an object (the recipient) and thereby incurs the fault;
subsequently, one wishes to seek purification from that same object. Although such words of confession are uttered, the initial act was speaking to another.
At that time, the offense is already established; it cannot be rendered non-existent through this confession. This excludes those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
That is to say, excluding persons of overweening pride who lack a deceitful mind, they do not fall into the category of the offense of lying.

This is because their afflictions remain temporarily suppressed as they cultivate the path, and they falsely believe within their own minds that they have truly attained and realized the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*). Therefore, regarding their departure...
Within the world-transcending dharmas, one gives rise to conceit in the mind. However, this overweening pride cannot be attained by those who break the precepts or are indolent;
it is only for those who maintain pure precepts and cultivate meditative concentration.

Without improperly discriminating between name and form, they first enter *vipaśyanā* with a heart of intense vigor, or attain *śamatha* through the power of skillful maintenance. Thus, the afflictions...
They do not arise. Thinking they have already attained the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), they give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
If they know for themselves that there is truly nothing realized, yet they deliberately speak falsely, this constitutes lying (*mṛṣāvāda*). Regarding the offense herein:
if a bhikṣu speaks thus, though it is false and unreal, by speaking directly to another person, or by means of a hand gesture, or by sending a messenger to speak, or...

If one sends a letter [to claim attainment], or makes signs to indicate it, and the other person understands, it is a *pārājika* offense; if they do not understand, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).

If one is in a secluded place but perceives it as non-secluded, or if one is in a non-secluded place but perceives it as secluded, yet claims for oneself, "I have attained the state of a superior person," it is a grave offense.
If one speaks thus toward devas, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, or animals capable of changing their form, it is likewise a grave offense.

If one knows [the truth], it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if one does not know, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If one has truly attained the Path and speaks of it to a monk who is not in agreement, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If one preaches the characteristics of the Dharma to others and says, "I have attained it," it is a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).

If one addresses a human being while perceiving them as a human being and speaks to them, it is a fundamental offense. If one is in doubt regarding a human being, or perceives a human being as a non-human being, or perceives a non-human being as a human being, [the same applies].

Some may doubt this, [thinking] that all such cases constitute *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses). Those who do not commit an offense include: preaching the Dharma to others without saying "I have attained it";
speaking in jest; speaking alone in a secluded place; speaking in a dream; or speaking erroneously. In these instances, the five conditions are not fully met.

Only when these conditions are fulfilled does the offense constitute a *pārājika*. First, there must be a monk who has obtained a dwelling place; second, there must be a person as the object; third, there must be an intentional mind of falsehood;

fourth, there must be the manifestation of signs through body or speech; and fifth, the other person must understand the meaning. When these five factors are complete, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding "those whose conditions are deficient," one should understand this according to the *Vinaya-viniścaya* (The Vinaya Compendium). It states: If a bhikṣu intends to manifest that he possesses superior dharmas within himself, yet says aloud, "There is a bhikṣu who has attained such and such superior and wondrous things," but does not say of himself, "It is I," he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: For the sake of gain and offerings, if one praises another’s perfection of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation in various ways, while secretly using it to glorify oneself, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

For the sake of gain and offerings, if one acts with composed deportment—whether sitting, rising, walking, or standing—and speaks with serene dignity to manifest the appearance of having attained the Path, desiring to make others know it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If someone asks a bhikṣu, "You... [and so forth].

"Are you an Arhat? If one remains silent, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*. One should say, "I am not an Arhat. The *Lekha-śāstra* states: "If asked whether one has attained the fruit [of the path], and one answers 'I have' while showing a fruit in one's hand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*."

If one says, "I do not fall into the three miserable realms," it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Even down to saying that one's observance of the precepts is pure and that no lustful desire arises—if this is untrue, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one has not recited the sūtras, yet claims to have recited them..."

One who is not a master of discourse but claims to be a master of discourse; one who is not a master of the Vinaya but claims to be a master of the Vinaya; one who does not practice meditation but claims to practice meditation—speaking broadly, one who has nothing at all to recite or study yet claims that they have something to recite or study—all such cases constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It would be better to eat ashes and charcoal, to swallow excrement and earth, or for a sharp blade to rip open one's belly, than to receive offerings by falsely claiming superhuman attainments (*uttarimanussadhamma*). As stated in the *Vinayamūla*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are two types of thieves in the world: first, those who are not actually of pure conduct but claim for themselves that they are of pure conduct;

second, those who, for the sake of food and clothing, speak falsehoods in the midst of the great assembly regarding what is unreal and not their own, falsely claiming to have attained superhuman attainments. Of these two, it is the latter—the one who acts for the sake of food and clothing—who is [the greater offender].
The greatest of thieves, because they steal the food and drink offered by others).
△ Finally, the summary question:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the four *pārājika* rules. If a bhikṣu commits any one of these rules, he is not [to be reckoned as a bhikṣu]."
He dwells together with the bhikṣus as before; his subsequent transgression is likewise.
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not dwell together [with the Saṃgha]. Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter? (Three times.
The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, because they are silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld.

The commentary states: "One who violates any single dharma" means that among the four *pārājika* dharmas, if one commits even one of them, one is no longer a bhikṣu and may not dwell together with the pure assembly. As previously stated, the same applies to subsequent violations.

Just as before when he had not yet received the full ordination and was a layperson, having no status as a bhikṣu, so too after he has committed a transgression against the precepts, he is no different from that former layperson;
this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

Having violated that rule, one incurs its offense. "The name of the offense is 'abandonment'" means that because one has abandoned the Buddha-dharma to a foreign land, one should not dwell together with others.
If these four matters are pure, one is fit to hear the subsequent precepts; therefore, it is necessary to pose these questions. The remaining meanings are as explained previously.
For all subsequent sections, one should understand them according to this pattern; they will not be repeated again. This.

Regarding the middle *pārājika* offense: although the name of the transgression is the same, the retribution differs. Why is this? It is because the objects of sexual misconduct are not uniform. They include animals and humans.

Among humans, there are those who have left the household life and those who have not. Those who have not left the household life are of two kinds: those who observe the precepts and those who do not.
Among those who have left the household life, there are five kinds; likewise, they include both those who observe the precepts and those who do not.

Regarding the precept of ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are such distinctions even among the noble ones (*ārya*). As in the case of the precept against stealing, the objects stolen are not of one kind;

there are distinctions between stealing from those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*) and those who remain at home (*gṛhastha*). Among those remaining at home, there are also distinctions when stealing another's property.

Even among those who have left the household life, there are distinctions in stealing. Furthermore, there are distinctions regarding the Three Jewels (*triratna*), just as there are in the case of the precept against killing.
There are distinctions among people: those who live at home and those who have left the home life; those who observe the precepts and those who do not; and even up to the noble ones (*ārya*).
As explained in the section on false precepts, when speaking to householders, it is a grave offense to claim to have attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*);

however, when speaking to those who have left the home life, it is a lighter offense. Therefore, although the name of the transgression is the same, its retribution differs. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

There are three kinds of offenses for committing a transgression: first, the offense of a course of action (*karmapatha*); second, the offense of misconduct (*duṣcarita*); and third, the offense of violating a precept (*śīla*).

Among these three offenses, Sudinna committed the offense of misconduct, because sexual intercourse is an unwholesome practice. He did not commit the offense of a course of action, because it was his own wife.
He did not commit the offense of violating a precept, because the Buddha had not yet formulated the rule. [This occurred] in the forest grove.

The Buddha incurred two offenses: he incurred the offense of misconduct because sexual intercourse is an unwholesome act; and he incurred the offense of a karmic path because the female macaque submitted to the male macaque.
He did not incur the offense of violating a precept because the Buddha had not yet formulated the rules of discipline. Other precepts may be understood by analogy with this case.
Furthermore, when one steals another's property, there are two ways in which the object is separated from its original location: first, by lifting it away from its original place...
Regarding the location: secondly, having lifted [the object] from its original place and returning it to that same place, one who carries it away incurs two kinds of offenses.

First, one incurs the offense of the karmic path (*karmapatha*), because of stealing another's property. Second, one incurs the offense of violating the precepts (*śīla*), because the Buddha has established the prohibitions.

Regarding "returning it to its original place": one incurs one offense. Since the object was first moved from its original location and then returned there, and because no harm was done to another's property, there is no offense of the karmic path (*karmapatha*);
one incurs only the offense of violating the precepts (*śīlavipatti*). This should be understood according to the underlying principle:

both constitute the offense of misconduct (*duṣcarita*), for theft is an unwholesome dharma (*akuśala-dharma*). The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* asks: "For what reason are the first three *pārājika* offenses listed with sexual misconduct first and theft last?"
They are explained in reverse order, which differs from other locations where the sequence is given as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.

Here, the sequence is taught according to the chronological order of the occasions for committing the offenses; furthermore, it follows the sequence because each preceding act induces the subsequent one.
Through unchaste conduct, one proceeds to steal; having already stolen, one then kills an enemy; and after killing, when questioned [about the crime].
Thus one utters false speech. Furthermore, those afflictions that are most powerful are presented first.
What are the characteristics of these four *parājika* offenses? They are: lack of renunciation, lack of forbearance, and lack of realization.
Among these, lack of renunciation is established as the first two: first, regarding sexual desire; second, regarding material possessions. Because of a lack of forbearance, one commits killing.
Because it has not been realized, it is false speech, as explained above; one should take the subsequent explanation as the intended meaning.
That is to say, because the afflictions bound to the earth (*bhūmi*) are particularly heavy, they were proscribed first. A bhikṣu must swiftly depart from the three realms.
Sexual desire is the root of birth and death and the cause of out-flowing turbidity; thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also teaches this as the primary instruction. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If..."
If the beings within the six realms of all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
You practice samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; if the lustful heart is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the paths of demons. You teach the people of the world to practice samādhi...
Samādhi: First sever sexual desire in the mind; this is called the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
If one who cultivates dhyāna-concentration does not sever sexual desire, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that it will become rice.
Even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it shall be known only as "Hot Sands. Why is this? Because this is not the foundation for food; it is composed of sand and gravel.
If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous awakening, it will all be rooted in lust.

With lust at its very foundation, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. By what path can you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata? You must—
Regarding the mechanism of lust: sever both body and mind; even the nature of this severance must be absent. Only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
As clarified in the sutras, you should observe this for yourself; contemplate it well and practice diligently, lest you suffer future regret.
II. The Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas (Opening: Three). First, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration; third, the concluding inquiry.
△ First, the general heading:
"Venerable sirs, these thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."

"Come. The commentary explains: *saṃgha* means "the community"; *pācittiya* (here rendered as *vāśeṣa*) means "residual. This refers to the four preceding *pārājika* rules, which carry the sense of being "without remainder.
If one commits even one of them, there is no remaining residue that can be remedied. These thirteen rules, in their essential nature, are...
There is a remainder. If one has committed an offense, there still remains a residue that can be remedied;
it must be dealt with according to the rules by relying upon the Saṃgha, and the offense must be cleared by relying upon the Saṃgha, rather than by relying upon one, two, or three bhikṣus.
Furthermore, one cannot be cleared of an offense by relying on a saṃgha of fewer than twenty members. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"It is like a person who has been killed by another; as long as the throat remains intact, it is called 'residual' (*śeṣa*). It is like two people entering together into the midst of a battle:
one is killed by another and his life is severed, while the other is also killed by another but the vital faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*) still remains slightly."
It can be severed. If one obtains a skilled physician and excellent medicine, it may be cured; if these are lacking, it cannot be cured.
It is the same for those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: there is a slight possibility of repentance.
If one obtains a pure assembly that performs the method of confessing and removing the offense according to the Dharma, this offense may be removed. If such a pure assembly is lacking...
"O Great Assembly, it cannot be eradicated; this is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension from the community).
[Section on Individual Enumeration] 1.
The Precept Regarding the Emission of Semen.
If a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his organ and emits semen, except in a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The commentary says: At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Kālodāyin’s lustful desires were intense;
following his thoughts and recollections, he manipulated [his organ] and emitted impurity. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "How can one, toward me who am pure..."
"You have gone forth within the pure Dharma, yet you perform defiled acts. You fool! With the very hands that receive the faithful offerings of others, you now play with your genitals and emit semen.
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who fell asleep with a distracted mind and emitted semen in a dream; he then doubted whether he had committed an offense against the Saṃgha.
[The monk] reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "There is no offense. However, there are five faults in sleeping with a distracted mind:
first, having bad dreams; second, the devas do not protect one; third, the mind does not enter into the Dharma;
fourth, one does not clearly perceive the signs of dawn; and fifth, one emits semen during sleep. There are five merits in sleeping with a virtuous mind; these are the reverse of the above."
Thus, regarding "intentionally discharging seminal essence": this refers to acting with a deliberate mind.

Because the wind of deluded thoughts and perverse recollections fans the fire of lust, the flesh, marrow, and fat flow; through heat, they transform into semen, which is then discharged by a deliberate mind, departing from its original location.

(The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states that the waist is the original location. It further says: "Not so; the entire body contains seminal essence, except for the hair, nails, and dry places, where there is no essence. If the essence departs... )

The original location, the path to the ultimate way, the non-path to the ultimate way, and the departure—even down to [the amount sufficient to] satisfy a single fly—constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This excludes cases occurring in dreams; that is to say, one does not commit an offense while dreaming.

This is because there is no substantial reality to be found within a dream. If a person who has not yet abandoned greed, hatred, and delusion falls asleep with a distracted mind, they will inevitably discharge impurity;
however, if they fall asleep with their mind focused in mindfulness, this fault does not occur. This refers to what is called "deliberately manipulating the organ."
This is the cause for the offense. With the exception of dreams, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*—the formal definition of the offense established by the re-binding of the rule.
(The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Dreams are false and unreal. If dreams were real, there would be no liberation for those practicing the holy life within my Dharma, because all dreams are unreal.
Therefore, those who practice the holy life within my Dharma attain the end of suffering. Regarding the offense herein: if, for the sake of pleasure, for oneself...

If one plays with [the seed] for any of these reasons—for the sake of a trial, for the sake of merit, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of rebirth in heaven, for the sake of giving, for the sake of seeds, or out of self-indulgence and pride, or for the sake of a pleasant countenance—then if such means result in the loss [of the seed], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if there is no loss, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. In this case, there are six kinds of mental intentions that move the body.
If one emits semen, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense in all cases. This refers to internal matter, external matter, and both internal and external matter;

as well as water, wind, and space. Regarding "internal matter," this refers to one's own body. Regarding "external matter," this refers to another's body. Regarding "both internal and external matter," this refers to one's own body and another's body together.
Regarding "water, wind, and space": if one directs the male organ against the current, with the current, or sprinkles it with water; or if one directs it against the wind, with the wind...
Wind, or blowing from the mouth; or if one moves the body in mid-air, there is neither internal form nor external form. Because of this spontaneous movement, one incurs an offense.
In all such cases, if one loses semen through the recollection of bodily movement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).
If a woman grasps a bhikṣu from the front or from behind, and the bhikṣu moves his body and emits semen, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if he does not move his body, it is not.
If it is lost, there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to manipulate [the organ] and it is lost, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);

if it is not lost, he incurs an *dukkaṭa*. If he instructs another person to manipulate it and it is lost or not lost, in all cases there is an *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three lower groups [śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if it is lost through improper mental attention, or if it is lost upon seeing a beautiful form without physical contact.
Whether while walking and touching her own two thighs, or her robe, or her skirt; or during bathing and rubbing;

or when afflictions are intense and emission occurs upon being touched by another—in all these cases, if she does not form the intention to discharge impurity and yet it is emitted, this nun incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
This is because the afflictions of women are deep and heavy, making them difficult to restrain and control.
Furthermore, it must be in a private, secluded place; only with many conditions and much effort can one emit [semen]. This differs from men, who can emit it according to the circumstances.
Therefore, the regulation is not the same, and the offense is also lighter. (The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one employs means during the waking state and emission occurs in a dream...")

Or conversely, one may intentionally experience pleasure; or, having previously applied effort, later cease the mental application; or, while applying effort, immediately withdraw the mindfulness as the semen is about to move—all these incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If one grasps another’s generative organ (*upastha*) and intentionally emits impurity, or measures one’s own generative organ, or grasps and squeezes it with the hand for pleasure, or rubs and touches it so as to cause arousal, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense in each case. If, with a defiled mind, one gazes at one’s own generative organ, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Lakṣaṇāvatāra-śāstra* states:

If semen is emitted from the stalk [of the organ], it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If desire arises and the body becomes aroused, but there is no thought of emission and one does not intentionally manipulate it to cause emission, one should reproach one's own mind.

If one sees another engaged in sexual intercourse or the mating of birds and beasts, and desire arises such that one loses the impurity, this is a matter for which one should reproach one's own mind. If, however, for the sake of experiencing pleasure, one employs further means to watch intently with the intent to cause emission, and emission occurs, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one sees a man and a woman naked, and desire arises such that one loses the impurity..."
One should reproach one's own mind. If, for the sake of pleasure, one goes to look [at her] and causes her to come out, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
**The Second Precept: Touching a Female Body.** If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, touches the body of a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her hair, or touching her—[it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].
"Each individual part of the body" refers to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin heard of the rule established by the Buddha that one must not emit semen.
He then waited for women to enter his room, where he would fondle them and kiss their mouths. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha... [ruled accordingly].
Having rebuked him, he established the precept. "With lustful intent" means that affectionate attachment has arisen.
"To touch the body of a woman" is the general heading. "Grasping the hand or grasping the hair" is the detailed explanation. "Touching each individual part of the body" is the concluding summary.
"Woman" refers to one who is a fit object for sexual intercourse. "Body" refers to [the parts] from the hair down to...
Feet; physical contact with the body, meaning to perform acts of touching by applying the body to the body. This consists of nine types:

grasping and rubbing (*parāmarśa*), pulling (*ākṛṣṭi*), pushing (*pratikṣepa*), upward stroking (*pratiloma-parāmarśa*), downward stroking (*anuloma-parāmarśa*), lifting (*utkṣepa*), lowering (*nikṣepa*), seizing (*grahaṇa*), and pressing (*niṣpīḍana*). Regarding "grasping and rubbing": it is rubbing the front and back of the body.
"Pulling" is drawing [the body] closer to oneself. "Pushing" is thrusting [the body] away behind oneself. "Upward stroking" is from the bottom to the top. "Downward stroking" is...
"Ma" refers to [the act] from top to bottom. "Ju" (lifting) means grasping and lifting upward. "Xia" (lowering) means grasping and causing one to sit down.

"Zhe" (grasping) means grasping and holding the front and back, the breasts and the thighs. "Na" (pressing) means pressing down upon the front and back, the breasts and the thighs. "Zhuoshou" (grasping the hand) refers to...
"Hand" refers to the area from the fingers to the arm. "Grasping the hair": "hair" refers to the hair on the head. "If one touches any part of the body": "touching" means making physical contact;
"parts of the body" refers to the other various limbs and members of the body, such as the shoulders, arms, navel, breasts, thighs, calves, nails, teeth, and so forth.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful attachment, touches a woman or...
If a person touches a bhikṣu with a mind of lustful attachment, when there is no intervening garment, for every instance of contact, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If there is an intervening garment on one side, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense. If both parties have an intervening garment and they touch through the clothing, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
This applies equally if one touches a female deity, nāga, yakṣa, or rākṣasa, or a female animal capable of assuming human form. All such cases are likewise treated.
If one touches a person with two sexual organs, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one touches the body of a male, or touches an animal that cannot transform its form, it is all *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one perceives a female and touches a male body, or perceives a male and touches a female body, it is all a *sthūlātyaya*. If this woman perceives another woman [as a male], [it is likewise].
If other women perceive this woman as such, it is all *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one touches the body of a dead woman whose corpse has not yet decomposed, it is *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If it is half-decomposed or mostly decomposed, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). If a bhikṣu, with a mind of desire, moves the part of the woman’s body upon which she is leaning, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a woman pays homage by grasping his feet and he perceives the pleasure of touch and moves his body, it is *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; otherwise, it is not.

Moving the body [to touch her] constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Striking a woman constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). If, with a lustful mind, one touches robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and so forth, up to touching one's own body, all constitute *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding a human female: if one perceives a human female as such, it is a *saṃghādisesa* (offense entailing suspension); if there is doubt regarding whether she is a human female, it is likewise a *saṃghādisesa*.
Furthermore, if one perceives a non-human female as a human female, or perceives a human female as a non-human female, or if doubt arises in these cases, all constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pārājika*; for the three lower assemblies (*śrāmaṇerī*, *śikṣamāṇā*, and *śrāmaṇera*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if there is contact or touching during the act of giving or receiving; or if one falls to the ground from a stumble and lands upon a woman; or if a woman is carried away by water.
If one rescues those who are being swept away, or those who have fallen into fire or pits, by approaching them with thoughts of compassion;

or if one rescues those who have hanged themselves, consumed poison, or committed suicide—for the sake of providing such relief—one commits no offense even if one does not intentionally experience the sensation of physical contact.

At that time, while the Buddha was wandering among the people, he saw a great mass of fire burning fiercely and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Suppose there were a person who were to grasp that fire..."
He grasped it and kissed it; immediately his skin, flesh, bones, and sinews were burned away and consumed.
Suppose there were another person who took a woman of the four castes, grasped her, and kissed her—of these two matters, which would be considered better? The bhikṣus said:
"To grasp those women and kiss them is what is considered good in the ways of the world; whereas if one grasps fire, it burns the skin and bones until they are completely consumed."
He experienced great agony that was unbearable. The Buddha said: "It would be better to grasp a blazing fire until one's sinews and bones are completely consumed.
Why? Because for this reason, one will not fall into the three evil realms; whereas if one is not a śramaṇa, one will."
Claiming for oneself to be a śramaṇa, one commits offenses even in secret; though internally empty and rotten, one appears outwardly complete and pure.

Such a person does not deserve the offerings of the faithful and will fall into the three evil realms, suffering for a long night. Therefore, one should maintain pure precepts when receiving the offerings of the faithful.
By providing all that is required, one enables the donor to obtain a great reward. This is the purpose for which one has gone forth.

A śramaṇa may also achieve [this] accomplishment. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a woman falls into water and cries out for help, a bhikṣu may grasp her with the perception that she is the ground;

this is not an offense. If he uses bamboo, wood, or rope to pull her out, it is not an offense. If the woman grasps the bhikṣu urgently, the bhikṣu should remain established in right mindfulness. If his mind becomes otherwise, and he grasps her while wearing coarse, thick clothing, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If he grasps her while wearing soft, thin garments, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a woman is being swept away by water, she should be rescued.

Even if lustful thoughts arise, one should simply grasp her at one place and not let go. Once she has reached the shore, one must not intentionally touch her; if one touches her again, one incurs an offense. This applies even to touching a woman depicted in embroidery, painting, or carved in wood.")

*Dukkaṭa*. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If a woman strikes a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu receives it with a mind of lustful delight, it is *dukkaṭa*. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "If a mother comes to embrace him, or if a daughter sits in his lap, or if he touches a woman’s lips with his mouth while on a narrow path—in all these cases, there is no offense.
Regarding the five kinds of animals that may be relied upon for crossing a river: elephants, horses, bulls, water buffaloes, and yaks. One should not rely on a female cow among the animals to cross."
The Third Precept on Haraṣa-vāda (Coarse and Lewd Speech):
If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, utters coarse and lewd speech regarding sexual intercourse to a woman,
for each instance of such coarse and lewd speech uttered, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The commentary states: The dependent origination is the same as before. "Lustful intent" is explained as above. "Woman" refers to one who understands speech regarding good and evil.
"Coarse and vile" refers to that which is base, impure, and contrary to the dharma of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Although all transgressions are termed "evil," this [lust] is specifically the cause and condition for coarse and heavy offenses; it is manifest as something base, impure, and unclean.
Because it will certainly bring about undesirable evil results in the future, it is specifically designated as "coarse and wicked. Regarding "sexual speech":
this refers to speaking of the attractiveness or unattractiveness of another's anus or urinary tract—speech that is associated with sexual desire and is improper.
"Engaging in coarse and wicked sexual speech with a woman" is the general heading; it refers to whatever coarse [speech] is uttered.

"Vile speech regarding sexual desire" is a term for specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the offenses therein, there are eight matters, all of which constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
These are: seeking it oneself, instructing another to seek it, questioning and answering, explaining and teaching, and reviling. As for "seeking it oneself":
a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, speaks to a woman, saying, "Give me your two paths (vagina or anus) to perform such-and-such an act," or he uses other similar words.
Regarding speech associated with sexual desire that instructs another to seek it: if a bhikṣu says to someone, "May the devas protect me;

let us perform such and such an act together," this refers to the questioner asking about the two paths [the anus and the mouth] being used for private intercourse with her husband or another man, and the respondent answering that those two paths were used for private intercourse with her husband. This is the explanation.
"Speaker" is as explained above. "Teacher" refers to instructing those two paths so that the husband and outsiders respect and love them.
"Abuser" refers to insulting and humiliating those two paths. As stated above, if the matter is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for each instance;
if it is not clear and distinct, it is a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one uses a signet ring, a letter, a messenger, or makes gestures to convey [the intent], [it is likewise].

If that woman knows [the truth], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if she does not know, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Excluding the two [sexual] organs, if one speaks of the excellence or defects of other parts, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one speaks toward a female deity, a *nāga*, a *yakṣa*, a *gandharva*, a female *kinnara*, a *mānuṣī*, or a hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*), if she knows [the truth], it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if she does not know, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one speaks toward a female animal that cannot change its form, or toward a male, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, utters coarse and wicked speech toward a woman—perceiving her as such—it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If he utters coarse and wicked speech while suspecting her to be so, or if she is not coarse and wicked but he perceives her as such, or if he entertains doubt, it is in all cases a sthūlātyaya offense. This applies to a human female.
If one perceives a human female as a human female, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If one suspects she is a human female, or perceives her as a non-human female, or if one perceives a non-human female as a human female, or again gives rise to doubt, or if one perceives a female as a male, or a male as a female—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives this woman as another woman, or perceives another woman as this woman, it is always a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If [the offender] is by nature...

To speak coarse and wicked words without a lustful intent constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for a monk; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; for the three lower groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases: when teaching a woman the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);

when this topic arises incidentally while reciting the Vinaya; or when speaking in a dream. [This applies] when intending to say one thing but mistakenly saying another. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a woman speaks vulgar and evil words...")

[The Buddha] said: "If a bhikṣu accepts [an offer] through speech and is pleased in his heart with the matter, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense even if he does not speak of it himself. However, if in a certain region vulgar or evil words are spoken yet are not considered offensive, there is no offense in any such case."
The Fourth Precept on Praising One’s Own Person to Solicit Offerings:
If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, speaks before a woman praising his own person, saying, "Sister, I practice the holy life."
"Those who uphold the precepts with diligence and cultivate wholesome dharmas may offer this method of sexual desire to me;
such an offering is the foremost and supreme. [This constitutes] a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
The commentary states: The setting for this account is the same as before. "Lustful intent" is explained as above.

"In the presence of a woman" means in the presence of a woman who is capable of understanding the meaning of words concerning good and evil. "Praising one's own body" refers to three kinds of self-praise:
first, praising oneself by claiming one’s own body is handsome and one’s complexion is beautiful; second, praising oneself by claiming one’s lineage...
"Caste" refers to the kṣatriya, householder, merchant, or brahmin lineage. "The three" refers to praising one's own cultivated wholesome dharmas.
"O great sister" is the term used to address her. "I practice the holy life" (brahmacarya) describes one's own ability to cultivate pure conduct;
because this practice is the path leading to nirvāṇa, it is called "holy" (brahma).
Regarding practice: one who upholds the precepts with diligence means that their own morality is complete, without deficiency, without breach or leakage, and free from defilement.

Regarding the cultivation and accumulation of wholesome dharmas: this refers to diligently cultivating and accumulating all excellent and sublime dharmas, namely the twelve dhūta virtues, as well as being able to recite and chant, possessing great learning, preaching the Dharma, maintaining the Vinaya, and practicing seated meditation. Through such pure cultivation...
By practicing thus, one’s precepts are perfected. Through the perfection of the precepts, one accomplishes all supreme and wondrous virtues.
The above has clarified the description of his own merits; hereafter, it clarifies the solicitation for offerings.

"One who can offer this method of sexual desire may provide me with an offering"—this clarifies that he is explicitly soliciting an unrighteous offering, distinguishing it from other matters. Such is the offering.
Regarding "the foremost and most excellent offering": this refers to the offering of sexual desire, which is the foremost and most excellent among all offerings.
Regarding the offense therein: if one praises one's own body before a woman, it constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
For every distinct instance of praising the body that is clearly articulated, there is a separate *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if the speech is not clearly articulated, there is no offense.

These constitute grave offenses (sthūlātyaya). If one employs hand gestures, writes a letter, dispatches a messenger, or displays signs such that the other person understands [the intent], all result in a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
if the other person does not understand, it is a grave offense. To seek offerings from any location other than the two [proper] passages constitutes a sthūlātyaya.

If one speaks clearly to a female deity, a female spirit, a female ghost, or a female animal capable of changing form, it constitutes a coarse offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if not clearly, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
To praise [one's own body] before a male human or an animal constitutes a transgression (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding a human female, if one perceives her as a non-human female, [the same applies].
Regarding doubts and the lightness or heaviness of the offenses for the other four assemblies, these are all as explained in the preceding precepts. As for those who do not commit an offense:
if one says, "This bhikṣu is virtuous and good; you should honor him with acts of loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind";

or if, when explaining the Vinaya, the words are similar or even mistaken (as in the case of the *kṣatriya* mentioned in the explanation of the precept on entering a royal palace among the ninety matters).
The Fifth Precept on Matchmaking:
If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for either side, conveying the intentions of a man to a woman or the intentions of a woman to a man—
whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit relations— even for a mere moment, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The commentary states: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Kāla who was well-versed in worldly affairs and acted as a matchmaker for others.
When the men and women he paired off with found a marriage that suited their wishes, they would joyfully provide him with offerings and praise;
however, when those they wedded did not find satisfaction, they would resent and revile him. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.

After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he established the precept: "Regarding those who act as go-betweens for both sides, this refers to a bhikṣu acting as a messenger for men and women, going back and forth to arrange marriages.

'Conveying the man's intent to the woman' and 'conveying the woman's intent to the man' means taking the intentions of both the man and the woman and communicating them to one another. Whether it be for the sake of establishing a wife or..."
"Adulterous intercourse" refers to becoming a wife, which constitutes being a wife for the duration of one's life. "Secret intercourse" refers to temporarily engaging in sexual union with another.
The phrase "even for a mere moment" indicates that it is not for a long duration; [it may last] for a single day and night.
There are thirty *muhūrtas* [in a day]. Even causing them to meet for the duration of a single *muhūrta* incurs the fundamental offense.
One who goes back and forth between the two parties to arrange a marriage is the messenger; one who conveys the intentions of the man and woman to one another is the principal agent.
This concerns the matter of arranging a marriage for a wife or engaging in illicit intercourse. As for the time frame, it extends even to a mere moment.
What, then, are the characteristics of an offense in this context? Suppose that man and woman dispatch a bhikṣu as a messenger, saying: "Act as our agent and take a wife for me."

If she says, "I have had a private liaison with you," or "for a moment," or "for the duration of a single thought-instant," and the bhikṣu accepts her words, goes himself to speak to her, and having accepted her words, returns to report them, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. This is how it should be understood: when a bhikṣu accepts such words.
One goes to inquire and returns with a report. Among these three methods, one may act as both the first and second [parties] oneself while dispatching a messenger for the third;
or act as the first and third oneself while dispatching a messenger for the second; or act as the first and last oneself while having another perform the middle part.

In all such cases, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. There are four ways by which these constitute matchmaking: first, speech; second, writing; third, sign language (finger-seals); and fourth, indicative gestures.

By employing these four matters within those three cases of "going and returning" (*yāna-āgamana*), one may act with a single matter to constitute all three, or use two or three matters in combination.
If one goes oneself, or sends a messenger to go and return, such that the other person understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If they do not understand, it is a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*); within those three cases, if two [of the four matters] are employed, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one performs a single act of matchmaking, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). According to the extent of the matchmaking—whether it be many or few instances—if the matter is clearly understood, each instance constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).

If it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). This applies even if one matches a woman among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas, or a female animal capable of transforming its form.
Regarding the two gateways and the two organs, all constitute grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*). Acting as a matchmaker for men or animals constitutes an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*).

If it is a human female and one perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If there is doubt regarding her being a human female, or if one perceives her as a non-human female, or if she is a non-human female and one perceives her as such, or if there is doubt regarding this, all constitute offenses of transgression (*sthūlātyaya*). If one carries another's letter and does not examine it, or if one acts on its behalf...
If one uses robes for other purposes or as a tool, it is entirely an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). A *bhikṣuṇī* commits the same offense; for the three lower assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense in the following cases: for the sake of reconciling those who are separated; for reconciling a husband and wife who are quarreling; for causing [the offender] to repent; or for the sake of one's parents who are ill.

Furthermore, if one is imprisoned in jail, or for the sake of a faithful upāsaka who is ill, or for the sake of the Three Jewels, a stūpa, or a sick bhikṣu, it is not an offense to read letters and carry them [to these persons]. These aforementioned five precepts all pertain to matters of desire (*kāma*).
Although the first precept does not involve a female object, one still obtains pleasure; the next two precepts arise through body and speech.
To experience sensual pleasure is the fourth precept. To seek sensual pleasure through skillful means is the fifth precept.

To live by taking advantage of the sensual pleasures of others is [the sixth]. (The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If parents are quarreling and the father sends the mother back to her own home, but later feels regret and says to the bhikṣu, 'I am old and have no one to attend to me morning or evening;

you may tell your mother to return and care for me,' and the bhikṣu accepts this mission and tells the mother to return and report to the father, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a man has a multitude... )

If a man has many wives, some of whom he favors and others he does not, and a bhikṣu says to him, "You should look after them all equally and strive to treat them with impartiality," and he replies, "I shall do as my teacher instructs," the bhikṣu incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a husband and wife are quarreling and the bhikṣu encourages them to reconcile, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. However, if the couple is discordant and there is a deficiency in matters concerning the Buddha or the Saṃgha, or for the sake of performing meritorious acts, encouraging their reconciliation is without fault. If he encourages a wife to return early to her husband’s home, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If two bhikṣus—one having a son and the other having a daughter—arrange their own marriages for them, both incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If a person keeps many horses but none of good breeding, and he asks a bhikṣu to say to a certain family, "They have fine breeding horses; [procure one] for me... [the bhikṣu incurs an offense].

To seek [a marriage]. If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between and succeeds in finding one, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Śīla-nidāna-sūtra* states: To bring together the male and female of livestock constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: If one says, "Why do you not seek a wife? and the intent is to act as a matchmaker, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense.

If one further says, "There is a daughter in that family; why do you not seek her? with the intent to act as a matchmaker, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one says, "Why does this man not enter the house [of his bride]? or "Why does this woman not serve her mother-in-law?

or "Why does this man not live in a separate household?"—any such speech that corresponds even slightly to the business of matchmaking constitutes an *dukkaṭa* offense. If a disciple says to a teacher, "I wish to act as a go-between for another," and the teacher gives silent consent, the teacher incurs a grave offense. Why?

Therefore, these four precepts follow this sequence. Generally, when a man does not yet know a woman's intentions, he first takes her hand to test her feelings. If she consents, he next grasps her arm, and so on, gradually touching other parts down to her throat and abdomen.

If she does not grant permission, one should speak vulgar words to entice her feelings; these two matters are for the purpose of dealing with a woman who lacks faith. If she is a woman of faith and reverence, knowing that she delights in merit, one should employ various virtuous words to encourage her in discussion.
These three cases concern one’s own defiled desire; the next one concerns others, acting as a matchmaker for men and women out of a motive for seeking food and clothing (to bring them together).
*The Commentary on the Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, Fascicle Two:
Phonetic Glossary. *Yi* (杙): Pronounced *yì*. A wooden peg; a stake. *Sai* (塞): Pronounced *sài*. To block; a barrier; a border. It means to separate or to be at the edge of a boundary.
The upper character of *xiáng* (桁) is pronounced *háng*. Shackles that clamp the feet and neck are both called *xiáng*. The lower character is pronounced *qiáng* with a departing tone;
it refers to setting up a trap on the road.
The two forms refer to a person with two sexual organs—that is, one body possessing both male and female organs.
The Fourth Part of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra with Commentary, Scroll Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Jiqi. ○ The Sixth Precept:
Regarding the Construction of Excessively Large Private Dwellings.
If a bhikṣu seeks to build a house for himself, without a patron and for his own use, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements. Regarding these measurements:
the length shall be twelve spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the internal width seven spans. He must then have other bhikṣus point out the location.
That bhikṣu should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
If a bhikṣu builds a hut for himself where there are difficulties or obstructions, without a patron and for his own sake, and does not have another bhikṣu designate the site—
If one constructs it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, he permitted the bhikṣus to construct private dwellings.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu from the country of Āṭavī who, having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, privately constructed a large dwelling.

It required immense labor and he constantly went about begging for materials; consequently, the householders grew weary of him and avoided him. There was another bhikṣu who wished to build a dwelling and cut down a tree himself;
the tree deity, losing its support, went to inform the World-Honored One. At that time, Mahākāśyapa arrived at the city of Āṭavī. All...
The lay devotees saw them from afar and each fled. Kāśyapa questioned them and learned the reason for their departure, reporting the matter in full to the Buddha.

After the Buddha had rebuked those bhikṣus, he established a precept: "One who seeks to build a house for oneself" means one who personally solicits materials such as timber, as well as craftsmen and the like, to build a house—either building it oneself or having others build it—and which has no owner.
This means that there is no donor, and one seeks alms by begging for oneself. "For oneself" means for one's own person, not for the sake of the Saṃgha.
"One should construct according to the proper measure" means constructing in accordance with the measurements prescribed by the Buddha;
thus, one avoids the fault of excessive labor and the hardship of being too small or cramped. Regarding these measurements, they specifically refer to twelve spans of seven [finger-breadths].
Regarding the measurement by hand: "Twelve *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha in length" refers to the length, meaning the depth of the building.
One *vitasti* of the Buddha is equivalent to three *vitasti* of an ordinary person (*vitasti* is pronounced *zhai*; it means to stretch out; that is, to extend the fingers).
"Seven *vitasti* in internal width" refers to the horizontal width inside the building. "One should assign the location using the fingers of a *bhikṣu*" and so forth.
"Monks" refers to the Saṃgha, or alternatively, to individuals specifically appointed [for this purpose]. "Pointing out" (uddiś-) means to indicate; "granting" (pradā-) means to bestow.
That monk who is constructing the dwelling should first personally inspect a site that is free from obstacles and hindrances.

Having done so, he should go to his original residence and request from the Saṃgha the inspection and pointing out of the location. He should make this request as follows, declaring: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, [Name],..."

"Monks, a monk is building a dwelling for himself; it has no owner and is intended for his own use. He now requests from the Saṃgha that a site free from difficulties and obstructions be assigned to him.
After he has spoken thus three times, the Saṃgha should examine whether this monk is trustworthy or not. If he is trustworthy...
One should then grant permission for its construction. If [the person] is not to be trusted, the Saṃgha should go to that place to inspect it.
If the Saṃgha does not go, one or two or three monks who are trustworthy within the Saṃgha should be dispatched to that place to inspect it.
If there are obstacles or hindrances, they should not grant permission. Since there are neither obstacles nor hindrances, the Saṃgha should grant permission for its construction.
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is personally soliciting materials to build a dwelling for himself;
it has no owner and is for his own use. He now requests from the Saṃgha the assignment of a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
