Therefore, one may keep a dog according to one's convenience). One should not ride elephants, horses, carriages, palanquins, or litters, nor carry swords or blades.

Those who are old or infirm should ride in hand-pulled carts or be carried by men; however, for the sake of avoiding danger, riding elephants or horses is permitted (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śūtra* states:

"If a bhikṣu, upon being requested, gives various items to kings, ministers, elders, or householders—whether for the sake of the Three Jewels or for his own benefit—it is called 'defiling another's family. Why is this? For those who have left the household life, there is [no such thing as...]"

One should be free from desire, maintain purity through self-restraint, and take the cultivation of the Path as one's primary concern. If one engages in the exchange of messengers with worldly people, it will disrupt and waste one’s correct practice; this is not appropriate for those who have left the household life.

Furthermore, to give gifts to laypeople (śrāmaṇera/brāhmaṇa) destroys the sincere and impartial goodwill of the donor. Those who receive the gift will feel joy, love, and respect, whereas those who do not receive it—regardless of whether they are sages or saints—will lack such feelings of love and respect.

This causes one to lose the profound merit and benefit intended for the former person. Moreover, it subverts and confuses the Buddha-Dharma. Generally, laypeople should provide offerings to those who have left the household life, yet here the monastics instead provide offerings to laypeople. Above, this loses the heart of the Sages; below, it confuses the True Dharma. Generally, laypeople constantly seek the Triple Gem as their field of pure merit, [and thus] sacrifice...

To sacrifice one's own flesh and blood for the sake of planting roots of goodness, yet because of the circumstances of giving to those who have left the household life, instead give rise to expectations toward such renunciants, thereby destroying the pure faith and respect of others and losing all the various offerings due to renunciants—if one were to give even a small amount of goods to a layperson and, despite that, erect a stupa made of the seven precious jewels with all manner of adornments, it would not equal sitting in quietude and purely upholding the precepts; this is truly making an offering to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

If one uses even a small amount of property to give as a gift to laypeople—even if it enables the construction of a vihāra as magnificent as Jetavana—it is not as good as sitting in quietude and purely observing the precepts; this is the purest form of making offerings to the Triple Gem.

If one uses a small amount of property to give as a gift to laypeople—were one to fully provide the four requisites to all the noble ones throughout Jambudvīpa—it is not as good as sitting in quietude and purely observing the precepts; this is the purest way of making offerings to all the noble ones.

If there are those with great power who wish to destroy stūpas or damage images, and they can be saved only through gifts, one should sell the land of the stūpa, its flowers, fruits, or whatever money the stūpa possesses, or acquire goods through other means, managing the situation as appropriate. If there are those with great power who wish to cause disruption and chaos within the Saṃgha...

Reduction. Regarding whatever items exist within the *saṃghika* (monastic) lands, they may be sold for coinage according to circumstances. Whether it be the regular monastic year (*saṃvatsara*) or the face-to-face year (*mukha-dvāra-saṃvatsara*), if there are those with great power who wish to effect a reduction, one should adjust it according to the produce that can be yielded from that land.

If one’s parents are fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), then providing them with offerings is permitted. If one is a laborer working for the *saṃghika* lands, then [the produce] should be given to him. If a donor wishes to provide food for the Saṃgha and desires to know the proper rules, this too should be granted. Furthermore, out of compassion, all who are orphaned, destitute, or begging should be given [alms].

Moreover, regarding all women—mothers, daughters, or sisters—it is not permitted to sit together on the same bed or mat, regardless of whether they are kin or strangers, because it would destroy one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). 4.

If one uses incense to fumigate the robes of the assembly, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*. Because women possess deep-seated defiled attachment, it is forbidden to allow elephants to fight, or even for chickens to fight.

If parents have passed away, weeping is entirely forbidden; if the fourfold assembly weeps, they incur a *dukkaṭa*, and a bhikṣuṇī incurs a *pāyattika*. This is because their hearts of affectionate attachment are so deep. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If a donor invites a bhikṣu to accompany them to a funeral, he must not go.

However, if a bhikṣu reflects to himself, 'I shall go to observe the burial and practice the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā*), and by means of this, I may perhaps attain the fruits of the Path,' then going in such a manner is without fault. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu should not offer worship at the shrines of various celestial deities."

Furthermore, one must not bully others or destroy their images. One should not circumambulate a temple to the right. If, however, one happens to pass by on the road and circumambulates to the right, one should recite a noble *gāthā* and clear one’s throat or snap one’s fingers to alert them.

Moreover, a bhikṣu should not sell medicine. If he is skilled in medical formulas, he should administer medicine according to the illness out of a heart of compassion. If he receives payment for giving medicine, or accepts employment as a hired laborer, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

Once various types of people have gone forth, they should not suddenly display their former arts and crafts, nor should they keep tools for such crafts. If he was previously a physician, he is permitted to keep a needle case and a pouch for holding knives. If he was previously a scribe, he is permitted to keep an ink bottle.
Thirteenth: The Precept on Not Abandoning a Malicious Disposition.

If a bhikṣu is of a malicious disposition and refuses to accept the words of others, and after the bhikṣus have admonished him in accordance with the Dharma regarding the rules of training, he still does not comply.
He himself does not accept admonitory speech, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me of what is good or bad;
nor shall I speak to the venerable sirs of what is good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist; do not admonish me. Other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not yourself refuse to accept admonitory speech. Venerable sir, you ought yourself..."
One should accept words of admonition. Venerable sirs, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s disciples prospers, admonishing one another, instructing one another, and confessing to one another.
When a bhikṣu is thus being admonished, if he persists and does not relinquish his position, that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times to relinquish it.
The case: Up to three admonitions; if he relinquishes it, it is well. If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The commentary says: When the Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī, in the garden of the householder Sunakṣatra, at that time the Venerable Bhikṣu Chanda was of evil character and would not accept the words of others.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to act toward him.
The *karmavācanā* of formal admonition was established as a precept for those of "evil nature who do not accept the words of others.

This refers to those whose innate disposition is coarse and violent, such that they do not receive the virtuous instructions and exhortations of other bhikṣus. "Within the disciplinary laws" refers to the seven classes of offenses:
first, the *pārājika*; second, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, the *pāyattika*; fourth, the *pratideśanīya*; fifth, the *sthūlātyaya*; [sixth, the *dukkaṭa*; seventh, the *dubbhāsita*].

"Rañca. (1) Six *duṣkṛta* offenses; (2) seven instances of improper speech. When he is thus admonished and instructed according to this Dharma and Vinaya, he stubbornly maintains his evil disposition and does not accept the words of others.
"The various bhikṣus" refers to those bhikṣus who uphold the True Dharma.
"Admonishing according to the Dharma" means exhorting and admonishing in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.

"One who does not accept admonitory speech" refers to one who, when others instruct them according to the Dharma through the Vinaya, obstinately refuses their words and acts as if they are not fit to be spoken with.
"Venerable sirs, do not speak to me of what is good or bad" means that regarding beneficial matters, there is no need for exhortation; and regarding non-beneficial matters, [do not speak].

To obstruct one another is likewise a word born of arrogance. When I say, "I shall not speak of the good or evil of these venerable ones," it is intended to demonstrate that I am free from involvement with others, and that others likewise should not involve me in their affairs.

All of these are words for forbidding others from offering admonition. "Cease for now" means to preemptively forbid others from speaking words they have not yet uttered, so that they shall not speak them.
"Do not admonish me" refers to one's own mind being unable to endure it, further manifesting this refusal to accept the counsel.
"That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu" means that one should further admonish and exhort him in accordance with the Dharma.
"One should not oneself refuse to accept admonition" is a word of exhortation. "One should oneself accept admonition" is a word of instruction.
"Venerable sir, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma" is a word of encouragement;
that is to say, one should properly instruct and admonish one another by means of the Dharma and the Vinaya. Thus [said] the Buddha.
Regarding the statement that "the assembly of disciples attains increase," this clearly demonstrates the benefit gained through mutual admonition.
Because they admonish one another, the Buddha’s disciples attain the growth of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). Because of this growth, the Buddha-Dharma flourishes.

Because it flourishes, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) endures for a long time. As for the phrase "mutually admonishing and instructing one another with repentance," this indicates an even greater degree of earnestness.
This further clarifies the mutual admonition and exhortation. "Admonition" (*codanā*) means to prevent what is unbeneficial. "Exhortation" (*avavāda*) means to cause one to obtain wholesome benefit.

"Repentance" (*pratikarman*) means to reform the past and cultivate the future. When such admonition is given and [the monk] stubbornly persists without relinquishing his position, it means that when this bhikṣu receives such individual admonition from others, he obstinately clings to his evil nature and does not change his ways. This is "evil" (*pāpaka*).
"By nature I will not accept the words of others, nor will I even allow myself to be admonished"—this is the origin of the offense.

"Do not personally refuse to accept admonition," and so on, up to "confessing through mutual succession"—these are the words of individual admonition. "Three admonitions" refers to the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-trikarman*) within the Saṃgha.
"Does not relinquish" is the textual formula for the formal establishment of the offense. Regarding the gravity of the characteristics of the offense herein:
As for the other four assemblies, their offenses, transgressions, and non-transgressions are all identical to those of the preceding precept.
If one is being reproached and admonished by an ignorant person, one should say to them: "The conduct of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya is also like this;
you should further study, inquire, and recite the sūtras. At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I shall now speak to you of eight [precepts]."
There are eight kinds of evil horses and eight kinds of evil persons. What are these eight?

There may be an evil horse to which one applies the bridle and whip, intending to make it go, yet it instead bucks and stumbles and will not move; or it leans sideways against both shafts and does not advance;
or it rears and falls to the ground, injuring its knees and breaking the shafts or the yoke; or it even walks backward.
They do not advance; or they stray onto wrong paths, breaking the wheels and snapping the axles;
or they show no regard for the driver, nor do they fear the whip, using their skill to kick out from under the bit and charging headlong, impossible to restrain;
or they stand on two legs and foam at the mouth, or they crouch backward and lie down. These are the eight kinds of evil horses. What are the eight kinds of evil persons? There may be a bhikṣu who...
When those [other monks] cite charges based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected, that bhikṣu says, "I do not recall; I do not recall.
Like a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip have been given, yet it continues to resist and stumble instead of moving forward;

or he neither speaks of having committed an offense nor speaks of not having committed one, remaining silent. Like that wicked horse leaning against both shafts of the carriage, it does not advance. Or...
"You yourself, Venerable One, have also committed this offense. How can you remove the offenses of others?

You are like that ill-bred horse which, reeling and falling to the ground, wounds its knees and breaks its harness. Or you say, 'Venerable One, you are yourself deluded and still require instruction from others;
yet you wish to instruct me. Like that ill-bred horse, you instead retreat backward rather than moving forward, or you answer by speaking of other matters."
He gives rise to anger, like a wicked horse that charges down a wrong path, breaking wheels and snapping axles;

or he shows no fear of the Saṃgha, nor does he fear transgression, refusing to heed the words of those who charge him with his faults. He then seizes his sitting mat, places it upon his shoulder, and departs;
he cannot be rebuked or restrained, just as that wicked horse fears neither its driver nor its whip, but merely bites at the bit.
They bolt about, uncontrollable; or they snatch the robes from the left while among the monks, raising their hands and speaking loudly:
"Is this how you intend to instruct me? They are like those wicked horses that stand on two legs and spit foam.
Or they say: "Elder, you have not even given me robes, bowl, bedding, or medicine; why then do you instruct me? Thereupon, they immediately abandon the precepts.
Taking the lower path, he goes to where the bhikṣu is and speaks thus: "I have abandoned the holy life; is it not well with you?
Like that wicked horse, he crouches and lies down again. These are the eight kinds of evil persons, who are like those eight kinds of evil horses.
I have fully explained the disciples who should be treated with compassion. You should dwell in empty places, at the foot of trees...
"Go! Practice meditative concentration; do not be negligent, lest you later fall into regret. This is my instruction and admonition.
(The aforementioned texts for the various *karmavācanā* are fully recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Karmavācanā-mūla*).
△ Finally, the formal conclusion and inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine offenses that are committed at once, and four that require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas and knowingly conceals it, he should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*."
Having completed the *parivāsa* probation, he is granted the six-night *mānatva*.
Once the *mānatva* has been performed, there remains the formal rehabilitation (*ābṛhaṇa*), which must be carried out before an assembly of twenty monks.
If even one person is missing and the assembly does not number twenty, the rehabilitation of this bhikṣu’s offense cannot be accomplished; nor can the bhikṣus [attain their own purity].
"Ha! This is the proper time. Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? (Ask three times.
Venerable ones, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus I shall hold it to be so."
The commentary states: "That which I have already explained" refers to the completion of the presentation of the matters I have spoken.

This is intended to allow the audience to deliberate further upon those offenses before taking a brief rest. Regarding "the first offense of the nine precepts": this refers to the aforementioned nine precepts, wherein the fundamental offense is incurred at the very moment the act is committed;
it does not require repeated admonition and failure to desist before the offense is fully established. Four... [and so forth].
"The three admonitions" refers to the latter four precepts; only after the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tri-karman*) has been completed does the offense accrue.
"To commit any one of the rules" means to transgress any one among the thirteen matters.
"Knowing yet concealing" means that although the mind clearly recognizes the matter one has committed, one intentionally hides it and does not disclose it to others.
"One who should be given *pārivāsika* by force": "force" means against one's will. *Pārivāsika* is translated here as "separate residence" (*biezhu*).
This refers to the rule that the Sangha must grant a period of separate residence according to the number of days the offense was concealed.
"Having completed the *pārivāsika*" means that after concealing the offense for a certain number of days, one must undergo that same number of days of separate residence.
In the interim, one must not commit the offense again; thus the practice according to the Dharma is completed. Regarding the granting of the *mānatva* for six nights as an enhancement:

*mānatva* here means "mental joy" (*manas-tuṣṭi*). This refers to the practice of performing the *parivāsa* (probation) to its conclusion, after which one is further granted the practice of mental joy for six nights.
While practicing this, the offense becomes purified, one's own mind rejoices, and it also causes the community...
The Saṃgha rejoiced. Knowing that this person had repented through this means and would no longer give rise to afflictions again, they became a pure person;
thus, the Saṃgha granted him absolution from his offense. If he had not concealed it, he need not undergo the *parivāsa* (probation);
rather, he simply performs these six nights of *mānāpya* (reconciliation) with a joyful mind. Since the days include the nights, it is called "six nights. He then practices the *mānāpya*.

"Completed" means that the six-night practice has been finished according to the Dharma, and the method was not violated during the interval. Regarding "the remaining matters such as the removal of the offense":

this refers to the fact that although one has performed the method for six nights—which is the expedient means for purifying the offense—there still remains the matter of the formal removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).
This should be performed before a community of twenty bhikṣus; if there are fewer than that, the ritual procedure is not valid.
If [the rite] is completed, that offense will not be removed, and the Saṃgha will incur the fault of practicing what is contrary to the Dharma.
Since the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, deeply understands the karmic nature of sentient beings, twenty pure monks are required for the offense to be extinguished; it cannot be liberated otherwise.

It is like a person who has been harmed by another yet still possesses a throat; unless they receive excellent medicine and a skilled physician who applies even a small amount of effort, [they will not survive].
It is impossible for them to live [in purity]. This case is also like that: it is not that one does not rely on the Dharma, nor is it that there is no pure Saṃgha;
yet, with only a small assembly and few conditions, for the pure precepts to arise again—this has no basis in reality.
"This is the time" means that this is the method for emerging from the offense. The rest of the text is explained as above. Regarding the ritual procedure herein: if a bhikṣu...

Regarding one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it: in accordance with the number of days it was concealed, they should be granted the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* for treatment.
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, perform the proper deportment by bowing at the feet of the monks, join his palms, and kneel on his right knee, declaring:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it for [X] days. [The procedure] should follow the years of concealment."

[State] the length of days and months as appropriate: "I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed a certain Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. Having concealed it for [a certain number of] days, I now request from the Saṃgha the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā*.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, Bhikṣu [Name], the *karmavācanā* for [a certain number of] days of *parivāsa*.
Thus he should say three times. The Saṃgha should grant it by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. If...
If one commits another offense while practicing *parivāsa*, one should request from the Saṃgha the practice of *mūlaparivāsa* (the re-initiation of the period of concealment).

The Saṃgha should grant this by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. (This is the case where a new offense is combined with an old offense; it is called the "method for breaking the concealment. If the method is not broken, then once the *parivāsa* is completed, one simply requests the six-night *mānatva*).
When the *parivāsa* is finished, one should request from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*. The Saṃgha should [grant it] by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is granted. Once the six-night penance has been completed, one should request absolution from the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha should grant absolution through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations).
If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense without concealment, one should request the six-night *mānāpya* (probation) from the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha should grant it through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
While undergoing the *mānāpya*, if one commits a further offense, one should request a *mānāpya* with *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (probation for the days spent in concealment); the Saṃgha [should grant it].

One should grant it by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (this refers to the method of combined treatment according to the new and old codes; this is called the "method of breaking the *mānatva*"). Once the *pārivāsika* (probation) has been performed, one should then carry out the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the original status).
One should request absolution from the offense. The Saṃgha should grant it through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).

If there are numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, whether concealed for one night or up to ten nights, it is permitted to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the concealment of those numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses for ten nights (having performed this according to the Dharma, one subsequently grants *mānāpya* and absolution from the offense). If one has committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses...
Regarding the offenses: if both are concealed; or if one is remembered and the other is not; or if there is doubt regarding one and no doubt regarding the other;

or if one is recognized and the other is not; or if when requesting the period of concealment (*paryuṣaṇā*), one is mentioned and the other is not—[the procedure] should follow what has been remembered.

If one has recognized, spoken of, and has no doubt regarding the offense, yet is granted the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* (act of concealment), and later remembers, recognizes, speaks of it again, and has no doubt, one should grant the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* according to the offense committed.

This applies likewise if one concealed it for two months but remembers it for one month and does not remember the other month, or even if one spoke of it for one month and did not speak of the other month. If a bhikṣu commits [an offense]...

Regarding the two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: [if a monk] leaves the monastic life (*pravrajyā*), and having left it, returns to receive the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), there may be cases where both [offenses] were concealed before and after [the interruption], or where the first was concealed and the second confessed, or where the first was confessed and the second concealed.

In such cases, one should grant the *parivāsa* (probation) ritual according to the number of days the offenses were concealed. Alternatively, if both were confessed before and after [the interruption], one should immediately grant the *mānāpya* (penance). "Before" refers to the period prior to leaving the monastic life.

At the time of the path (referring to the later time of receiving the full precepts), there may be cases where one previously concealed one offense but did not conceal another, yet later both are concealed;
or where that which was previously concealed is subsequently concealed again, while that which was previously confessed is also subsequently confessed;

or where that which was previously concealed is subsequently confessed, while that which was previously confessed is then concealed; or where one previously concealed one and confessed one, yet later both are confessed. As it is said:

In all such cases, one should grant the *paryuṣaṇā-karman* (the rite of concealment) according to what has been concealed. Once the period of concealment has been completed, both [the preceptor and the disciple] should then be granted *abhiprīti* (reconciliation).
This applies whether one remembers [the offense] and the other does not, one suspects it and the other does not, or one recognizes it and the other does not.
Regarding "one confessed" and "one not confessed," each is treated as above—either one concealed or one unconcealed—forming four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).

Together there are twenty permutations. This applies likewise when practicing the *parivāsa* (probation), when the *parivāsa* is completed, when practicing the *mānāpya* (rehabilitation), and when the *mānāpya* is completed;

each of these also forms twenty permutations (adding the subsequent cases of one concealed and one unconcealed, there are a total of one hundred permutations). Having become a *śrāmaṇera*, one returns to receive the full [ordination].

The same applies to the hundred phrases regarding the *śīla* (precepts). Regarding those who are insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by pain; those who have not been charged for not seeing their offenses; those who have not been charged for not confessing their offenses;
and those who have not been charged for not relinquishing evil views—each of these has one hundred phrases (totaling eight hundred phrases).

Or, if one abandons the path while practicing *praticchādana* (concealment), and later returns to receive the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*), they should subsequently continue the concealment from the previous day. Or, if one should be subjected to the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status), that person abandons [the practice].

[If one] goes forth from the path (after which one should be subjected to *mūlāpakarṣa*), or if one has completed the period of concealment (*parivāsa*) and then goes forth from the path (after which one should be granted *ābhimānika*), or if one goes forth from the path while practicing *ābhimānika* (after which one should continue the counting of days), or if one has completed the practice of *ābhimānika* and then goes forth from the path (after which one should be granted *āpattivyutthāna*).

The same fivefold formulation applies to those who become *śrāmaṇeras* up to those who are suspended for not relinquishing evil views. [This continues] from "going forth from the path while practicing *parivāsa*" until this point.

[There are forty phrases. If there is a bhikṣu who commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense—namely, one that constitutes a *pārājika* [if concealed] or one that constitutes a *pāyattika*, even down to a *duṣkṛta*—and he conceals it, this is considered "not concealing" [in the sense of being a minor offense].
He should be instructed to perform a *duṣkṛta* confession, after which he should be granted *mānāpya*.
Or, if there is one who commits a *pāyattika* offense, such as one that constitutes a *pārājika* offense and so forth, and he conceals it...

Regarding concealment (*saṃvara*): in all cases, one must first be instructed to perform the confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense, and subsequently perform the formal confession for the primary offense according to the Dharma.

If one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it with the intention of concealing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, after instructing them to perform the confession for the *duṣkṛta*, one shall grant them the *parivāsa* (concealment) *karmavācanā*.

If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, whether one does not remember the number of offenses committed nor the number of days, or remembers the number of offenses but not the number of days, in all such cases, one should be granted concealment (*paryuṣita*) for the period from the time of the offense until the present.
If one remembers the number of days but not the number of offenses, one should grant concealment according to the number of days.
The same applies whether there is doubt or no doubt, and whether the offense is recognized or not. If a bhikṣu [approaches] the Saṃgha...
When one requests to undergo *mānāpya* (probation) but commits a further offense during that same day and conceals it, the Saṃgha should say to him:

"You must undergo *mānāpya* once more. If he has undergone *mānāpya* for one night, or even up to six nights, and commits a further offense during that interval which he conceals, he should be granted *mānāpya* again.
Subsequently, he should be granted the *mūlāpakarṣa* (renewal from the beginning), and only then should he be rehabilitated.

Regarding the offense: when a bhikṣu conceals his own offense, up until the point of its purification (*āpattivyutthāna*), they must not perform the formal act of concealment (*parivāsa-karman*) or the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning) against one another. Purification requires a quorum of twenty persons.

For a bhikṣu practicing concealment, there are eight matters that cause the loss of a night (*rātriparihāṇi*), for which he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*): first, going to another monastery without informing them; second, [meeting] a visiting bhikṣu...
1. Not informing [the resident monks] when arriving; 2. Going outside on account of some business without informing them; 3.

Walking slowly within the monastery grounds without informing them; 4. Not sending a messenger to inform them when ill; 5. Two or three people staying together in one room (one should instead stay separately in a small hut);
6. Staying where there are no other bhikṣus; 7. Not informing them at the time of the fortnightly *poṣadha* confession; 8. The time for making the announcement (*ārocana*).

Regarding these thirty matters, the procedures for relinquishing property, confession, and *karman* are all placed after the concluding text. If he does not return it, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If there is...

If someone instructs one not to return [an item], it is an *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies equally if one makes a formal gift (*śuddha-dāna*), sends it to another person, makes it into the three robes (*tricīvara*), makes it into miscellaneous minor garments, intentionally destroys it, burns it, makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined;

in all such cases, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, the offense is the same. For the three lower groups of disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if [the instruction] is not followed.

Within ten days, one may perform a formal act of purification (*śuddhika-dāna*). If the robe is given away to another, stolen by a thief, lost, burnt, washed away, or if one perceives it as no longer pure, and thus does not perform the purification or give it away, there is no offense.

If the person to whom the robe was entrusted dies, goes far away, leaves the monastic life, is taken away by a thief, or is harmed by wild beasts, and so forth—if in such cases one does not perform the purification, there is no offense. (The character *cháng* [長] is pronounced with a departing tone; it means "the rest.")

Furthermore, the *Mātṛkā-vinaya-śāstra* states: "How does one obtain a long robe (*atireka-cīvara*)? It means that if it has entered the hand, or is upon the knee, or upon the shoulder, one forms the thought: 'This is my robe. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If two people share an object and have not yet divided it..."

There is no offense. However, once the portion has been divided, if one does not perform the ritual of purification (*pariṣkāra*), there is an offense after ten days have passed. If a donor invites a sick bhikṣu for a meal and also offers robes, and that bhikṣu entrusts someone else to fetch his share of the robes, the person holding the robes may delay giving them to him for a long time without incurring an offense.

There is no offense. If one hears that another has sent clothing but has not yet received it, there is no offense even if a long time passes. If one has had clothing woven for another, and although the weaving is finished, the other does not give it for a long time, there is no offense. If one has purchased clothing, even if the price has been settled, there is no offense if it has not yet been received.

If one seeks goods for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha or the Sangha, and they are gathered in one place, there is no offense even if a long time passes before they are used. If one travels through a dangerous place and leaves clothing behind before departing, there is an offense if one retrieves it after ten days have passed;

the same offense applies if someone else takes it and gives it back. If one is pursued by bandits and abandons the clothing to flee, and someone brings it back after ten days have elapsed, there is no fault. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Sometimes a donor says, 'This is my property; you should use it.'"

Even if one does not perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), there is no offense in using it. This applies equally to items belonging to oneself that have been entrusted to another, or to cases where one has not yet formed the intention that they are "obtained. There is no offense in these instances. Regarding the five-day period for obtaining robes: if one becomes insane on the very day the robe is obtained, the five-day limit is extended once the mind returns to its normal state.

Other points regarding what is permissible or prohibited should be considered according to the specific circumstances. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one obtains a robe on the first day and discards it on the second, and continues in this manner until obtaining a robe on the ninth day and discarding it on the tenth—yet the robe obtained on the tenth day is neither discarded nor formally accepted [as one's own]..."

If one does not perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), then upon reaching the eleventh day at the conclusion of the period, there is an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). This means that while all the robes obtained during the first nine days are forfeited through purification, the single robe obtained on the tenth day constitutes an offense of forfeiture because it is connected to the preceding sequence of causes and conditions.

If one obtains a robe on the first day and forfeits it on the first day, and obtains another robe on the second day—because these two days' acquisitions are not continuous—one may subsequently obtain robes for ten more days in succession.

If one obtains a robe on the first day, forfeits it on the second day, and does not obtain another robe on the second day, but obtains a robe on the third day, then these three days' acquisitions may likewise continue in succession until the tenth day, provided they are not separated by a break in continuity. If a bhikṣu has already forfeited his robe and repented for the offense, yet his intention to seek further robes remains continuous and uninterrupted, and he should [seek them] again...

If one obtains cloth, that cloth constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in relation to the previous cloth. Once the cloth has been relinquished and the offense confessed, the continuity of intention is severed. On that same day, whether the previously sought cloth arrives or an unexpected cloth arrives, it does not fall under the category of "continuity," because the intention has been severed.

If one relinquishes the cloth on that very day and confesses the transgression on that very day, yet the intention to seek cloth remains unsevered, then even if cloth is obtained after a month, it all belongs to the "continuity" and constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in relation to the previous cloth; the offense is incurred on the very day the cloth is obtained, without needing to pass further days.

If one relinquishes the cloth today and the offense is already confessed, and the intention to seek cloth is also severed, but on a later day a new cause or condition for seeking cloth arises, it does not fall under "continuity," because the intervening intention was severed. If one relinquishes the cloth at the time of the ground-clearing ceremony (*bhūmi-pariśodhana*), [the same principle applies].

The offense has already been confessed; the continuity of the intention has been severed. If one subsequently seeks and obtains a robe toward evening, this robe must be relinquished, and one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. If the robe has already been relinquished and the subsequent continuity has already been severed, even if one obtains robes over many days while the offense remains unconfessed, these robes must be relinquished and a *duṣkṛta* confession performed.

Because the former was a continuity of days and the latter is a continuity of intention, one incurs the same offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The three robes should neither be fewer nor more. If one keeps fewer than required, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*; if one keeps more, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The commentary explains:

"The phrase 'the ground is cleared' refers to the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*). Taking two *kṣaṇas* before sunrise as the limit, this constitutes the dawn light, meaning that its white color is visible. Furthermore, it is defined by being able to see the lines on the palm."
[...limited sequence). Next, the matter of the *kaṭhina* robe is explained. *Kaṭhina* here means "merit" (*guṇa*). This refers to receiving this robe;
by the power of this robe, one is able to uphold five meritorious matters during the five-month period.

It is also called the "robe for rewarding the good and punishing the evil," meaning that when a bhikṣu has performed meritorious deeds during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), this robe is used to reward him. As for those who violate the retreat...

It is not permissible to punish those who dwell among a community that acts contrary to the Dharma. When a bhikṣu has completed the rains retreat (*varṣā*), there are four matters he ought to perform:
namely, the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the dissolution of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha-vimocana*), the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*), and the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe.

(If the boundary markers are submerged by a great flood, or if the Saṃgha must all leave the boundary due to danger from bandits, or if the assembly desires the boundary to be wider or narrower, one should first dissolve the previous boundary and then re-establish it; if they do not so desire, this need not be done. Once the *kaṭhina* robe has been accepted, one obtains five privileges.
There are five benefits: first, keeping extra robes; second, staying overnight apart from one’s robes; third, eating in a separate group; fourth, eating by turns;
and fifth, entering a village before or after a meal without informing a bhikṣu. How does one receive the *kaṭhina* robe?
If one obtains a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a rag-robe (*pāṃśukūla*), and if it is a new robe—or if it is an old robe with a new patch—[it may be received].

Performing the purification (*viśuddhi*): if it has already been washed, once washed, one performs the purification by folding it. It must not be obtained through wrong livelihood; it must not be obtained through deceit; it must not be obtained through signs;

it must not be obtained through provocation. It must not have been kept overnight; it must not be subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) before being purified. It must be in accordance with the Dharma from the very day it is received.

It has borders sewn around the four edges, five strips (*pañca-paṭṭa*), and ten sections (*daśa-khaṇḍa*). If it exceeds these [measurements], it may also be accepted (referring to the seven-strip robe). Two...

From eleven sections up to twenty-five strips (one hundred and twenty-five sections), one should wash them oneself, dye them the color of a *kāṣāya*, stretch and smooth them out, and cut and sew them into ten sections.
One should receive [the robe] before the assembly of monks within the boundary (not before a single person, nor received by a single person alone).

It is not received before two, three, or four persons, nor is it received by two, three, or four persons. In any dwelling place, down to the most humble, one must obtain five virtuous bhikṣus within the same boundary (*sīmā*): one person is appointed to receive [the robe], and four perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); thus the reception is accomplished. One may not receive it oneself outside the boundary.

If more than five people are present and they communicate their consent (*chanda*), the reception is accomplished. If one goes outside the boundary and returns, and hears that the Saṃgha has finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, one may immediately express sympathetic joy (*anumodana*); this also constitutes a valid reception. If many people offer clothing and requisites, one should take the best single item to make the *kaṭhina* robe;
the remainder shall be divided according to the ritual procedure. One should make the following announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today, the assembly of monks..."
"I request that the Sangha accept the *guṇa-cīvara*. If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, may the community of monks in harmony accept the *guṇa-cīvara*.

This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). [Next, one must appoint a person to hold the robe. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are five qualities by which one should not be appointed: first, partiality due to affection; second, partiality due to hatred; third, partiality due to fear; fourth, partiality due to delusion; fifth, ignorance as to whether [the robe] has been accepted or not. One who possesses the opposite qualities should be appointed.

Furthermore, there are five types of bhikṣus who may not serve as the holder of the *guṇa-cīvara*: first, one who has not completed his full term of residence (*anupasaṃpanna*); second, one who has broken the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā-bheda*); third, one who entered the retreat late (*paścima-varṣā*); fourth, one who has been suspended (*pravāsanīya*); fifth, one who is living in isolation (*pārivāsika*). The root Vinaya states: 'One should ask who is capable.'"

[One who] holds the *kaṭhina* robe [should say]: "If you answer, 'I, so-and-so, am able,' then among those in the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should appoint him in this manner):

'Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha. Thus is the motion (*jñapti*)."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the *kaṭhina* robe for the sake of the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the *kaṭhina* robe for the sake of the Saṃgha, remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, please speak. The Saṃgha has consented; the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the *kaṭhina* robe for the sake of the Saṃgha is concluded. The Saṃgha...

Because he has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. (The Sangha should then perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and bestow the *kaṭhina* robe upon the robe-holder; it should be done as follows.)
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This dwelling-place has obtained robes that may be distributed; the present Saṃgha should divide them.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha bestow these robes upon the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This bhikṣu shall take these robes on behalf of the Saṃgha to make them into a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain them at this dwelling-place. Thus is the motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Sirs.
Venerable sirs, listen. This monastery has obtained robe-cloth that is to be distributed. The present assembly of monks should divide it.

The Sangha now bestows this cloth upon the bhikṣu so-and-so; this bhikṣu shall take this cloth for the Sangha and, having made it into a *kaṭhina* robe, maintain it here at this residence. Which elders consent to the Sangha bestowing this cloth upon so-and-so...?

The monk who has received the *kaṭhina* robe for the purpose of making merit remains silent. Whoever does not approve, let him speak. The Saṃgha has approved and finished bestowing the robe upon the monk so-and-so.
Because the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. (The monk holding the robe should rise and take hold of it;

as the hands of the various monks reach toward the robe, at the point where the signs are clearly perceived, he should speak as follows: "This robe the community of monks shall accept and make into a *kaṭhina*."
[This] robe: "The Sangha now accepts this robe to make it into a merit-robe (*puṇya-kāṭhina*). The Sangha has finished accepting this robe to make it into a merit-robe.
(Recite this three times. Those bhikṣus should say: "That which has been accepted by the recipient has been well-accepted; whatever merit and renown there is herein belongs to me.
The person holding the robe should respond, "So be it. If one obtains an unfinished robe, one should...
Within the Saṃgha, one shall appoint a bhikṣu by means of a formal act (karmavācanā) to perform [this task] (it should be appointed as follows): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to prepare the *guṇavatī-cīvara* for the Saṃgha. This is the motion (*jñapti*)."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] by the Saṃgha to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha, remain silent.
Whoever does not consent, please speak. The Saṃgha has already consented; the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] by the Saṃgha to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha is concluded. The Saṃgha.

Because of patient silence, this matter is thus upheld. (Once the robe has been made, it is received according to the previous rules. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "On the sixteenth day, when the dawn light appears, one takes the *kaṭhina* robe, cuts it, and brings it to the community of monks.

The bhikṣus should tell the owner of the robe about the need for needles, thread, and dye, as well as the number of bhikṣus required to make the robe. The donor should provide food and drink. Those who receive the *kaṭhina* robe on behalf of the Saṃgha should know the method for receiving it.

If the robe has already been cut, it should first be washed; then, together with many bhikṣus, they should cut, sew, and finish it. It should be dyed and completed that very day. Once the purification (*pariśuddhi*) has been marked, it should be received. If the robe is not yet finished, all bhikṣus should be summoned to complete it together."

One must not speak of obstacles to the practice of the Dharma, except in the case of those who are ill. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Even those capable of performing only two or three stitches should all assist in its making. Once it is completed, the person responsible for spreading the robe should adorn the *guṇa-cīvara* (the robe of merit) with ointments, incense, and flowers.

Having made these offerings, he should place it upon a clean tray and carry it toward the head of the assembly. Standing before the *sthavira*, he should hold the robe up and remain there. After the formal announcement has been made three times, he should then spread out the robe before the *sthavira*.

The Elder said: "Excellent, the distribution of robes! Most excellent, the distribution of robes! This shall bring us gain and benefit, which I shall obtain. Thus it was said, down to the last member of the assembly. The person distributing the robes should not take these robes to the places for defecation or urination, nor to the fire-houses.

He should not stay in the open air, nor go outside the boundary. Even if he has a reason to travel, he should not spend the night away. There are ten kinds of persons with whom it is not proper to share the *kaṭhina* robe: first, one who has not completed the rains retreat; second, one who has broken the rains retreat;

third, one who sat for the rains retreat after [the others]; fourth, one who sat for the rains retreat in another location; fifth, one who was not present at the time of the distribution of the robes; sixth, one practicing the *yadbhūyaskāra* penance; seventh, one who has completed the *yadbhūyaskāra* penance; eighth, one practicing the *mānāpya* penance; ninth, one who has completed the *mānāpya* penance; tenth, one undergoing training (*śaikṣa*).

Furthermore, there are ten persons who obtain the material benefits (*lābha*) but do not receive the spiritual advantages (*anuśaṃsā*). This refers to replacing the fourth person mentioned previously with a *śrāmaṇera*, thus making ten. There are five types of persons who obtain neither the benefits nor the advantages:

namely, the three kinds of persons subject to suspension (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*), those who have spent the summer retreat elsewhere, and those belonging to the faction of the unrighteous (*adharma-pakṣa*) at the time the Saṃgha is split. The *Sudharman-vinaya* states: "If a residence has fewer than five persons, or if they do not know how to perform the formal procedure (*dharmasamādāna*), one may summon monks from another monastery to complete the quorum for receiving [the robe] and performing the *karmavācanā*.

However, those monks shall not receive the *kaṭhina* robe, nor shall they receive a share of the robes. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* permits a single person living alone to perform [the ceremony]. When that person takes the robe, he should say: "This is the *kaṭhina* robe."

"I receive it now. Thus he says three times. At the time of cutting [the cloth], he should say: "I shall receive this *kaṭhina* robe. When sewing it, when washing it, when dyeing it, when marking it, and when purifying it with a blade, he should likewise speak as above.

Once it has been completed, he should mentally reflect and say aloud: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], receive this *kaṭhina* robe. Thus he says three times. When the four months of winter have ended, the Saṃgha should suspend the *guṇavatī-cīvara*.
It should be suspended in this manner: having performed the preliminary formalities, he makes the announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today the community suspends..."

Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe: If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, hear me. The Saṃgha now, in harmony, shall take out the *kaṭhina*. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

[Once it has been taken out, one no longer obtains the five benefits; all surplus items must be relinquished, or otherwise rendered pure (*śuddha*), etc. Otherwise, after ten days have passed, one incurs the offense of relinquishment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If it is not taken out...

If one exceeds the limit for the *kaṭhina* robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There are eight causes for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe: first, departure; second, completion [of the rainy season retreat];
third, non-completion; fourth, loss; fifth, cessation of expectation; sixth, hearing [the end of the period]; seventh, exiting the boundary;

eighth, exiting together [with the community]. Furthermore, there are two ways of relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe: when a monk who holds the *kaṭhina* robe spends the night outside the boundary, or when the Saṃgha...
[They] emerge together [from the *kaṭhina* ceremony] (as explained in detail in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*).
○ The Second Precept on Sleeping Separated from One’s Robes:
If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the *kaṭhina* robe relinquished, should remain separated from any one of his three robes;
If one leaves [the robes] overnight, except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus went wandering among the people and entrusted their robes to a bhikṣu who was a friend.
That bhikṣu frequently dried them in the sun. The other bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha established this precept for them.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who suffered from the disease of consumption (śoṣa).
He possessed a very heavy *pāṃsukūla-saṃghāṭī*, and having a matter requiring him to go among the people, he was unable to carry it while traveling. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha on his behalf.

The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to grant the sick bhikṣu the *anāpatti-cīvara* (the non-forfeiture of robes) through a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). That sick bhikṣu should then go before the Saṃgha.

[In the midst of the assembly], having performed the formal rites and prostrated at the feet of the senior monk (*sthavira*), he kneels with his right knee on the ground and joins his palms to request the formal authorization.
He says: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], am afflicted by such-and-such an illness. This saṃghāṭī robe made of discarded rags is heavy;

yet there is a necessary reason for me to travel among the people, and I am unable to carry it while traveling. I now request from the Saṃgha the authorization for the 'non-loss of robe' (*acchinna-cīvara*) rule. (Having said this three times, the Saṃgha should grant it for him.)

[Karmavācanā] Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. A certain bhikṣu has contracted a certain illness. He possesses a heavy *pāṃsukūla-saṃghāṭī*, and because of a necessary matter he wishes to travel among the people;
however, he is unable to carry it while traveling. He requests from the Saṃgha the *anāpatti-vattha* (the rule regarding not being separated from one's robes).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent. I thus announce this: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
This bhikṣu, named So-and-so, has contracted a certain illness. He possesses a saṃghāṭī robe made of discarded rags which he finds heavy.
Having a necessary reason to travel among the people, he is unable to carry it while traveling. He now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act of establishing the 'non-loss' rule for his robes."
The Procedure for the Non-Loss of Robes (*Avisāra-dharmā*). Now, the Saṃgha grants the monk so-and-so the formal act of non-loss of robes.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting the monk so-and-so the formal act of non-loss of robes, remain silent. Whoever does not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has granted the monk so-and-so the formal act of non-loss of robes; the Saṃgha consents, as it is silent.
Therefore, this matter is to be maintained in this way. The robes have been finished; the *kaṭhina* robe has been removed, as explained above. Regarding the three robes:
first, the *antarvāsa* (here translated as "lower garment"); second, the *uttarāsaṅga* (here translated as "upper garment"); third, the *saṃghāṭī* (here translated as "double-layered robe").
These three robes are collectively called *cīvara* in the Western Country (India), so they are designated by their color.
These are all called *kāṣāya*. The reason for establishing these three names is to symbolize the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma;
to manifest the three periods of time; to sever the three poisons; to transcend the three realms; and to deliver beings from the three states of existence.
This is intended to manifest a dharma never before seen, thereby distinguishing it from non-Buddhist paths, and to cultivate few desires and contentment.
The three robes are neither too many nor too few; they are sufficient to sustain the body for the practice of the Way. They are also intended for the three seasons of winter, spring, and summer:
one wears the heavy robe in winter, the medium robe in spring, and the light robe in summer; during the great cold, all three robes are worn together.

"It may be used to ward them off" (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The three robes are the insignia of the śramaṇas, the worthy and holy ones; therefore, my disciples, by means of these three robes, are fully able to ward off great cold and great heat, and to shield themselves from flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies, thereby maintaining a sense of shame and integrity and not destroying the noble lineage.

If one’s nature cannot endure the cold, it is permitted to wear old, worn-out garments, or to have them quilted as desired; this is the practice of having few desires and few concerns"). "Separated" (*li*) means that the body and the robe are in different locations.
"Each individual robe" refers to any one of the three robes being separated [from the body]. "Spending the night in a different location" [means staying overnight apart from the robe].
This refers to staying overnight in a different territory; at the appearance of the dawn, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

This is based on the fact that once the three robes have been formally accepted and maintained, if one is separated from even one of them for an overnight stay, it is termed "losing the robe," and thus one incurs the offense. This excludes cases where there has been a formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*).
This refers to the circumstance of being ill; if the community performs the ritual action [of *sīmā-bandha*], there is no offense. Regarding the boundaries therein:

if one does not lose one's robe, then within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) there is a single boundary; a tree is a single boundary; a threshing floor is a single boundary; a wagon is a single boundary; a boat is a single boundary; a village is a single boundary;

a house is a single boundary; a hall is a single boundary; a storehouse is a single boundary; and a granary is a single boundary. (Regarding "tree": it means that which is equal in height to a person and sufficient to provide shade.)

Sitting cross-legged. *Kṣetra* (field): that place where the five grains are cultivated. *Śakaṭa* (cart): that place where carts turn around. *Nau* (boat): that place where boats turn around. *Grāma* (village): there are four kinds, as mentioned above. *Mandapa* (hall): that which is largely open to the air.

*Koṣṭha* (storehouse): where various goods are stored. *Kośa* (granary): where grain and rice are stored). If one loses a robe, then within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) there are various boundaries, up to the various boundaries of the granaries, as well as the boundary of this monastery and not the boundary of that monastery, and so forth.
The granary boundary. It is not that granary boundary, nor do the various boundaries mutually negate one another.

If, at the edge of any of the aforementioned boundaries, one uses a stone or a brick with the strength of an average person to throw it, the area reached by that throw is called the "boundary of influence" (*sīmā-vaipulya*).
If one places a robe within a monastery and stays overnight under a tree, or even stays overnight in a storehouse, or if one places a robe in a storehouse...

In such places, if one stays overnight within a monastery, or leaves one's robes in one location while staying overnight elsewhere, and does not relinquish the robes, nor hold them in hand, nor remain within reach of where a stone could be thrown, then at the appearance of dawn, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for being separated from those robes—except for the three robes.
To be separated from any other robe constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If there is no village and one is in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), one may leave [the robes]...

If one leaves one's robes among eight trees and stays overnight in another location without relinquishing the robes and other items, and the dawn appears, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

(Regarding "not relinquishing the robes": this refers to having a reason to go out briefly with the intention of returning, but being detained by difficult circumstances so that one cannot return on the same day. In that case, one should borrow another person’s extra set of three robes (*trīṇi cīvarāṇi*) at that place and formally accept them.

One should mentally relinquish the previously accepted robes, and only then accept the borrowed robes. If there are no monks' robes available, a nun's robes may also be used. One should intend to relinquish the borrowed robes and return them the next morning. Upon reaching one's original location, one should again accept one's own robes. If there are no other robes available to borrow, one should mentally relinquish [the previous ones].)

Regarding the observance of robes: it is better to incur the *dukkaṭa* offense of violating one’s dignified deportment by being without a robe while observing the precept, rather than incurring the grave *pāyattika* offense of being separated from one's robe. As for the phrase "between eight trees": the distance between one tree and the next is seven *dhanus*; thus, the distance between eight trees is fifty-six *dhanus*. One *dhanu* is four cubits (*hasta*) of an average person;

this space between the eight trees constitutes the boundary for one's robe. The Mūlasarvāstivāda school states: "If traveling on a road, the limit is forty-nine *vyāma*; when standing, sitting, or lying down, the limit is within a circumference of one *vyāma*. This is the extent within which one does not lose possession of the robe.

Even if one sits or lies down between two boundaries, as long as even a corner of the robe does not leave the body, it is not called 'losing the robe. This robe subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) should be relinquished.
The confession is as before; the Dharma is identical to that of the preceding precept. The Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
If they do not return it, and he wears it repeatedly until it is ruined, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for all of it. For the other four assemblies, the offense is the same as before.
There is no offense if the dawn has not yet appeared, while he is holding the robe in his hand, or until he reaches a place where a stone could be thrown.

Furthermore, one loses [the status of] having lost, burned, washed away, or destroyed [the robe]. If the road is dangerous and difficult, or if one is captured and bound, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*)—as the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"Regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*): while the illness has not yet been cured, one may stay overnight separated from the robe. If the illness is cured and one wishes to return, but the road is dangerous and difficult so that one cannot return, yet one constantly maintains the intention to return, then even though the illness has been cured, the robe is not lost.

However, if one forms the firm resolve not to return, the robe is lost; if ten days pass, one commits the offense of keeping an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*). If the illness is cured and one returns to the place where the robe is, but the illness flares up again and one wishes to go once more, one immediately relies upon the previous formal act. No [new act is required].

It must be performed by means of a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Consequently, the establishment of the "boundary for not losing one's robes" (*acīvarāpanā-sīmā*) is explained. At that time, there was a monk who had renounced desire and wished to go and dwell in a forest cave (*araṇya-guhā*).

Fearing he might commit the offense of staying overnight apart from his robe, the Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to establish a boundary for not losing one's robes, excluding areas separated by fast-flowing water.
This is performed by a formal motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karmavācanā*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. In this place, which constitutes a single residence and a single recitation..."

The precepts. If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to establish the *akalpiya-cīvara-sīmā* (the boundary where robes need not be kept with one), excluding the village and the area outside the village.

This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen. At this place, which is a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts, the Saṃgha now establishes the *akalpiya-cīvara-sīmā*, excluding the village and the area outside the village. Which elders among you consent to the Saṃgha establishing [this] at this place?

In this single residence, for the purpose of a common recitation of the *Poṣadha*, the *Acīvarāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary where robes need not be kept) is established, excluding the village and its outskirts.
Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has consented that this place shall be a single residence with a common recitation of the *Poṣadha*.
The boundary for not losing one's robe is established, excluding the village and the area outside the village. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

(This boundary for not losing one's robe has no separate characteristics; it is established within the same residential Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). First the Great Boundary is established, and subsequently the boundary for not losing one's robe is established. However, there are three types of monasteries:

if the Great Boundary is coextensive with the monastery, or if the boundary is smaller than the monastery, it need not be established. If the boundary is larger than the monastery, it should be established according to the Dharma; then, the robe is contained within the boundary. Excluding the village and the area outside the village.)

Regarding the "boundary" (*sīmā*): this refers to excluding the village and the area outside the village, taking the open space and the dwelling place, and performing the *akopya-karman* (the ritual for not losing one's robe). Initially, the *agrāmaka-karman* (the ritual for designating a non-village) was established so that robes were included within the village;

later, due to the arising of certain circumstances, the village was subsequently excluded. Now, regardless of whether a village exists or not, the law requires it to be excluded. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* clarifies this meaning: the village is excluded for five reasons.

If the ritual was performed and established when there was originally no village, and a village subsequently enters from outside the dwelling place of a *karmadāna*, then wherever that village reaches, it is no longer part of the robe-boundary. If the original village departs again, the robe-boundary remains inclusive. If there was originally a village that was not included, and the village leaves, the robe-boundary is restored to its full extent because of the village.

Regarding going and coming: because it is neither a formal bond nor a formal release. If a bhikṣu’s body is in a village and his robe is also in a village, he should go to where the robe is. If his body is in a village and his robe is in an araṇya, he should exit the village boundary. If his body is in an araṇya and his robe is in a village, [he should likewise go to where the robe is].

One should go to the place where the robe is kept. If both one’s person and the robe are together in an araṇya (forest hermitage), there is no offense. If one wishes to release [the boundary], one should first release the *a-nasita-cīvara-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing the robe), and then release the *mahā-sīmā* (the great boundary).

One should perform the release as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This place is a single residence with a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant permission."
The formal motion for dissolving the *acelaka-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe) is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

This place is a single residence with a single recitation of the precepts. The Saṃgha now dissolves the *acelaka-sīmā*. Which elders among you consent to the Saṃgha dissolving the *acelaka-sīmā* at this place?"

Those who consent to the dissolution of the *akālacīvara-sīmā* (the boundary for not being separated from one's robe) within this same dwelling place and this same *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) remain silent.
Whoever does not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has consented; the dissolution of the *akālacīvara-sīmā* within this same dwelling place and this same *poṣadha* is concluded.

Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) is relinquished, the boundary for not being separated from one's robe is also relinquished.")
If one has relinquished [the robe] but not yet left the robe-boundary (and the great boundary has not been relinquished).
○ The third precept concerning robes kept for more than one month:
If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina cloth has been withdrawn, and that bhikṣu obtains an out-of-season robe and wishes—
It must be accepted. Once accepted, one must quickly have it made into a robe. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, one may keep it for up to one month in order to fulfill it.
If one keeps it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu whose saṃghāṭī robe had become old, worn out, and tattered. Within ten days, he was unable to procure a replacement;
fearing that he would commit the offense of possessing an extra robe (dīrgha-cīvara), his fellow students informed the World-Honored One.

Thereupon, the Buddha permitted bhikṣus to keep an extra robe for the purpose of fulfilling their needs. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus (ṣaḍvargika) kept many kinds of surplus robes. Together with...

[This was] insufficient. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha established a precept for them. When the robes were finished and the kaṭhina cloth had been withdrawn, it was explained as before:
"If a bhikṣu obtains an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara), he may accept it—meaning he may obtain it from laymen or laywomen, or from male or female renunciants.
What is called 'season' and what is called 'out-of-season'? If one does not receive [the robe] during the [proper] period..."
Regarding the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit): one month after the *pravāraṇā*, or five months after the *pravāraṇā*, if one receives a robe of merit, this is called the "proper time.
To exceed this limit is called "improper time. To obtain a robe during this improper time is called an "improper-time robe.
Regarding "if one desires it, one may accept it": "desires it" means to have a longing or wish to obtain the robe; "accepts it" means...

"It is permissible to keep [the robe-material]. "Having received it, one should quickly make it into a robe" means that once the robe-material has been obtained, one should, according to what is missing or damaged among the three robes, promptly complete it into a robe and accept it for use; it must not exceed ten days.
"If it is sufficient, it is well" means that if one obtains cloth of equal quality such that its measurement is complete and capable of forming a single garment without any deficiency.
Furthermore, if one is insufficiently supplied, one may keep [the robe] for one month.

That is to say, if one lacks robes and has a source from which they expect to obtain them, it is permitted to wait until thirty days have passed in order to fulfill the requirement. Regarding the offenses within this:
If within ten days one’s requisite robes are complete, they must be cut, or sewn together with thread, or stitched into a robe, or given as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), or sent to another person.
Otherwise, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, for however many robes [are incomplete], one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If the requisite robes are not yet complete, but become complete on the eleventh day, then one should act accordingly.

One must perform tasks such as cutting and tailoring on the aforementioned day. Otherwise, at the appearance of the dawn on the twelfth day, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the quantity of the robes.

This applies likewise until the twenty-ninth day. Upon reaching the thirtieth day, whether the robes are sufficient or insufficient, whether they are of the same type or not, one must perform tasks such as cutting and tailoring on that very day; otherwise, [an offense is incurred].
On the thirty-first day, when the dawn light appears, the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense is incurred. This robe must be relinquished and confessed;

the Saṃgha should then perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) to return this robe to the bhikṣu. Regarding other offenses or non-offenses, as well as the transgressions of the four assemblies, all are identical to the previous precept.

(*The Śāriputra Vinaya-vibhāṣā* states: "If on the twenty-ninth day one obtains a robe that is finer than the expected one, and the previous robe was coarse—provided the previous robe has been formally dedicated (*pariṣkāra*)—the newly obtained robe may also be kept for one month, because the expectation [of the same] remains."*)

If one expects to obtain coarse robes, one may further delay for one month. In this manner, proceeding as desired, they may do so at will; however, to maintain uniformity, it must not exceed one month. Next, the method for making robes is explained:
At that time, the Buddha instructed Ānanda to teach the bhikṣus to cut and sew robes according to the regular patterns of field ridges and furrows.
The disciples of all Buddhas of the past and future shall wear such robes, just as I do today; by cutting with a knife, one becomes a śramaṇa.

Regarding robes: so that they may not be plundered by enemies or bandits, the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to make the *ānavaśī* (lower robe), the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), and the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) with cut-and-sewn strips.
He also permitted the making of an uncut *ānavaśī*. [The *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual for Robes) states: "The appearance of the strips is like the ridges of a field;

just as water is stored there to nourish fine seedlings, so too does wearing this robe produce merit. The Buddha commanded that it be modeled after this; its significance is not in vain. The commentary explains: Those who open up waterways today are precisely following this precedent of excavation.]
This was not the original regulation). One may sew the leaves together like bird’s feet, or sew along the edges of the leaves like horse-teeth stitches.
It should have five strips, not six; it should have seven strips, not eight; it should have nine strips, not ten.
Up to nineteen strips; it should not have twenty strips. If it exceeds this number of strips, one should not keep it (according to other schools, it is permitted up to twenty-five strips).
If it is a new garment, one should make the *antarvāsa* and the *uttarāsaṅga* single-layered, and the *saṃghāṭī* double-layered.
If it is an old garment, it is permitted to make the *antarvāsa* and the *uttarāsaṅga* double-layered.
Monks, the saṃghāṭī should consist of four layers. As for *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) clothing, the number of layers may be as many or few as one desires;
however, one should not use a minor garment in place of the three robes (*tricīvara*). It is permitted to make an *antarvāsaka* from a cloth four cubits long and two cubits wide;
to make an *uttarāsaṅga*; and for the *saṃghāṭī*, if one obtains a seamless robe (*ekāṃśa*), its width...

If the cloth is long, it will be insufficient when cut to make a robe; therefore, it is permitted to apply patches (*pattra*). One should dye it to a discolored hue (*kaṣāya-varṇa*) to serve as a śramaṇa’s robe.

When the robe is worn out, it should be mended. It is permitted to wear patchwork (*nakha*). One may use double-layered thread for the borders and sew on patches according to the size and shape of the holes, whether square or round.
According to the Vinaya texts of other schools, there are nine grades of the *saṃghāṭī* in total; the first three grades consist of nine...
Eleven strips; thirteen strips. The altar partitions consist of two long and one short strip. The middle three grades consist of fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen strips.
The final three grades consist of twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five strips, each with four long and one short strip.
The *uttarāsaṅga* consists of seven strips, with two long and one [short].

Short [length]: the *antarvāsa* (inner robe) consists of five strips, with one long strip and one short strip. The Buddha said: "The three robes (*tricīvara*) should be formally accepted and maintained.
If there is doubt, one should relinquish them and accept them again. If one possesses the three robes but does not maintain them [through formal acceptance], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
