Whether for the Saṅgha, for a group, or even for a single person, or if one takes hold of gold or silver on behalf of an image, in all such cases it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). There is no offense if one does not accept it oneself and does not instruct another to accept it.

If a layperson brings gold or silver as a gift to a bhikkhu, the bhikkhu should reply, "I am not permitted to accept this. If the layperson says further, "Venerable Sir, my intention to give has already been resolved; I cannot take it back," he should set it down on the ground and depart. Having departed, the bhikkhu must remain there to watch over it. If a layperson comes and asks about it, he should inform them of the facts as they are.

If that layperson says, "Since you, Venerable Sir, may not accept it, please give it to your disciple," the bhikkhu should remain silent. The layperson may then take it up and carry it away to exchange it for food, drink, clothing, or pure requisites, and the bhikkhu may then accept these items.

If there is no one capable of understanding the Dharma, and gold and silver are within the house, keep the door closed so they are not lost. If there is someone who sells robes and bowls, the bhikṣu should summon them and show them the gold and silver, saying: "I, this poor monk, require these robes and bowls; here is the gold and silver for them."

The lay devotee (gṛhapati) should know for himself: if there is no one to sell robes or alms bowls, but someone comes with non-seasonal drinks, seven-day medicines, or lifetime medicines, he should go to where the gold and silver are and say, "There is this gold and silver;

the Saṃgha requires these medicines. The lay devotee should know for himself that once the medicines have been obtained, the Saṃgha may consume them, but this bhikṣu may not consume them. No others—whether laypeople, pure attendants (śuddhakarman), or even animals—may eat them. Why? Because they are the property of the Saṃgha.

If the owner of the gold and silver cannot obtain the medicines and leaves, there is no other means by which they may be accepted. If he sees an upāsaka, he should call him and instruct him to throw [the items] away. If he asks, "Why do you throw them away? I shall pick them up," the bhikṣu should reply, "As you wish."

[The Buddha] said: "If that person understands the Dharma and, having exchanged his robes and bowl, comes to offer them to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha may accept them. If there is no upāsaka who can be instructed to throw them away, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations) to appoint a single bhikṣu who possesses five qualities.

This bhikṣu shall take this gold and silver, cause him to close his eyes and throw it away, and must not record its location. If he records the location, he commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: 'The Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint a bhikṣu as the person to discard the gold, silver, and coins.

That bhikṣu should discard these items in a pit, in fire, in flowing water, or in the wilderness; he must not mark the spot. If he takes them and places them elsewhere, he must not take hold of them again. That bhikṣu should not question the Saṃgha.'"

Regarding this item, what should be done? The Sangha should not instruct, "Make it thus" or "Make it so. If they do not discard it nor inquire about it, but instead have a *kappiyakāraka* (a person who makes things allowable) trade it for items for the Sangha’s food and clothing and bring them to the Sangha, the Sangha may accept them. If they are to be distributed, [the procedure follows].

Only those who have committed an offense are not permitted to receive a share. As for those who have not committed an offense, even if they give [money] to a bhikṣu, if the bhikṣu is unaware of it, a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) shall receive it to purchase pure items. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is permitted for a sick person to have a *kappiya-kāraka* keep [the funds], provided he does not become greedily attached to them.

If an object subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) has been forfeited before the Saṃgha, it must not be returned to that bhikṣu, nor may the Saṃgha divide it among themselves. If there is a large amount, it should be placed within the category of "inexhaustible goods" (*akṣaya-nīvi*). If it generates interest or profit, one may use it to build a dwelling or provide clothing, but it must not be consumed as food.

Whenever a bhikṣu obtains money, or when he receives the value of robes at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he must not take it with his own hands; he must have a *kappiya-kāraka* manage it. If no *kappiya-kāraka* is available, he should point to the ground by his feet and say: "This [is it]."

Once it is known that [the object] has been placed on the ground, one may personally take grass, leaves, bricks, tiles, or other such items and cast them from a distance over it to cover it. One should then wait for a *karmadāna* (attendant) to arrive and inform them, according to what is used in that particular country—whether it be copper coins, iron coins, coins made of foreign resin, or leather coins.

Bamboo tally sticks: one must never hold them. In some countries they are used, yet their characteristics are not perfected; in other countries they are not used, yet their characteristics are perfected. To hold them in either case constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "To take precious objects with one's own hand."

If it is small, it should be discarded. If it is large, even if one obtains a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) who shares the same intention, one should say to them: "Because this is impure, I should not take it; you should take it. Once the lay attendant has taken it, they should say to the bhikṣu: "This object is given to the bhikṣu.

The bhikṣu should say: "This is an impure object; if it were pure, I would accept it. If one cannot obtain a lay attendant who shares the same intention, one should make it into bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions. One should enter among the monks and say: "Venerable sirs, I took treasure with my own hand and have committed a *pāyattika* offense.

I now confess it; I do not dare to conceal it, but repent of my transgression. The Saṃgha should ask: "Have you abandoned this treasure? He should answer: "I have abandoned it. The Saṃgha should ask: "Do you see your offense? He should answer: "I see it. The Saṃgha should then say: "Henceforth..."

"Do not do it again. If he says he has not yet relinquished it, the Saṃgha should issue a formal injunction to make him relinquish it. If they do not issue the injunction, the entire Saṃgha incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he does not relinquish it despite the injunction, that bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) states:

Once the attendant (*naiṣadyika*) has taken [the object] and says to the bhikṣu, "This item is for the bhikṣu," and the bhikṣu says, "This is an impure object; if it were pure, I would accept it," this constitutes the declaration of purity (*paryavadāna*). Having declared its purity, he may then enter the assembly of monks to repent his transgression.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one receives the price of a robe offered by another, and desires it, one may accept it. Having accepted it, one should maintain it with the mental attitude that it belongs to that person. However, one should seek out a *kappiyakāraka* (a 'purifier')—either a *śrāmaṇera* or a lay follower (*upāsaka*)—and ask them as follows:"

"Can you act as my pure donor (*śuddha-dānapati*)? If he says he can, one should entrust the matter to that person's mind and keep the object; it should be held by a messenger and not grasped by oneself. Even if one travels far away, as long as that person remains alive, they shall always be the pure donor.

If one has not yet found a pure donor to act as the pure donor, one should hold the object before a single *bhikṣu* and speak these words: "Venerable sir, please bear this in mind. I, [name], have obtained this impure object. I shall take this impure object and exchange it for pure wealth.
Having said this three times, one may use it according to one's needs without harboring any doubt. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If no pure donor can be found, one should hold gold..."

Regarding silver and other such items, one should stand or remain before a single bhikṣu and speak as follows: "Venerable sir, please bear this in mind: I, the bhikṣu [Name], have obtained this impure wealth; I shall now take this impure wealth and exchange it for pure wealth. This should be said a second and a third time.

Then, one should either carry it oneself or have someone else carry it. If a bhikṣu obtains gold, silver, or the like while on a journey, for the sake of provisions for the road, he should carry it himself or have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) or a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) carry it.

It should be understood that for a *śrāmaṇera*, regarding gold, silver, and the like, there is only a prohibition against personal possession; it does not prohibit holding or grasping them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu causes a śrāmaṇera to grasp gold, silver, or coins for the first time, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If he sees that the śrāmaṇera has already grasped them previously and subsequently causes him to grasp them, there is no offense. My interpretation is as follows: According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha*, the allowance for possession through formal ritual procedures was established by the Buddha’s great compassion for disciples of inferior faculties in the final age. Those who possess such items must feel deep shame and remorse.

Give rise to a mind of weary detachment and do not harbor greedy attachment. Bestow [wealth] upon the two fields of merit; use it when it is beneficial. You should not be deeply attached to chests and bags, lest at the moment your eyes fall to the ground, the life-faculty be difficult to sever—like a bird wishing to fly into the void that is instead trapped by a clam;
this is truly to deceive and harm oneself.
The Nineteenth Precept on the Buying and Selling of Precious Objects:
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain, Upananda went to the marketplace and exchanged money for money.
He took it away. When the householder saw this, he criticized and disparaged him. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha established a precept:
"Regarding various buying and selling"—this does not refer to trading for a single item, but rather refers to [trading] wrought gold, unwrought gold, and wrought silver.
"Unrefined silver" refers to that which is used for mutual exchange. "Refined" refers to gold and silver fashioned into various vessels;

"unrefined" refers to that which has not yet been fashioned into such vessels. Alternatively, one may exchange money for gold and silver, or exchange gold and silver for money, or exchange money for money.
There are eight kinds of money: namely, gold, silver, copper, iron, white wax, lead, tin, wood, and *hu* (barley).
This refers to currency. "Precious objects" refers to gold, silver, coins, the seven types of jewels, necklaces, and so forth.
Regarding the method of relinquishing these, as well as the resulting offense for the fourfold assembly, it is explained in the same manner as the precept on handling precious objects.

There is no offense if one uses money to purchase ornaments for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, or exchanges ornaments for money (*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: At that time, the bhikṣus obtained inexhaustible goods and placed them in a room or storehouse. The donors...)

Someone came and asked, "Venerable sir, for what reason do you still not repair the monastery? The bhikṣu replied, "Good sir, it is because we have no money or goods. The host said, "Have I not offered inexhaustible goods? He replied, "Those inexhaustible goods are currently in the monastic storehouse.

The host said, "This is not right. Does my home have no place to store them? Why do you not exchange them to seek profit? He replied, "The Buddha has prohibited seeking profit. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "If it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, one should seek profit. Having heard the Buddha's words, the lay devotees with faith, for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, offered inexhaustible goods. These three actual substances should likewise be circulated to seek profit.

Any benefits obtained should be used to make offerings to the Triple Gem. When giving these items, one should clearly provide double the value as collateral, record the terms in a formal contract, establish guarantors, note the date, and record the name of the presiding elder.

And as for the names of the administrators (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), even if they are lay followers (*upāsaka*) endowed with faith, one should likewise require double the deposit. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Seek out reliable guarantors and clearly draft a formal contract. On the final day of the year, one should inform the Elder (*sthavira*) and the administrators, ensuring that all are made aware of it;
furthermore, one may also inform those lay followers who possess faith."
**The Twentieth Precept on Trading:** If a bhikṣu engages in various forms of trading, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Commentary:* At that time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Upananda took ginger from a market stall and exchanged it for food.
Furthermore, [a monk] beat up old clothes and traded them for new garments with non-Buddhists (tīrthika). The non-Buddhists later regretted the deal and refused to return them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept: "To trade" means to buy cheaply and sell dearly. "To sell" means to increase the price.

"Various kinds of trading" refers to [trading] medicinal substances taken at the proper time (kāla-bhaiṣajya), those not taken at the proper time (akāla-bhaiṣajya), and those taken for seven days (saptāha-bhaiṣajya), and so forth.

Regarding the trading of physical goods, life-sustaining medicines, robes, and other such items among one another: as for the offense herein, if a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture);

if he does not [engage in such trade], it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The method for relinquishing and confessing, and the rules for returning the items, are as explained in the *Dīrghacīvara* (Excess Robe) precept.
Since the preceding precept concerned trading with gold, silver, money, or precious gems, it required that these be relinquished to a *kalpaka* (lay attendant). This [present case]...

If one trades robes for medicine, it is therefore required that they be relinquished to the Saṃgha. This offense applies equally to bhikṣuṇīs; for the three lower groups of followers, it constitutes a duṣkṛta (wrongdoing).

There is no offense if one trades with members of the five groups of renunciants after having personally ascertained the value and ensuring there is no disparity between the items, following the rules of market exchange, and not trading with anyone else; or if one causes a *śuci-puruṣa* (pure person) to conduct the trade; or if...
One who regrets [the transaction] should return it. If one exchanges ghee for oil, or oil for ghee—the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that "various kinds" refers to:

asking the price oneself or sending someone to ask; offering a high price oneself or sending someone to offer a high price; or lowering the price oneself or sending someone to lower the price—when such impure speech is used, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. Upon obtaining the goods, there is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If an object is worth fifty coins but is sought for a hundred, and the bhikṣu says, "I will take it for fifty," such a request is not considered "lowering the price. If one knows that the other person intends to buy the item, one must not snatch it up and buy it; to do so constitutes an offense of *vinayātikrama*.

If a bhikṣu, upon seeing a bowl being sold, thinks, "This bowl is excellent; it will always bring profit in such-and-such a place," he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense at the time of purchase. If he thinks, "I have this wealth, but there is no *pariśuddha-puruṣa* (pure person) [to act as a go-between]; this is a pure transaction," he may purchase it and depart without offense.
If a bhikṣu serves as the *māsaka* (steward) for the Saṃgha and, while traveling to markets to trade for ghee, oil, and all other goods, uses impure speech, he commits a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If he purchases ghee, oil, and so forth for his own sake, and does not employ pure speech in any way, he commits a *naiḥsargika* offense upon obtaining them. If a bhikṣu exchanges with another bhikṣu using impure speech to purchase, or if he uses impure speech in the presence of any of the ninety-six types of renunciants, [he likewise commits an offense].

If one tells the buyer, "There is no offense whatsoever," and a donor, for the sake of a bhikṣu, gives money to a shopkeeper and says, "If a certain bhikṣu comes every day to ask for something, give it to him as you please," then when that bhikṣu later comes to ask for it...

There is no offense in using pure or impure speech [regarding the price] when seeking items. If the goods sought by a bhikṣu are not available at the shop, and the shopkeeper gives him money to purchase them elsewhere, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) if the bhikṣu uses impure speech while seeking the goods at that other location.

If a bhikṣu, when purchasing grain, thinks, "The price will rise later," he commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of purchase and a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* at the time of sale. However, if he thinks, "I fear the grain will be expensive at such-and-such a time;

I shall purchase this grain now so that I may rely upon it for reciting sūtras, sitting in meditation, and practicing the Path," and when the time comes the grain becomes very expensive, there is no offense if he eats what is surplus, gives it to his *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, or uses it to perform meritorious deeds. The same applies to buying bowls, medicine, and so forth.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one buys for profit but does not sell for profit, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of purchase, but no offense at the time of sale. If one buys without seeking profit but sells for profit, there is no offense at the time of purchase, but a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of sale.

If one travels to another region having purchased goods with no original intent to seek profit, even if a profit is realized upon selling them when arriving at that place, there is no offense. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "When buying or selling, if one does not speak according to reality, or uses false or adulterated measures and scales to deceive others, one incurs the offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*).

At the moment of obtaining the goods, one commits the offense of theft (*steya*). Whenever one intends to buy or sell property, one must first fix the mind so as to have no desire for profit; whatever profit is gained in accordance with the circumstances is entirely without offense. Even if the goods are intended for the three robes (*tricīvara*), one should not calculate for profit."

One should not engage in buying and selling. Furthermore, at places where laypeople conduct market transactions, one should not personally negotiate the price; rather, one should have a layperson who is faithful and respectful, or a *śrāmaṇera*, act as the buyer, in which case there is no offense. If no such person is available, one may personally negotiate the price.

Whether two or three times, one may return the price; it should not exceed this. If one colludes with others to set high or low prices, or if one does not truly wish to buy yet falsely increases the other's price, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one wishes to engage in trade, one should employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person)."

Regarding speech: one should say, "I shall exchange this item for that item," and furthermore, one should think in one's mind, "May he obtain my profit, while I do not obtain his profit. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one uses an article subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) to purchase food, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for every mouthful;

if one purchases clothing to wear, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for every instance of wearing it. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The sin of trading is the most grave among all *pāyattika* offenses. It would be better to be a butcher than to engage in trade. Why?

A butcher merely harms animals, whereas a trader deceives and harms everyone—whether monastic or lay, wise or foolish, observant of precepts or violators of them—without exception. Furthermore, such a person constantly harbors evil intent; even if they deal in grain, their mind is always filled with covetous hope."

It causes the world to suffer from famine and the calamities of frost and hail. If one stores salt or other goods, their mind will constantly harbor expectations for rebellion and disorder in distant regions, and the royal highways will become blocked. Such are the evils of those who engage in trade; these traded goods, even if used to prepare food for the Saṃgha, should not be consumed by the monks.

If they are used to build monasteries for the four quarters of the Saṃgha, one must not dwell within them. If they are used to construct stūpas or images, one should not pay homage toward them. Furthermore, it is said that only the Buddha intentionally pays homage to them; ordinary bhikṣus who uphold the precepts should not do so.

One should not make use of this object. If this bhikṣu dies, the Saṃgha should perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to divide these goods. Question: Since he did not make use of these goods while alive, why are they divided as soon as he dies? Answer: This is a commercial transaction.

The transgression is grave. If one were to continue living, because the Saṃgha would consume these goods, the practice would persist without interruption; within the field of merit that is the Saṃgha, such use is not permitted. This would cause [the deceased] to realize there is no merit in this life and lead to the incurrence of heavy retribution in the future.

For these reasons, [the heirs] dare not do so again. Since the bhikṣu has died, there is no longer any motive for buying or selling; therefore, it is permitted to take the goods through a formal ritual (karmavācanā).
The Twenty-first Precept on Keeping an Extra Alms Bowl:

If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms bowl without having made it a formal gift (apariśuddha-dāna), he may possess it for up to ten days. Should he keep it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The group of six monks kept alms-bowls; they retained those that were fine and set aside those that were not.
When the lay devotees went to their quarters and saw the many bowls, they spoke with derision, saying, "It is like a potter's shop."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who established a precept: "It is not permitted to keep an extra bowl. At that time, Ānanda obtained a bowl of high value and wished to give it to Kāśyapa;
however, Kāśyapa was away. Fearing he would commit the offense of keeping an extra bowl, he went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked how many days it would be before Kāśyapa returned. He replied, "In ten days' time. Thereupon, [the Buddha] permitted the keeping [of an extra bowl] for up to ten days.
"Daily" means that one regards [the bowl] as belonging to oneself. "Extra" refers to possessing more than the single bowl currently held and maintained;
this is what is called "extra. There are two kinds of bowls: first, iron; second, clay. Their colors are also of two kinds: first, red; second, black.
Their capacities are also of two kinds: the large bowl holds three *dōng* (pecks), and the small bowl holds... [two pecks].
One and a half *dō* (calibrated according to the Tang *dō*: one *dō* for a large bowl, half a *dō* for a small bowl). This is the measure of a bowl; it should be accepted and maintained.
However, the original Vinaya text does not provide the text for the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*). According to other schools, there is a ritual procedure for acceptance.

One should face a single *bhikṣu*, place the bowl with its opening upward in the left palm, and cover it with the right hand, saying: "Venerable Sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the *bhikṣu* [Name]..."

A. This *pātra* should be accepted according to its proper measure for the sake of long-term use. [This is] stated three times. If there is a reason it must be relinquished, it should be understood as being according to the procedure for relinquishing robes.
Regarding the term *pātra*: this is a vessel that accords with the Dharma, meaning in terms of its substance, color, and measure.

All three are appropriate for use. Regarding their substance, they are made of iron or clay; regarding their color, they are red or black; regarding their capacity, they are three *dō* or two and a half *dō*.
If they exceed three *dō* or fall short of two and a half *dō*, they are not of the proper measure and are not permitted to be accepted or maintained.
"Impure giving" refers to not performing the two kinds of pure giving—either directly or through an intermediary. "May be kept for ten days" means:
One may keep [an extra bowl] for ten days, but not beyond that. If it exceeds ten days, at the appearance of dawn on the eleventh day, there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

Regarding the bowls obtained during those ten days—whether they have been formally assigned (pariṇata) or not, or even if they were lost or forgotten—each and every detail is as explained in the precept concerning extra robes (atireka-cīvara); there is no difference in their characteristics, and thus they are not repeated here.
The method for relinquishing and repenting, as well as the cases where there is no offense, are all exactly the same.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps [an extra bowl] for even one night, she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the three lower assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If she obtains a *kaṃsa*, a small bowl, or a medium-sized bowl, it is permitted to keep them without having performed the ritual of pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*). A *kaṃsa* is a small, shallow bowl; that is to say, a *kaṃsa* is inserted into a small bowl. Small...
The small bowl may be placed inside the medium bowl; the medium bowl may be placed inside the large bowl. One should not keep a wooden bowl, for that is the practice of non-Buddhists.

One should not keep a stone bowl, for that is the bowl of the Tathāgata’s tradition. One should not keep a bowl made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or other precious gems, for that is the practice of laypeople.
One should not paint grapevines, lotus designs, or svastika symbols upon the bowl. One should not [do so].
One’s own name [should not be written on it]. One should not wrap the four sides or the mouth of the bowl; one should not wrap the entire bowl.
One should wrap two-thirds of it, leaving one-third uncovered. If there are many holes or cracks, one should wrap them all. If food enters a hole, it may be picked out as it goes in;
once it has been picked out, there is no offense regarding what remains that cannot be removed. It is permitted to make a bag to contain it, or to make a strap to carry it.
One should carry the bowl under the arm, with the opening facing outward. If the bowl is cracked or broken, it is permitted to repair it.

If one goes forth as a monk who makes bowls, he is permitted to make bowls for the bhikṣus and permitted to keep the tools for making them. It is permitted to fumigate the bowl; one should construct a fumigation furnace.
Whether using a cauldron or a jar, coat them with various kinds of clay mixed with apricot kernels and hemp seeds. Level the ground with ash to create a fumigation altar for the bowl.
Set up a support and place the bowl upon it; cover the bowl with a bowl-stand and heap ash around its four sides.
Press it down with the hand to make it firm. If using firewood or cow dung, pile them around the four sides and burn them.

One should fumigate in this manner (*Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: if using *tila* seeds or sesame seeds, crush them and smear them upon the bowl-oven; place the bowl inside and fumigate it. Once the fumigation is complete, the oven should be carefully lifted and not allowed to be seen by the rain).

The *Nidāna* states: "The keeping of a bowl-cage is permitted. There are two kinds of cages: first, those made by craftsmen, namely potters; second, those made by oneself, namely by cutting a jar or a large pitcher in half. One should use straw chaff to make mud and coat the outside entirely. Use sesame dregs to..."

Apply clay to the interior and wipe it smooth; wait for it to dry. Place rice husks inside and close it with a lid, sealing the rim with clay. One may prop up the bowl using some object so that smoke escapes from within the lid. Cover the opening with ash and pile up cow dung on top; set fire to it from above. One should personally watch the fire;

if one entrusts another person to watch it, the bowl will still not take on the proper color. It should be washed repeatedly before being fired again. One should sweep the ground clean, taking care not to harm any insects. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The almsbowl is the insignia of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

one must not place impure things within it. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should carry the bowl according to the rules for bowls: one must not use it to discard refuse, to hold leftover food, to hold drinks taken after midday, or to hold incense or medicine; it should be lifted with purity and guarded with care."

As with the eyes, one should not use a bowl for drinking after midday; however, it is permitted to use it as a drinking vessel made of copper, iron, or clay. It is also permitted to have a separate vessel for slurping rice gruel. Furthermore, it is said that there are three types of bowls:

the superior holds three *pātra* of rice, excluding soup and vegetables; the inferior holds one *pātra* of rice, excluding soup and vegetables; and the middle is between these two. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that placing a partition inside the bowl is not permitted; however, if a partition is made using a cake or rice, there is no offense.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that if one keeps an extra white iron bowl, an unbaked clay bowl, or any bowl that does not meet the prescribed measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states that there is no offense if [the bowl] is smaller than the measure, larger than the measure, or intended to be given to another person who is about to receive the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). To provide relief...

Regarding their use, although one does not differentiate between them, there is no offense in any case. If one keeps two small bowls for storing soup or vegetables, or for drinking water, as well as a salt dish and a spoon, there is no offense whatsoever. Furthermore, within the large bowl, one may keep small bowls according to what they can contain;

if it accords with one's needs, keeping many is not an offense. One should further keep one large bowl to prevent the occurrence of deficiencies. The World-Honored One permitted only one—neither too many nor too few—which is in accord with the Middle Way, providing for the body while cultivating one’s practice. Know this.

One should receive and use [the bowl] with care, as if protecting one's own eyes. When traveling on a road, one should not carry it exposed or wrapped in the corner of one's robe; rather, it should be placed in a bag and carried by hanging it over the shoulder. If staying within a monastery, one should provide a niche or cave for it.

For those dwelling in an araṇya (hermitage), one should weave bamboo or reeds into a basket, coating its interior and exterior with clay and cow dung, and place the bowl inside. The commentary states: "The term 'one pātra' translates here as 'one sheng' (升); according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, this would be equivalent to seven he (合)."

**The Twenty-second Pācittiya: On Seeking a Bowl with Fewer than Five Repairs** If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has fewer than five repairs and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it. The Saṃgha shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among those present and give it to him.
"One should hold [the bowl], even to the point of repairing it when it is broken; this is the proper time. Commentary:
When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, the bowl of Upananda broke. He entered the city and went from house to house among the lay devotees seeking a bowl.
Each of the lay devotees bought a bowl and gave it to him. He broke one bowl after another until he had obtained many.
The bowl. At another time, when various laypeople gathered and learned of this, they all criticized and disparaged it. The Buddha established a precept for them:
"One who possesses a bowl" refers to one who currently holds and uses a bowl as their own. "With fewer than five patches" means not reaching that number.

"Five patches" refers to each patch being separated by a distance of two finger-widths. "Patch" (綴) means to join together; it refers to stitching, attaching, and mending. Not... [the rule continues].

"Leaking" refers to being capable of holding rice and soup. "Seeking another new bowl because one considers it superior" means that although one currently possesses a bowl that does not leak, one seeks a second bowl from another person out of greed for something new, beautiful, and excellent.

If a bowl has fewer than five patches but does not leak, and one seeks a new bowl [for such reasons], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If it has five or more patches... [it is not an offense].
[This constitutes] an offense of outflow (*sāsrava*). Seeking a new bowl [in such a case] is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). "That bhikṣu" refers to the person who has committed the offense.

"Should go before the Saṃgha to relinquish it" means that it must necessarily be done in the presence of the Saṃgha; furthermore, the relinquishment must take place at this very residence and not at any other residence.

Having relinquished it, he should perform confession. The Saṃgha should then perform a formal act (*karman*) to grant him a bowl. If this bowl is of high value or of fine quality, it should be retained.
Set it aside. Take the one that is the very lowest and most inferior and grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

Once the *karman* has been performed, that bowl should be passed in order among the Saṃgha. If no one takes it at all, it should be returned to that bhikṣu, who shall be made to keep it for as long as he lives.
The bowl he previously possessed should be kept according to the Dharma; this [new] bowl must not be kept.
Since it is intended for constant use, one should act accordingly. One should announce the matter to the Saṃgha and ask them as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I shall inquire about this bowl in order with the Elder.
Having made this announcement, one should hold the bowl out to the Elder. If the Elder wishes to take this bowl, he should accept it.
The bowl of the senior monk (sthavira) should be given to the next-ranking monk. If it is given to that bhikṣu, he should accept it;
he should not refuse to take it out of concern for the Saṃgha, nor should he, on account of this reason, keep the very lowest bowl.
If he accepts it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense. If the second senior monk takes this bowl, he should take the bowl of the second senior monk and give it [to the third].
If [the bowl] is given to that bhikṣu by the third elder, that bhikṣu should accept it;
he should not refuse it out of regard for the Saṃgha, nor should he, on this account, accept the very lowest bowl. If he accepts it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
In this manner, it is passed down successively until it reaches the junior-most bhikṣu. If one takes this bhikṣu’s bowl and returns it to that same bhikṣu, or if one takes...
The bowl of the most junior monk should be given. It should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation):

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha now gives this bowl of the most junior monk (*if it is the bowl of this particular bhikṣu, one should say: 'The Saṃgha now gives this bhikṣu’s inferior bowl'*)."
"Let it be received and kept by monk so-and-so until it breaks. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
The Saṃgha now gives this bowl of the lowest-ranking seat to monk so-and-so to receive and keep until it breaks.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha giving this bowl to this monk, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak. The Saṃgha has consented."
The bowl has been given to the bhikṣu [Name]. Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. (According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya:

first, perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* [the formal motion with one subsequent proclamation] to appoint a bhikṣu endowed with five virtues to distribute the bowl of the offender. The appointed person should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) in the midst of the Saṃgha, saying:

"Venerable sirs, I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall distribute the bowl of the offender. May the venerable ones each bring their own bowls to the midst of the Saṃgha tomorrow. On the following day, the bhikṣus each bring their own bowls to the midst of the Saṃgha. The bhikṣu distributing the bowls takes the bowl of the offender and approaches the Elder; he then praises it.)

That bowl is pure and complete, fit for use. Whether the senior monk accepts it or not should be understood as explained above. This continues until a single bowl is obtained at the end of the procession, which is then entrusted to that bhikṣu with instructions to guard it.

"Until it breaks" means that it should be held; this does not refer to formal ritual acceptance (*karmavācanā*), but rather that he must carefully protect this most inferior bowl until it breaks, maintaining and using it throughout that time. "This is the proper time" means:
This is the method for holding the lowest-grade alms bowl that one should maintain. That bhikṣu must guard this bowl:
he must not place it where tiles or stones might fall; he must not place it beneath a leaning staff or beneath a leaning sword;
he must not place it beneath hanging objects, on the road, upon stones, beneath fruit trees, or on uneven ground; nor may he hold it with only one hand.

One should bring the two bowls close together, leaving a space between them sufficient for a finger’s width. One must not open the door while holding both bowls with one hand, except when exercising care.
One must not place them inside the threshold, beneath the door leaf, beneath a rope bed or a wooden bed, between beds, or in the corners;
these are exceptions for temporary placement. One must not stand and shake the bowls, nor even let them strike one another, so as to cause them to break. One must not [do so].

One should intentionally break it or cause it to be lost, thereby rendering it unfit for use as an alms-bowl (*pātra*). A *bhikṣuṇī* commits the same offense; for the three lower groups of disciples, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

There is no offense in the following cases: if the bowl has fewer than five patches and leaks; if one seeks a new bowl because of this; if one requests it from a relative or from those who have left the household life;

if one requests it on behalf of another; if another requests it for oneself; if one obtains it without having requested it; or if one receives it when it is being distributed to the Saṃgha according to seniority.

If one purchases an animal for its own value (the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya states: "The bowl-carrying bhikṣu shall hand over his bowl to that bhikṣu and say: 'This bowl must not be kept as a personal possession, nor should it be treated as a separate property'").

Nor should one give it away to others. One should examine it carefully and use it slowly and properly until it is worn out. One should keep two bowl-covers (*pātra-puṭa*): place the fine one in this spare bowl, and place the old one currently in use in the other. When going for alms, one should take both bowls;

if one receives fine food, place it in the spare bowl, and if one receives coarse food, place it in the old bowl. One should eat from the old bowl. One should first wash the spare bowl, and likewise, when drying or storing them, always prioritize the spare bowl.

When placing them inside a niche or fumigating them with incense, always place the spare bowl first in the superior location. When traveling on foot, have someone carry the old bowl while one carries the spare bowl oneself. If there is no one to hold it, place the spare bowl [in a secure spot].

The new alms bowl should be placed on the left shoulder, while the old bowl should be set at the right side; one should carry it away oneself. This disciplinary measure shall remain in effect for as long as one lives, or until the bowl breaks, during which time it must be carefully guarded. If one does not follow this rule of practice, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose bowl was broken into many pieces. He drilled holes in them and joined them together with fine cords. After eating, he would untie and wash them; having washed them, he would join them back together again, thereby neglecting the cultivation of wholesome qualities.

The Buddha said: "If a bowl is difficult to obtain, you may repair it as you wish. However, if it is easy to obtain elsewhere, you should discard it and seek a better one. There are five methods for repairing an iron bowl with rivets: first, filling the hole with a fine needle; second, attaching a small iron plate and hammering it in to make it firm; third, joining it like the teeth of a fish; fourth, folding the edges like a hem.

[The bowl] is broken. [First,] the interior and exterior are clamped together. Fourth, the hole is covered with iron plates and fastened all around with nails. Fifth, powdered filings are used; there are two kinds: first, iron filings from a grindstone, and second, stone powder. To repair an iron bowl first, and to repair a ceramic bowl next:

when applying the powder to seal the hole, one takes oil and the powder in an iron bowl and grinds them thoroughly with an iron hammer before using them to fill the hole. It is then heated over a fire until it hardens. If it remains rough or coarse, apply more oil and fumigate it according to the prescribed method.

If the ceramic bowl has cracks or pores, use sugar mixed with clay to fill them and dry them by heating over a fire. If it is cracked or broken, carve it into the shape of a drum-shape (drum-waist) and fill it with an iron drum. Cover the top with clay and use it after fumigating it with fire. Thus it is said.
Regarding the term "sugar" mentioned here, it refers to candied sugar (i.e., lump sugar).

**The Twenty-third Precept: On Having an Unrelated Weaver Weave Robes.** If a bhikṣu personally solicits thread and has an unrelated weaver weave three robes for him, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Thullaccaya* (grave offense);
*pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). The commentary states: When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, Upananda wished to sew a saṃghāṭī robe.

He entered the city and went to the houses of various lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), seeking thread everywhere. Having been given much thread through his begging, he took it and gave it to a weaver, instructing him to weave it.
When making the three robes, one might personally perform the spinning and personally supervise the weaving. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged it.
The Buddha therefore established a precept: "As for 'begging for oneself,' it means going about from place to place to personally seek and beg for it.
As for 'thread,' it refers to the ten kinds of cloth thread mentioned above. 'Non-relative' is as explained above. 'Weaver' refers to a person who weaves cloth."
The three robes are explained as above. Regarding the offenses herein: if both the weaver and the provider of the thread are not relatives;

or if the weaver is not a relative while the provider of the thread is a relative; or if the provider of the thread is not a relative while the weaver is a relative—in all these cases, an offense is committed.
Whether one supervises the weaving, weaves it oneself, or makes the *vāna* (weaving frame), it is all a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). One must relinquish [the robe] and repent.

The method of restoration is the same as that explained for the precept concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*). A bhikṣuṇī commits the same offense; for the three lower assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
There is no offense if the weaver and the one who provided the thread are both relatives, or if one weaves for oneself a bowl-bag or a meditation belt.

Girdles, hats, socks, and cloth for wrapping sandals, etc. (According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*: if one begs thread from a non-relative, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one causes a non-relative to weave it, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;

if one weaves it oneself, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one pays a price for it, there is no offense. If, with a deceitful mind, one describes one's own superior virtues and obtains an object thereby, one incurs both a *duṣkṛta* and a *pāyattika* offense simultaneously. If one possesses actual virtues, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* and a *pāyattika* offense. This applies even if the weaver is a relative.)

Because one does not know the proper time, causing others to become distressed, or manifesting strange signs, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in all such cases. The Sarvāstivādins say: if one has few robes and it is the proper time to beg for robes, one should not beg for thread to make robes; however, there is no offense if thread is required for sewing robes or making a belt.

**The Twenty-fourth Precept: Exhorting to Weave Fine Robes** If a monk, when a householder or a householder’s wife has employed a weaver to weave a robe for that monk, should go to the weaver’s place before having been invited by them of his own accord and say, "Weave this robe for me; give it to me."
"It is very fine weaving; make it broad, large, and firm, and I shall give you a small amount of payment.
If that bhikṣu gives him payment—even as much as the value of a single meal—and [the weaver] obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery. A certain householder produced high-quality thread and had a weaver weave a robe for Bāḷhika (Upananda).
The weaver went to the monastery and informed him; he then immediately went to the householder’s home.
He further requested thread from his wife and gave it to a weaver, instructing him to weave a garment that was vast, exquisite, and extremely durable, while promising to increase the weaver's wages.
Once the garment was finished, the householder saw that it was not the one he had previously ordered to be woven.
He then inquired and learned the reason for this, and immediately censured the practice. The Buddha consequently established a precept.

At that time, there were lay devotees who invited monks to a *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony), but the bhikṣus, being hesitant, did not dare to accept; nor did they dare to request anything other than what was offered.
Therefore, he further established the rule that one must not first accept an invitation to a *pravāraṇā*. "Exquisite weaver" means to make it refined and wonderful; it also refers to making the robe.
The meaning of "vast and firm" (*vipula-dṛḍha*): "Vast" (*vipula*) means to measure the length of the feet; "great" (*mahat*) means to measure the width of the feet; "firm" (*dṛḍha*) means solid;
"fine and dense" (*sūkṣma-saṃhata*) means subtle and compact. Regarding "even for the price of a single meal":
this refers to the labor cost of providing even the very least, namely a single meal. The remaining phrases are explained as before. Within this—

Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for a *pravāraṇā*, goes to seek robes and obtains them, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If he does not obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The method for forfeiture, confession, and restoration is as stated above. Bhikṣuṇīs commit the same offense. For the three lower assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one requests from relatives or from those who have left the household life; or if another requests on one's behalf, etc. (*Vinaya*).

The *Vibhāṣā* states: Regarding this robe, regardless of whether it is of the proper measure or not, one incurs an offense in all cases. If one instructs a weaver to weave a robe for oneself but does not provide the payment for the food [of the laborers], yet obtains a fine robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
However, if one uses one's own thread and has a weaver weave it, there is no offense.

**The Twenty-fifth Precept: Taking Back a Robe After Having Given It** If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, either takes it back himself or instructs another to take it away, saying, "Give me back my robe;
I will not give it to you," and if the other bhikṣu returns the robe and he takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Previously, Upananda had given a robe to a disciple of Nanda.

Later, because he called him to go [somewhere] and the disciple did not comply, Upananda became enraged and forcibly seized the robe back. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established this precept:
"When one has previously given a robe to a bhikṣu," this indicates that it was not a temporary gift, nor was it a loan for wearing; rather, it refers to a formal resolution made from the outset.

"He gave it to another. Later, "he became angry" indicates a lack of affection; because the object contradicted his own desires, he gave rise to resentment and created an evil mental karma (*manas-karman*).
"If he took it himself," this indicates an evil physical karma (*kāya-karman*) committed.
"If he instructed another to take it," this indicates an evil verbal karma (*vāk-karman*) committed. "Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you."
This refers to hoping to obtain a previously held robe, yet instead seeking it back [from another]. "If a bhikṣu returns the robe" means the robe has already been separated from that bhikṣu’s person.
"He takes the robe" means taking the robe into his hand and forming the thought that he has acquired it for himself. Regarding the offenses herein:
if he seizes it and hides or stores it away, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); if he does not hide or store it away, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If it is placed on a tree, a wall, a fence, a stake, a shelf, a bed, a loom, or a floor mat, taking it away from its original location constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;

taking it without removing it from its location constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The method for relinquishing the item and performing the confession is the same as above. A *bhikṣuṇī* commits the same offense; for the three lower groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one is not acting out of anger, or if the person to whom the robe belongs knows of one’s intention to repent and immediately returns the robe.
If another person exhorts him to return the robe; or if it is unreasonable for the one who borrowed the robe to take it back by force; or if there is fear that the robe will be lost or damaged;

or if that person has broken the precepts, broken right view, or broken proper conduct; or if he has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), or has been expelled (*pabbājanīya-kamma*), or is liable to be expelled;
or if, for the sake of these matters, there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—in all such cases, one may take it back.

Taking [the robe] and not returning it. There is no offense [if the following apply]: (according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if one takes back from a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) who has been granted training, or from one undergoing *parivāsa* (probation), or from one who is joyful in mind, or from one who is blind, one-eyed, deaf, or mute;

or if one takes the robe of one who has been expelled for holding evil views or expelled for misconduct; in all such cases, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If one takes back from one who is insane, mentally deranged by illness, or one who has committed the four *pārājikas*, the five *ānantaryas*, or the five types of persons, as well as the robes of the other four assemblies, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.

If a nun takes back a monk’s robe, it is an *dukkaṭa*; if she takes back the robes of a nun or others, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The essence of this precept is: first, one fundamentally gave the robe to another; later, for the sake of causing distress, one temporarily takes it back. This is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If the robe is returned to the other, one must perform a *pāyattika* confession. If one first fundamentally gave the robe to another, and later fundamentally took it back.

One incurs an offense according to the value of the money [involved]. If one first temporarily gives a robe to another and subsequently takes it back, there is no offense. If, out of anger and with the intent to cause distress, one temporarily seizes it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). However, if a teacher temporarily seizes it for the purpose of subduing a disciple and causing them to abandon unwholesome dharmas, there is no offense.
**The Twenty-sixth Precept: On Medicines Exceeding Seven Days.** If a bhikṣu has medicinal remnants—namely ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—he may consume them for up to seven days.
If he consumes them beyond the seventh day, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. During the autumn months, the bhikṣus were afflicted by wind-related ailments;
their bodies became withered and they developed malignant sores. The Buddha permitted them to consume the five kinds of medicine—whether at the proper time or not—at the occasion of being ill.
At that time, Piṅgalavatsa’s disciple accumulated and stored a great quantity of the five kinds of medicine, which spread everywhere.
"Indiscriminately. When the householders saw that the lodgings were foul and filthy, with such provisions strewn about in disorder, they all felt revulsion and reproach.

On account of this, the Tathāgata established the precept. "One who is ill" refers to one whose body is afflicted by disease, for whom a physician has prescribed the consumption of a certain number of medicinal substances.
"Remnants" refers to what has been received from another and then—whether eaten or not—left over until the following day; at that point, it is termed [remnant].
"Remnants" refers to the five kinds of medicinal substances: ghee (*sarpis*), oil, fresh butter (*navanīta*), honey, and rock sugar (*śarkarā*).
Ghee is the milk of cows, buffaloes, and the like, produced by churning; alternatively, it is produced by placing medicinal herbs or leaves into the milk.
Oil refers to oils derived from hemp, sesame, radish, and so forth. Fresh butter is the milk of cows, buffaloes, and the like [in its unrefined state].
It is produced as follows: that which is immature first transforms from milk into curd; curd transforms into fresh butter (*navanīta*);

fresh butter transforms into clarified butter (*ghṛta*); clarified butter transforms into the finest essence (*sarpis*). This finest essence is the supreme medicine. As for "honey," it refers to the honey of various bees.
As for *śarkarā* (stone-honey): it is the hardened product of boiled sugarcane juice that has been refined; this is called *śarkarā*. It is of two kinds, black and white.
The white variety is purely sweet in taste and can cure feverish diseases. The black variety is slightly bitter in taste and can cure cold-natured diseases.
As for various types of sugarcane syrup—whether thick or thin, unrefined, or diluted with water—all of these are likewise [considered *śarkarā*].
It is comprised within stone honey (*śarkarā*). If sugarcane juice has not yet fermented, it is permitted to drink it outside of the proper time;

once it has fermented, it is not permitted. Sugarcane itself is permitted as food during the proper time. At one time, a bhikṣu saw others making stone honey by mixing it with various other substances;

he did not dare to eat it outside of the proper time. The Buddha said, "I permit you to eat it outside of the proper time. Such is the proper method of preparation. If one suffers from wind-related ailments, [one may use] oil.
Fat can serve as medicine. There are five kinds of fat: namely, bear, fish, donkey, pig, and *makara* (sea-monster) fat.

These should be received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and strained at the proper time, following the procedure for consuming oil. One should filter them until they are pure and clean, receive them from another, and formally accept and maintain them.

They may be consumed as one wishes until the illness has been cured. It is not permitted to receive, cook, strain, or consume them at an improper time. This applies equally to clarified butter (*sarpis*).

Rock honey (*śarkarā*) can eliminate febrile ailments; honey treats phlegm (*kapha*) as well as water-retention diseases. Old granulated sugar (*phāṇita*) also removes phlegm. Ghee and honey likewise treat wind-phlegm.
Thin molasses (*guḍa*) can eliminate the three diseases of wind, phlegm, and heat. Regarding "those which may be consumed for up to seven days":
this means that the day one first receives the medicine from another and it enters one's hand is counted as the first day, continuing until...
For seven days. Within the seven-day period, whether it be at the proper time or the improper time, one may take and consume [the medicine] oneself.
This statement of "seven days" indicates the maximum duration; however, when first receiving the medicine, one must perform the formal ritual (*adhikāra*).
One should hold the medicine before a *bhikṣu* and say: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the *bhikṣu* [Name], because of the cause of a certain illness..."
"This is seven-day medicine. Because it is to be consumed while kept for seven nights, I now receive it from the Venerable One" (recite this three times;

if one intends to consume it for fewer days, one may state the specific number of days accordingly. According to the *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha*, it must be within the permitted time: having washed one's hands and received the medicine, place it in the left hand and cover it with the right hand, performing the ritual act before the other person).
"If one consumes it after the seven days have passed" means that one has exceeded the prescribed limit. Regarding the offense herein: from the day the medicine is obtained... until [the seventh day].
Within those seven days, whether one obtains it or not, whether it is a pure gift or an impure gift, regardless of how much there is, when the light of the eighth day appears,
it becomes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in its entirety— even if it is given away to others, lost, destroyed, or otherwise disposed of.
The method for relinquishing and returning [the medicine] is exactly as explained in the *Dīrghacīvara* rule; the only difference here is that this concerns medicine and the seven-day limit.

If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) but does not relinquish the medicine, and instead trades it for other medicine, there is one offense of forfeiture and one offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
The Saṃgha shall perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to return the medicine to this bhikṣu, who should then use it to anoint his feet or light a lamp. [This applies to] a bhikṣuṇī as well.

The same offense applies. For the three lower groups of practitioners, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: if one uses ghee or oil after seven days have passed to smear on a door hinge;
or if one gives honey or rock sugar to a park keeper; or if, upon reaching the seventh day, one relinquishes it to a *bhikṣu* to eat. (Regarding "smearing on the feet":

this refers to applying oil at a time when it can alleviate wind-disorders (*vāta*). Furthermore, as this area of the heel connects with the tendons of the foot, applying oil there can cause the eyes to become clear and bright. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It should be relinquished to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha shall relinquish it to a layperson. [The *śramaṇera*... )

Furthermore, if it is used for lighting a lamp, that bhikṣu may not use it; no bhikṣu at all may consume it. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If a śrāmaṇera has been given alms-food for less than seven days, and on the eighth day there is an urgent illness requiring its use, one may request food from the śrāmaṇera;
there is no offense. Regarding medicines, they do not exceed four types. The first is *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (timely medicine), which refers to rice, parched grain flour, cakes, and fruit.

Roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, and so forth, which may be eaten from dawn until midday, but are not permitted to be consumed outside of that time—these are called "medicines of the proper time" (*kālabhaiṣajya*).
Second are the "medicines of the improper time" (*akālabhaiṣajya*), namely the eight kinds of syrups: first, pear syrup;
second, jambu fruit syrup (shaped like a watermelon, purple in color, sour and sweet); third, jujube syrup; fourth, sugarcane syrup; fifth, *vīra* fruit syrup; sixth, *śā*... [text fragment]
7. Lodhaka juice (the clear liquid of lotus root); 8. Pālūṣa juice (a fruit resembling the jujube and also similar to the *āmra* fruit); 9. Grape juice.
Aside from these eight juices, other liquids such as those from mandarin oranges, pomelos, pomegranates, plantains, and so forth, which do not cause intoxication, may also serve as juice.

These should be strained using a clean vessel until they are clear like the color of water, purified by dripping water [into them], and then received from the hands of a person who has performed the purification rites.
Facing a single bhikṣu, one should recite the ritual formula: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name]..."
"Due to the cause of a certain illness, this [substance], which is non-time [medicine] (*vikālabhojana*), is for the purpose of being consumed outside of the proper time.
I now receive it from the Venerable One. (Recite this three times. Having received it, one may eat it after midday. This is called non-time medicine;

it is not permitted to receive it on one day and store it until the next day to drink. Whoever drinks it shall be dealt with according to the law. Third is the seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), as described above.
Ghee and the like, having been received from another and having undergone the formal ritual for a bhikṣu, may be taken with one's own hands and consumed for a maximum duration of seven days;
these are called "seven-day medicines" (saptāhika-bhaiṣajya). Fourth are the "life-long medicines" (yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya), namely:

harītakī (commonly abbreviated in secular usage as "hazizuo"), vibhītaka (resembling a peach, its medicinal function being identical to that of harītakī), āmalaka (the *yuganzi* fruit), śrīparṇī, and pippalī.
Roots such as *bhaṭā*, black pepper, and other roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits that are suitable for medicinal use—including various pills, powders, decoctions, and ointments;
all that is salty, bitter, sour, or pungent, even down to ashes and soil—that which is unfit for food, yet is appropriate medicine for the causes and conditions of a chronic illness:
having received this from another and performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) before a bhikṣu, and so forth...
"For as long as life lasts, it is permitted to take [these medicines] oneself. One should add the formal ritual formula as follows: 'Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], because of the cause of a certain illness, shall take these [specific] medicines for as long as life lasts, for the purpose of keeping them overnight and consuming them over a long period.
I now receive them from the Venerable One' (recite this three times). If the four types of medicine are mixed together, one should act [as follows]."
The first medicine is to be taken as it is. If the latter three medicines are mixed together, they should be taken as the second medicine.
If the latter two medicines are mixed together, they should be taken as the third medicine. If the last one is mixed with the very last one, it should be taken as the fourth medicine.
However, these four medicines are all permitted for consumption solely for the purpose of treating illness. At the time of taking them...
One should conceive the thought that one is treating a disease before being fit to eat; this is just like the first type of medicine.

One accepts food for the purpose of healing the ulcer of hunger and accomplishing the work of the Path, not for the sake of sweetness or nourishing the body. As the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"If one uses time-medicine (*kālabhaiṣajya*) and so forth to assist in forming a seven-day medicine, there is no fault in taking it as a seven-day medicine. Or, if one uses seven-day medicine and so forth to assist in forming a lifetime medicine (*yāvajjīvika*), there is no fault in taking it as a lifetime medicine. Or, if one uses seven-day medicine..."

[These] assist in the formation of *kālāhāra* (food to be consumed during the proper time). It should be taken as *kālāhāra*, because its potency is predominant and it assists [the primary substance] in its formation. If the potencies of the various components were equal, one would determine [the classification] according to their names.

The *Mūla-karman-ṭīkā* states: "However, when sugar is prepared in the Western Regions (*pāścātya-deśa*), rice grits are always added; when rock honey (*śarkarā*) is prepared, milk and oil are added. The Buddha permitted these as 'non-time' (*akāla*) foods, opening them for consumption to prevent coarse behavior and to provide sustenance for those on long journeys.

In the islands of the South Sea, they boil tree sap into wine and then make sugar balls, which are eaten entirely at non-proper times. Based on this principle, even if East Asian candied sugar is used at a non-proper time, it should still be permissible to eat. Why? Because while the sugarcane itself is *kālāhāra*, its juice is considered 'non-time. Although rice and *maku* (leaven) are said to be..."

At that time, why would the consumption of sweetmeat balls (*modaka*) be prohibited after noon? Although a detailed examination reveals this to be logical, in practice, people each act according to their own inclinations. Thick, turbid apricot soup is certainly not permitted within the prescribed limits; honey-boiled yam is definitively subject to the prohibitions. The *Vinayasamgraha* states:

At that time, the juice of the sugarcane itself serves as a *yāmakālika* (medicinal) substance; the sugar is for seven days; once it has been burnt and reduced to ash, it is for the duration of life (*yāvajjīvika*). Other substances should be understood by analogy with these. There are six kinds of fermented sour liquids (*sukta*): first, great vinegar (*mahāsukta*); second, barley vinegar (*yavasūkta*); third, medicinal vinegar (*bhaiṣajyasūkta*); fourth, small vinegar (*kṣudrasūkta*);

fifth, curd-liquor vinegar (*dadhimanda-sūkta*); and sixth, churned curd-liquor vinegar (*manthitadadhimanda-sūkta*). When drinking them, one should add a few drops of water to purify them and strain them through a silk cloth. If their color is like that of bamboo or reeds, they may be consumed at the proper time (*kāla*), at improper times (*vikāla*), or when ill.

If you are free from illness, you may drink it as you wish. Regarding various fruits and the like intended for making fermented drinks (*mantha*): if they are received during the proper time (*kāla*), one should crush them with clean hands, mix them with water, and clarify them; these may be drunk only during the proper time. If one prepares them oneself outside of the proper time (*vikāla*), drinking them outside of the proper time is permitted.

If one has an unordained person (*anupasampanna*) prepare them, they may be drunk at both proper and improper times. If one wishes to make a fermented drink that can be consumed until the following day (*yāmika-mantha*), one should prepare it during the proper time, receive it during the proper time, perform the ritual consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in the presence of another person, and then take and drink it oneself until the end of the first watch of the night.

If this time has passed, one must not drink it. As for those drunk during the proper time, it matters whether they have been strained or not; however, for those drunk outside of the proper time, they must necessarily be clarified by straining. The six types of fermented acids (*sukta*) should be understood according to these same principles. There are five kinds [of these].

A person may possess seven-day medicines under the following five conditions: first, a traveler; second, one who has fasted; third, a sick person; fourth, a guardian of a monastery; and fifth, a laborer. When traveling, if granulated sugar is mixed with rice, one should remove the rice by hand and eat it.

If it is placed within roasted flour (maṣa), it should be washed with water. If it adheres, scrape it off with a bamboo slip and wash it again; eating it thus incurs no offense. If it cannot be made free of taints, first wash it with water, then crush it with the hands and throw it into pure water, straining it with a cloth;

it may then be drunk at improper times. However, regarding these sugars and the like, whether at the proper or improper time, and whether one is ill or not, eating them incurs no offense. This applies equally to sugarcane, oil, sesame, and so forth, provided they are not... [text ends].

If honey is received at the proper time but pressed out at an improper time, even if it has been filtered and kept as a reserve, it should not be consumed. However, if honey is purified by sprinkling water upon it, it may be eaten at will, both during the proper time and at improper times.

If there is a cause for illness and a physician instructs one to take "unusual" medicine, one should also take it in order to eliminate various toxins; this should be procured by those with faith. If one takes garlic as medicine, one must not use the Saṃgha’s bedding or the areas for defecation and urination.

One should not enter the midst of the Saṃgha, nor prostrate to the Buddha or circumambulate the stūpas. If laypeople come, one should not preach the Dharma to them, nor go to their invitations. One should stay in a peripheral room. Once the medication has been finished, one should remain for seven more days to allow the foul odor to dissipate, then bathe the body and clothes to ensure they are both clean and pure. As for that [place]...

Regarding one's dwelling: it should be swept, sprinkled, and cleanly plastered. If one has consumed *húcōng* (Allium ascalonicum), one should abstain for three days; if *zésuàn* (Allium tuberosum), for one day. When ill, one should wear various incenses and apply fragrant ointments to the body; however, one should not enter the assembly nor preach the Dharma to laypeople.

Once the illness has been cured, these items should be discarded immediately. One must bathe both body and clothing before resuming normal activities. If someone with faith offers incense as a gift, it is appropriate to accept it, place it at the head of the bed, or apply it to the door panels, occasionally smelling it with the nose;

this can cause the eyes to become clear. Flowers may be treated in the same manner. Once the seven-day medicine has been formally accepted, one should form the mental resolve: "I shall consume this medicine for seven days. If one consumes it without having made this formal resolve, one incurs an *āpatti* of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) with every swallow. If [one uses it] merely for the sake of a fine appearance... [or] to delude others... [text continues].

If one consumes [medicines] for their flavor, or seeks physical robustness, or with a deceitful mind, taking various medicinal drugs constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, while actually consuming them, one should inform fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*), saying: "I have already finished taking medicine for one day; six days remain, and I shall take it.

This should be announced for each day up to the seventh. *Yi* (the commentator) says: "The word 'again' (*punar*) refers to the improper time (*vikāla*). 'Maintaining' (*dhāraṇa*) means performing the ritual act of formal acceptance (*vidhi-samādāna*) in the presence of others."

**The Twenty-seventh Precept: Regarding Seeking and Using a Rain-Bathing Robe Too Early.** If a bhikṣu has one month remaining of the spring season, he should seek a rain-bathing robe; he may use it for bathing once half a month remains.
If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bathing robe more than one month in advance, or uses it for bathing more than half a month in advance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[The Buddha said: "Tī. The commentary explains: When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, the Mother of Viśākhā invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha. At that time, it rained heavily.
The Buddha ordered the bhikṣus to bathe in the rain. A maidservant came to announce that the time had arrived; from afar, she saw the bhikṣus.
They all bathed naked, which they claimed was the practice of non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthika). He returned and informed his master, who again commanded him to go and invite [the Buddha].
When the Buddha arrived at his house and had finished receiving the offerings, he immediately made a request: "May the World-Honored One permit me to provide food for the visiting bhikṣus."

The Buddha granted permission for all eight types of provisions to be supplied for life: food for a monk traveling on a long journey, food for a sick monk, medicine for a sick monk, food for one tending to the sick, rice-gruel to be provided to monks, rain-bathing robes to be provided, and bathing robes to be given to bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) immediately sought these at all times—spring, summer, and winter—constantly.

[The Buddha] prescribed the rain-bathing robe (*varṣāśāṭī*). [A monk], not relinquishing his rain-bathing robe, used it for other purposes. Even though he already possessed a rain-bathing robe, he bathed naked.

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept: "When one month of spring remains"—meaning that of the four months of spring, three months have already passed and one month remains;
that is, from the sixteenth day of the third month until the tenth day of the fourth month.
It is on the fifth day. "One should seek the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-bath robe)" means that one should beg for it during this month.
When heavy rain occurs, one bathes while wearing it; therefore, it is called the rain-bath robe.

"It should be used for bathing during the half-month" refers to the latter half-month, meaning it is only permitted to be used starting from the first day of the fourth month. [This is] after one month has passed.
"Seeking beforehand" means seeking before the sixteenth day of the third month.
If someone brings a gift on their own initiative before that time, one should perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification) and keep it until the time for seeking arrives.
"Using it for bathing more than half a month before" means using it before the first day of the fourth month; this is to prevent the difficulty of making preparations at the last moment.
As the rainy season approaches and the days for the summer retreat draw near, it is permitted to seek rain-clothing (varṣāśāṭī) one month prior to the end of the preceding summer.
One should not exceed this time, nor should one seek it during the summer retreat itself. This is because during the retreat, one’s primary focus should be on practicing the Path;

one must not engage in the pursuit or acquisition of goods, as such activities would obstruct and cause the abandonment of one's principal practice. Furthermore, until the fourth month has arrived, it is not considered a major [offense].

During the rainy season, bathing is therefore not permitted. From this it should be understood that one must not bathe while wearing robes during light rain, nor may one enter other bodies of water to bathe while wearing them.
Regarding the offense herein: if one seeks [the robes] before the sixteenth day of the third month.

If one uses [the rain-cloak] before the first day of the fourth month, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The rules for relinquishing and the method for repentance and restoration are the same as those mentioned above.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense, because nuns do not possess rain-cloaks. There is no offense if, having relinquished the rain-cloak, one then uses it for another purpose;
or if one wears a bathing-cloak while bathing; or if there is no rain-cloak; or if one makes a bathing-cloak from it (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This garment...").

One must not accept [the rain-bathing robe] as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*). One must not perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhaka-dāna*) with it.
