One must not wear it when entering rivers or ponds, nor when bathing during light rain. Furthermore, one must not bathe naked; one should instead wear a *saṃkakṣikā* or other old garments.

One must not wear the rain-bathing robe for various other activities; it should only be worn for bathing when there is heavy rain. If the rain suddenly stops while one is still covered in moisture, one may wear it to enter other bodies of water to bathe.

When eating, if one wishes to apply oil to the body, or during illness, or in places where many people pass, one may tie both ends together to create a barrier. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it must be relinquished. A single bhikṣu should make this proclamation within the Saṃgha: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe. Thus three times.

It is said: if one discards it on the sixteenth day, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense. Once discarded, it may be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*). One may also perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) before a monk who is a kinsman, and enter other bodies of water to bathe; there is no offense in making various kinds of garments [from it]. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"There are two purposes for keeping a rain-bathing robe (*varṣā-śāṭī*): first, during the rainy season, to shield the four sides while bathing therein; second, when the weather is hot, to likewise shield oneself while bathing therein. Furthermore, since it rains frequently during the summer months, one may constantly wrap the three robes in it while carrying them about.

If it is an intercalary month, one should not seek [the robe] before the second month. It is stated that a bhikṣu incurs no offense for not keeping a rain-bathing robe. [The author] comments: According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, for those who observe the *pūrvavārṣika* (early) retreat, as previously mentioned...

Regarding the proper time, one should seek [the robes] and should store them. It is not permitted to continue using them until the half-month prior to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. For those who observe the later *varṣā*, they may seek them according to their preference, either before or after [the retreat], but they must not continue using them until the half-month prior to the latter *pravāraṇā*.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, for both those who observe the earlier and later *varṣā*, it is forbidden to store or use them as of the fifteenth day of the seventh month. As for the term *saṃkakṣikā*, it refers to the short inner skirt.

**The Twenty-eighth Precept: Regarding the Retention of Urgent Alms-garments Past the Designated Time.** If a bhikṣu, while the ten days of the final month of the three-month summer retreat have not yet elapsed, receives an urgent alms-garment (*ātyayika-cīvara*), that bhikṣu, knowing it to be an urgent alms-garment, shall accept it.
Having accepted it, he may retain it until the time for [the distribution of] robes. If he retains it beyond that time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Śikṣāpada*: An offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in the country of Vairaṇyā, having completed the summer retreat, he permitted the bhikṣus to receive their summer robes.
However, the group of six [monks] constantly begged for robes at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and they even begged for robes before the retreat had concluded.

They also received robes. At that time, after Upananda had completed his retreat in one location, he heard that those who were observing the retreat in another location had obtained a great deal of robe-material.
He immediately went there and shared in the distribution of robes at various places; having received a large portion, he brought it back.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "One must not constantly beg for robes at all times, nor while the retreat has not yet concluded."
Regarding the begging for robes and the receiving of robes: one must not remain in residence at this location while receiving a share of robes from another place.

At that time, King Prasenajit dispatched two long-serving senior ministers, Śoṇa and Uttara, to go and suppress the rebels. The ministers thought to themselves, "We do not yet know whether we shall return from this campaign.
We should prepare food and offer robes to the Saṃgha in advance. The bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat...
Not daring to accept the robe as the period was not yet complete, he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to accept an urgent gift of robes.

For this reason, he established a precept for the bhikṣus: "The ten days before the completion of the three-month summer retreat" refers to when the first three months of the summer *varṣā* have not yet concluded and ten days still remain before the time of the *pravāraṇā*, which is the beginning of the seventh month.
The six days refer to the period from the sixth to the fifteenth day. Regarding "urgent robe-gifts" (*ātyayika-cīvara*): they are acquired upon acceptance, but lost if not accepted.
This refers to when a person, due to urgent or difficult circumstances, offers a robe to the Sangha to seek merit and blessings, such as when preparing for a military expedition.

If one encounters a serious illness, or if it is the time for a woman about to give birth, giving at such times as these is [the "urgent robe offering"]. If this period has passed, one no longer gives;
therefore, it is called the "urgent robe offering" (*ātyayika-cīvara*). The phrase "knowing this to be the urgent robe offering" indicates that it is not any other type of robe.
As for all other robes, they must be received only after the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded.

Even if a donor offers them during the retreat, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint one person as the robe-keeper (*cīvara-paṭiggāhaka*) for the Saṃgha; these shall be distributed once the retreat is over. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Except for robes offered in times of urgency, all robes given during the *varṣā* must wait until the time of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony). To distribute them during the retreat constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding those who should receive them, it means they are eligible to receive them.
Regarding the time for robes: if one does not accept them, the person offering them loses the merit and benefit, and the bhikṣu also loses the benefit of the robe.
For this reason, accepting them is permitted. "Having accepted" means having received the robe so that it enters one's hand.
"Up until the time for robes, one should store them" means storing or keeping them; this refers to the period after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony until one has accepted the *kāṭhina* robe.

The month [of Kārttika] and the five months during which the *kaṭhina* robe is received constitute the "robe season. During these two periods, one may keep extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) without violating the precepts;
therefore, it is said that one "should keep" them. (The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: The reason the one-month period is called the "robe season" is that it follows the conclusion of the rainy retreat.)

The donor provided abundant food, drink, clothing, and offerings to the assembly of monks, while the bhikṣus themselves engaged in various tasks such as washing and dyeing robes. Due to these circumstances, all [monastic rules] were relaxed for one month; therefore, it is called the "robe season" (kālacīvaram).
If one keeps it beyond the limit, it means exceeding five months and fifteen days.

If there is no *kaṭhina* robe, by the fifteenth day of the eighth month, this robe must be relinquished, or given as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), or if the three robes are incomplete, it should be used for formal acceptance and maintenance.
Otherwise, at dawn on the sixteenth day, there is an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If there is a *kaṭhina* robe, [the period extends] until the tenth day of the twelfth month.

On the fifth day, this robe should be relinquished as previously prescribed. Otherwise, on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month at the appearance of the dawn light, it becomes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Regarding the distinctions in the characteristics of these offenses:

if ten days remain before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and one receives an urgent gift of robes, one should keep them until the proper time for robes. If nine days remain and one receives an urgent gift...

Regarding robes: it is permitted to keep them until the time for the robe-offering, with an additional one day. In this manner, even if there is only one day remaining before the time for the robe-offering, if one obtains an urgent gift of a robe (*ātyayika-cīvara*), one may keep it until the time for the robe-offering, with an additional nine days. Thus, by combining the preceding and following periods, one may keep it for a full ten days without offense.

If one exceeds the ten-day limit prior [to the robe-offering], one commits an offense. If one exceeds the limit after [the robe-offering] and continues to keep it, even for just one [day], one commits an offense.

If one also commits [the offense] on the same day, it must be relinquished and confessed; the procedure for returning the robe is the same as above. A *bhikṣuṇī* commits the same offense. For the three lower assemblies, it is an *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if, for the sake of preventing theft, loss, burning, or being swept away by water, one exceeds the time limit; or if one has the perception that there is theft, loss, and so forth;

or if there is danger from bandits, wild beasts, rising waters, treacherous terrain, royal peril, threat to life, or threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if the person who received the entrustment...

Death; or departing on a journey, abandoning the path, and so forth. If such circumstances arise after [the robe has been offered], there is no offense (*mūla-vinaya*). It clarifies the five kinds of "urgent robes" (*ātyayika-cīvara*):

those given for one's own illness, for another's illness, when about to die, for the deceased, and when about to depart. The *Sarvāstivāda* school says: if a king, prince, queen, high official, or general gives things to the Saṃgha, because such a virtuous mind is difficult to encounter;

or if a woman wishes to marry, or a sick person gives, it will benefit both the living and the dead. Or, due to other urgent and difficult circumstances, they are called "urgent robes. This leads to an explanation of the three months of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Regarding duties that ought to be performed: a bhikṣu should not travel through human settlements at all times, as this obstructs and abandons the work of the Path, tramples and injures the lives of living beings, and, by failing to have a fixed place of residence, invites worldly censure. He should observe the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*).

When there are no compelling reasons, he should observe the "prior" retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), residing for the first three months, specifically from the sixteenth day of the fourth month until the [sixteenth day of the] seventh month.
On the fifteenth day, if there is a matter [that prevents one from entering retreat], one may observe the *paścimikā* (latter) *varṣā*;

one shall reside for the final three months, that is, from the sixteenth day of the fifth month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month. When intending to enter the *varṣā*, one should personally deliberate whether the monastery...
Whether it be in an araṇya, or among trees, or in mountain caves and the like, can you dwell happily without fear, poisonous insects, various perils, or the noise of clamor?
Will you be able to complete the summer retreat? Is there anyone upon whom you may rely?

During the summer, you should rely on a master who extensively recites both divisions of the Vinaya; if such a person is not available, there must be one who understands the Sūtra-piṭaka and the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
"No. Can you compassionately and constantly instruct me so that I do not become negligent? Furthermore, may there be no cause for doubt or uncertainty regarding what remains unresolved.
Should I happen to commit an offense, may there be no lack of a place for its purification, and may there be no one within the assembly who would cause a schism or delight in contention?
May there be no causes or conditions for the breaking of precepts, for the sake of my holy life and livelihood."
Having deliberated thus to ensure that there are no obstacles, one then addresses the person upon whom one relies, saying:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], now enter the three-month summer retreat at this monastery (if it is within a village, one should say 'at such-and-such village';
if it is in a separate room, one should say 'in such-and-such room'), for the purpose of repairing dilapidated dwellings. Thus.

This is said three times. If it is the *paścima-varṣā* (latter retreat), one should change [the phrase] to "the latter three months. The remaining wording is identical [to the other sections]. (According to other schools: after the three recitations have been made, the person upon whom he relies should say, "Go;

do not be negligent. He replies, "I shall uphold it. According to the *Karmavācanā-mūla*, one should further ask: "Upon which master of the Vinaya do you rely? He replies: "Upon Master So-and-so. [The master] says: "If you have doubts, you should ask. He replies: "So be it.

For the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one must rely on a master who has recited the entire Vinaya (*piṭaka*), and not on a mere resident; to do otherwise constitutes an offense (*pāyattika*). Regarding the instruction to repair dilapidated rooms, this applies specifically to monastic dwellings; if it concerns a donor's property, [the rule does not apply].

In a house, a mountain cave, or at the foot of a tree, one may adjust the terminology according to the specific circumstances. The procedures for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) for the other four assemblies are all identical to the above text; the only difference is the name used in the address. If there is no person upon whom one can rely, one should perform the mental recitation of the retreat.
The text follows the same principle as above, with the sole exception of the initial phrase of address (this refers to the person upon whom one relies;

it means that when there is no bhikṣu in the dwelling to rely upon for the ritual, it does not mean one must receive instruction from such a person. If there is no one there from whom one can receive instruction...).

[This refers to] when the location is cramped or crowded. As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should be able to travel back and forth within seven days; one may mentally rely on [a distant place] as one's formal dependence (*āśraya*).

At that time, a bhikṣu who had no person to rely upon informed the local authorities, but he himself forgot to perform the mental act of reliance (*manasikāra*). He did not know whether it was valid or not. The Buddha said:

"If he has come for the sake of the rains retreat (*varṣā*), then the retreat is established. At that time, various bhikṣus went to a place for the rains retreat and entered its boundary, whereupon the dawn appeared.

"I do not know whether it is established or not. The Buddha said: "If one has come for the sake of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), then the retreat is established. It is the same when entering the monastery grounds (*ārāma*).

It is likewise when one foot has entered the boundary and one foot has entered the monastery grounds. (This refers to the two periods of sixteen days before and after; according to the Vinaya texts, the intermediate *varṣā* is also permitted.

If it is the intermediate period, then from the seventeenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the second month, one may perform the formal act (*saṃgha-karma*) on whichever day is appropriate. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: 'Once the fifteenth day has arrived, the official in charge (*vaiyāvṛtyakara')..."*

The person should sweep and plaster the dwellings to make them clean. When the assembly has gathered, they should announce: "Tomorrow, O Bhikṣus, you should enter the summer retreat; all matters pertaining to the summer season should be kept in mind until the sixteenth day.

The officer in charge should observe the number of people and prepare tally-sticks (*śalākā*). He should wash them with scented water, smear them with fragrant clay, place them in a clean tray, arrange fresh flowers upon them, and cover them with a clean cloth. Then, having struck the *gaṇḍī* to assemble the great assembly, he should place the tally-sticks before the Elder (*sthavira*).

Next, the regulations for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) should be proclaimed. An official who knows the assembly shall go on circuit to announce: "Venerable sirs, those who are of one mind and desire it should observe the rains retreat here. During the summer, the community of bhikṣus must not interrogate one another regarding offenses, nor should they establish illegal regulations that cause the bhikṣus to dwell in discomfort.

One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma. Then, the person distributing the voting sticks (*śalākā*) shall hold the tray of sticks before him, while the person collecting the sticks shall follow behind holding an empty tray.

The Great Master, the Teacher, first places one tally. Next, the entire assembly rises from their seats, crouches down, and examines the matter with careful scrutiny. Having received the tally, they hold it with both hands and place it upon an empty plate. If there is a śrāmaṇera, his preceptor [acts as follows].

Alternatively, the preceptor (ācārya) should take up the tally-stick on their behalf. Next, the tally-stick for the deity who protects the monastery is cast down. Once all have participated, the tally-sticks should be counted, and one should address the assembly, saying: "In this residence, there are currently this many bhikṣus who have received tally-sticks."

Śrāmaṇeras, such-and-such a donor, and such-and-such a steward; in such-and-such a village or quarter, which is a place for alms-seeking—then all bhikṣus should observe that place for alms-seeking. Having observed it, they should reflect to themselves: "In this place, I am fit to observe the rains retreat (varṣā);

it shall not give rise to suffering, and should it arise, I shall dispel it. If there is illness, there shall be an attendant; I shall be provided with medicine. Whatever is required shall be fully supplied.

Having made this reflection, one should go to a secluded spot, stand before a single bhikṣu, perform the full ritual deportment, squat down, join the palms, and recite three times to receive the rite of the rains retreat (*varṣopagamana*). Once the rains retreat is concluded, the visiting bhikṣu...

Come. One should neither move [the furniture] nor depart. If one wishes to enter the rains retreat at a residence, one should first go personally to inspect the dwellings and bedding, and only then accept the room.
Prior to the commencement of the retreat, a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) should be performed to appoint a person to distribute rooms and bedding.
Once appointed, that person should count the monks, count the rooms, and count the bedding. Having completed the counting, they proceed to...
Before the Elder, he spoke thus: "Venerable One, please take this dwelling and bedding according to your pleasure.
Having finished giving them to the Elder, he then gave them to the second Elder, and so on in succession until reaching the lowest-ranking monk.

If there is a remainder, it should be further divided by the senior monk (*sthavira*), and this process may be repeated up to three times. If there is still a remainder, one should open up the dwelling place for visiting monks (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*).
If virtuous monks arrive, [the remainder] should be given to them; however, one must not divide the communal assembly hall, the heated bathhouse (*jantāghara*), or the summer hall (*gimhāna-sālā*).
And as for the walking hall: if one obtains a dilapidated dwelling, it should be accepted; one must repair it according to one's ability.
If one wishes to observe the rains retreat in a quiet cave, one should first go there and make a sign, or write one's name, saying: "So-and-so wishes to observe the retreat here.
When departing, one should erase the sign and the name. If the dwelling is so narrow that it cannot accommodate [the residents], it is permitted to share the space down to the size of a single bed.
[The bedding] shall be divided; even down to the seating area, it should be shared among all. One must not move the fixed beds, mats, or bedding from this room to another room.
However, if there are many such rooms, one is permitted to ask the long-term residents or the master of the monastery or stupa, and upon their permission, the items may be moved.
Upon departure, one should return to the original location. One should not observe the rains retreat in the open air or in trees;

however, it is permitted to stay under a tree, provided the tree is taller than a person's head and its branches and leaves are sufficient to shade a single sitting place, as well as within a small hut.

In a mountain cave, in the midst of trees, or in the open air—where one may sit with knees tucked in without obstructing the head, and where the feet are shielded from water and rain—one should dwell in retreat (*vassa*).
If one dwells among cowherds, oil-pressers, woodcutters, or on boats during the summer, it is permitted to follow them wherever they go.
If one is in a village during the summer, [one should remain] in that village.
Divide [the community] into two groups. Each group shall reside where the necessary provisions are fully supplied; when one group moves, the other should follow.

According to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*), it is permitted to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in a place free from five faults: first, being too far from a village, making it difficult to obtain necessities; second, being too close to a city, which hinders the practice of the path; third, having many mosquitoes and ants; [and so forth].

This results in harm to both oneself and others. Fourth, there is no person upon whom one can rely; such a person possesses five virtues: first, causing those who have not heard [the Dharma] to hear it; second, causing those who have already heard it to attain purity; third, being able to decisively sever the net of doubt;

fourth, possessing unhindered penetration; and fifth, possessing right view. Fifth, there is no donor to provide medicine and food. Generally, those observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*) should not leave their boundary for even a single night during the summer. If a donor invites one to a distant place and one cannot return on the same day, one is permitted to go for seven days.
One must not go solely for the sake of food and drink, except for other specific causes and conditions. If...
It serves six purposes: first, until medicinal herbs have been administered; second, returning on the seventh day; third, when the five groups of monastics request the confession of offenses;

fourth, when the three lower groups of monastics request the reception of the precepts; fifth, when summoned by kings, ministers, lay devotees (upāsakas), parents, relatives, acquaintances, and friends;
sixth, for the purpose of tending to the sick; seventh, for seeking companions for recitation; and eighth, for the sake of the Three Jewels.
Regarding this matter, it is permitted to go for seven days. It should be received in this manner: assuming the proper deportment, one should speak to a single bhikṣu, saying:

"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a focused mind. I, the bhikṣu [Name], now receive the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, returning here within this period to observe the rains retreat.
I inform the Venerable sir so that he may know. (Recite this three times. If the previous matter does not require seven days, it may be...)

It is designated according to the specific circumstance. Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) procedure for receiving the seven-day leave (*saptāha-kalpa*): if there is no Bhikṣu present, it is permitted to receive it from the fourfold assembly; however, one may not receive it through mental resolve alone. This excludes five types of persons:

namely, forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), those living in solitude, those traveling on long journeys, those who have been ill for a long time, and those staying among their kinsmen during times of famine. Without a reason authorized by the Buddha, one is not permitted to stay overnight outside the boundary, even for a single night. It is permitted for the fivefold assembly to enter the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).

When the fivefold assembly receives the days [of the retreat], if they must travel to a destination, they must return within the boundary as soon as their business is finished, because there is no formal legal procedure [to remain otherwise]. If the location is distant and they cannot return within seven days, it is permitted to receive the procedure for exceeding the seven days. If...
For a half-month or a month, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) should be performed as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let monk so-and-so receive the seven-day rule (or the fifteen-day or month-long rule) to go outside the boundary."
For the sake of a certain matter, I shall return here to observe the rains retreat. Thus do I announce it. Venerable Sangha, listen.

This bhikṣu named [Name] has received the *saptāha-atireka-dharma* (the rule for being away for up to seven days, or fifteen days, or one month) to go outside the boundary for the sake of a certain matter, and will return here to observe the rains retreat.
Which elders of the Sangha consent to the Sangha’s hearing this bhikṣu named [Name] receive the *saptāha-atireka-dharma*... [fifteen days...]?

[For] one day or seven days (or fifteen days or one month), [a monk] goes outside the boundary for a certain purpose. Those who intend to return here to observe the rains retreat should remain silent.

Whoever does not consent should speak. The Sangha has consented that the bhikṣu so-and-so receives the "seven-day rule" (or fifteen-day or one-month rule) to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose and return here to observe the rains retreat. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is settled.
Thus it should be maintained (one should know that the three aforementioned types of receiving the [rainy season] retreat do not extend into the night, unlike other codes).

If one has received the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary and is detained by others, or if water and land routes are impassable due to various difficulties, and although one intends to return, one fails to return within the allotted days, this is not termed "losing the year" (*vassa*).
If there is a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) or a threat to life at the place of retreat, or if for my sake...

Therefore, one should leave [the monastery] for the purpose of breaking up a schism, or for the purpose of stopping a schismatic act, or for the purpose of reconciling that Sangha, or because one cannot obtain food, drink, medicine, or attendants as one desires.
If such circumstances exist, one should go; this applies even if one is already in the place where the summer retreat (varṣā) is being observed.
Hearing that great gains and offerings are available elsewhere, he immediately goes there. This bhikṣu does not obtain the preceding year [of the rains retreat];

having violated his original commitment, he incurs an offense. Or, he departs without cause; or, having accepted the seven-day rule, he exceeds seven days. He breaks the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (early) retreat;

having violated his original commitment, he incurs an offense. Upon returning within the seven days, the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* retreat is established, and he does not violate his original commitment.

It is essential [to remain]. There is no offense. If, at the end of the period, one stays outside the boundary for seven days, whether one returns or not, the prior *anvārambhaṇa* (early) retreat is established;

there is no offense. The same applies to the subsequent (*paścima*) retreat. If one has entered the retreat in this location, but hears that the Saṃgha in another location has obtained a large share of the retreat offerings (*lābha*), and goes to stay there, one immediately loses this location. After staying there for a short time, if one returns...

If one loses that place, or if one has accepted an invitation for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) and perceives a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should go and inform the donor and request to move elsewhere.
If permission is granted, it is well; if not, one should depart. At that time, the bhikṣus established a rule for their communal dwelling during the *varṣā*:
they were not to converse, prostrate, or exchange greetings with one another. The Buddha said: "When you dwell together..."
Like enemies, they are just like white sheep. I have taught the bhikṣus through countless skillful means to instruct one another, to receive each other’s words, and to awaken one another in turn;
you should not thus collectively accept the dharma of the mute, becoming equal to the non-Buddhists.

If one practices the dharma of the mute, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense (*saṃghāṭī-vinaya* states: if while traveling on the road, the day for entering the retreat has arrived before reaching the residence, then on the road...).

If one is staying by the side [of a tree], or under a tree, or in a vehicle, one should accept the *anvāśraya* (temporary residence) and remain until the appearance of the dawn light. Upon reaching the designated dwelling place on the day of the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*), one should kneel with palms joined before a single bhikṣu and recite three times to formally accept the later retreat.

If one travels on the road and does not accept the earlier retreat (*pūrvikā varṣā*) on its appointed day, there is one *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline). If one reaches the dwelling place on the day of the later retreat and does not accept the later retreat, there is a second *vinayātikrama*. Such a person has broken the retreat and shall not receive the distribution of robes.

If rooms and quarters are assigned during the spring or winter seasons, one should occupy them according to seniority when a *sthavira* (senior elder) arrives. However, when rooms are assigned specifically for the retreat period, one must not occupy them according to seniority when a *sthavira* arrives. If one drives another out, one commits an offense. One is forbidden from speaking with such a person.

If one wishes to employ skillful means to remain with few affairs and not speak, one may do so for half a month. Upon reaching the day of the *poṣadha*, one should engage in conversation and exchange greetings regarding matters and responses. After the *poṣadha* ceremony has passed, one should continue as before.

Once a bhikṣu has completed the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he should perform the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding what is called *pravāraṇā*: it means that during the three months [of the retreat], one might have committed an offense without being aware of it;
now, one allows the Saṃgha to freely proclaim one's own faults concerning offenses seen, heard, or suspected. As...
This is the Dharma-Confession (*dharmapratideśana*), also called *pravāraṇā*. It means that, among the three matters, one may raise any issue at will;
it is the sense of confessing offenses and removing transgressions. If there are five or more persons residing in a monastery, one should appoint a messenger to announce the *pravāraṇā*.
The Elder (*sthavira*) should first, during the morning meal or the midday meal, proclaim: "Venerable Saṃgha..."
Listen. On such-and-such a day, at such-and-such a time, in the month of [month], the Saṃgha has assembled at such-and-such a place for the *pravāraṇā*.

Listen: the *pravāraṇā* shall take place in the *Poṣadha-hall*. It should be on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day. One should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one proclamation) to appoint a person to conduct the *pravāraṇā*.
Such a person must possess five virtues, namely: being free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; and knowing whether the *pravāraṇā* has been performed or not yet performed. Harmony...
Once the assembly of monks has gathered, he should ask: "Can you, [Name], act as the one who grants the invitation to self-examination (*pravāraṇā*) for the community of monks?
If he replies that he can, he should be appointed in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha appoint the monk [Name] to act as the one who grants the invitation to self-examination. This is the motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen."
The Sangha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to act as the one who bestows the invitation for self-criticism (*pravāraṇā*).

Which elders among you consent to the Sangha’s appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to act as the one who bestows the invitation for self-criticism? Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak.

The Sangha has already consented to the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to act as the one who bestows the invitation for self-criticism. Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus settled.

This person shall hold [the bowl] (with the permission of other sections, the number may be two or three, but must not exceed this). If it is the Elder or one possessing the five virtues, they should first announce [the matter].
Thereafter, they perform the *pravāraṇā*. They make the following formal motion (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. Let the Saṃgha, being in harmony, perform the *pravāraṇā*. This is the motion. Having made this motion, there are those who possess the five virtues.

Having approached the Elder, each person in turn should perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults). He should rise from his seat, bare one shoulder, remove his sandals, kneel with both knees on the ground, and join his palms.
Facing the one endowed with the five virtues, he should speak as follows: "Venerable Sir, today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*. If there is any offense seen, heard, or suspected, may the virtuous elders, out of compassion, speak to me.
If I see an offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma. (Recite this three times. Having completed the *pravāraṇā*, they return to their seats.

If one is elderly or ill, they may perform the *pravāraṇā* in their own seat as is convenient for their body. If one forgets during the recitation, each [verse] should be granted to them. For those unable to listen to the *ekottara-karman*, one should write it on paper and read it to them. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "If one is the person performing the *pravāraṇā*..."

The senior elder (sthavira) should bare one shoulder, bend his body, and say to the second senior elder: "Venerable sir, today is the time for the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā). At that time, the second senior elder should bare one shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, grasp the feet of the senior elder, and three times perform the invitation ceremony.

If a junior monk acts as the one performing the invitation ceremony, he should bare one shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak thus: "Senior elder, today is the time for the invitation ceremony. The senior elder should likewise bare one shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and three times perform the invitation ceremony.

In this manner, it proceeds through all the monks until the invitation ceremony is completed. Then, one should go before the senior elder and announce: "The Sangha has unanimously completed the invitation ceremony. Thereupon, they should withdraw as usual after paying their respects. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The one performing the invitation ceremony goes to his own seat."

In this place, one should receive the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults). One must not wait until the *saṃgha-pravāraṇā* has been completed before performing one's own *pravāraṇā*. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, and other sources, it is permitted that once the *saṃgha-pravāraṇā* is finished, those acting as the *pravāraṇā-dhāraka* for the *saṃgha* may perform their *pravāraṇā* with one another.

The *Vinayaviniscaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "If the assembly is small, one person should be appointed to receive the *pravāraṇā*. If the assembly is large, two or three people should be appointed. If two are appointed, one shall receive the *pravāraṇā* from the *sthavira* (senior monk), and the other shall receive it from the middle of the assembly down."

If three persons are present, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) proceeds from three locations. If there is only one person performing the *pravāraṇā*, he should perform it in the presence of another who has already performed his own *pravāraṇā*. If there are two or three persons, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* procedure with one another.
If the eight difficulties (*aṣṭau āpattayaḥ*) or other circumstances arise, as in the case of the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts), an abbreviated *pravāraṇā* is permitted.

If the difficulties are still far off and there is time for an extensive recitation, it should be performed extensively. If the difficulties are imminent and the threefold proclamation cannot be completed, [it must be abbreviated].
It should be stated again; yet it must not be stated more than once. It should be stated only once. If one does not do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If a difficult situation is imminent and it is impossible to state it only once, the bhikṣus should immediately make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and each perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it three times.
The announcement is made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now [perform] each [of us]..."
The *pravāraṇā* by means of three utterances together. The announcement (*jñapti*) is made as follows.

Having made this announcement, each person performs the *pravāraṇā* by means of three utterances together (that is, speaking face-to-face in pairs). It is repeated; the same applies to a single utterance.

If there is an imminent danger such that one cannot perform the three utterances individually, nor can one make the announcement, one should simply depart for that reason. If there are four persons, the announcement cannot be made.
Regarding the appointment of those who perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults): they should face one another and perform the *pravāraṇā* for each other, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind: today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure regarding the *pravāraṇā*. (This is to be said three times.

If there are three or two persons, it is performed in the same manner, with the exception that the first phrase is modified to reflect the number of persons facing one another. One must not perform the *pravāraṇā* separately from the assembly, nor may one perform the *pravāraṇā* while having committed an offense, as such does not accord with the Dharma. If one has committed an offense, one should...)

After the confession (*pāṭidesanīya*), the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is then performed. Four persons may not receive the consent (*chanda*) of a fifth person; they perform the *pravāraṇā* among themselves, even to the point that one person may not receive the consent of a second.
This is the *pravāraṇā* by mental reflection (*manasikāra*). If there is only one person, he should mentally reflect and speak aloud:

"Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure in my *pravāraṇā*. (This is to be said three times. One bhikṣu remains behind. On the day of the *pravāraṇā*, he should go to the hall where the precepts are recited (*poṣadha-śālā*) and perform tasks such as sweeping and sprinkling water, according to the procedures prescribed for the recitation of the precepts. He shall wait for visiting guests to arrive.

They shall perform the *pravāraṇā* together; if none come, they shall perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of the threefold formula themselves. It is permitted for those who have entered the later retreat (*paścimikā*) to receive the *pravāraṇā* from those who have entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvikā*).
Once the *pravāraṇā* has been performed, one should remain and wait until the completion of the month, reaching the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

If items obtained during the summer retreat, including bedding and other requisites, are to be distributed, it is permitted to receive them. One should not count the years of seniority (*varṣa*) until the three months are complete.
If those who have entered the retreat earlier and later reside together, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* at the location where the *sthavira* resides. Or, the *sthavira*...

Whether arriving earlier or later, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) according to those who have resided there first. Among those who have resided there first, there may also be earlier and later arrivals;
one should perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the majority. If traveling on a road, it is well if one can perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony with others.

If harmony cannot be achieved, one should move to another location together with fellow teachers and friends, and having performed the formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), perform the *pravāraṇā*.

Regarding the *Pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults): when departing, one should dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*) before leaving. If there is anyone who has committed an offense involving the four *pārājika* rules, they should be expelled before the *pravāraṇā* is held.
If one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one should grant them the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā*, or the *mānāpya* (penance), or the *āvarhaṇa* (rehabilitation).

Once [the formal act] has been completed, one should then perform the *pravāraṇā*. If one has committed an offense belonging to another category [of the Prātimokṣa], one should first perform the confession before performing the *pravāraṇā*.
If there is certain to be a dispute on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, or if it might cause a schism in the Saṃgha and so forth, one should not perform the *pravāraṇā* on that very day;
rather, one should postpone the *pravāraṇā* for a short while and listen to the *pratiṣedha-pravāraṇā*. One should not seek permission [to delay]; the *pravāraṇā* itself is [the means].

Listen. If the person who obstructs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) is impure in the three karmas, lacks wisdom, is not discerning, does not know how to ask questions, and is unable to answer, other bhikṣus should say to him: "Stop; there is no need to raise this matter of dispute.
They should not heed this person's words and should instead proceed with the *pravāraṇā*. If that person’s three karmas are pure and so forth, they should ask him: "By what..."
Regarding the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*): Is it on account of broken precepts? Is it on account of broken views? Is it on account of broken decorum?
What has he seen? What has he heard? What does he doubt? If he is unable to answer these fully, then according to what was raised, he shall be given the offense for groundless accusation.
If he can provide a full answer, the Sangha should punish him according to his offense; only then should the Sangha perform the *pravāraṇā*.

If there is a sick bhikṣu who obstructs another sick bhikṣu, or if those who are not ill obstruct one another, they should be told: "The Buddha has spoken thus; you must wait until the illness has healed.
They should speak in accordance with the Dharma, and the other party should likewise speak in accordance with the Dharma. It should be done in this manner.

...and only then perform the *pravāraṇā*. If there are many bhikṣus who, having dwelt in retreat with diligence, have attained superior fruits and realizations, they may fear that by performing the *pravāraṇā* on this day, they will no longer be able to enjoy such bliss.

In such a case, they should perform a *jñapti* (formal motion) to extend the *pravāraṇā*, so that the *pravāraṇā* occurs when the fourth month is complete. If, however, there is another location where bhikṣus are quarreling and not in harmony, and they wish to—
Come here for the *pravāraṇā*. If this community is to perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day, shorten it to the fourteenth;
if on the fourteenth, shorten it to the thirteenth. If you hear that they are coming today, assemble the Saṃgha and perform the *pravāraṇā* quickly.
If you hear that they have already arrived within the boundary (*sīmā*), go outside the boundary and perform the *pravāraṇā*. If you hear that they have already entered the monastery...
Inside [the boundary], one should prepare bathing implements and the like to allow them to bathe; then, secretly exiting the boundary, one performs the *pravāraṇā*.
If guests call for the *pravāraṇā*, one should reply: "We have already completed our *pravāraṇā*. Once the resident bhikṣus have finished their *pravāraṇā*, the guests may not obstruct it;
however, while the guests are performing their *pravāraṇā*, the resident bhikṣus may obstruct it. By employing such skillful means, one may accomplish this.
Good. If [the conditions] are not met, one should perform the formal announcement for the *upariṣṭa-pravāraṇā* (the postponed *pravāraṇā*). The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let it be known that today the Saṃgha shall not perform the *pravāraṇā*;

we shall perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight. Thus is the announcement. If guests and residents remain until the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, they should perform the second postponement announcement.

The senior [monks] perform the *pravāraṇā*. If a guest arrives after [the invitation has been issued] on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon and still does not depart, one should act according to the Dharma and the Vinaya by forcibly performing the *pravāraṇā* in harmony.
If the number of guests and residents is equal, it is the same as the procedure for the *poṣadha*.
It should be known that one must not perform the *karmavācanā* or the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in the presence of bhikṣuṇīs or those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, one should not perform the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) again; for the *pravāraṇā* is itself the recitation of the precepts.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have completed their rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), they should, by means of a formal motion and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), appoint one bhikṣuṇī to go among the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha.
Regarding the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*): she goes before the Saṃgha, pays homage to the Saṃgha, and with body bent and head bowed, joins her palms and says:
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed the summer retreat; the Bhikṣu Saṃgha has completed the summer retreat.

The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha invites the Saṃgha for criticism regarding the three matters of offenses seen, heard, or suspected. May the Venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, speak to me. If I see an offense..."
One should perform the confession according to the Dharma. After it has been recited three times, the Elder says:

"Venerable Saṃgha, do you see any offense of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha that may be raised—whether seen, heard, or suspected? Speak to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha so that they may perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma."

Be diligent and do not be negligent. (The bhikṣuṇīs should pay homage to the saṃgha and then return. If the two assemblies of monks and nuns each have fewer than five members, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, the bhikṣuṇīs should go to the place of the bhikṣus, pay homage, inquire after their well-being, and then withdraw.
Śrāmaṇeras should perform the *pravāraṇā* toward the bhikṣus; śrāmaṇerīs and female trainees (*śikṣamāṇā*) should perform the *pravāraṇā* toward the bhikṣuṇīs. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If among the assembly observing the rains retreat there is one person who entered the retreat early, when the fifteenth day of the seventh month arrives, the entire assembly should collectively undergo the *pravāraṇā* with that one person. Once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, they remain seated until the fifteenth day of the eighth month. If everyone entered the retreat late, all should [perform it] on the tenth day of the eighth month."

On the fifth day, the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) is held. If the assembly consists of ten thousand or twenty thousand, they should gather in one place and perform the *pravāraṇā* therein before the appearance of the dawn light. If the great assembly consists of sixty thousand or eighty thousand and there is fear that it will not be completed, they should reduce the number and go outside the boundary to perform the *pravāraṇā*.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: When the summer retreat is about to end and seven or eight days remain until the day of the *pravāraṇā*, one should issue a public announcement in the nearby villages and hamlets, or write it upon paper, so that those far and near may all know [of the approaching date].

Whether old or young, the fivefold assembly of renunciants as well as the various donors shall all together prepare for the matters of offering. The junior bhikṣus should sweep, sprinkle, and adorn the monastery buildings and the caityas. By the night of the fourteenth day, they should have those who hold the sūtras recite them throughout the night.

On the following day, knowing the proper time, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; it must not exceed the appearance of dawn. Having performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one subsequent announcement) to appoint those possessing the five virtues, these virtuous ones should distribute living *kuśa* grass to serve as seats for the Saṃgha.

Then, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made. At that time, each person should mindfully receive a handful of *kuśa* grass, lay it down crosswise and inverted, move their body forward, step upon it with both feet, take a small amount with their hands, and hold it up before them, reciting this three times.

Then the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of mutual invitation) is performed. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, grass is also spread upon the ground to serve as a seat. Once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, the five groups of renunciants and all the lay travelers together take knives, needles, thread, towels, silks, and so forth, to collectively perform the *pravāraṇā* offering for the benefit of the assembly present.

The reason for presenting knives and needles on this day is that one seeks clear intelligence and sharp wisdom. At that time, those possessing the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) should hold knives, needles, and thread, or various other requisites of a śramaṇa, and stand before the *sthavira* (senior elder), speaking these words:

"Venerable Sir, may these various items be given as a *pravāraṇā* gift to those who have completed their *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat)? If, at this place, any other beneficial articles are obtained, [they shall be shared by] the harmonious Saṃgha."

"Is it appropriate to divide [the offerings]? The entire assembly answered simultaneously, "It is appropriate to divide them. If it were otherwise, both the appointed bhikṣu and the great assembly would incur an offense against the Dharma (*vyatikrama*). The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states: On the fourteenth night, one must invite a master of the sūtras to ascend the seat and recite the scriptures.

At that time, the monastic and lay communities gather like clouds; lamps are lit to maintain the light, and incense and flowers are offered as worship. At dawn, everyone goes out together to circumambulate the village and city, each with a devout heart, paying homage to the various *caityas*.

Carriages and platforms carry the sacred images; drums and music fill the sky; banners and canopies are interlaced and fluttering, obscuring the sun. Only after returning to the monastery at the hour of *yūzhōng* (noon) do they perform the Great Fast (*mahā-pūjā*). After noon, everyone gathers to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. First the bhikṣus, and afterwards the bhikṣuṇīs.

The assembly. Next, the three groups [of monks] below [the *upādhyāya*] may, once the *yathāsukha* (as they please) ceremony is concluded, go their separate ways as they wish. This signifies that the summer retreat (*varṣa*) has been fully completed; there is no need to remain for another night. Yi says: This is the intention of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya.

Nanshan [Daoxuan] explains that according to this school, one is not permitted to leave the boundary during the retreat, because it would constitute a breach of the summer retreat and a separation from one's robes. Since the night has not yet ended, one must wait until the fifteenth day when the night has passed and the dawn light (*āloka*) appears on the sixteenth day;

this is called the completion of the summer retreat. Question: Why is the period fixed at only three months? Answer: First, throughout a lifetime, the physical form depends on nourishment; therefore, the first three months are established [as the retreat], while the final month is opened [for travel] so that one may obtain clothing for the body. Second, if the retreat were concluded at the end of the fourth month, then on the sixteenth day of the fourth month...

[The ceremony] can only be successfully completed [if performed at the proper time]. If there is any lapse or omission, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) cannot be concluded. Because the prescribed method is so strict, it is difficult to apply as a constant standard. Therefore, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, opened the period from the sixteenth day of the first month to the sixteenth day of the second month, allowing the monthly continuous observance to be completed.

The *Zhijue hua chao* states: "In various sūtras and vinayas, the sixteenth day of the seventh month is considered the year of birth for the bhikṣu’s fivefold Dharma-body; thus, the fifteenth day of the seventh month is the end of the winter retreat (*la*).
Since bhikṣus have left secular life, they do not calculate by secular years, but rather count their summer retreats (*xiālā*)."
**The Twenty-ninth Precept: Regarding Separation from One’s Robes Beyond Six Nights during the Kārttika Month** If a bhikṣu,
at the conclusion of the three-month summer retreat, when the month of Kārttika has been completed, resides in an araṇya (wilderness) that is subject to doubt and fear,
and while residing in such a place, wishes to leave one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling—

[The rule concerning] being separated from one's robes. If monks have a legitimate reason to stay apart from their robes for up to six nights, should they exceed this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, after the monks had completed their summer retreat (*varṣā*), during the month of Kārttika...
When dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage), there were many bandits. The Buddha permitted dwelling in such places provided that one leaves each and every robe inside the dwelling.
At that time, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks left their robes inside the dwellings, entrusted them to their acquaintances and fellow bhikṣus, and then went out.
The other bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha established this precept: "The end of the three months of the summer retreat" refers to the tenth day of the seventh month.
The five days conclude [the retreat]. As for the "one month of Kārttika" that follows: *Kārttika* is translated here as the Pleiades (*Mṛgaśiras*).
This refers to the month when the Pleiades constellation is aligned with the moon, specifically from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month;

it is the one month following the four months of the summer retreat. Regarding "fulfilling": this means that those who have completed the subsequent summer retreat must remain for the full duration of the one month of Kārttika.
Even if one follows those who have completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end of the preceding *varṣā*, one must still remain for this full month in order to complete the ninety days.
If there is fear or apprehension, it is permitted to stay apart from one's robes for six nights;
this does not mean that one may stay apart from one's robes once the month of Kārttika has already ended. Otherwise, it would contradict the texts of the other four schools of Vinaya.
This is contradictory. Other schools all state that the latter month has not yet been completed. However, this one month is the time when autumn bandits arise in the Western lands;

furthermore, it does not apply to those who observe the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), because those observing the earlier retreat may also stay away from their lodgings for one month without receiving the *kāṭhina* robe.
As for "forest-dwellers" (*āraṇyaka*), it refers to those who live five *li* away from a village in a secluded place.
"Secluded place" (*araṇya*) means: those who have doubts think there may be thieves here who intend to come and plunder their clothing and belongings;
"fearful" means they dread losing their clothing and belongings because thieves frequently come to this place to rob them.
"Place" refers to the hermitage or monastery of an *āraṇyaka*; "dwelling" means residing therein for the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*).
Furthermore, for a bhikṣu to dwell in such a place means to dwell in a place where there is doubt and fear.
Regarding the "three robes," these refer to the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka.
To wish to leave behind one robe means to leave any one of the three robes behind. To "place within a house" means to entrust the robe to someone inside a dwelling.
"Within a lay household in the village" means inside the private residence of a householder. "Having a cause and condition" refers to having matters related to the Three Jewels and so forth.
"Staying overnight apart from one's robe" means being separated from the robe that has been entrusted to someone else.

"Up to six nights" means that if there is a cause and condition such as those mentioned above, staying apart from one's robe is permitted for a maximum duration of six nights. "If it exceeds this" means exceeding [the limit].

The six-night limit constitutes an offense immediately. Regarding the violation herein: once the six nights of being separated from one's robe have elapsed, if by the time the light of dawn has not yet appeared on the seventh night, one has neither relinquished the robe, nor is holding it in hand, nor is staying within reach of a stone’s throw, then at the moment the light of dawn appears, one commits an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
With the exception of the three robes, to be separated from any other robe constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

The procedures for relinquishing, repenting, and returning the robe are the same as above. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense, because for nuns there is no rule regarding dwelling in an *araṇya*.
There is no offense in cases such as being robbed, lost, washed away, or burned; or when a boat crossing is impassable, or due to various obstacles and difficulties. (The *Vinayavibhāṣā* states:

From the sixteenth day of the seventh month, for the subsequent six nights, it is permitted for a monk in an *araṇya* who is observing the rains retreat to sleep apart from his robe. The reason this is permitted is that in foreign lands...)

There are times when bandits plunder; within this one-month period, it is the time when such bandits strike. For this reason, [the Buddha] permitted [the practice]. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If there are many monks in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) and the dwellings are secure and well-fortified, it is not necessary to entrust one's robes to a village.

Once the entrusted robes have been kept for six nights, one may go to check on them; having seen the robes, one returns to the hermitage. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One is not permitted to entrust the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) or the five robes; however, one may entrust the seven robes (*saptaka-cīvara*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One may entrust whichever robe is most important, but one must not entrust all five robes, as they are worn upon the body.
Nor may one entrust two robes, because one cannot wear only a single robe when performing prostrations, entering the monastic community, or going for alms."
The thirtieth precept concerning the misappropriation of the Sangha’s property:
If a bhikṣu, knowing that it is the property of the Sangha, seeks to appropriate it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery. There was a householder who constantly practiced giving;
he wished to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as excellent robes. At that time, Upananda said to him, "Those who give to the Saṃgha receive much merit.
You should now offer the food to the Saṃgha, but you may offer the robes to me. The householder agreed. The next day, he invited the Saṃgha to his home. Having seen the various [monks],...
The Venerable Kāśyapa, fully endowed with dignified deportment, raised his voice and said, "How can I create an obstacle for one who has thus made the robes of the Saṃgha so well-arranged?
The bhikṣus questioned him and learned the reason; they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha established this precept:
"One who knows" means either knowing by oneself or knowing through the words of another; it excludes those who do not know. "The Saṃgha" refers to...
Regarding "the community of the Buddha’s disciples" and "objects": these refer to the six requisites for a bhikṣu’s sustenance, down to drinking vessels and water containers.
Regarding "objects belonging to the Saṃgha": these are things made for the sake of the Saṃgha, already given to the Saṃgha, or already promised to the Saṃgha.

"To seek for oneself and enter into one's own possession" means knowing that the objects belong to the Saṃgha, yet diverting them to provide for oneself. As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knows this is [property] of the Saṃgha...

Regarding objects: if one appropriates for oneself what was intended for another, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This includes cases where property belonging to the Saṃgha is diverted to a stūpa, or property belonging to a stūpa is diverted to the Saṃgha;

as well as property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, property belonging to the present Saṃgha, property belonging to the community of bhikṣus, or property belonging to the community of bhikṣuṇīs.

Regarding items belonging to this person or items belonging to that person, if one exchanges them with one another in this manner, it is all *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), because they have not entered into one's own possession;

thus, a light offense is incurred. If one has already promised [to give], and one perceives it as having been promised, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If one has promised but is in doubt, it is *dukkaṭa*.

If one has not promised, yet perceives it as having been promised, or is in doubt, it is all *dukkaṭa*. The procedure for forfeiture, confession, and the returning of the object is the same as above. This concludes the comparison.

The same offense applies to a bhikṣuṇī. For the three lower groups [of practitioners], it is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). There is no offense in the following cases: if one was unaware; if permission had already been granted, yet one forms the perception that it has not;
if permission was granted for a small amount, yet one encourages the giving of more; if permission was granted for a few people, yet one encourages the giving to many;

if one intended to give coarse items, yet encourages the giving of fine ones; or in the case of speaking in jest, speaking by mistake, speaking to oneself, speaking in a dream, or intending to say something else.

This is a mistaken explanation of that [passage]. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If someone comes wishing to give a gift and asks a bhikṣu, 'To whom should I give? he should reply, 'Give it to whomever you respect in your heart. He asks again, 'Where does the fruit of retribution become greatest?

He replies, 'Giving to the Saṃgha yields the greatest fruit of retribution. He asks again, 'What kind of monks are pure, uphold the precepts, and possess merit? He replies, 'There are no monks among the Saṃgha who violate the precepts or are impure. If a person brings an object to give to a bhikṣu, he should say, 'One who gives to the Saṃgha obtains great fruit of retribution.

If [the donor] says, 'I have already given to the Saṃgha; now I wish to give specifically to the Venerable One,' then to accept it is without fault. However, if one knows the object was intended for the Saṃgha and diverts it toward oneself...")

This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This object must not be returned to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha should instead utilize it. If one diverts it to another person, it is a *pāyattika*. According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda, diverting the property of others toward oneself also incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one diverts the property of others to another person, or to the Saṃgha, or if one diverts the property of the Saṃgha to another person, or to another Saṃgha, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of diversion, and also an *dukkaṭa* upon acquisition. Regarding "another person," this refers to one, two, or three bhikṣus. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

if one diverts the property of this stūpa toward that stūpa, it need not be recovered, as the merit is identical; one need only perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta*. If one diverts the property of this saṃgha toward that saṃgha, it need not be recovered.

Because the *saṃgha* is the same [in both cases], one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. If one diverts the *pravāraṇā* robes belonging to this *saṃgha* toward another *saṃgha*, they should be taken back; because the objects belonging to the *pravāraṇā* are distinct, one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. If one does not return them, the value shall be calculated as an offense. The same applies to *mukhadvāra* robes.

If one diverts property belonging to another toward other persons, it should be taken back and given to the original owner; one should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. If one does not return it, the value shall be calculated as an offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "To divert the property of this monastery to that monastery;

to divert the property of this room to that room; to divert the property of this corridor to that corridor; to divert the property of this space between pillars to another space between pillars; to divert the property of a space between pillars to a doorway; to divert the property of a doorway to the upper story."

Even if one redirects [the property] to the rooms, corridors, pillars, gates, or pavilions, it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in each case. If one redirects the property of this image to another image, or redirects the property of this stūpa to another stūpa—whether it be the base of the stūpa, the pillars, the walkway, or the tiered levels—it is likewise so.

To overturn an alms bowl, a square pedestal, a wheel-marked object, or even a precious vase, turning them one after another, constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense if they are turned back by the power of a king. To divert the property of one poor person to give it to another poor person;

to divert the property of a non-human being to give it to another non-human being; to divert the property of a non-human being to give it to a human; to divert the property of a human to give it to a non-human being; or to divert the property of a renunciant to give it to a layperson—or conversely—constitutes an offense of wrong-doing in each case. If one cannot find [the intended recipient], there is no offense.

One should understand that the mutual diversion and giving of the property of men, women, eunuchs, and the other four assemblies follows the same principle as above. This concludes the explanation on the ownership of offerings and the rules for distributing items. If there is anyone...
If one builds a dwelling for oneself and gives it to a single person, or gives it to many people, or after giving it to the Saṃgha,
subsequently transfers it to others— whether giving it to many people, to the community of monks,
to one's own school, or to another school— all such cases are termed illegal giving, illegal receiving, and illegal residence. If there is someone who...

To take pleasure in building a private dwelling and giving it to a single person, or to many people, or to the Saṃgha, or to both divisions of the Saṃgha—this is considered giving according to the Dharma, receiving according to the Dharma, and abiding according to the Dharma. However, if one builds a private room within the grounds of the Saṃgha...
When an elder arrives, one should rise and yield the way; if one does not rise and yield, one should return the property to the Saṃgha, for there is no further justification for it.
To take the property of the Saṃgha as one's own is improper. Regarding all property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters:

it should not be divided, it should not be taken into personal possession, and it should not be bought or sold. Nor can it be sold by the Saṃgha, nor by a multitude of people, nor even by a single individual. If that...

If one enters [the property] oneself, or divides it, or sells or buys it, in all such cases it is not accomplished; one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. What constitutes the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions?
It includes the monastery, the articles belonging to the monastery, the dwellings, the articles belonging to the dwellings, jars, pots, cauldrons, and kettles.

Axes, chisels, lamp-stands, and various other heavy items; rope beds, wooden beds, large cushions, small cushions, bedding, miscellaneous articles, timber, bamboo, and grass—all these are not permitted to be divided.

However, it is permitted to divide fruits and flowers. If flowers have been offered to the Buddha, or if the *saṃgha* present obtains clothing and goods that may be divided, one should calculate the number of persons and mix the high-quality with the inferior so that [the distribution is fair].

Regarding those who have arrived: the counting sticks (*śalākā*) are cast to divide [the robes]. If there is a visiting bhikṣu who arrives before the counting sticks are cast, he should be given a share;

if he arrives after the counting sticks have been cast, he should not be given a share. If visitors arrive repeatedly while the robes are being divided, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to appoint one person to divide them.
Once appointed, one should again perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to entrust the items to that person and have him divide them.

[Regarding] the method for assigning [the robe] to the Saṃgha (including the rules for the distribution of robes, etc., which are fully recorded in the Mahāvibhaṅga and the Karmavācanā texts): if there are only four persons, it is unnecessary to appoint an assigner.

One should directly perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one announcement) for the division. Once the ritual procedure is completed, the items shall be divided equally according to the number of people present.
If the Saṃgha is in harmony, they should give an equal share to the śrāmaṇeras. If they are not in harmony, they should give them half a share. If they do not consent, one should...
Give one-third and one-fourth. If they do not give, it should not be divided. To the monastery attendant, give one-fourth; if he does not give, it should not be divided.
If there are three people, they should divide it together by means of three verbal declarations, saying: "Venerable sirs, please bear in mind:
whatever robes or non-seasonal robes are here at this residence, they should be divided among the present Saṃgha. In this place...
"There is no Saṃgha; this is my portion. This is to be recited three times. If there are two persons, it is also the same.
If there is only one person, he should mentally reflect and speak these words; the text follows the above, except that the words addressed to another are omitted.

If there is a bhikṣu present in the residence, and one has the perception of a bhikṣu or harbors doubt, yet desires to divide the community into separate factions, it does not constitute a formal division; one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If there is a bhikṣu [but...]
If there is no bhikṣu, but one perceives it as such, there is no offense; the act is not completed.

If there is no bhikṣu, yet one has the perception that there is one, or if there is doubt, the act is completed and one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If there is no bhikṣu and one perceives there is none, the act is completed and there is no offense.

Whether the receiving of robes is completed or not, and whether an offense is incurred or not, it is likewise. If the two communities of monks and nuns obtain property that may be divided, they should divide it.
It shall be divided into two parts. If there are no bhikṣuṇīs, even if there are only śrāmaṇerīs, it should likewise be divided into two parts.
If there are no śrāmaṇerīs, the bhikṣu-saṃgha should divide it. If there are no bhikṣus, and only śrāmaṇeras exist, it should also be divided into two parts.
If there are no śrāmaṇeras, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha should divide it. If there are no bhikṣus...

There was no transgression. All monasteries, fields, gardens, fruit trees, separate rooms, and the property belonging to those separate rooms—copper jars, copper vats, cauldrons, pots, lamp stands, and all other heavy items, as well as beds, mats, pillows, and so forth, along with the monastery attendants.
Carriages, sedan chairs, bathing jars, mendicant’s staffs, fans, and all such implements and tools belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions and should not be divided.
However, robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and containers for storing robes should be divided among the monks present at the site.

If a caregiver brings the six personal effects of the deceased to the assembly of monks, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to award them to that caregiver.
If the deceased possessed many sets of the three robes (*tricīvara*), one should give him those that he habitually wore. The Sangha should examine this attendant;
if he has been an excellent caregiver, the best set of the three robes should be given to him;
if he was mediocre, the mediocre set; if he was inferior, the inferior set. If the deceased had debts, it is permitted for the attendant to use his extra robes to repay them. Or...
There are no extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*). One should sell the three robes (*tricīvara*) to repay [the debt]. If there is a surplus, it should be given to the attendant.
The attendant should ask the patient: "Which are the three robes? Which are the extra robes? To whom do you owe money? Who owes you money?"
To whom should you give it? If you do not ask, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma. A caregiver for the sick should possess five qualities:
first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and being able to provide what is permitted; second, not loathing or despising the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit;
third, possessing a heart of compassion and not acting for the sake of food or clothing; fourth, being able to endure... [the long-term care].

One should prepare medicinal decoctions until the illness is cured, or even until death. Fifth, one should be able to preach the Dharma for the sick person, causing them to rejoice and increasing their own merit in wholesome dharmas.
One who possesses these five qualities may take the clothing and belongings of the patient;
they should give whatever six types of items are currently available. If these are absent, one must not substitute them with other items. If the patient...
When a person is at the point of death, they may say: "I give these various possessions of mine to the Buddha, to the Dharma, to the Saṅgha;
or to a stūpa, or to an individual. Whether I die and give them away, or whether I do not die and return them [to you]. The Buddha said: "One should not give in this manner.
They should be distributed among the *saṃmukha-saṃgha* (the present community). If a bhikṣu dies in a village where there is no monastery, and if there are faithful [laypeople] in that place..."
A lay devotee (*upāsaka*) or a garden keeper should take charge of recording [the deceased’s belongings] and wait for members of the fivefold assembly of renunciants to come;

when they arrive, he should give them [the items]. If no one comes, he should send them to a nearby monastery. (The property of the deceased should be divided among the *saṃgha* present; it should not be kept beyond the end of the rainy season retreat.

The method for dividing the property of the deceased is as previously described in the method for distributing robes—whether for the *saṃgha*, for three people, or even down to a single individual, this should be understood. If a bhikṣu has completed his summer retreat in a different location...
