Furthermore, if one resides in another location, one should take the requisites for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) from the place where one has resided for the greater number of days. If the duration of residence in both places is equal, it is permitted to take half from each.
Having already received one’s share of the robes at this location while observing the *varṣā* retreat, one should not receive a share of robes at another location as well.
If a bhikṣu departs before the distribution of robes at the end of the summer retreat, he should entrust one person to take his share.

The Saṃgha should grant it to him. If there was no entrustment, or if the entrustment was made vaguely, or if the one who received the entrustment forgot it, none of these constitute a fault on the part of the Saṃgha.

If a single bhikṣu resides in a dwelling and acquires a large amount of requisites for the summer retreat, that bhikṣu should form this thought: "This is my property. Whether another bhikṣu arrives or not, he should not [give it away].
It is settled. If the Saṃgha has obtained a large quantity of robes and later the Saṃgha splits into two factions, they should divide it into two portions.
If the Saṃgha splits before the robes have been obtained, one should inquire of the donor; according to what he says, one should give them to him.
If he says he does not know, or says "give to both," one should divide it into two portions. If the Saṃgha obtains robes that are divisible, and there is a bhikṣu...

From this faction, one should not give a share to that faction. If a bhikṣu dies while on his way to that faction before he has arrived, his robes and bowl are to be given to the place he intended to go.
If a bhikṣu who has been subject to formal censure (ukkhepanīyakamma) passes away, his robes and bowl are to be given to the community of monks who performed the joint formal act of censure.
If the Saṃgha has split into two factions and a donor invites them both to a meal at a single location...
Furthermore, regarding the gift of robes or the gift of thread, one should follow what the donor has provided.

If the Sangha has obtained robes for the summer retreat and the Sangha is divided into two factions, the robes should be divided according to the number of people in each group. If the Sangha is divided before the robes for the summer retreat have been obtained, they should likewise be divided according to the number of people.
Whether the robes for the summer retreat have been obtained or not, if one goes to another faction, one should give [the portion] to them. In all such cases...
There are eight kinds of gifts of robes: if given to the community of bhikṣus; if given to the community of bhikṣuṇīs; if given to both communities;

if given to the community of monks from the four quarters; if given to the community within a specific boundary; if given to those who have performed the same formal ritual (karmavācanā); if given by naming individuals;
or if given to a single person—in each case, they should be assigned according to the portion to which the gift belongs. If a bhikṣu does not desire [the robe], [it should be handled accordingly].

Without anger, without fear, and without delusion, one who knows what has been apportioned and what has not yet been apportioned—such a person the Saṃgha should appoint to distribute rice gruel, to distribute light meals, to distribute the five types of formal meals, to appoint those for invitations to assemblies, to spread bedding, to distribute bedding, to distribute bathing robes, and to distribute robes;
they may take or give, and they may appoint bhikṣus as messengers or appoint śrāmaṇeras as messengers—all such matters are treated in this same way. There are these five [qualifications].
If one distributes property for the Saṃgha according to the Dharma, one will be reborn in heaven as swiftly as an arrow shot.

If one acts contrary to these five dharmas when distributing property for the Saṃgha, one will enter hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. (Regarding the distribution of property herein—whether the property belongs to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters, the Saṃgha present before one, many individuals, or a single person;

whether it is at the proper time or not—at such subtle and minute details, it is difficult to describe them fully. One must not act hastily; one should carefully examine the *Mahā-vinaya* and the *Karmavācanā* texts before performing the rite. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, when a śrāmaṇera dies, the property belongs to the upādhyāya. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when a śrāmaṇera dies, [the property belongs to] the present...)

The preceding monks should divide [the inheritance]. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If a bhikṣu dies, whatever benefit of food and drink there may be—even down to a single leaf—along with whatever benefit of clothing and requisites there may be—even down to what is spun into a lamp wick—all these may be divided equally.

If there are garments of superior quality or high value, they should not be torn; rather, they should be sold for their price and the proceeds divided. If a bhikṣu arrives during the five designated times, he should be given a share of the benefits: first, at the time of striking the *gandī*; second, at the time of reciting the three-part *Anityatā-sūtra*;

third, at the time of paying homage to the *caitya*; fourth, at the time of casting lots (*śalākā*); and fifth, at the time of making the formal motion (*jñapti*). If the assembly is not gathered in harmony, or if there is no one to preside over the legal procedure, one should perform the 'initial and final' rite: that is, taking a small amount of the deceased's property, such as two coins or the like, and giving it [to the arriving monk]."

The foremost elder and the lowest-ranking monk shall each receive a portion to serve as a definitive record; thereafter, the assembled Sangha shall divide it among themselves as is customary, without requiring further formal procedures. If someone arrives after the initial and final rites have been completed, they should not be given a share.

Even if [the property] existed during the first four periods but not during the last two, a share must still be granted. Once the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, all those currently within the boundary who are entitled to a share must receive their benefit.

If no formal announcement has been made and the initial and final rites have not been performed, then all disciples of the World-Honored One who are Śrāvakas—whether currently residing in Jambudvīpa or elsewhere—all have a share in whatever fields, houses, shops, bedding, mats, copper, or iron there may be.
Bamboo and wooden utensils, leather bedding, and shaving implements; slaves, food, drink, grain, wheat, and beans—these shall enter the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Directions.

As for large and small bowls, basins, needles, awls, knives, ladles, hearths, various bags, water-pots for pure and impure use, oil containers, and all clothing and robes—whether they be Dharma-robes or bathing garments, whether dyed or undyed, as well as footwear and the like, those of red, white, or dark blue colors should be distributed among the present Saṃgha. All superior colors should be entered into the Buddha Hall.

Items for use in making offerings to painted images, as well as various medicinal herbs and the like, should be placed in the monastic storehouse to provide for the sick. Precious gems and jade should be divided into two portions: one portion shall enter the Dharma (the Sūtra-piṭaka), and one portion shall enter the Saṃgha.

Items belonging to the Dharma may be used to transcribe Buddhist sūtras and to maintain the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*). As for those items that enter the Saṃgha, they should be distributed among those currently present; however, all sūtras and śāstras must not be divided and should be stored in the scriptural repository (*sūtra-kośa*) for the common reading of the Saṃgha from the four directions.

Any books of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) should be sold, and the proceeds should be distributed among those currently present. Regarding all items involving promissory notes or contracts: if they can be collected early, they may be divided immediately; if they cannot yet be collected, the notes should be stored in the monastic storehouse to be used for the needs of the Saṃgha from the four directions at a later time. If there is gold or silver, whether in finished or unfinished form...

Utensils, cowrie shells, and various coins shall all be divided into three parts: one for the Buddha, two for the Dharma, and three for the Saṅgha. Items belonging to the Buddha should be used for the repair of the Buddha hall and the stūpas; the remaining two portions should be understood as previously described.

If a bhikṣu is ill and says, "After my death, you may take this object and give it to that person," this is a worldly custom and does not constitute a valid entrustment; these items must be divided. If the object is handed over directly to the intended recipient, it is considered a gift well-bestowed.

The corpse should be cremated as an offering; once the recitation of sūtras is completed, the items may then be divided. If the deceased had entrusted an object, it shall be divided among the community at the place where the object is located. If items obtained from the site of a stūpa of a Śrāvaka disciple are acquired, they should be used to restore and maintain that very stūpa. If...
There may be some remaining; these should be divided in the presence [of the assembly].
△ Finally, the formal inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:"
"Regarding this matter, we are pure" (recited three times). "Venerable sirs, because there is silence, we are pure regarding this matter; thus it shall be held.
The commentary states: the concluding phrasing here is as explained in the previous section. This concludes the brief explanation for each individual precept above.

[The] characteristics. Now, the method of repentance shall be explained in its entirety. This method of repentance applies to both the monastic community (*saṃgha*) and the individual (*pudgala*), and its meaning encompasses the three types of relinquishment (*tyāga*):

first, the relinquishment of material things (*dravya-tyāga*), which means distancing oneself from the conditions for transgression; second, the relinquishment of the mind (*citta-tyāga*), which means distancing oneself from the causes of transgression;

and third, the relinquishment of transgression (*āpatti-tyāga*), which means eliminating the karma of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). If material things are not relinquished, the method of repentance is not accomplished; if the mind is not relinquished, then...
If the causal stream is not severed and the offense is not relinquished, then the defiled conduct is not discarded. Among these three [factors], if even one is lacking, it is not pure.
Furthermore, once wealth and goods enter one's hands, one incurs the offense because they arise through the mutual defilement of prior forces.
Thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The robe has already been relinquished and the offense has already been confessed; yet one seeks a robe."

If the intention is not interrupted, whether it be on that very day or even after a month, should one obtain original or acquired wealth, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* in its entirety.
Because the mental continuity remains uninterrupted, the offense is incurred on the very day the robe is obtained; it does not require the passage of days.

If one relinquishes the robe and performs repentance on that same day, the intention is severed. Even if the intention to seek a robe arises again on a subsequent day, there is no offense, because the intervening intention has been severed.

Therefore, if the robe has already been relinquished and the intention to seek it has ceased, even though the offense has not yet been confessed, should one obtain the original item or a different property after many days, one must relinquish it and perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense. In all cases of relinquishment, one must resolve to abandon it with a mind free from attachment.
If the original property is returned, it is treated as if newly acquired; one may then either take possession of it or perform the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification) according to the Dharma.

It may be kept. Now, among these thirty *naiḥsargika* offenses, with the exception of the two involving precious objects, one does not perform the relinquishment in the presence of a person who has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

As for bedding made of wild silkworm silk, it must be cut to pieces and discarded forever. For the remaining items, they should be relinquished according to their original location—whether to the Saṃgha, to a group of many, or to a single person—but they must not be relinquished to a separate assembly.
If they are so relinquished, the relinquishment is invalid, and one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Regarding the offense: when relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should carry it to the midst of the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove one's sandals, pay homage to the Elder, kneel with palms joined, and make this declaration of relinquishment:

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept [a certain number] many extra robes for more than ten days [or, if the number is known, one should state it according to that number;

if the robe-material cannot be counted, one says "many"], and have been separated from them [or, if the case involves returning property of the Saṃgha into one's own possession, one should state the specific name and matter accordingly].

I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha (recite this once). Having completed the relinquishment, I then request confession from the Saṃgha, making the request as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen."
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept [a number of] extra robes for more than ten days [specify the type and quantity of the items as appropriate].
I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. These robes have now been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Within this matter, there are [a number of] *pāyattika* offenses.
I now request the Saṃgha to grant me absolution. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, permit me, Bhikṣu [Name], to perform this confession. (Having recited this three times, he then...)

Within the Saṃgha, one should request a pure bhikṣu to serve as the presiding master for the confession. The formal petition for this purpose, as required by the Vinaya, exists in all versions of the *Karmavācanā* texts. One should approach that bhikṣu with full decorum and petition him, saying: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept [a certain number of] extra robes for more than ten days [specify the particular case as appropriate].

I have committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). These robes have already been forfeited to the Saṃgha. Within this matter, there are [a certain number of] *pāyattika* offenses."
I now request the Venerable One to act as the presiding master for my confession. May the Venerable One act as my presiding master for the sake of compassion.
(Recite this three times. The presiding master shall not grant permission immediately; he should address the Saṃgha, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

This bhikṣu [Name] intentionally kept [a number of] extra robes exceeding ten days [specifying the particular item as appropriate], thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. These robes have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha."

With single-minded attention, I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept [a number of] extra robes for more than ten days [specify the particular circumstance].
I have committed a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. These robes have already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Regarding this matter, there are [a number of] *pāyattika* offenses;

One should go before three pure bhikṣus, perform the formal ritual, and speak these words of relinquishment:

Having relinquished it, one should confess the original offense. First, one should request a presiding confessor (*karmavācaka*). The request is as stated above. The presiding confessor should then ask the other two bhikṣus: "If [the two]..."
"Elder, please listen as I accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so. [The two bhikṣus should respond: "It is well. [The presiding confessor then says to the one confessing their offense:

The person from the borderlands [is exempt]. All other details are as above. However, regarding this *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, if one does not immediately confess at the time of the transgression, and subsequently uses the object, there arises a secondary offense involving the forfeiture of the property, as well as the offense of concealment (*praticchādana*).

As detailed in the *Śanbu jiemobu* (Supplementary Karmavācanā), there are eight categories of *duṣkṛta* offenses in total: two primary categories arising from the root offense, and six categories arising from concealment. The first two categories of concealment arise from the concealment of the formal act of forfeiture; the middle two arise from the concealment of using an impure robe;

and the final two arise from the concealment of remaining silent during the *poṣadha* recitation by the Saṃgha. These are all calculated based on the passage of the first and second watches of the night and beyond. According to the original *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Vinaya Karmavācanā), which enumerates the various offenses according to their sequence from beginning to end, there are a total of twelve distinct stages.

There are three sets of three offenses. The first set of three consists of: (1) a *pāyattika* for a long duration; and the two types of concealment, namely the fundamental and the successive. The second set of three consists of: (1) a *pāyattika* for declaring oneself pure when the Saṃgha recites the *Prātimokṣa*; and the two types of concealment. The third set of three consists of:

The fourth set of three consists of: (1) a *pāyattika* for declaring oneself pure during the Saṃgha’s *Pravāraṇā*; and the two types of concealment. The fifth set of three consists of:

(1) a *pāyattika* for declaring oneself pure during a face-to-face *Pravāraṇā*; and the two types of concealment. Third: one commits the *dukkaṭa* offense of not being fit to hear the precepts due to having committed an infraction oneself, as well as two instances of concealment. The eighth "three" refers to the *dukkaṭa* offense of lying through silence during the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts when questioned twice or thrice at the two designated times, as well as two instances of concealment.

The third [category] of the ninth [section]: the offense of *duṣkṛta* for declaring one's own purity through mental recitation (*manasikāra*) during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), as well as the two types of concealment (*chādana*). The third [category] of the thirteenth [section]: the offense of *duṣkṛta* for declaring one's own purity through mental recitation during the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), as well as the two types of concealment.

The third [category] of the eleventh [set] consists of: (1) one’s own *duṣkṛta* offense of receiving another’s confession, and two offenses of concealment. The third [category] of the twelfth [set] consists of: (1) the *duṣkṛta* offense of wearing a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, and two offenses of concealment.

Regarding these various offenses, they may or may not exist; one must personally examine them. According to the number of offenses committed, one should act in accordance with the text. Now, the confession is opened into three stages. First, the joint confession of twenty-four offenses of concealment:

namely, from the original *thullaccaya* down to the two *duṣkṛta* offenses of wearing a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe at the end of the twelfth set. This is because these offenses are of the same category. Second, the joint confession of the seven sets of *duṣkṛta* offenses, such as the improper recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, for which the same applies.

Because these seven types are identical, the third [section] is the collective confession of the five categories of *pāyattika* offenses, such as the offense of keeping extra robes (*dīrgha*) beyond the limit. One who wishes to perform this confession must first confess the concealment (*pracchādana*) from its inception;

next, one shall confess the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). Now, first we shall confess the twenty-four offenses of concealment. One should do so with utmost sincerity and deep remorse, performing the ritual in this manner:

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept [such-and-such a number of] extra robes for more than ten days [specify the specific type as appropriate]. I have committed [such-and-such a number of] *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses. Having already committed these offenses, the Saṃgha..."
When the *poṣadha* was being recited, he declared himself pure; yet he had committed [so many] *pāyattika* offenses. When the *poṣadha* was recited before another person, he declared himself pure;
yet he had committed [so many] *pāyattika* offenses. When the *pravāraṇā* was performed by the Saṃgha, he declared himself pure; yet he had committed [so many] *pāyattika* offenses.
When the *pravāraṇā* was performed before another person, he declared himself pure; yet he had committed [so many] *pāyattika* offenses. He himself possessed these offenses.

While preaching the precepts for the assembly, one commits [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses. Having committed these [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses oneself, it is improper to hear the recitation of the precepts;
one commits [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses. When the Saṃgha recites the precepts, there are two instances of three inquiries; one commits [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses of silent falsehood.
When reciting the precepts through mental reflection (*cetanā*), one declares oneself pure; one commits [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses. Mental reflection on oneself...

He has arbitrarily declared himself pure. He has committed such-and-such a *duṣkṛta* offense. He has accepted the confession of another while being guilty of such-and-such a *duṣkṛta* offense himself.
He has worn a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe [without the required forfeiture], committing such-and-such a *duṣkṛta* offense. He fully recognizes all these various offenses;
therefore, by failing to disclose them and allowing them to pass until nightfall, he commits the *duṣkṛta* offense of concealment (*praticchādana*).

I do not recall the number [if the number is known, one should state it according to that number]. After the second night has passed, I have again committed the *duṣkṛta* offense of concealing a subsequent transgression.
I do not recall the number [if the number is known, state the number]. I now repent and dare not conceal it. Through repentance there is peace and happiness;
without repentance there is no peace and happiness. I call this transgression to mind and disclose it; knowing it, I do not conceal it.

[Recite] the *Zang* [formula]. Now I reproach my own mind and give rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*). (One recitation. Although it is called "reproaching the mind," the words must be expressed through the manifestation of the three karmas for the offense to be extinguished.

Although it is a self-reproach, one must nevertheless request a witness from another; this differs from the self-reproach for a *duṣkṛta* committed by mistake. If following the *Shanbu* [Vinaya] and other codes, one must likewise seek reproach from another for minor offenses.

Next, perform the confession for the seven types of *duṣkṛta* offenses, such as those regarding the improper recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, according to the full ritual procedure). I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept [such-and-such] long robes in excess.

If more than ten days have passed [the specific number being designated according to the particular type of item], one commits as many *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses. Having committed these offenses, [one must confess].
While preaching the precepts for the assembly, one commits [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses. Furthermore, having personal offenses oneself, one is unfit to hear the precepts;

During the *cetanā-pravāraṇā*, one declares oneself pure; one commits [so many] *duṣkṛta* offenses. *Cetanā*...

May the Venerable One bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure. (Recite this three times. The presiding confessor says: "Reproach yourself."

As for "names," this refers to the distinctions among the six classes of offenses.)

"Kind" (jāti) refers to the thirty distinct matters, such as keeping extra robes or being separated from one's robes. "Nature" (svabhāva) refers to the difference between being singular or manifold; thus the Vinaya says: "One name, many kinds; self-nature and non-self-nature; abiding in distinct differences."

Section Five: The Five Pāyattika Dharmas (Opening Three). First, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration; third, the concluding inquiry.
△ First, a general heading for the various Venerable Ones: These are the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas, recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The commentary states: *Pāyattika* means "falling. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "Falling into burning, boiling, and concealment."
It obstructs the eight hot and eight cold hells. The *Mūla-vinaya* states:
"Those who commit this offense fall into the evil realms of hell, the animal kingdom, and the hungry ghosts, where they undergo the suffering of being burned and boiled.
Furthermore, if one does not diligently confess and eliminate this offense, it will obstruct all wholesome dharmas. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Pāyattika means..."

This means "burning and boiling" in the sense of falling into the evil destinies (*apāya*). Furthermore, *pāyattika* (falling) refers only to the act of falling, while "burning and boiling" points to the specific place where one falls.

Although other offenses are also instances of falling, they receive the designation "falling" based on conventional linguistic usage, just as the word *go*, which primarily denotes the act of moving, is also conventionally applied to humans and other things where the sense of movement is applicable.
The sound "go" (cow) applies to the object that is a cow; the same principle applies to the term *pātayantika*. Therefore, there is no fault.

Furthermore, regarding all training rules (*śikṣāpada*), it is universally admitted that during the preparatory stage (*prayoga-avasthā*), there is an offense of *pātayantika* for disrespecting the Noble Teaching (*ārya-śāsana*). Based on this partial instance, [the same logic holds].
The meaning of "falling" (pārājika) applies to all [the precepts].
△ Within this, they are listed individually.
○ Thus, the first is the precept against false speech.
"If a bhikṣu speaks falsely knowing [the truth], it is a *pāyattika*. The commentary states:
When the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the country of the Śākyas' Red Marshes, the Śākya son Hastibala was debating with non-Buddhists.
If he was not as [eloquent] as they were at that time, he would contradict his previous statements; likewise, when questioned within the Saṃgha, he did so again.
This violated his previous words. The non-Buddhist brahmins collectively raised criticism and disdain. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
"Knowing" means being aware through one's own mind; it does not refer to a mistake.
"False speech" means speaking contrary to one's mind to another person, uttering deceptive words. Within this, there are eight kinds of false speech, namely: [saying] one has not seen.

Not hearing, not touching, not knowing, yet claiming "I see, hear, touch, and know"; or seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing, yet claiming "I do not see, hear, touch, or know"—these instances of seeing are visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
hearing is auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*); touching is the triad of olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses (*ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāyavijñāna*);
and knowing is mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Thus, these six consciousnesses are grouped into four names based on the eye and ear.
The three faculties of mind (*manas*) are sharp by nature; their functional power is predominant, and they can apprehend objects at a distance.
Therefore, each is designated as a distinct name. The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body are dull by nature; their functional scope is limited, and they apprehend only proximate objects.

Therefore, they are collectively termed "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*). Regarding the offense herein: if one speaks and the meaning is clearly understood, it is an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*); if it is not clearly understood, it is not.

Dukkaṭa (offense of wrong-doing). If, when the precepts are being recited, one remembers an offense even after it has been asked about three times, yet does not disclose it, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense.
This applies equally to bhikṣuṇīs; for the three lower groups of disciples, it is likewise a dukkaṭa.

There is no offense if one speaks according to the facts, or if one speaks based on a perception that arises from what has been seen, heard, touched, or known (in total, there are five types of false speech; for instance, there is false speech that constitutes a pārājika, such as claiming for oneself [attainment of the fruits of the path]).

Regarding the "superior human state" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*): there is false speech that constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, such as slandering another with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense. There is false speech that constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, such as slandering another with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, as well as other offenses mentioned herein.

There is false speech that constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, such as claiming to have realized the superior human state when one has not, or slandering another with groundless charges when the matter is not clear. There is false speech that constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense, such as during the recitation of the precepts when the three questions are asked, or in cases where the matter is not clear.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "False speech is when the mouth and the mind are at variance; it is also called empty speech. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one intends to delude another, one incurs an offense for each instance of speaking. When the intention to deceive arises, one incurs the offense of 'reproach of the mind' (*cittavipratisāra*). And so forth.

When one speaks, if the person before does not understand, both incur the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one expresses the matter through speech and the body also makes it known, both incur the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*). A disciple of the Buddha always speaks the truth; one should not swear an oath to clear oneself.

This is because it expresses one's lack of faith. Even if one is falsely accused or slandered, one should not make a solemn oath. The *Vinaya-mūla* states: "At that time, the group of six monks encountered a minor matter and immediately uttered a curse, saying: 'If I have committed such an act, may I fall into the three evil realms.'"

"You will not be born into the Buddha-dharma. If you do such a thing, you too shall fall into the three evil realms and not be born into the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha said, "It should not be done. However, I permit you to speak these words: 'If I have committed such an act, I take refuge in the Buddha; if you have committed such an act, you too take refuge in the Buddha.

If a layperson sneezes or comes to prostrate at one's feet, one should pronounce a blessing, saying, 'May you live long. If a junior person sneezes when they have left their seat, one should say, 'May you be free from illness. If it is a senior person who sneezes,"
One should say "Vandāmi" [I pay homage].
○ The second precept concerning disparaging speech:
If a bhikṣu disparages another according to their class or type, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The group of six monks settled a dispute by reviling a bhikṣu with various insults.
The bhikṣu felt ashamed and abashed; he lost his composure and was unable to speak. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established this precept:
"To speak disparagingly" means to utter words of humiliation from one's mouth to scold and revile another, intending to cause that person shame.
Furthermore, within this category of disparagement, there are seven matters: namely, low birth, lineage, occupation, craft, transgressions, afflictions, and illness.
Regarding "birth" (*jāti*): this refers to those of low status, such as professional executioners, scavengers, bamboo-workers, and carriage-makers.
Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*): this refers to various other low clans; or, even if one was not originally of a low clan, it refers to those who have practiced low crafts.

These are also of low caste. As for their occupations, they include the sale of pigs and sheep, slaughtering oxen, falconry, net-hunting, committing robbery, apprehending criminals, guarding cities, and administering criminal justice—these and other such lowly professions. As for their crafts and skills, they include working with iron.

"Woodworking, tile-making, leatherwork, shaving, and the like are various lowly crafts. 'Transgressions' refers to committing the seven classes of offenses, from the *pārājika* down to verbal misconduct.
'Fetters' refers to anger, resentment, vexation, and envy, up to the five hundred fetters and afflictions.
'The sick' refers to those who are blind, one-eyed, bald, crippled, lame, deaf, mute, and so forth."
This extends even to those afflicted by scabies, leprosy, abscesses, and other various ailments. Regarding the offense herein:

if one reviles another face-to-face using any of the seven aforementioned matters—such as saying, "You are a master-thief," or "You are a murderer," up to "You are deaf and mute"—or if one reviles them through metaphorical insinuation; [this constitutes an offense].
"You are like a master-killer," up to "you are like one who is deaf and mute.

If one insults by comparing oneself, saying, "I am not a master-killer," up to "I am not one who is deaf and mute," and thus disparages another bhikṣu, in all such cases one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If the meaning is not clearly understood, it is an *dukkaṭa*. This applies whether one insults by speaking of wholesome qualities, by means of metaphors, or by comparing oneself.
Whether understood or not, it is entirely an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Regarding one who speaks of the Dharma while reviling:
"You are an *araññavāsin*, a *piṇḍapātika*, a *paṃsukūlika*, even a practitioner of *jhāna*; you resemble those such as *araññavāsins*, whereas I am not like those such as *araññavāsins*.
A *bhikkhunī* commits the same offense; for the three lower groups of disciples, it is an *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if it is for the sake of mutual benefit.
It is spoken for the sake of the Dharma, for the sake of the Vinaya, for the sake of instruction, or for the sake of intimacy;

it may be spoken in jest, spoken inadvertently, spoken alone, spoken in a dream, or spoken erroneously. (According to the Mahāsāṃghika and Sarvāstivāda schools, if one speaks with a mind of contempt, even if speaking of the aforementioned castes or crafts, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one contempts the other four assemblies or any laypeople, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* offense.)
**The Third Precept on Divisive Speech:** If a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, it is a *pāyattika*. *Commentary:* The setting is as before.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks would repeat what was said in private to one person and then report that private conversation to another.
He spoke thus, and consequently, where there was no prior quarrel among the assembly, one arose; and where a quarrel already existed, it could not be extinguished.
The bhikṣus, having investigated and understood the cause, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept: "As for the act of divisive speech (*paiśunya*):
this refers to conveying words from one party to another so as to produce strife and discord, thereby creating a rift. Regarding the offense herein:"
Regarding the seven matters mentioned above, if one uses any one of them to say to another:
"So-and-so says you are a master murderer," or even "a deaf-mute," if the statement is clearly understood, one falls into an offense; if it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. There is no offense in the following cases: when one breaks away from evil spiritual friends or evil associates;
when one breaks away from those who desire to cause a schism in the Saṃgha or who perform illegal and non-disciplinary *karmavācanas*;

or when one breaks away from those who desire to destroy a stūpa or a monastery, or from those whose speech is repeatedly meaningless and unbeneficial. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one forms the intention to separate from them, whether they actually separate or not, it is a *pāyattika*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* [states... )

It is said: To repeat the words of the fourfold assembly, as well as the words of all laypeople, constitutes *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing). If one does not repeat the words from one side to the other, but merely speaks to both parties to cause a rift, it is also *duṣkṛta*. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:

If a layperson within a monastery intends to commit an evil act to harass a bhikṣu, one should speak with stern reprimand to subdue them. If they are not subdued, one must not go directly to the king; first, speak to that evil person’s acquaintances, and next to the princes and ministers.
If that person abandons their evil ways, then stop; do not allow the matter to proceed.
The Fourth Precept on Sleeping in the Same Room with a Woman:
If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. The Venerable Aniruddha went to a village where no other bhikṣus resided and heard...
There was a house belonging to a courtesan who habitually provided lodging for travelers. [The Venerable One] went there to stay the night; he sat cross-legged with his mindfulness fixed before him.
During the first watch and the last watch of the night, the courtesan came to seek him as a husband. The Venerable One did not answer her, nor did he look at her.
She then stripped off her clothes and came to seize him. The Venerable One leapt into the air, and the courtesan was filled with shame. She put on [her clothes].
She adjusted her robes, joined her palms, and repeatedly confessed toward the sky. The Venerable One descended from his seat and preached the sublime Dharma for her;

she attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-entry) and requested to receive the Three Refuges and Five Precepts to become a laywoman (*upāsikā*). When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept:
"A woman" refers to a human female who possesses consciousness and whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has not been severed. "A dwelling" refers to one that has four sides.
A wall or partition, with a roof above; or a front porch that lacks walls; or although there is a roof, it is not complete;
or although the roof is complete, there are openings. Regarding the offense herein:
if a bhikṣu has already stayed overnight and a woman arrives later, or if the woman has arrived first and the bhikṣu arrives later, or if both arrive together, or if [the structure] is slanted...
If one lies down, resting the side against the ground, or turns over during sleep, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in every instance.
If one sleeps in the same room as a female deity, a *nāga*, a spirit, a ghost, an animal, a eunuch, or a person with both sexual organs, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense in every instance.

If a woman stands during the day while a bhikṣu lies down, it is also an *dukkaṭa*. The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].

Not knowing that there is a woman inside the room; or if the house has a roof but lacks four sides of enclosure, or is half-enclosed, or slightly enclosed, or fully enclosed but lacks a roof, or has a slight roof, or is half-enclosed and half-roofed, or slightly enclosed and slightly roofed, or is in the open air;
whether walking, sitting, lying down due to illness, or being seized and bound by others. (The Vinaya-saṃgraha states: If...)

The woman is on the upper floor and the bhikṣu is below, or vice versa; or the ladder has been removed; or the door is firmly locked. If the ladder has not been removed, one should secure it with a bolt and key. Or, even if they are in the same room, one should use objects to screen them off so that the path between them is cut off.

If it is not otherwise, when the light of dawn appears, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for all [cases]. If a female deity or a female *nāga* whose form is visible, as well as a female animal, shares a lodging with one, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for all [such cases].

There is no offense if the female animal is small and incapable of sexual intercourse. If there is a parent, husband, or other guardian who protects her, there is no offense in sharing a lodging. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If they share the same roof but have different partitions; or if it is a great assembly preaching the Dharma; or if it concerns a mother, sister, close relative, or one who is ill."
If there is a man who is capable of understanding and accompanies one, and one does not lie down [with him], there is no offense in any case.
The Fifth Precept on Staying Three Nights with One Who Has Not Received Full Ordination:
If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received the full precepts (upasaṃpadā), exceeding two nights and reaching a third night, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at the city of Khānumata. The group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) were lodging together with several elders in a lecture hall.
One of the six monks fell asleep with a distracted mind; as he turned over, his body was exposed. When the elders saw this, they mocked and ridiculed him.
All the bhikṣus felt ashamed and remorseful, and they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. Later, the bhikṣus used a...
Hulu had not yet received the full ordination (upasampadā), so he was sent out to stay overnight in a latrine.

The Buddha then permitted the bhikṣus to stay together with those who have not received the full ordination for two nights. If they reach the third night, before the first light of dawn has appeared, they should rise and move away.
If they reach the fourth night, they must either leave themselves or cause that person who has not received the full ordination to leave. Regarding those who have not received the full ordination:
"Others" refers to persons other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs. "To stay overnight together" means to stay in the same room;

"room" is explained as above. Regarding the offense herein: if they arrive one after another, or if they arrive simultaneously, and lie on their sides or turn over while sleeping, it constitutes a full offense.
If one stays with a male deva, nāga, yakṣa, ghost, or animal for more than two or three nights, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. As for those who do not commit an offense, it is also as stated above (*Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"If one is not permitted to stay two nights, there will inevitably be various causes of distress or even the loss of life; out of compassion, one may stay two nights together. However, to protect the Buddha-dharma, staying for three nights is not permitted.

If, after staying together for more than two nights, one stays with another person on the third night, it is a *pāyattika*. This is because of the continuity with the previous person. If, after staying together for two nights, one moves to another place and stays there for one night before returning to stay together again, there is no fault. If one remains seated throughout the night, there is no offense.")—the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says the same.

It is said: When the fourth night arrives, one should stay in a different room or in the open air. If it is windy, rainy, snowy, or cold in the open air, one should return to the room and sit until the end of the night. If one is old or ill and unable to sit, one should use a screen that reaches from the top of the head to the armpits and down to the floor;

it should be made of a dense material so that not even a kitten can pass through. If traveling on the road and no screen or curtain is available, one may rely on a trustworthy person who has not yet received full ordination and say to them:

"You sleep while I sit. When you wish to lie down yourself, you should call me to wake up. Or [I shall say]: "I will sleep while you sit. If you fall asleep, you will have no merit. The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: When reaching the third night and being required to go out to stay overnight, one should not be sent outside the monastery or away from the eaves; one need only leave [the immediate vicinity].

Regarding the allocation of space within one's own quarters: if you fear that an evil bhikṣu might become a cause for the breaking of precepts, you should have the śrāmaṇera go to the quarters of a virtuous friend. If no such person is available, you should expel the wicked bhikṣu together with him, or take the śrāmaṇera yourself and go to another place to stay overnight.

If, having already entered the rains retreat, you are unable to go elsewhere, you should form the mental resolve for the sake of protection; staying overnight under these circumstances is not an offense. If there are difficult circumstances and no other bedding is available, you should fold the seven-robes (saṃghāṭī) into four layers and lie upon them.

Fold the great robe (uttarāsaṅga) and place it beneath your head, or use it to cover your body; use the five-robes (antarvāsaka) as an inner garment. Whenever you lie down to rest, place your right side against the bed, with your two feet overlapping, keeping the body steady and motionless, while maintaining the perception of light.

Abiding in right mindfulness, with a mind free from affliction, one’s robes shall not be disarrayed. One should know moderation regarding sleep and maintain the thought of rising early. During the first and last watches of the night, one should constantly cultivate wholesome qualities. This is the method for a śramaṇa’s reclining and rest, provided there is no suffering from illness.
One should not lie down during the day. (For a sick person, there is no offense even if they stay together for more than two nights.
○ Sixth: Reciting the Precepts Together with One Who Has Not Received Full Ordination.
If a bhikṣu recites the precepts together with one who has not received the full precepts, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in the town of Āṭavīka, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) were together with several elders in a lecture hall reciting the Buddha’s sūtras.
Their voices were so loud that they were no different from the chanting of Brahmins; they disturbed those engaged in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. "One who has not received full ordination" is as explained above. "Reciting together" means [reciting] in unison.

The method for reciting the sūtras according to phrases and syllables is as follows. Regarding "reciting together by phrase" (*padasama*): this refers to two people reciting the same phrase simultaneously, neither before nor after the other;
or, when one person has finished reciting a phrase, the second person recites it immediately following the first. Regarding "reciting together by syllable" (*vyañjanasama*):
this refers to two people reciting the same syllable simultaneously, neither before nor after the other; or, when one person has not yet uttered a syllable, the second person recites it concurrently.
The second person summarizes and explains the preceding [text]. Regarding "the Dharma of the Sūtras":
this refers to that which was spoken by the Buddha, or spoken by Śrāvakas, sages, or devas, and which has been approved by the Buddha—all such are called the Dharma. Among these, as for the offense:

If one recites together with a person who has not received full ordination—whether by oral instruction or by written transmission—if it is clearly articulated, one falls into an offense of defeat (*pārājika*);

if it is not clearly articulated, it is an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*). If one recites together with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, sons of gods, or animals capable of transformation, whether the speech is clearly articulated or not, it is entirely an offense of wrongdoing.
If the teacher does not instruct, saying, "I have finished speaking; you may speak now," the teacher incurs an offense of wrongdoing.

[The offense] is committed. The remaining four assemblies incur the same fault as above. Those who do not commit an offense: after I have finished speaking, you speak; or one person finishes reciting while another writes it down;

or if two people share the same task and recite together, even if they speak erroneously. (The *Mahīśāsaka*, *Daśabhāṇavāra*, *Pañcavargika*, and *Mūlasarvāstivāda* schools agree with this section. It is not permitted to recite the Dharma together with those who are not fully ordained.

According to the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*, the group of six monks spoke the words of the Vinaya to a śrāmaṇera. Consequently, the Buddha established the rule that one must not speak [the Dharma] to those who are not fully ordained.)

Regarding the rules for reciting the Dharma: the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* (Lüshe) holds the same view. It states that among these rules, those corresponding to the *Vinaya* (piṇi) apply here. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* (*Shanjianlü*) says: "If one recites together with the written text compiled by a Dharma Master, there is no offense. From this, one should know that the Five Categories and Seven Groups [of offenses] may only be heard by bhikṣus;

for others, it is not their lot, just as a king’s secret treasury is not shared with external officials. If one explains them to someone who is not yet ordained, both parties suffer loss, and it further obstructs their renunciation, such that they shall never be able to receive full ordination.

Regarding the recitation of the Sūtra-Dharma, one should follow the permissions and prohibitions of the Vinaya and exercise skillful means accordingly. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (*Wufenlü*) states: "If one teaches the Sūtras to a person who has not yet received the precepts, and they recite together, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika). 'Reciting together' means reciting at the same time, or reciting while receiving the sound [of the teacher]."

[The recitation] has not yet ceased; he has already begun to recite it. Or, while his recitation is not yet finished, this person begins to teach [the same]. For every phrase, there is an offense of falling (pāyattika). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If two people both possess mastery of the sūtras and recite them together, there is no offense. However, they must not chant in unison. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states:

There is no offense if one stammers, if one speaks rapidly by nature, or if they recite together for the purpose of establishing the correct text and phrasing. Furthermore, when teaching, if one first informs the other, saying, "Do not speak at the same time as I," there is no offense even though they recite together.

If one teaches the Dharma using a melodic, chanting tone, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, if one is preaching the Dharma or offering praise in a secluded place, there is no offense in reciting the sūtras with a melodic intonation. One should not, however, praise or recite non-Buddhist scriptures or secular texts. If, for the sake of...

To subdue those of other paths, one should know when one possesses sufficient strength. One should divide the day into three periods: during two parts of the superior time, one should study the Buddha-dharma; during one part of the inferior time, one should practice the external scriptures. One should not calculate the three periods based on months or years.

If one recites texts in the manner of a Brahmin—using their specific sections, rhythms, and intonations—one incurs an offense against the Dharma. However, if one uses the local dialect or national customs to chant and recite for the purpose of leading others, there is no offense. If one reads the sutras, a high desk should be placed in front to support the scriptures, and fragrant flowers should be solemnly arranged before them.

As for a teacher of the Dharma, if they preach to others without being invited to do so, they incur an offense against the Dharma. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One may listen to and study books, but one must not, out of a desire for excellence, neglect one's duties; this is for the purpose of subduing outsiders."

Because it is for the sake of the Path, one is permitted to read external texts; however, one is not permitted to follow the views of secular scholars, nor is one permitted to render the Buddha’s words into the language of external texts. One who violates this commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "One is not permitted to intermingle the discourses of non-Buddhists with the Buddha’s sūtras."
Listen to and understand the local dialects; recite and study the Buddhist scriptures.
The Seventh Precept: Regarding speaking of another’s grave offense to one who has not yet received full ordination.

If a bhikṣu knows that another has committed a grave or evil offense and speaks of it to a person who has not received the higher ordination (the *mahā-śīla*), except when authorized by a formal monastic decree (*saṃgha-karman*).
*Pāyattika*. The commentary says:
When the Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain, there were certain bhikṣus practicing *parivāsa* (probation) and *mānāpya* (reinstatement).
They sat in the lower seats, while the group of six bhikṣus spoke to the laypeople, saying, "These individuals have committed such-and-such offenses; therefore, the Saṃgha has punished them."
He sat down facing downward. When that bhikṣu and the other bhikṣus heard this, they were all filled with shame and remorse. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
At that time, Śāriputra was appointed by the Saṃgha to speak of Devadatta’s transgressions before the king and the assembled populace.

Having heard of the Buddha’s establishment of the precept, he gave rise to a sense of fear and caution. The Buddha said, "There is no offense for one appointed by the Saṃgha. Because of this, [the matter] was further...
This refers to the *saṃghakamma* for the removal of the formal act (*kamma*). "Knowing" means that one’s own mind clearly recognizes that another person has committed such an offense;
it does not mean being unaware of it. "Another" refers to a person who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*). "Gross offenses" refers to *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
"To speak to one who has not received the full ordination" means to declare it before such a person, thereby exposing the transgression committed by the former individual.
"Excepting the formal act of the Saṃgha" means that, apart from the ritual procedure performed by the assembly to dispatch someone to proclaim a fault or offense, there is no violation.
Regarding the offenses herein: if one speaks and the meaning is clearly understood, one falls into an *āpatti*; if it is not clearly understood, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
If one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense by confessing another offense—other than a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*)—to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one has committed a grave offense oneself and confesses it to one who is not fully ordained, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.

With the exception of monks and nuns, if one confesses the grave offenses of any other person to one who is not fully ordained, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. This applies when there is a grave offense and the perception of it as such.
A *pāyattika* offense; [if there is] doubt, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*. If it is not a grave offense but one perceives it as such, or if there is doubt, in all these cases one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.

For the other four assemblies, the offenses incurred are the same as above. There is no offense if one does not know; or if a layperson has already heard of this grave offense and so forth (the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If the *karmavācanā* for this bhikṣu is performed and he becomes the one whose offense is proclaimed, and another bhikṣu speaks [of it], there is a *dukkaṭa*. If one causes it to be spoken toward this person, at this place, yet it is spoken toward another person or at another place... [there is no offense].

Those who speak [of such matters] all incur *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the appropriate time, according to the specific offense for which the *karman* is prescribed, there is no offense in speaking. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: The purpose of appointing someone through *karman* to announce this to the assembly is to prevent harm and the destruction of the Triple Gem;

to prevent the increase of factions of those with broken precepts; to cause them to abandon evil friends and draw near to virtuous friends; and furthermore, to protect the minds of the assembly so that they do not collectively assume that everyone acts wickedly, nor that all *bhikṣus* are generally covered by the thought of frequently committing offenses.

Moreover, it is to ensure that laypeople do not subsequently engage in further unbeneficial actions because of this. If one goes to a household of laypeople about whom one previously had no knowledge, and forms the perception of not knowing them—or if one suspects them—based on another's coarse [behavior], [one incurs no offense].

If one speaks of [another's] faults while knowing them, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If, regarding a household known to be such, one forms the perception that it is not so, or entertains doubt, yet speaks of it to others, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.

If another does not know [of the fault], but one forms the perception that they do, there is no offense. If one speaks of one’s own grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to a *bhikṣuṇī*, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* in all such cases. Even if one has received formal authorization (*karmavācanā*), if one speaks of it to someone who already knows [of the matter] out of a private grudge, this is also a *dukkaṭa*.

From this, one should understand that whatever speech a renunciant utters must be for the sake of benefit; one should not speak of others out of private resentment. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "It would be better to destroy a stupa or damage an image than to speak of a bhikṣu’s transgressions to one who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*). If one speaks of such transgressions, one destroys the Dharma."

Because of the body: if one speaks of the names of the offenses of the two [upper] classes, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; if one speaks of the actual matter of the offense, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*. If one speaks of the names or the matters of the offenses of the three lower classes, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The Eighth Precept: Proclaiming One’s Own Realization of the Dharma to Those Who Have Not Received Full Ordination.
If a bhikṣu proclaims to one who has not received the full precepts a state of superhuman attainment, saying, "I have seen this; I have known this."
"Truthfully" means: a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The origin story (*nidāna*) is as explained in the first section regarding the precept on false speech.

The distinction here is that one speaks of the Dharma realized by oneself to a person who has not yet received full ordination; therefore, it does not fall under the category of "false speech through deception. This is the transgression.
"Human Dharma" refers to the "superior human Dharma," meaning these noble and beneficial dharmas that transcend all ordinary and ignorant beings;
there is none who can surpass them. Why is it said they "transcend humans"? It is not said they transcend devas, for the Buddha appeared in the human realm.
The precepts are established among human beings because humans possess the *prātimokṣa* discipline; furthermore, humans are superior to devas.
This is because humans are able to cultivate wholesome dharmas and frequently realize the noble path, whereas the various devas are attached to pleasure and cannot practice with diligence.
Thus, by saying that one has "surpassed humans," it is already implied that one has surpassed the devas. "Reality" (*satya*) refers to what is truly real.

This is the actual realization of this Dharma. Regarding the offenses herein: if such a thing truly exists and one speaks of it to someone who has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*), or sends a messenger with a hand-seal or written signs, if the meaning is clearly understood, it is an offense of downfall (*pārājika*); if it is not clearly understood, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one speaks of it to a monk who does not consent [to hear it], that also constitutes an offense of wrong-doing. Other cases of offense or non-offense follow accordingly.
All are as explained in the fourth *pārājika*. The distinction therein is this: what constitutes an abandonment (*pratikṣepaṇa*) there constitutes a *pāyattika* here;

what constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* there constitutes a *duṣkṛta* here. This is the difference in their characteristics. Regarding the other four assemblies, the offenses incurred are the same as above. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says:

"If one truly attains the four fruits [of the path], or even if one attains the *aśubha-bhāvanā*, and speaks of it to others, one falls into an offense. If, however, for the sake of fame or profit, one says...")

If one says, "I maintain the precepts purely; I have truly mastered the Tripitaka; and regarding the sūtras I have recited, their meanings as I understand them, and my ability to provide answers to questions, I can explain these to others," one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for each such statement. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that there is no offense when speaking at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: To manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) before laypeople constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). However, there is no offense if one manifests rare phenomena to clarify the holy teaching, or to proclaim one's own virtues, or if one does so because one wishes to subdue the minds of those sentient beings being converted.
The Ninth Precept on Speaking Excessively with a Woman:
If a bhikṣu speaks more than five or six words of Dharma to a woman, except when a man capable of understanding is present, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, Kālodāyin spoke with a woman in private while preaching the Dharma.
Those who saw this became suspicious. Consequently, the Buddha established a precept. Thereafter, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and dared not preach the Dharma to women.
Furthermore, even when a man was present, they still did not dare to speak beyond a certain limit. Therefore, he further established the rule regarding the "five or six words," and so forth.
"Women" refers to those capable of understanding words of both good and evil. "To speak" means to proclaim and set forth with the mouth. "Dharma" is as explained above.
"Exceeding" means to speak further and at greater length than the scope of five or six statements. Regarding "five or six statements":

the five refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); for example, saying that form (*rūpa*) is non-self, and that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are non-self.
"I. Six refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). As it is said: "The eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent.
If there are further factors associated with these five or six, they are termed the "discourse on the five or six.

A man who possesses knowledge refers to a layman (*avadātavasana*) who understands and discerns both coarse and non-coarse matters, whose mind is free from lustful excess, and who may serve as a witness.
This is because there would be no false teaching directed toward such a person, and furthermore, it would prevent public censure.

If all those who have gone forth were not designated as witnesses, it would be because their status is identical [to that of the accused]. Regarding the offense herein: it is to preach the Dharma to a woman.

If [the recipient] understands five [precepts], it is permissible; if they exceed five and reach six, it is permissible; if they understand six, it is permissible; if they exceed six and reach seven, it is permissible.

Whether [the recipient] understands clearly or not, and regarding the offenses incurred by the other four assemblies, all are identical to the preceding precept. There is no offense if one speaks of five or six precepts together; if one speaks beyond that in the presence of a man who understands;
or if one bestows the five precepts and explains the dharma of the five precepts in the absence of a man who understands.

The method for bestowing the eightfold precepts of the fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*), as well as the exposition of the eightfold precepts of the fast; the exposition of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);
the ten unwholesome dharmas (*daśākuśala-dharma*) and the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśala-dharma*); and the appropriate responses to questions on the meaning posed by women.

If [the listener] does not understand, one should explain it extensively. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If, after having spoken five or six words to a woman, one says, 'Sister, the Dharma is correctly complete with this much,' and rises from one's seat and departs, even if there is another occasion for her to return and sit down again, one should not speak to her.")

[If] one has committed [an offense], but after finishing five or six words of speech, another woman arrives and one speaks for that subsequent woman, and continues in this manner to speak for an unlimited number of women, there is no offense in all such cases.

If one is reciting a sutra oneself and a woman comes to listen, or if a woman asks about the meaning [of the teaching] and one must ensure she understands it, there is no offense even if one exceeds five or six words. The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Speaking of the merit and rewards of giving, or offering blessings and prayers, does not constitute an offense. If one speaks of mundane, ordinary matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
One may preach the Dharma to a bhikṣuṇī; since it is for the purpose of instructing the assembly, there is no fault."
The Tenth Precept on Digging the Earth:
If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika. The commentary states:
When the Buddha was at the city of Khānumata, the group of six bhikṣus (ṣaḍvargika) were repairing a lecture hall for the Buddha; they dug all around it with their own hands.
Regarding "ground": the householder criticized and complained, saying that the sons of the Śākya were severing the life-root of others.

Because of this, the Buddha established a precept. He then instructed people to dig the ground, saying, "Dig here; place it there. The Buddha further formulated a rule for this. "Ground" refers to ground that has already been dug.
"Unexcavated ground" and "already excavated ground": the latter refers to ground that has previously been dug up, where insect life has dispersed and grasses and trees do not grow;

this is termed "ground where nothing grows" (*ajātapṛthivī*). "Unexcavated ground" refers to ground that has never been dug up, or ground that was once dug up but has remained so for four months, having been moistened by rain or other water, such that insect life and grasses and trees [have returned].
If it has grown back as it was, it is still called "unexcavated ground," which in meaning is "ground where plants grow" (*jāti-bhūmi*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"If ground that has previously been excavated becomes moistened by rain or dampened by other water, and three months have elapsed, it is called 'ground where plants grow. If it is not moistened by rain or dampened by water, but six months have elapsed, it is also called 'ground where plants grow. Other than this, it is not 'ground where plants grow.

According to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, ground consisting of four parts sand and stone and one part soil, as well as ground that has been scorched by fire, are all not "ground where plants grow. Regarding the offense herein: if one uses a hoe, or a pickaxe to dig, or...

Striking with a mallet, piercing with a sickle or knife, or even injuring with the fingernails; driving stakes into the ground or setting fire upon the earth—all these constitute *pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).
If one does not instruct, saying, "Look at this" or "Know this," it constitutes *dukkaṭa* (an offense of wrong-doing).
The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. There is no offense if one says, "Know this" or "Look at this," or if one is dragging timber.
Regarding bamboo: if a fence falls over, one may prop it upright; if bricks or stones have been overturned, one may take cow dung, earth from a collapsed bank, or earth from a rat's burrow;
or if one removes soil from a walking path (*caṅkrama*) or from within a dwelling;

or if one walks back and forth on a path, sweeps the ground, or levels the ground with materials—provided one does not dig intentionally, there is no offense in any of these cases. However, such is the rule for a bhikṣu.

If one wishes to take something, one should use pure speech (śuddhavāda), saying, "Know this; look at this," so that the other person may know for themselves and look for themselves what is to be dug up and where it is to be placed.
One must not say directly, "Dig this" or "Place this. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: For the three lower assemblies, digging the earth without purpose constitutes a *dukkaṭa*;

however, there is no offense if one takes dry soil. When a bhikṣu requires anything, he should say to the *kappiya-kāraka*: "Know this. If they do not understand, he should speak again, saying: "Look at this. If they still do not understand, he should speak again, saying: "I require...")

It is so. If [the other] does not understand, one speaks again, saying: "This is for me. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) states: "Whenever one wishes to take vegetables, grass, or wood, one should say from afar: 'Bring clean [items] from such-and-such a place where there are good ones. If one goes to the edge and points them out, it is an offense (*pātayantika*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If, at the edge of a river or on a slope, one causes [something] to fall by stepping on it, for every step that causes it to fall, it is an offense. If while walking along the edge of a slope the earth collapses, there is no offense. If there is a clod of earth that one person cannot lift, breaking it constitutes an offense; if it is heavier than what one person can lift, there is no offense.

If a *bhikṣu* managing affairs fears that the property of a stūpa or the property of the Saṃgha will be lost and wishes to bury it in the ground: if it is in an open place with living soil, he must not dig it himself, but should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) do so. If it is in a covered place with dead soil, he may dig it himself."

Digging up a hidden treasure; the same applies to driving in a wedge and pulling it out. If the dead soil has been soaked by rain, one may not take it oneself; one must have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) take it. Only after the area has dried beyond the limit reached by the rain-soaked earth may one take it oneself without fault. Digging into sandy ground to a depth of half a [handspan] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); digging into pure sand is without fault.

This should be understood to apply analogously to stones, ginger-stones, dung, and ash. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one digs in a muddy place, even down to the depth of the knee, for each individual act of digging there is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one draws lines on the ground, even down to the depth of a mustard seed, for each individual line drawn there is a *duṣkṛta*. However, if a bhikṣu acts as a master craftsman and wishes to newly construct a *stūpa* or a monastery (*saṃghārāma*), drawing lines on the ground to mark the locations for images, there is no offense. If other bhikṣus draw such lines, they commit an offense. If it is raw gold..."

In places where silver and other ores are found, or where realgar, red ochre, white plaster earth, raw stone, black stone, sand, or salt flats are located, there is no offense for one who digs. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "To pull out a stake constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). However, if it is a *bhikṣu* engaged in construction work..."

When wishing to establish the foundation, one should select an auspicious star and a favorable moment. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person), one may personally drive a stake into the ground to mark the boundaries; if it is driven in four finger-widths deep, there is no offense.
The Eleventh Precept on Destroying the Village of Spirits:
If a bhikṣu destroys the village of spirits, it is a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. There was a bhikṣu who, while repairing a dwelling, cut down trees himself. The Buddha...
"To establish the precept": "To destroy" is a general term for hacking, cutting, burning, boiling, breaking, uprooting, and lacerating. "Ghosts and spirits" refers to those who are not human.
"Village" refers to all grasses and trees, meaning that all ghosts and spirits dwell in dependence upon them.
It is like a village. There are five kinds of villages, namely the five types of seeds from which life arises:
first, root-seeds, such as ginger, turmeric, *nakha*, and *hāridrā*, which are produced from roots;
second, stem-seeds, such as the poplar, the willow, the bodhi tree, and the *pippala* tree, which are produced from stems; third, joint-seeds...
The first refers to those produced from joints, such as *chēngyì* (fragrant herb), *luólè* (coriander), and *liǎo* (smartweed).

The fourth refers to those produced from hollows, such as sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and lotus roots. The fifth refers to those produced from seeds, meaning that the seed itself gives rise to another seed, such as rice, wheat, beans, and mustard.
(The *Jiè yīnyuán jīng* states: "There are spirits who rely on tree roots, and some rely on...")

On tree branches; some rely on the inner bark, some on the fissures in the bark, some on the buds, some on the leaves, some on the flowers, and some on the fruits. All medicinal herbs and trees have deities dwelling within them, for they consume their fragrance.

Regarding the offenses herein: if one takes any of the five types of living seeds while perceiving them as living, and cuts them oneself, parches them oneself, cooks them oneself, or instructs another to do so, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in every case.
This applies whether one has doubts, or perceives them as non-living, or if they are actually non-living.

If one perceives [living beings] as such, or harbors doubt, whether acting oneself or instructing another, it is all *duṣkṛta*. (If it is not living matter but one perceives it as such, there is no offense. This phrase is omitted in the Vinaya, but according to the underlying principle, it should be present.

These six types of perception regarding the object apply universally to all other precepts; one should consider them accordingly. If the objects are living plants or non-living plants, the perception of the object should be analyzed into five permutations.
Whether one cuts, fries, or cooks them oneself, or causes another to do so, the gravity of the offense should be understood as explained above.
If one drives a stake into a tree, sets fire to living grasses or trees, or cuts more than half of living grasses or trees, one falls into an offense of transgression (*āpatti*).
If one cuts grasses or trees that are half-dry and half-living, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If one does not say, "Look at this," or "Know this," it is an offense of wrong-doing.

For the other four assemblies, the acquisition of offenses is the same as above. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "For the three lower assemblies, killing living grasses or trees without cause is a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is applied accordingly.")

It should be understood that for these three classes of persons, there is no prohibition when there is a purpose, but they are forbidden when there is no purpose (the same principle applies to those born in the land).

There is no offense if one says, "I know this" or "I am watching this," while cutting withered or dry grass and wood, dragging timber or bamboo, erecting fences or barriers, moving bricks or stones, striking the ground with a staff, clearing a path covered by grass by parting it with a staff, or sweeping the places where one walks, comes, or stays;
in all such cases, if there is no intentional purpose and the cutting occurs by mistake, there is no offense.
One should not eat fruit that has not been purified. One should perform five kinds of purification before eating it:
first, purification by fire (even a single touch with fire); second, purification by knife (damaging the fruit with a blade); third, purification by a wound (a natural blemish on the fruit);

fourth, purification by bird-pecking (damage caused by a bird's beak); fifth, purification by non-seed-ripeness (unfit for sowing, or not yet mature). Among these, after the first and last two types have been purified—
One may eat [the rest] entirely. For the remaining three types, one should remove the seeds before eating. Furthermore, there are five kinds of purification:
