first, having a small portion of the skin peeled; second, having the skin completely peeled off; third, rotting (decayed); fourth, splitting (cracked open); fifth, withering and drying up.

One should not consume impure vegetables, nor should one perform the purification oneself, nor should one handle them with one's own hands. One should have another person perform the purification and then place them on the ground.

One should have someone perform the ritual of purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*). Once the purification has been performed, one should not eat it without having received it [through the formal act]. (The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If grapes, melons, or fruits are gathered into a single heap...")

In three or four places, one should support it with fire; this constitutes purification (*pariśuddhi*). If using a knife or fingernails, each must be purified separately. If one purifies [the food] oneself by means of a knife or other tools, there is no offense at the time of eating, but at the time of performing the purification, one incurs an offense.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If eating roots that grow from seeds, they should also undergo five kinds of purification: namely, peeling, cutting, breaking, washing, and fire. If eating stalks or leaves, three kinds of purification are required: namely, knife, fire, and washing. When performing the purification, one should perform a 'collective purification' (*saṃkṣipta-pariśuddhi*). Within a single heap or a single vessel, if one [item] is purified, it is called collective purification.

If weeds grow in the courtyard of a monastery, it is permitted for a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) to take charge of them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "In certain lands where grain is heaped up, fearing that non-humans (*amanuṣya*) might steal it, one surrounds it with ash and fire."

Regarding "consciousness": this itself constitutes purification. It is like a monastery master who has grain in his storehouse that has not yet been purified; fearing that young bhikṣus do not know the Dharma, he has a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) purify it by fire. When the grain in the storehouse is exhausted, the bhikṣus may always say, "Pound it [to remove the husks]," and they do not commit an offense.

If duckweed covers the surface of the water so that one cannot part it with the hand to take water for use, one should seek a place where cattle or horses have passed. If such a place does not exist, one may seize a clod of earth and throw it, saying: "Go as far as the Brahma Heaven!

Once the clod or stone has fallen and opened a space in the water, it may be used without fault. If one overturns duckweed floating on the water, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense. If one seizes it and throws it onto the bank, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If one picks up dried cow urine together with living grass, it is a *pāyattika* offense. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* says: to cover living grass with ash, soil, or sand is an *dukkaṭa* offense. If one says to another person, "Take these fruits; I wish to eat them," it is an *dukkaṭa* offense. If one swallows raw fruit that has not been purified, it is a [pāyattika] offense.

It is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If one bites it and causes it to fall, it is a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation). Taking a fungus from a tree is an *dukkaṭa*. Striking a ripe fruit so that it falls is an *dukkaṭa*; striking an unripe fruit so that it falls is a *pācittiya*. The *Suddharmaprakāśana-vinaya* states: "If a sprout grows after the fire-purification (*aggiparicatta*), the place where the sprout grows must be purified again."

One must not go to where sprouts grow to fetch food. If one requires flowers or fruit, it is not an offense to climb a tree branch and have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) gather them, provided one does not cause the branch to break. If the tree is too high for the *kappiya-kāraka* to reach, the bhikṣu may embrace the *kappiya-kāraka* so that he can gather them; this is not an offense.

If a tree falls and crushes the bhikṣu, even if he has a knife or axe in his hand, he should rather die maintaining his resolve than cut down the wood or dig up the earth to save his own life. Why is this? Because digging earth or cutting wood constitutes a *pācittiya* (offense of expiation).

A wise person would rather die maintaining the precepts than live while violating them. If one must cut down a tree or dig the earth to rescue another bhikṣu, there is no offense. If someone sets fire to a monastery and one digs up grass or soil to extinguish the flames in order to protect the dwelling, there is no offense.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If, while walking upon living grass or ground covered in green moss, one forms the intention to damage the vegetation, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for every portion damaged.

If one merely has the intention to walk, there is no offense. If one pulls up mushrooms from the ground, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. If mold or mildew grows on jars, pots, clothing, mats, or bedding, and one forms the intention to destroy it, [one incurs an offense]."

If one acts with remorse, it causes others to perceive the matter as pure; only then may one enjoy the object without offense. Whenever a *bhikṣu* acting as a steward intends to fell a tree for the purpose of construction, seven or eight days prior, he should set out various sacrificial offerings beneath that tree and recite the *Triśaraṇa-gāthā*.

An elder *bhikṣu* should offer prayers of benediction, preach upon the ten paths of wholesome action, and extol virtuous deeds. Furthermore, he should announce: "If there are devas who have long resided in this tree, you should seek another dwelling, for this tree is now being utilized for the sake of the Triple Gem.

After seven or eight days have passed, he should have a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) cut it down. If, at the time of felling the tree, some unusual sign appears, he should praise the merit of giving and renunciation and speak of the faults of stinginess and greed. If [the sign] still...

Regarding those that manifest distinct characteristics, they must not be cut down; however, if they lack such characteristics, they may be cut. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are three precepts of great benefit to the Buddha-dharma: one must not carry burdens, one must not kill plants and trees, and one must not dig the earth.

If these three precepts were not established, all kings would compel bhikṣus to perform manual labor. Because these three precepts exist, all sovereign rulers and kings cause them to set their minds at rest."
**The Twelfth Precept: Causing Distress through False Speech.** If a bhikṣu falsely utters deceptive words to cause distress to another, it is a *pāyattika*.
*Commentary:* When the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, Chanda committed an offense. When the bhikṣus questioned him about it, he immediately...
Regarding other matters, he replied: "To whom did you speak? What did you say? What principle were you discussing?
Were you speaking to me, or to someone else? Who committed the offense? From what did the offense arise? I see no offense; how can you say that I am guilty?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *jñapti-karman* for "speaking otherwise" (*anyavāda*) against him.
The precept was established as follows: "If a bhikṣu speaks evasively, it is a pāyattika offense.
Once the Saṃgha had enacted this prohibition against speaking evasively, he subsequently began to harass the community of monks: when summoned, he would not come; when not summoned, he would come.
When he should rise, he would not rise; when he should not rise, he would rise. When he should speak, he would not speak; when he should not speak, he would speak. The Buddha again...
The Saṃgha shall perform a formal act of *jñapti-karman* for causing vexation; thus these two matters are combined to establish the precept (the *karman* text is as in the Vinaya).
"Falsely" means to answer in a manner that does not accord with the facts. "With other words" refers to evasive speech;
it means that when the bhikṣus question them according to the Dharma, they give rise to resentment in their hearts and respond with evasive remarks.

"To whom did you speak? What did you say? and so on, up to "I do not see my offense. If one speaks such extraneous words before the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made by the Saṃgha, it is entirely an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one speaks such extraneous words after the formal motion has been made, it is entirely a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
Regarding "distressing another": this refers to intentionally desiring to cause distress to the person in question. To call out... [text ends]

Regarding "coming or not coming": if one comes when not called, or even speaks when one should not speak, if one thus disturbs the Saṃgha before the formal announcement (jñapti) has been made, it is entirely an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If one thus disturbs the Saṃgha after the announcement has been made, it is entirely a falling offense (pāyantika).
If an Elder calls someone to come and they do not come, they incur an offense of wrong-doing. As for the rest...
The same offense applies to bhikṣuṇīs. For the three lower groups of followers, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). There is no offense if one does not understand because of impaired hearing;
if there are discrepancies in the person’s speech; if one asks them back and they appear to speak irrelevantly;

or if they intend to perform an illegal or improper *kamma*, or intend to perform a *kamma* that would be disadvantageous to their two teachers or friends, and one does not join in harmony with them when summoned.

Regarding "Come" or "Do not come": if one wishes to know the instruction, when told "Do not come," one should nevertheless come. If one is eating in a single sitting, or if one is ill, when asked to rise, one should say:
"Venerable sir, please forgive me; because of such circumstances, I do not rise. Or, if there are various obstacles, when instructed "Do not rise," one may nevertheless rise.
If questioned with a malicious intent or the like, one should not provide an answer, as it would constitute an act contrary to the Dharma and Vinaya.

Regarding *anartha-karman* (unbeneficial formal acts), such as instructing someone not to speak and yet speaking oneself, and other similar instances of causing provocation—none of these constitute an offense (*na āpatti*).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If, within the Saṃgha, one asks one thing and answers another, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Among a large group, before two teachers, or in the presence of elders, if one asks one thing and answers another, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"If, toward the Saṃgha or those of venerable status, one violates and provokes them with a defiled mind regarding a teaching that accords with reason, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If one utters words of violation and provocation regarding a teaching that does not accord with reason, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. If one has been appointed to oversee communal affairs, and with a defiled or evil mind, fails to do what should be done or does what should not be done..."

If one acts [in such a way], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each instance; with a mind free from defilement, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If one treats the two teachers or the precepts with contempt, one incurs a *pāyattika* for each; if one treats other bhikṣus with contempt, it is a *dukkaṭa*, even down to [disregarding] the teacher’s instruction to sweep the ground."

If one does not sweep, or sweeps in accordance with instructions but then sweeps contrary to them, it is all an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu sees hunters pursuing deer or other game entering the monastery, and they ask, "Have you seen any deer pass this way?", he should not answer, "I saw them.

If it is cold weather, he should reply, "You may enter the heated room for a moment to warm yourself by the fire. If it is hot weather, he should reply, "You may enter the cool room for a moment to drink water and rest for a while. If they say, "I am not tired;

I am asking about the running deer," he should first look at his own fingernails and reply to them, "I see my fingernails. If they ask again, he should look into the great void and reply, "I see the great void. If...

He says, "I am not asking about fingernails, nor about empty space; rather, I am asking whether there is any fault in killing a sentient being. The bhikṣu should then look in all four directions and reflect thus: "In ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are fundamentally devoid of sentient beings.
He should then reply to him, "I do not perceive any sentient being. (In these cases, there is no offense.)
Thirteenth Precept on Scolding and Abusing:
If a bhikṣu scolds or abuses [another], it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting of the缘 (nidāna) is as in the second section regarding the precept on groundless slandering. Māluṅkyaputra was appointed by the Saṃgha.
He was in charge of the monks' bedding and the assignment of meals for the monks.

At a place where he could see but not hear, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra spoke with derision, saying, "The son of Māra has attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who established a precept.
Later, at a place where he could hear but not see, he again reviled him, saying he had attachment and so forth. [The Buddha] then combined these two matters into one.
He established the precept for this. "To harbor resentment" means to feel an inner inability to endure and thus to detest, loathe, revile, or disparage another.
This may occur either face-to-face or in private; here, the meaning is taken as face-to-face.

"Face-to-face" refers to a situation where one is within sight but not within hearing, yet speaks of [faults such as] favoritism and so forth. "To revile" means to utter unwholesome words and to scold.

To revile another—either face-to-face or behind their back; here, "behind their back" is the intended meaning. To revile behind one's back means to speak of them as having attachment and so forth in a place where they can hear it within earshot but cannot see it with their eyes.
Regarding the offense herein: if one reviles face-to-face or reviles behind their back, if the speech is clearly understood, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation);
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This applies even if an elder instructs [one to do so].

If you harbor resentment and revile [the person], or if you accept the instruction yet harbor resentment and revile, you incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). For the other four assemblies, the offense incurred is the same as above.
There is no offense if the person actually committed such an act and one speaks thus out of fear that they might later feel regret, in order to urge them to confess according to the Dharma;
or if spoken in jest, while speaking to oneself, in a dream, or by mistake. (According to other Vinayas, it is stated that reviling a person appointed by the Saṃgha incurs a *pācittiya* offense.)
[To reprove others for this] constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense).
○ The Fourteenth Precept on Spreading Monastic Bedding and Not Replacing It:
If a bhikṣu takes a monastic rope bed, wooden bed, bedding, sitting cushion, or mat spread out in the open air, or instructs another to do so...
[If a monk] spreads [a seat], leaves it, and neither picks it up himself nor instructs another to pick it up, it is a *pāyattika*.

The commentary explains: When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, seventeen groups of bhikṣus took the monastic sitting-mats, spread them out in the open air, and practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).
Without gathering them up, they departed for another invitation. Consequently, they were covered by wind-blown dust and soil, and infested by insects.

Birds pecked at it until it was ruined, becoming filthy and impure. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept: "To take" means to take it oneself or to instruct another to take it.
"The Saṃgha" refers to four or more bhikṣus. In this context, items such as rope beds and the like are considered property of the Saṃgha.

"Property of the Saṃgha" refers to that which was made for the Saṃgha but has not yet been relinquished to them, or that which belongs to the Saṃgha, meaning it has already entered [into their possession].

"Monks, it has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. As for the rope bed (*śayyā*), there are five types: namely, those with curved legs, straight legs, bent legs, those that fit through a doorway, and those without legs.
Wooden beds are likewise. As for bedding (*śayanāsana*), it is used either for sitting or for lying down.
A sitting cushion (*upadhāna*) is for the purpose of sitting. An open space (*abhyavakāśa*) is a place without coverings. To spread (*prajñap-) means to arrange."
"To depart" means to leave one's dwelling place. "Not to lift it up oneself" means not to collect or store it oneself.
"Not to instruct another to lift it up" means not to entrust someone else with the task of collecting it.
If there is a matter of necessity and one wishes to go, one should entrust it to a resident bhikṣu or a manager, saying: "I now have a matter of necessity."
When one is about to depart, one should entrust [the items] to a virtuous person (bhadanta) for protection and supervision.

If there is no one at all, one should place them in a secluded spot and then depart. If there is no secluded spot, one should settle them safely and then cover them with coarse materials before departing.
One should depart immediately upon being able to return. If it rains heavily and one returns quickly so that the items are not damaged, one may go. If it is moderate rain...
One may go if there is little rain and little travel, or if one can return. Regarding the offenses herein:
if one travels without employing the aforementioned expedients, at the moment one steps out the door, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one foot is outside the door and one foot is inside the door, and one intends to go but does not, or returns with regret, it is entirely an *dukkaṭa* offense.

If two people sit together on one bed, the junior person should fold it up and leave. If the junior person intends that the senior person should fold it up, but the senior person does not, the junior person commits a *pāyattika* offense;
furthermore, because it is contrary to proper decorum (*anācāra*), he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the senior person intends that the junior person should fold it up, but the junior person does not, the senior person commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If two people neither go first nor last and both fail to put things away, both incur an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).

If there are other empty rope beds, wooden beds, squatting stools, small tables, bathing benches, or the outer and inner covers of bedding, or floor mats, or if one takes ropes, wool, or hemp and places them in the open air, yet departs without putting them away, in all such cases one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If one spreads out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha...

If one leaves [the bedding] exposed in the open air without putting it away and enters a room to sit in meditation, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). The same offense applies to the other four assemblies.

There is no offense if one departs after having entrusted [the bedding] to another, if one departs for safety’s sake, or if one goes and returns immediately; these cases should be understood as above.

Furthermore, if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one is permitted to depart without putting it away. In all other cases, such as with empty beds, one must put them away before leaving.

And they departed. If two persons sit together, the one of lower rank should withdraw. When discussing the Dharma and Vinaya, if they differ by three *vassa*, they are permitted to sit together on wooden benches;
if they differ by two *vassa*, they are permitted to sit together on small rope benches.
Two persons should not sleep on the same bed, except in the case of illness. Two persons should not lie on the same bedding and covers; however, if there is no one else available, it is permitted.

Spread [the bedding] upon it. Each person shall separately place a woolen blanket for lying down. During the cold season, there is but a single coverlet; it is permitted to wear separate undergarments internally, while externally they are covered together.

To violate this incurs an offense. (According to the *Vinaya-mūla*: failing to guard communal property constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; if it concerns the personal property of another or one's own property, failing to guard it constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.

The person to whom the charge is entrusted must be a bhikṣu; others are not fit. It is also permitted when there is a specific reason. The *Vibhaṅga-vinaya* states: even a well-disciplined great śrāmaṇera may be entrusted with it. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: if no bhikṣu is present, one should inform [the layperson].)

If there is no *śrāmaṇera* (novice), one should entrust [the items] to a nearby donor. If there is no donor, one should look toward the four directions and only depart after having hidden the key to the door. If one encounters a *bhikṣu* on the road, one must point out the location of the key.

If, while on the road, another person offers to carry them for you, and upon arriving at the monastery, you fail to put them away during the first watch of the night, or even until the appearance of the dawn light, and you retrieve them without damage, you incur an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If you retrieve them after they have been damaged, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of downfall). There are five types of persons who are unfit to be entrusted with [items]:

those lacking shame and remorse, those with enmity, those who are aged and infirm, those suffering from illness, and those who are not fully ordained (*upasampanna*). Regarding all clothing belonging to the Saṃgha, it is improper to use it without interposing another object as a lining. As for that which...

Regarding replacement items: these must not be discarded or neglected. If monastic bedding or furnishings are damaged, one must not fail to repair them. Any holes or tears should be sewn and patched; if a part is torn or broken, it should be joined back together.

If an item cannot be repaired, it should be used as a lamp wick, or even used to fill gaps and crevices, so that the merit of the donor may increase. When bhikṣus listen to the Dharma at night, they must not sit on the same mat or rug in close proximity with bhikṣuṇīs, laypeople, or śrāmaṇeras.

However, there is no offense if there are difficult circumstances. One who has not yet completed his summer retreat (an *anupavāsaka*) must not share a seat with one who has completed three summers. One who has completed one summer may not share a seat with one who has completed four summers. Those who have completed two summers or more may all share a seat with those who have completed three summers or more.

Regarding sitting together: if the space in a layperson’s house is narrow, there is no offense even if one sits together with one's preceptor. On a single bed, it is permitted for up to three people to sit; on a large wooden stool, two people are permitted to sit; and on a small square seat, only one person may sit.
One should not sit upon a wooden stool by piling them up one on top of another).
○ The Fifteenth Precept: Regarding Not Putting Away Bedding in a Monastery Cell.
If a bhikṣu, within a monastery cell, spreads out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha—whether spreading it himself or instructing another to spread it—and then sits upon it [without putting it away].
If one lies down, and upon departing does not lift up [the bedding] oneself nor instruct another to lift it up, it is a *pāyattika*.

The commentary says: The setting of the Buddha is as before. At that time, there was a visiting bhikṣu who said to a resident bhikṣu, "I have spread out the monastic bedding in a peripheral monk’s cell and stayed overnight. Later, without informing the owner, he departed; consequently, the bedding became moldy.
[The bedding] was ruined; it was gnawed by insects and its color had changed. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
"Monastery quarters" refers to the dwelling place of the Saṃgha, capable of accommodating the four modes of deportment. "Bedding and requisites," etc., are explained as above.

If one has spread out monastic beds, mattresses, pillows, or even down to the sleeping mats, when departing one should personally put them away. If one entrusts them to another, saying, "Please guard and protect these for me," [the responsibility remains with the original owner].

Case: If there is no one present and one does not fear that anything will be lost, one should move the bed away from the wall, prop up its legs high, place the pillows and bedding inside, and cover them with coarse materials.
If one fears they might be damaged, one should place the bedding and other items on a clothing rack, stand the bed upright, and depart.
Regarding the offense herein: if one departs without performing the aforementioned actions, at the moment one crosses outside the boundary.
This constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. If one foot is outside the boundary, or even if one has resolved to go but does not go, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for the duration.
If one intends to return immediately but stays outside for two nights, and on the third night fails to return to one's own quarters before the dawn light appears, [one incurs a *pāyattika*].
If one does not send someone back to inform the guardian of the goods, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. For the other four assemblies, the offenses are the same as above.
There is no offense if one departs after performing the aforementioned sequence of actions; or if the time for returning is not long; or if there are various obstructing circumstances (*antarāya*).

One must not return alone; one should dispatch a messenger to return, etc., as explained above (*Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If bedding belonging to the Saṃgha has been spread in an inner chamber, if there is no enclosure, one may return after going beyond the distance of one stone-throw;

otherwise it is an *dukkaṭa*. If one returns after two stone-throws, it is a *pācittiya* offense. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "When intending to depart, one should sprinkle and sweep the floor inside the dwelling to make it clean, and sun the mats and pillows until they are dry.

One should inform the person in charge of the beds and mats. If one stays overnight in a layperson's house, one should give instructions upon departure. If the bedding is made of grass, when departing one should ask where this grass is to be placed and arrange it according to the host's word. If the host says, 'Just go,' I [the text]..."
Cooking. [One should depart after withdrawing one corner of the seat].
○ The Sixteenth Precept on Forcibly Taking Up Residence:
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu is already staying at a dwelling, comes later and forcibly spreads out bedding within it to stay overnight.

One should think: "If he finds it cramped or unpleasant, he will naturally avoid me and depart. To act with such a motive, and for no other reason, constitutes an *ābhisamācārikā* offense; it is a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. At that time, the group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling on a road toward a village where no bhikṣus resided.
The group of seventeen said to the group of six, "You are our seniors;
you should go first to seek lodging. The group of six replied, "You all may go yourselves; I will not seek lodging. At that time...

The group of seventeen monks went there immediately and spread out their bedding to stay the night. Later, the group of six monks arrived; they disputed the order of seniority and ordered them to rise.
When they would not rise, the group of six forcibly took seats among them, spread out their own sitting mats, and stayed the night.

The group of seventeen monks spoke out in a loud voice, saying, "Venerable sirs, do not do this! When the other bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept for those who know [the situation]. Or...
One knows this either by oneself or is informed by another; this shows it is not through ignorance.
"The prior resident monk" refers to a monk who previously stayed and slept there.

"A latercomer" refers to a monk who arrives later and, relying on his power, acts forcefully—that is, he casts his body down and sits or lies upon that bedding. "In between" refers to the area near the head.
"By the side of the feet" or "by the two sides" refers to bedding, such as mats of grass, mats of leaves, or even bedding spread directly upon the ground.
"With a thought" means giving rise to an unwholesome mind with the desire to cause another to move away of their own accord.
"If they find it cramped and so forth" means that, being oppressed by the suffering of being crowded, they will naturally leave me of their own accord. Thus he acts.
"Due to this cause and condition, and no other" means that by creating such unwholesome strong conditions as described above, one causes another to avoid [the act] themselves;
it is not due to any other circumstance. "Not part of proper deportment" means that it is something a bhikṣu should not do, and therefore incurs an offense. Regarding the transgression therein:
for every time one turns over onto one's side and lies upon the bed, it is a *pāyattika*. For the remaining four assemblies, the incurrence of the offense is the same as above. No.
Regarding the offense: if one was previously unaware; or if, after speaking, one remains [there]; or if it is spacious and does not cause obstruction;

or if a relative or acquaintance instructs one to spread out [a mat] therein; or if one is ill and lying down; or if there are difficulties such as being imprisoned or confined. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the dwelling place is small...")

A single bhikṣu should spread his bedding within the space between two pillars. If one who arrives later lies down upon another’s bed, and if he is a senior (sthavira), he should be told: "Venerable sir, do you not know that the Blessed One has established the precepts?

If he is a junior (navaka), he should be rebuked: "It is not well; you do not understand the characteristics of the precepts. You do not know that the Blessed One has established the precepts. Why have you come later and lain down upon another’s bed? If a bhikṣu is walking for exercise in another location and sees a bhikṣu who arrived earlier, he should move away.

If one disturbs a bhikṣu, he incurs a pāyattika offense; a bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense; the other three assemblies incur a vinayātikrama offense; and a layperson incurs a vinayātikrama with mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If, for the purpose of annoying another, one closes a door..."

Opening doors; closing doors; opening windows; lighting fires; extinguishing fires; lighting lamps; extinguishing lamps; chanting *brahman* hymns; reciting incantations; reading scriptures; preaching the Dharma; engaging in debate; or performing any action that causes others displeasure—committing such acts constitutes an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: In the latrines for defecation and urination, one should enter first regardless of seniority; whoever arrives there first shall enter first. At the place for washing the feet, one must follow the order of seniority. Regarding the utensils of the Saṃgha, down to the dyeing vessels, whoever uses them first must wait until they have finished their task; one should not [use them] according to seniority.

Regarding seniority: one who has been previously used [as a seat] should not be displaced. Furthermore, one should not place a small amount of dyed liquid in a vessel with the intention of letting it sit there. When reciting the scriptures, if someone has already taken their seat before you, you should not make them rise and move aside based on seniority.
Monastic razors, once used, should be returned to their original place and not left out. Those who do not act according to these rules all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The Seventeenth Precept on Dragging Someone Out of a Room:
If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu and wishing to displease him, personally drags that person out of a communal monastery room or instructs another to drag them out,
it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. The group of seventeen monks entered the monastery, swept and sprinkled the rooms, spread out bedding, and stayed overnight.

Later, the group of six monks arrived and forcibly pulled them [out]. Being angry and displeased, they drove them from the rooms. The Buddha established this precept for their sake. Regarding "pulling out":
it may mean pulling them out by hand, or driving them so that they must leave on their own. The rest is explained as above. In this matter, there is an offense.
If one drags many people out through many doors, there are multiple offenses of falling (pāyattika). If one drags many people out through a single door, there are multiple offenses of falling.
If one drags a single person out through a single door, there is one offense of falling; if out through many doors, there are multiple offenses of falling.
If one throws another's belongings outside the door, or if one shuts another inside the door, both constitute an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). The remaining four [cases] are as follows.
The offenses for the assembly are the same as above. There is no offense if one has no heart of resentment or malice; if one departs in the proper sequence;
or if, by the third night, one sends away a person who is not fully ordained; or if one sees that the person has broken the precepts, lacks proper deportment, or has been formally accused by another.

Regarding those who have been expelled and those who deserve expulsion: if, for this reason, there is a threat to one's life or to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there is no offense in expelling such persons.

(The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one brings someone whom [the resident] dislikes to live in the same room with the intent that they leave of their own accord, whether they leave or do not leave, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense. To drag out members of the other four assemblies [of the Saṃgha] constitutes an offense.")

Dukkaṭa (offense of wrong-doing). If a bhikṣuṇī drags out members of the two higher assemblies (bhikṣus and śikṣamāṇās), it is a pāyattika (offense of expiation); if she drags out members of the three lower assemblies (śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and upāsakas), it is a dukkaṭa. However, there is no offense if she drags out one who is shameless and reckless, or if she drags him out for the purpose of subduing a disciple. The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states:

If there is a bhikṣu who is quarrelsome, who can cause disputes to arise and cause disputes to increase, and whose precepts, views, conduct, and manners are largely deficient—if such a person is dragged out in anger, even if done without a virtuous intention, it constitutes a dukkaṭa.

If one drags out a pure bhikṣu from a place that is not a monastic residence, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. If a person has broken the precepts, the great assembly should collectively expel him. If one fears further quarreling, one should create a state of alarm and, by means of skillful methods, take his robes and bowl to remove him.

If one leads someone out—whether a disciple or another person—with a mind of reprimand, hoping to cause them to reform and desist, there is no offense when leading them out of the room. However, one should not force them out of their dwelling place. If they have committed no violation of the precepts but are merely difficult to converse with, one should employ the "method of pulling the bridle" to subdue them.

One should dispatch a wise person to go to them and offer exhortation, causing them to cease their evil ways and come forward to repent and apologize. If, however, they are full ordination recipients (*upasaka*) who do not show respect and are incapable of being instructed, [the following should be done].

One should provide six items [of clothing] and drive them away. If they are *śrāmaṇeras*, one should give them the two robes (the upper and lower) and likewise drive them away. If nāgas or snakes suddenly arrive at the dwelling, one should snap one’s fingers and say: "O worthy ones, you should depart to a distance; do not disturb the bhikṣus.

If they do not leave after being told this, one should catch them with a soft object and remove them; one must not bind them with hair-ropes or the like, nor cause them injury. One should release them calmly in a thicket of grass; once they have entered their hole, only then should one depart.

Regarding the discarding of fleas, lice, and the like, one must not simply throw them on the ground as one pleases. One should place them upon old cloth or fabric, having first observed whether it is cool or warm. If such material is unavailable, one should place them in a crack in a wall or a hole in a pillar, as appropriate.

Regarding their own sustenance, the *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* states: If there are bedbugs, place them among fresh green grass; if there are none, place them in a cool, shaded spot. If there are other insects, they may be placed in a suitable location. No living being should be abandoned by hanging it up, causing it to faint. The *Mūla-vinaya* states:

One should not pick up lice and discard them on the ground in a place where many people reside. Because elderly or infirm bhikṣus grew exhausted from repeatedly rising to discard the lice, it was permitted to make tubes from ivory, horn, bamboo, reed, wood, or similar materials.

One should pick up the lice and place them inside. Once the lice have emerged, one should provide a lid and fasten it with thread, securing it within the leg of the bed. [The commentary] explains: One should not store them in the tube for a long time, causing them to starve or freeze; rather, one should take them out and place them in a suitable location. [The text] says "to drag."

Regarding the method of "restraining with a halter": this means to temporarily set the person aside, neither speaking with them nor engaging in joint activities. It is like a wild horse that is difficult to tame; one should immediately tether it to a hitching post and abandon it [for the time being].)
○ The Eighteenth [Offense]: Sitting or Lying on a Bed with Detachable Legs on an Upper Story.
If a bhikṣu, in a room or on an upper story, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with detachable legs, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting of the Buddha is as before. At that time, a bhikṣu was staying on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sitting on a bed with removable legs.

He was not composed in his posture; because the floor of the gallery was thin and the legs of the bed came loose, he fell onto a bhikṣu who was sleeping below, injuring his body and causing blood to flow.
The Buddha established this precept for him. Regarding "a dwelling": it refers to either a communal monastic cell or a private cell, specifically a room on an upper story of a multi-storied building.
According to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* translated by Yaśas, there is no character "ruò" (if) above or below the character "fáng" (room).

Regarding "double-storied buildings" (*chónggé*), this refers to multi-level rooms, lofts, or pavilions; it specifically denotes those where the top of the standing bed does not reach the upper level.

Based on this, such pavilions must have been lofts that were dilapidated, thin, and unstable, or perhaps pavilions made of bamboo, reeds, or grass. As for "removing the legs of the bed," this refers to beds with removable or detachable legs.
If a bed has detachable legs, the frame is thin and not secure, and it is further unstable; thus, faults arise from this.
If the bed has detachable legs but the frame is sturdy, there is no fault. If the frame is not solid, one may fix the legs with a narrow waist-piece, or secure them with wedges and bindings.
Or one may support it with wooden boards; this is not a fault. Although the bedstead is sturdy and secure, one must still remain composed and careful.

For the rule of a bhikṣu is that in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must always maintain mindfulness and act with deliberate care. If one gives rein to the mind and acts with agitation or playfulness, one immediately incurs an offense.
Regarding the transgression herein: for every time the side touches the bed, and for every time one turns over, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling), except when one is removing the bedding.
Regarding beds with protruding legs: if one sits on a single-seated bed, a plank bed, or a bathing bed, it is entirely an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
For the other four assemblies, the offense is the same as above. There is no offense if one sits on a bed with swiveling legs, straight legs, curved legs, or no legs at all;
or if the supports of the bed are large; or if there is a wooden floor covering on an upper story; or if the bed is placed upside down; or if the legs have been removed from the bed.
[The section on] the feet, etc.
○ Nineteenth Precept: Using Water with Living Beings to Irrigate Mud or Grass.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, personally irrigates mud or grass, or instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*.

[The Buddha] said: "Tī. The commentary explains: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, Chanda constructed a large building using mud mixed with water containing living organisms. He instructed others to mix it.
Consequently, the Buddha established this precept. "One who knows" means either one knows through self-examination or one knows through the words of another. "Water" refers to...
Regarding ponds, rivers, wells, water, and even liquids such as gruel or vinegar: "insects" refers to those visible to the eye within the water, or those seen after filtering.
"Pouring" means to drench; it is also a synonym for "using. There are two types of use: internal and external.
Internal refers to things such as food and drink; external refers to pouring, sprinkling, irrigation, washing, and bathing.
This is categorized as an external application; its internal application is governed by the subsequent precepts. Regarding the offenses herein:

if one knows that water contains insects, yet uses it to moisten mud or grass, or casts grass and soil into it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If there are insects in the water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If there are insects in the water but one suspects it, or if there are no insects but one perceives them as such, or suspects it, [the same applies].

One incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*. For the other four assemblies, the offenses incurred are the same as above. There is no offense if one does not know there are insects, or if one perceives them as being insect-free;
or if the insects are large and one touches the water with the hand to make them leave; or if one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground, etc.

(According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the Sarvāstivāda school, if there is doubt regarding the presence of insects, one also incurs the full offense (*pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*), which differs from this particular school. Other precepts regarding doubtful offenses should be understood by analogy with this case. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "For each insect that dies, one falls into an offense. [This applies to] the roots.")

The Fundamental Vinaya states: In ponds, rivers, or places with water, there are often many insects and fish. If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, diverts the water, the insects incur the offense of a *pārājika* (a grave downfall) according to the number of lives lost; if they do not die, it is an *dukkaṭa* (an offense of wrong-doing). If one dams this water source so that the flow is cut off...

If insects die at the bottom [of the vessel], the offense is the same as previously described. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Even if there are no insects in the water, one must not discard it recklessly; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. One must instead sprinkle it out or pour it toward the edge of a drain, within a distance of one cubit (*hasta*), which is the proper place for disposal. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu requires water for constructing a dwelling or a heated bathhouse, he should draw it from a pond, river, or well using a filter until the vessel is full. He must then inspect it to ensure there are no insects before using it. If there are still insects present, he should filter it again with a cloth bag and examine it closely."

If there are still insects after three layers [of filtration], one should dig another well and observe it closely as before. If there are still insects, one should abandon the work at hand and go elsewhere. The birth of insects is impermanent;

they may have been absent previously and now exist, or they may exist now and later cease to be. Therefore, a bhikṣu should observe daily and use water only when it is free of insects. The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "When wishing to construct a dwelling, one should first examine the water using a fine cloth folded into a single-layered bag."

Once those who are diligent in observing the precepts have finished straining the water, they should hold the vessel up toward the sun and examine it closely. If there are still insects present, they should make a filter-bag of three layers. If there are still insects after three layers, one should not remain in that place. Generally, there are three ways of killing living beings:

killing for the sake of greed for hair, horns, hide, or flesh; killing out of resentment, hatred, or malice; and killing without any desire for gain and without any ill will or malice—this is called killing through delusion. To use water containing insects in this manner is what is meant by killing through delusion.
**The Twentieth Precept on Roofing a House Beyond Three Layers:** If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling,
including the door, windows, and other decorative fittings, he may direct that the roofing of straw be applied up to two or three layers.
If it exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense.

The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. He constructed a large hall, covering it with straw; he covered it again and again, exceeding three layers without stopping, until the roof collapsed.
A householder saw this and disapproved. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who established the precept:
"To construct" means either to build it oneself or to instruct others to build it. "A large hall" refers to one that exceeds the prescribed dimensions or uses excessive materials.
As for "door-leaves," these are the panels of a gate. As for "windows and casements," these refer to openings pierced through walls to admit light.
As for "other decorative furnishings," this refers to carvings, engravings, and colorful paintings, as well as all other such ornaments.

According to the architectural style of dwellings, towers, and pavilions in the Western Regions (India), they consist of plank houses with flat roofs, with walls plastered with lime and covered with bricks or tiles, or sometimes thatched with reeds or grass.
As for the boards and wood, doors, windows, walls, and fences—there are various marvelous constructions and diverse forms of ornate decoration.
"Directing" means instructing and showing. "Covering with thatch" means roofing a house. There are two kinds of covering:
namely, vertical covering and horizontal covering. "Leveling at two or three joints" refers to limiting the measurement to two or three layers of joints.
"Exceeding" means to go beyond the limit; therefore, one incurs an offense. Regarding the violation herein:
if, after two sections have been covered by pointing out [the path], while the third section is not yet finished, one should go to a place where one is neither seen nor heard.

If one does not go, and the third section is completed, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika). If one leaves the place where one is heard and goes to a place where one is seen, or leaves the place where one is seen and goes to a place where one is heard...
In all cases of misconduct (*duṣkṛta*), the offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. There is no offense if the third section of the concealment has not yet been completed;
if one goes to a place where [the act] was neither seen nor heard, or if one is unable to go due to being obstructed by various difficulties, there is no offense.

(According to this school and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one departs before the third section of the concealment is finished, there is no offense. Other schools hold that the offense is established only upon reaching the fourth section. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If, when building a wall, it is made of wet mud...")

Beginning with the leveling of the ground and the laying of the foundation, one should erect the walls. One should apply two or three layers of plastered bricks; to exceed this number constitutes an offense. However, if the materials are fired bricks, stone, or wood, or if the donor wishes for a swift completion, there is no offense even if the number of layers exceeds the limit.

While explaining the rules concerning dwellings, at that time the five bhikṣus bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, in what kind of rooms and bedding should we reside? The Buddha—

The Buddha said: "It is permitted to dwell in an araṇya, at the foot of a tree, in an empty room, in a mountain valley, within a cave, in the open air, beside a stack of grass, at the edge of a forest, by a cemetery, or by a body of water. Or, if one spreads grass or leaves;

or if a donor has built a great lecture hall, a multi-storied pavilion, or various types of rooms for the Saṃgha, it is permitted to use them. When a bhikṣu wishes to build a dwelling, whatever materials are required..."
I permit all of these. I permit the making of beds, mattresses, and pillows—whether square, round, or triangular.
I permit the making of doors, door pivots, door panels, bolts, and keys. I permit the making of windows, window shutters, lattice screens, and fastenings;
for the fastenings, I permit the installation of horizontal bars. For young novices, I permit the installation of partitions within the rooms. I permit the making of large beds and small beds.
For sitting alone, one requires either a plank or a floor mat; for the *poṣadha* hall, its construction is permitted.
When many people gather for the *poṣadha*, long benches, long planks, grass seats, or mats spread upon the ground—or even sitting on leaves—are permitted.

Furthermore, the construction of a long hall for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) is permitted. If one is old, sick, or infirm, it is permitted to seek out a rope with both ends tied together and walk along that rope.

When walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), the hands are chafed by grasping the cord. It is permitted to make a loop. Alternatively, one may pass the cord through a bamboo tube and grasp the tube while walking in meditation.
When one becomes exhausted from walking in meditation, one should place beds at both ends [of the path]. One should construct a separate area for washing the feet.

Within the monastery, it is permitted to construct a pond, provided it is covered with a roof above and has railings on all four sides. It is permitted to construct a separate building for holding water. A sick bhikṣu should not remain [there].
One should reside in a large room on the upper floor. One should construct a separate small hut and install therein a chamber-pot and a spittoon.
If cattle or sheep enter the monastery, it is permitted to construct a moat or enclosure; one may build a bridge of boards and wood with railings on both sides.

It is permitted to construct channels for water passage or to dig wells. One should construct a well-railing and cover it with a roofed structure. It is permitted to stay in a screened area near such a building.
One should construct a bathhouse. It should be provided with doors and windows; there should be openings at the top to allow smoke to escape.
One should construct a bathing platform and pave the floor with bricks or stones. One should separately build a room for storing robes, a room for warm water, and a room for storing firewood.

When entering the bath, one should sit according to seniority. One should not bathe together with laypeople (*avadātavasana*). However, it is permitted to bathe if one praises the Triple Gem, or if one listens to the [Dharma] four times.
One should bathe while being shielded from view by various obstructions, such as walls, trees, grass, or water.
If one suffers from the cold while bathing, one should build a separate fire-hall and install a brazier within it. One must not decorate the hall with embroidered images of men or women;
however, it is permitted to use various other colors and patterns of birds and beasts (as detailed in the explanatory notes). One should not... [end of fragment].

If one intends to build a house for as long as one lives—even a most excellent, grand, multi-storied hall—one is permitted to undertake the construction for twelve years, provided it is completed within six years;
for other projects, the duration should be adjusted according to their size and scale.

A bhikṣu engaged in construction should not accept a monastery building from the Saṃgha at all times; he is permitted to do so only after the three months of the summer retreat have concluded, following the seniority of the assembly.

Regarding the allocation of seats: one should not take up residence in various different administrative quarters (karmadāna-vihāra). One should stay in a single location for the ninety days of the summer retreat (varṣā).
An administrator (karmadāna) should not reside in a place where many people live, nor should they seek an administrative quarter for performing minor repairs.
During the summer retreat, once one has accepted a regulated dwelling, one should not accept another room; one should remain in that very place.

Regarding the dwelling: one may construct a dwelling for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). If a monastic dwelling has become dilapidated and a layperson says, "If you give this to me, I shall repair it for the Saṃgha," the Saṃgha should authorize its transfer by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation).

The *karmadāna* (officer in charge of affairs) who departs before the Saṃgha has distributed the dwellings should designate someone to take possession of them; he should point out and assign specific rooms, and he must not keep them for himself.
White clothing and vessels; plows; or nets. One should not make sitting benches, earthenware jars, or earthen measures such as *sheng*, *dou*, or *he*.

(The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It is not permitted to possess fields, houses, or shops. If there are offerings, it is permitted for the Sangha to accept them and have a *karmadāna* [pure person] manage them.")
**The Twenty-first Precept: Teaching Nuns Personally.** If a bhikṣu, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, teaches and exhorts bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*.
*Commentary:* When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī requested of the Buddha that he permit [the bhikṣus] to...
The Buddha instructed Ānanda that, in turn, the senior monks should go to admonish and teach the nuns, preaching the Dharma to them.
When it was the turn of the Venerable Panthaka, he was to go; however, the Venerable had mastered only a single verse.
Upon arriving there, he recited that one verse three times, and three times he entered the fourth dhyāna. Those arhats—
The nuns were all greatly delighted. The group of six nuns then began to mock and revile them. The Venerable One immediately ascended into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations;

he preached the Dharma and departed. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went themselves to provide instruction, yet they spoke of other matters instead of the true Dharma, discussing only worldly treatises and secular affairs. The group of six nuns were extremely [offended].

Rejoicing, Mahāprajāpatī went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, the Saṃgha shall appoint a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs through a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
At that time, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus immediately went outside the boundary and appointed one another to go [and instruct].
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Only after one has accomplished ten qualities may one then teach."

[The Buddha] granted [the permission] for bhikṣuṇīs. Consequently, he established the precepts (the ten rules; as set forth above in the six methods of skillful means). "The Saṃgha" refers to those who share the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa and the same formal acts (karmavācanā).
"Not delegated" means not having been dispatched by a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) within the Saṃgha.
"Instruction" refers to teaching them by means of the eight rules that must not be transgressed. [This applies to a bhikṣuṇī] even if she is one hundred years old.
1. Upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, one should rise to meet him, inquire after his well-being, prostrate to him, and invite him to sit.

2. One must not revile or slander a bhikṣu. 3. One must not bring up a bhikṣu’s offenses, whether by means of formal recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*), by means of a confession (*pratijñā-kāraka*), by obstructing another's search for an offense, by obstructing the *poṣadha* ceremony, or by obstructing the *pravāraṇā*. Nor should one speak of another’s faults; however, a bhikṣu may be permitted to speak [of them] himself.
1. The faults of a bhikṣuṇī. 2. She loses her precepts by requesting [ordination] from the community of bhikṣus. 3.

If she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must perform the *mānatva* penance for half a month within both communities of monks. 4. During that half-month, she must request a person to provide instruction from the community.
5. She should not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) where there are no bhikṣus. 6. Upon concluding the retreat, she must go to a place where there are bhikṣus.
Among the monastics, one should seek three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected—during the *pravāraṇā*.
These eight rules should be respected, honored, and praised; for as long as life lasts, they must not be transgressed (also known as the Eight Rules of Reverence). Regarding violations herein:

if one goes to preach the Eight Rules of Reverence when the Saṃgha has not appointed one, or on a day other than the day of instruction, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. To preach [them in such circumstances] is a violation.

Regarding other matters, these constitute offenses of transgression (*pāyattika*). If the Saṃgha appoints someone to go [on a mission], they should arrive at the appointed time; the nun should also meet them at the appointed time.

If one does not arrive at the appointed time, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If the nun does not go out to meet [the visitor] when the time arrives, she also incurs an offense of wrong-doing.

The nun should go out half a *yojana* to meet [the visitor] and provide for their needs; if she does not do so, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense in cases such as those mentioned above regarding the Saṃgha.

He was dispatched. If various obstacles or hindrances prevent him from arriving on time, [he is not at fault]. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one does not appoint someone to instruct the nuns, for every instance [of failing to do so], it constitutes an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*). )

To instruct the other two daughters [of the Buddha] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one enters the nuns' quarters to provide instruction without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, one incurs a transgression for every step taken inside; if even one foot has crossed the threshold, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This excludes cases where a bhikṣuṇī is ill.

The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana-vinaya*) states that there are eight qualities by which one is qualified to instruct nuns: first, maintaining the precepts without violation; second, guarding the *prātimokṣa* and practicing the unsurpassed Dharma; third, being fully endowed with dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and not sustaining oneself through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

One does not go to five places: fourth, seeing even a minor transgression, one gives rise to a mind of dread; fifth, one firmly maintains a mind of non-retrogression; sixth, one possesses extensive learning; seventh, one’s extensive learning is firm and stable; eighth, one discerns and expounds the Dharma as being good in the beginning, middle, and end.

Possessing a pure, singular, and stainless holy life (*brahmacarya*), with right view free from deviation, one should recite the two sets of precepts with clear meaning and characters, and with a fluent and harmonious voice. One is thus respected and honored by the nuns and is well able to preach the Dharma in accordance with their needs.

If one does not preach the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) but instead first preaches other teachings, it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When instructing the nuns, one must not do so from sunset until the appearance of the morning light. One must not go to a secluded or private place, nor to an exposed place; rather, one should go to a place that is neither too secluded nor too exposed—such as a lecture hall or beneath a tree.

One must not go on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month, nor on the first, second, or third day. One should go to provide instruction from the fourth to the thirteenth day. Furthermore, one must not instruct those who are not in harmony.

Having joined the assembly of *bhikṣuṇīs*, once arrived, one should ask whether the *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha is in harmony. If they say it is harmonious, one should dispatch a messenger to summon them. If they cannot come, one should grant them the *anuśāsanī-chanda* (the consent for instruction).

One must not provide partial instruction, nor should one provide instruction in long-winded speech. Regarding "instruction" (*anuśāsana*): whether it be *Abhidharma* or *Vinaya*. The *Mūla-vinaya* states: "Instruction means instructing them by means of the three trainings of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)."
The twenty-second precept concerning instructing bhikṣuṇīs until sunset:
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting for the Buddha is as before. At that time, the Venerable Nanda was appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the community of nuns.
Because the Venerable possessed a beautiful voice, those who heard him preach the Dharma took great delight in it; consequently, he continued until sunset.

When the nuns departed from Jetavana and entered the city, the city gates were already closed. They therefore stayed overnight within the moat surrounding the city wall. At dawn, when the gates opened...
He entered the city ahead of them. When the elders saw him, they spoke with resentment and slander, saying that he had stayed overnight with the bhikṣus.

Consequently, the Buddha established this precept (this refers not to the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda). "Appointed by the Saṃgha" means appointed through the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* among the assembly of monks.
"Until sunset" means the sun has already set and night is about to fall; it is not an appropriate time for instruction or admonition. If it is as follows...
Instruction is termed "untimely. Regarding the offense therein: if one provides instruction until sunset, one incurs a *pācittiya* (offense of expiation).
Excluding formal instruction, if one recites a sutra, rehearses a sutra, asks questions, or engages in other matters until sunset, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
This applies except for [teaching] bhikṣuṇīs; if one teaches a sutra or engages in other matters for any other woman, [the same applies].
If it reaches sunset, it is also an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If it is sunset and one perceives it as such, there is a *pācittiya* (offense involving forfeiture).
If it is sunset and one is in doubt, or if it is not sunset but one perceives it as such, or if it is not sunset and one is in doubt—all these result in an *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if one stops before sunset; or if it is at a ferry crossing where a *bhikṣuṇī* preaching the Dharma is permitted; or if traveling with merchants and preaching the Dharma at night.

If one goes to a nunnery to preach the Dharma; or if, on the day of the *Poṣadha* (confession ceremony), one is invited to come as an instructor (*śāstṛ*) and happens to encounter a preaching of the Dharma and listens to it;

[the *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Even if it is within the permitted time, if the assembly of nuns stands rather than sits, or if their busy activities have not ceased, or if they are physically constrained, yet one preaches the Dharma for them, this is also called 'improper time' (*akāla')"].

Or if a donor originally intends to invite a Dharma Master to preach throughout the night; or if the nunnery is directly opposite a city gate; or if the city gates are not closed; or if the residence is located within the city; or if the nuns are among laypeople.
[He] abandons [the offense]. (In all these cases, there is no transgression).
○ The twenty-third precept concerning the disparaging of the instruction of nuns:
If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus, "The bhikṣus teach [the Dharma] for the sake of food and drink," [he commits an offense].
Regarding the term "bhikṣuṇī": it is a *pāyattika* offense.

The commentary explains: The setting is as before. At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the instructor was coming, they went half a *yojana* to welcome him, provided him with lodging, prepared food, beds and seats, and bathing facilities. The group of six [monks] did not receive the appointment from the Saṃgha.
A mind of jealousy arose, and he said: "The bhikṣus have no genuine sincerity; they instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs solely for the sake of food and drink.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established this precept: "To speak in such a manner is a word of derision and disparagement.
Regarding "food and drink": this is a general term for both proper and improper food, and it is one of the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).

Regarding the offenses herein: if one says that the bhikṣus teach the nuns for the sake of food and drink, or that they instruct them in the recitation or transmission of scriptures for the sake of food and drink, and the meaning is clearly understood, all incur a *pāyattika* offense. If the meaning is not clearly understood, they incur a *dukkaṭa*.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if the fact is actually so, or if it was spoken in a dream, or through a mistake.

Regarding the statement "and so forth" (*ādi*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "If one says it is for the sake of medicine, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinayātikrama* offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states, "If one says that one instructs a bhikṣu—or members of the three lower assemblies—for the sake of making offerings, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one says that a bhikṣu practices the twelve *dhūtas*, sits in meditation, recites sūtras, or performs various meritorious deeds—all for the sake of the benefit of making offerings—it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for every such statement."

**The Twenty-fourth Pāyattika: The Precept on Giving Robes to a Bhikṣuṇī Who Is Not a Relative.** If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for goods, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. In the city, there was a mendicant bhikṣu who was fully endowed with dignified deportment.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī saw him and repeatedly invited him to accept food, but he did not accept. Later, this bhikṣu obtained a share of a robe.
Intending to repay her for her previous invitations, and thinking she would not accept it otherwise, he immediately gave the robe to that bhikṣuṇī, who accepted it at once. This bhikṣu...
The Bhagavān frequently reproached that nun in the presence of others. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept:

"Regarding one who is not a relative (*apratigṛhīta*)," this means one who is not a relative; thus, having no sense of regard or consideration, they do not deliberate upon whether the bhikṣu possesses robes or not, and accept them as soon as they obtain them.
"Robes" refers to the ten kinds as explained above, with the exception of those obtained through exchange; this refers to mutual [bartering].
Exchanging [robes] is not an offense. Regarding the offenses herein: if one gives a robe to a nun who is not a relative, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.

If the other four assemblies give [a robe] to one who is not a relative, they incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Those who do not incur an offense are: giving to a relative; or exchanging with one another. (The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:

"If one gives a robe to a relative nun who has broken the precepts or holds wrong views, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one gives a robe to a non-relative woman or a girl, it is a *dukkaṭa*. However, there is no offense if it is for the purpose of managing household affairs, for the purpose of skillfully preaching the Dharma, or..."

If one gives robes for the sake of reciting many sutras or precepts, there is no offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one sees someone who has encountered calamity and lacks clothing, one may give it to them; or if one gives out of the occasion of preaching the Dharma or receiving the precepts, there is no offense."
The twenty-fifth precept: Making a robe for a nun who is not a relative.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense.

The commentary states: The setting is as before. At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who wished to have a *saṃghāṭī* robe made. She took it to the monastery, and Kālodāyin accepted it and began to cut it.
He then fashioned the image of a man and woman engaged in sexual intercourse. When the bhikṣuṇī returned, he folded the robe and gave it back to her, saying:
"You must not open or look at this robe carelessly, nor show it to others. When it is time for the announcement (*śuklā-vastu*)," [he continued].
When it was time [to go out], she should follow behind the community of nuns. The nun acted according to her instructions; when the time arrived, she put on her robes and followed behind.

When the lay devotees saw this, they clapped their hands and laughed loudly. The nuns became aware of the situation and informed the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept:
"Regarding those who are not relatives—this means that because one is not a relative, there is no heart of protective care, which leads to harm and loss."
Regarding "performing acts that are not beneficial": this refers to sewing, cutting, washing, and dyeing. As for the offense herein:
if one makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative, then for every portion cut by the knife, as well as for every stitch and every needle, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.

If one opens and looks at it, pulls and drags it, irons and straightens it, rubs and strokes it, grasps its corners, pulls it to align it, smooths it out, or uses a border, a cord, or joins a thread—these all constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses;

for the other four assemblies, they are *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one does so for the sake of the Saṃgha or a stūpa, or if one borrows, wears, washes, dyes, or repairs it with the intention of returning it to the owner. (The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "At the very moment one takes the robe, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.")
The Seventh Fascicle of the Commentary on the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra).
Phonetic Glossary:
*Jué* (钯); the first character is pronounced as *kuāng* (匡) with a falling tone (*rùshēng*), and the second character is pronounced as *zuō* (捉), meaning "to pare" or "to shave."
*Tiāo* (pronounced *tiǎo*, with the second tone): the character *qiàn* (嵌) belongs to the entering tone; it means a gourd thorn. *Què* (橛): the pronunciation is *jué*;
it refers to a piece of wood, specifically a wooden stake or peg.
*Shuān* (栓): the same as the character *què*; it refers to a piece of wood driven into the ground.
*Kǒng* (鑛) is pronounced *kuàng*.
*Zhě* (赭) is pronounced *zhě*, meaning red earth.
*Shàn* (墡) is pronounced *shàn*, meaning white earth.
*Āo* (拗) is pronounced *qiǎo* (切). Its sound is that of *āo* (凹) in the third tone; it means to snap or break. *Lā* (拉) is pronounced *là* (蠟);
it means to pull, to break, or to crush. *Bèilěi* (蓓蕾):
the first character is pronounced *bèi* (倍), and the second is pronounced *lěi* (壘). It refers to flower buds beginning to bloom.
The pronunciation of *qù* (醭) is *pū*; the pronunciation of *lù* (漉) is *liù*;
the pronunciation of *gē* (墼) is *jí*. It refers to unbaked bricks or tiles (*zhuānbāi*).
*Tān* (pronounced with the *shī-lián* rhyme) and *shǎn* (entering tone): to thatch a roof with woven straw.
*Láo* (pronounced *láo*): to weave bamboo or wood; this is another name for a *mò* (grindstone).
The Commentary on the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, Fascicle Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Jiqi. Section:
The Twenty-sixth Precept Regarding Sitting in Secret with a Nun.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. At that time, Kālodāyin went to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā and sat together with her in one place outside the gate.
Householders criticized and disparaged this. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established this precept.
"Alone" means that a single bhikṣu sits together with a single bhikṣuṇī. "In a secluded place" refers to a screened or concealed location, as explained in the *Aniyata-dharma*.
Regarding the offense herein: if one sits alone in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one stands, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

[The offense of] *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) is incurred by the other four assemblies. There is no offense if one has a companion, or if one falls to the ground due to sudden illness while walking, and so forth.

(According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, even other modes of conduct [such as standing] may incur a *pāyattika* offense. The Sarvāstivādins state that for every time one rises and then sits down again, one incurs a corresponding number of *pāyattika* offenses. If one sits with two other women in a secluded place, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.)
The Twenty-seventh Precept on Traveling with a Bhikṣuṇī:
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment to travel along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī, from one village to another, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The "appropriate times" are: when traveling with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or terror; these are called the appropriate times.
The commentary states: At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. The group of six bhikṣus and the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were traveling together through the countryside.
When the laypeople saw this, they all looked upon them with disapproval. Consequently, the Buddha established a precept. Later, while the bhikṣus were on the road...
They happened to meet by chance; out of apprehension and caution, they did not dare to travel together. The Buddha said, "There is no offense if it was not prearranged.

At that time, both the community of monks and the community of nuns wished to go to the country of Vaiśālī. Because they could not travel together, the nuns were left behind and were plundered by bandits.
It was for this reason that he permitted [traveling] at different times. "Prearranged" (期) means to have made a mutual agreement or appointment regarding the departure.
"Reaching a certain place" means that those who share the same path do not follow a different route. "The path" refers to the section of road between villages.
"Those who travel" refers to those who proceed together along the way. "From one village to another" refers to traversing the boundaries of inhabited settlements.
"Except at other times" refers to circumstances of difficulty, such as when there are traveling merchants.
Traveling together [with a nun] is not an offense. Regarding those who are suspicious, fearful, or terrified, it is as explained in the section on the thirty [offenses].

Among these, an offense occurs if one makes an appointment with a nun to travel together, even for the distance between villages; according to the number of people and the extent of the boundaries, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
If traveling through uninhabited areas outside of villages, even for a distance of ten *li*, there is a *pāyattika* offense. If it is less than the distance of one village... [text ends]
[The distance] is reduced by ten *li*. If there are multiple villages between [the points], they share the same boundary for travel.

If one intends to depart through some means and agrees with another on an appointment to adorn themselves, it constitutes an *duṣkṛta* offense for all; for the other four assemblies, it is a *sātisāra*.

There is no offense if one is constrained by force and so forth. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one does not make an appointment but happens to travel together on the same road, one should maintain a distance such that their speech cannot be heard by the other. If they hear each other and then return [to the path], one incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense. If with..."
