Once you have obtained a *viśuddhika*, any money or precious gems obtained thereafter need only be declared pure (*viśuddhi*) before the bhikṣus;

it is not necessary to state the name of the *viśuddhika*. Having performed the declaration of purity, you may keep the items for as long as you wish. If the *viśuddhika* dies or travels far away to another country, you should seek another *viśuddhika*. With the exception of money and precious gems, all surplus property (*atireka-dhana*) must be made pure before the five groups of monks (*pañca-varga*).

You should seek one who maintains the precepts, is learned, and possesses virtue to serve as the *viśuddhika*. Should you later obtain an object, you must declare the name of the *viśuddhika* before a single bhikṣu and perform the rite of declaring purity. If the *viśuddhika* dies or travels far away to another country, you should again seek another *viśuddhika*. [The exception of money and precious gems applies.]

All criminals, as well as those who are blind, deaf, mute, blind from birth, afflicted by disease, or mentally impaired—indeed, any recipient of pure offerings who wishes to be purified and act as a witness, yet does not give rise to strife—such persons as these are not in accordance with the Dharma.
The Sixtieth Precept: Not Dyeing New Garments.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new garment, he must apply one of three types of dye to alter its color. Within each category of color, he may choose whichever he prefers. For example, blue.
If one wears a new garment that is black, madder-colored, or not discolored by dye, it is a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. The group of six monks wore white garments while walking about, which caused householders to criticize and resent them;
consequently, the precept was established. Regarding "new garment": if it is a new garment, or if it is first obtained from another person, it is entirely termed a "new garment. (If from...)
If a person obtains a robe of color that conforms to the Dharma, according to principle there should be no offense; however, it must be purified by marking (*parikarman*) before being worn.
Regarding what should be dyed in one of the three types of discolored colors: these refer to blue (*nīla*), black (*kāṣāya*), and madder-brown (*māñjiṣṭha*).

"Discoloring at will within each color" means that among these three colors, one may choose whichever one pleases. As for "blue," it is not a very deep blue nor a pure blue. As for "black," it refers to mud-colored [dye].
[The Buddha said: "It must be dyed. However, the use of pure black mud-dye is not permitted, as it resembles the robes of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
It should be combined with red earth, red stone, or tree bark. As for *mūlāna*, it is the name of a tree; it is also called *linlan*.
Its bark dyes cloth to produce a reddish color. Regarding the offense herein: if one obtains a new garment and wears it without having dyed it in these three colors, [it constitutes an offense].

...is an offense of falling (pāyattika). If one possesses heavy robes, light robes, a bowl bag, a sandal bag, a needle and thread bag, a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, socks, or a headcloth, and keeps them without having performed the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), it is entirely an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If one entrusts an undyed robe to the house of a layperson, it is also an offense of wrong-doing. For the other four assemblies, the acquisition of offenses is the same as above. There is no offense if...

This violates the aforementioned regulations. If the color of the robe fades, it should be dyed again. (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one obtains a blue garment, it must undergo two kinds of purification: either with mud or with madder. If one obtains a garment dyed with mud, it likewise requires two kinds of purification: either blue or madder.

If one obtains a garment dyed with madder, it likewise requires two kinds of purification: either blue or mud. If one obtains a yellow, red, or white garment, it should be purified by the three aforementioned methods. The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Down to the cloth for wiping the bowl, the towel for wiping the feet, the bowl bag, the waistband, and so forth—all must be dyed to change their original color (*dūṣya-varṇa*) and kept after having been marked with the 'purification by dots' (*tilaka-śuddhi*). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Except for the three robes (*tricīvara*), all other garments may be worn without fault provided they have been marked with the 'three-dot purification' (*tri-tilaka-śuddhi*)."

If it is not pure blue, but light blue or azure, one may perform the ritual of *piṇḍa-śuddhi* (purification by marking) and make it into an inner undergarment (*saṃkakṣikā*). It may be worn provided it does not appear on the outside. If making a garment for visible wear, one must not use red, yellow, or white; nor may colors that are not pure or are large [in hue].

It is the same for all other garments, bedding, and requisites, with the exception of *puṭa* (sandals) and leather shoes; all must be worn after performing the "three-dot purification" (*trimaṇḍala*). Whoever wears them without performing this purification incurs an offense. If one wears a garment of lawful color that has been marked with the five primary colors (*pañcamahāvarṇa*), it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Apart from the five primary colors, there are pure yellow, indigo, turmeric, blue-black, and all shades of green, which also may not be worn. Furthermore, even if they are marked with the three dots, garments that are yellow, red, or white also constitute a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

When performing the ritual of purification (*śodhana*), it must be at least four finger-widths in size and no smaller than a pea. It may be one, three, five, seven, or nine [patches], but it must not be shaped like a flower. When washing a robe, if mud falls upon it, or if a crow or bird steps on it with muddy feet, it is then considered purified.

If one obtains many small, miscellaneous new items and sews them together into a single patch, they are purified as one unit. If they are patched separately, each must be purified individually. If it is a newly made *saṃghāṭī*...

Peach. If one corner is purified (*kappiya-karaṇa*), it is purified; if a strip or half a strip is patched, it is likewise purified. For the two lower robes and all other garments, even those with new fine patches, they must also be purified.

The commentary states: Whenever one obtains any garment of improper color, it should be purified by dyeing it with three colors. If one obtains any garment of proper color, it should be purified by marking it with three colors. *Śāṭaka*: this is translated as "inner garment"; it resembles a short skirt.
The Sixty-first Precept: Killing Animals.
If a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. Kāḷudāyin, having no fondness for crows, made a bamboo bow and shot at them.
The Buddha established the precept for this reason: "Intentionally" means not by mistake. "To kill" means to sever the life-faculty so that it no longer continues.
This includes either doing it oneself or instructing another to do it, even by means of poison, lethal implements, or the like.
This is explained in detail as in the first chapter. Regarding "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*): this is a term used according to the conventions of time and place;
it should properly be called "those who move horizontally" (*tiryañc*), because their forms are horizontal and they travel across the heavens; thus their movement is also horizontal.

They are not called "animals" (*paśu*) because they are raised by others, but rather because they are all birds, beasts, fish, turtles, insects, flying creatures, crawling things, and so forth—indeed, all that possess life. This is [the meaning].
Regarding the offenses herein: if one acts with the intent to kill and takes the life of an animal, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one employs the means to kill but does not actually kill, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). The same offense applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*. For the three lower groups of disciples, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if there was no intent to harm at all, but the life was accidentally taken. (The *Mātṛkā-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one intends to cut a vine but mistakenly cuts a snake...")

There is no offense. If one intends to cut a snake but mistakenly cuts a vine, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). If one intends to kill this insect but kills that insect; or intends to cut this insect but cuts the ground; or intends to crush this insect but crushes the earth—in all such cases, it is an *dukkaṭa*. Yi says: "Examine the precepts: there are both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) offenses."

Its essence is endowed with non-action (*avijñapti*). This nature of non-action is attained upon the completion of the three *karmavācanās* at the time of receiving the precepts. Having attained this nature, one spontaneously ceases from evil and spontaneously practices good without depending on further effort;

therefore, it is called "non-action. Consequently, one obtains the precept against killing in relation to all sentient and non-sentient beings; one obtains the precept against stealing in relation to all sentient and non-sentient beings; and so forth, until one obtains the precept against digging the earth in relation to all ground, and the precept against destroying in relation to all grasses and trees.

In this way, each of these two hundred and fifty rules of training pervades the entire Dharma-realm. To uphold even one of them brings merit equal to empty space; how much more so when the *śīla* (precepts) are fully complete! Therefore, the merit of a renunciant who upholds the precepts for a single day and night is inexhaustible.

Regarding what are called "inherent precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*): their nature is such that they are offenses regardless of whether one has received the precepts or not. Violating them is inherently evil by its very nature, and upholding them is inherently good by its very nature; it is not only through the Buddha’s regulations that there is good and evil.

Therefore, these are also called "ancient precepts" (*paurāṇa-śīla*). Regarding "prohibitive precepts" (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*): originally they were not sinful causes; it was the Buddha who established them as precepts to prohibit certain actions. If one commits such an act, one incurs an offense; if one does not commit it, one incurs no offense. They do not apply to those who have not received [the precepts], such as grasses and trees. In secular life, these acts are not prohibited.

The destruction [of a precept] is distinct and carries no further offense. Once a bhikṣu has received the precepts, the "unmanifest" (avijñapti) arises; if he maintains them, he accrues merit, but if he destroys them, he incurs guilt. Furthermore, this prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) coexists with all natural offenses (prakṛti-sāvadya).

Through repentance, the prohibitive offense is extinguished, yet the natural offense remains. For example, cutting grass and harming livestock both belong to the same category of *pāyattika* (offenses involving falling); through repentance, both offenses are cleared away, yet the transgression for taking life still persists. Therefore, natural and prohibitive offenses differ in their classification and belong to separate categories. Among the two hundred and fifty precepts, [this distinction applies].

Regarding offenses by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*): these include, for example, the four *pārājika* offenses of the first chapter; the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and *pāyattika* offenses of the second chapter, such as sexual misconduct, harsh speech, groundless slander, and so forth;

and those of the third chapter, such as taking robes, lying, disparagement, divisive speech, idle chatter, reviling, forcibly taking away bedding, dragging another out of a room, using water containing living organisms, killing, intentionally causing distress, concealing offenses, criticizing the precepts, eavesdropping on disputes, and striking a bhikṣu in anger. As for the remaining offenses, most are prohibitions by convention (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). One should reflect upon them according to their underlying meaning. As stated in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*: "That which was established by the Buddha..."

There are three kinds of precepts: first, natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); second, proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*); and third, those that are both. A natural offense is one that is comprised within the evil karma of body, speech, or mind; or it is committed due to secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) or as a derivative of the primary afflictions (*kleśa-niṣyanda*).

Furthermore, within this transgression, it is comprised of intentional action and involves the growth of defiled karma (*kliṣṭa-karma*). When there is a continuous stream of the characteristics of guilt coexisting with this, it is called a natural offense.

An offense different from these three causes—whether committed through the inability to distinguish [the rules], through loss of mindfulness (*smṛti-pramoṣa*), or through unintentional error—is such that, in its absence of afflictions or their derivatives, and in the absence of moment-to-moment growth, it is called a proscribed offense. If it possesses both characteristics, it is called an offense that is both proscribed and natural. If a person can [act] according to the principle...
One who understands the meaning of this precept is proficient in the Vinaya (and does not look to others' faces).
○ The sixty-second precept concerning drinking water containing insects:
If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks or uses water that contains insects, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. The group of six monks took water containing various insects for drinking and consumption.
The Buddha established this precept for them. "Knowing" means either knowing through one's own observation or being informed by another.

"Water" refers to all types of water, meaning everything from rivers, ponds, springs, wells, and ditches, down to fermented soy sauce, vinegar, curd, and grain gruel. "Insects" means either seeing them upon inspection or...
One sees [the insects] after filtering. As for drinking and using [the water], this constitutes internal consumption. External consumption is as prescribed in the preceding precepts.

Regarding the offenses herein: if one knowingly drinks or uses water containing insects, or fermented liquids such as insect-infested vinegar and the like, one falls into an offense of defeat (pārājika).
The perception regarding the object is as previously stated. The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a water-strainer in the shape of a ladle, or triangular, or as a water-jar strainer. If fine insects emerge, I allow you to place them in a sand-bag.
After filtering, the insects and sand should be returned to the water. One should not travel even half a *yojana* without a water-strainer."

If one has none, one should strain water using a corner of the *saṃghāṭī* (the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: if a bhikṣu lacks a water-strainer or similar equipment, he should not go to another village or monastery within a distance of three *krośas*.

However, if it is known that at the destination there will be no shortage [of clean water], and one does not take [a strainer] with him, there is no offense—meaning if one knows that the monastic community (*saṃghika*) there always has pure water, or if it is known that rivers or wells are free of insects; furthermore, there are five kinds of eyes).

One must not look at water. There are five types of eyes for which this is prohibited: first, eyes afflicted by sores; second, eyes with cataracts; third, eyes that are deranged; fourth, eyes impaired by old age or illness; and fifth, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Because the divine eye differs from human perception, looking [at water] is not permitted. For how long a duration?

One should inspect the water; that is, during the time it takes for a bamboo cart drawn by six oxen to turn around, or from the moment the mind has become pure, one should observe and know it to be free of insects. Even if one drinks without filtering, there is no offense. However, to drink without inspecting or filtering is in all cases improper to use. One should know that there are five types of filtering materials:

first, the square strainer (*caturaśra-paṭa*), which should be made of fine, dense silk, measuring one or two feet depending on the occasion. Second, the *dharmagaḍuka*, which is the "yin-yang" jar. Third, the *kuṇḍikā*, which is a jar with its mouth covered by silk and its neck tied with a thin cord;

one should submerge it in water, draw it out when full, and must still examine it for insects before using it. Fourth, the water-drawing strainer (*udakabhāṇḍaka*), which is a small circular strainer. Fifth, the corner-of-the-robe strainer (*cīvarakoṇaka*); this should be taken...

A fine silk cloth measuring about one *tala* in length is used either to tie around the mouth of a jar or to place over the rim of a bowl; it is required for the purpose of filtering water when providing sustenance, and is not merely a corner of one's *kāṣāya*.

If following a flowing river, one may travel up to five *krośas*; if on a non-flowing river, up to three *krośas*. Even without a filter, there is no offense in proceeding if one has gone that distance. If following a flowing river, once the water has been inspected and found free of insects, one may drink or use it as desired for a distance of one *krośa*, provided that no other river flows into it along the way.

For non-flowing water or rivers flowing upstream, once the water has been inspected, it may be used within a distance of one *vyāma*. There are five kinds of pure water: first, pure by the Saṃgha; second, pure by an individual; third, pure by filtration; fourth, pure by a spring; and fifth, well water.

Regarding purity: it means that the well water is constantly free of insects. If one knows that the person [fetching the water] is a precept-holder who cherishes and protects life, there is no offense in drinking or using the water even if one does not examine it.

Once the water has been examined, it may be used continuously from sunrise until the first light of dawn appears. When examining the water, if the insects are so minute they are difficult to see, one should indicate them with a blade of grass or a stalk; do not point at them with a finger. Having finished drawing the water, place the filter (strainer) in a bowl. If near a river or pond, pour the water directly into it; if on dry land, pour it back into the well.

One must not hold the filter in the air over the well, as this would cause the insects to suffocate or result in their injury. One should use a water jar as a vessel for releasing living beings, lowering it slowly into the well. The filter must be washed clean and dried in the sun.

Expose it to the sun until dry. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there are extremely minute insects in the water, one must not use it to wash one's hands, nor for the performance of the great or small excretions.

If one cannot trust [the local people], one must not tell them to filter the water; the bhikṣu should filter it himself. Tripitaka Master Yijing stated: "The water filter is counted among the six essential items; one must not fail to carry it. If traveling three or five li, one must not go without it. If one knows that a monastery does not filter its water, it is improper to eat or drink there.

To die of thirst on a long journey would serve as a sufficient warning and mirror for the Tathāgata’s holy teachings. Compassion is their foundation. Within the ordained precepts, there are both natural (*prakṛti*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa*) offenses. A proscribed offense is light in accordance with the specific circumstance, whereas a natural offense, by its very nature, ought to be treated as grave. Among natural offenses, killing..."

This is the primary reason; therefore, the wise should especially preserve and protect [life]. If one treats this as something trivial, what could possibly be considered grave? If one can act in accordance with the teachings, one will obtain the fruit of long life in the present and be reborn in a Pure Land in future lives.

Even if one has mastered the Tripitaka, attained realization through the four dhyānas, constantly contemplates non-arising, and clarifies the mind in the principle of emptiness—if one does not protect life and fail to uphold the teachings according to the instructions, one will ultimately not escape the Buddha’s reproach.

As for the first of the ten evil deeds, who would take its place to receive the retribution? Furthermore, consider seeing a sheep being led into a temple; it may only have been slaughtered a few times, yet people gather to watch its release and longevity, snapping their fingers and praising it as virtuous. Yet they do not realize that within the temple rooms, water is used daily to kill thousands and tens of thousands of living beings. Since...

Knowing that the principles and teachings are not to be treated lightly, one ought to investigate them minutely and examine them closely. One should protect oneself and benefit others, guarding well and reflecting wisely. Furthermore, there are those who cause people to plow fields and plant crops, scheming for minor gains while failing to see the great transgressions involved;

both land and water are harmed, and countless living beings are killed. As for such guilt and fault, what can be done? It is as if one were already bound hand and foot at the gate of the underworld, left to the disposal of others. Thus, a sutra says: "Those who kill living beings shall fall into the three miserable realms; even if they manage to become human again, they will have short lifespans and many ailments."

Alas, what suffering! Who shall endure it? If there be those capable of doing so—how excellent, how most excellent! This may truly be called the final dharma age of Śākyamuni, wherein we together form the causes for compassionate mindfulness; and at the initial realization of Maitreya, we shall all together realize the fruit of non-arising.
63. The Precept on Intentionally Annoying Others:
If a bhikṣu intentionally annoys another bhikṣu so that the latter is unhappy for even a moment, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. A group of seventeen monks went to ask a group of six monks:

"How does one enter the first dhyāna, up to the fourth dhyāna? How does one enter emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does one attain the fruit of stream-entry, up to the fruit of non-arising? The six monks replied:
"According to what you have said, you would be claiming for yourselves that you have attained the higher stages."

Regarding the rule for persons: one who has already committed a *pārājika* offense is no longer a bhikṣu. When the group of seventeen monks went to inform the Venerable Upāli, "If such a question were asked, what offense would he have committed?
he replied, "He has committed no offense. [The Buddha] then perceived that the Venerable Upāli was causing doubt and distress to the group of seventeen monks.
He informed the Buddha, who established the precept: "One who intentionally causes distress" means that with a deliberate mind, one causes another to fall into doubt or regret. And...
It gives rise to vexation. Or, it gives rise to doubt regarding the time of birth; for example, if one asks another, "How long has it been since you were born?
and they reply, "For such a length of time," one says to them, "You were not born that long ago; you were born like other people. Or, it gives rise to doubt regarding the age in years;
if one asks, "How many years old are you? and they reply, "I am so many years old," one says to them, "You are not [that] many..."

Regarding the number of years: as with other recipients of the precepts, you have not yet reached that number of years. Consequently, there may be doubt concerning the reception of the precepts. It is asked:

"Since you have not yet reached twenty years of age at the time of receiving the precepts, and furthermore, the assembly was separate within the boundary, there may be doubt concerning the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).
It is asked: "At the time you received the precepts, the *jñapti* (motion) was not accomplished and the *karmavācanā* was not accomplished; it was an illegal separate assembly."
Or, regarding an offense, one gives rise to doubt and says: "You have committed a *pārājika* offense," up to and including a *duṣkṛta* or a "bad speech.
Or, regarding the Dharma, one gives rise to doubt and says: "What you have asked constitutes a *pārājika* offense; you are no longer a bhikṣu.
"A moment" (*muhūrta*) refers to thirty such moments making one day and night. This means causing another...

Even for as little as a moment, the mind remains unsettled. Regarding the offenses herein: if one intentionally uses such matters to cause doubt and vexation, and speaks them clearly, one falls into a *pāyattika* offense;
if not clearly, it is an *dukkaṭa*. For the other four assemblies (*parṣad*), the acquisition of offenses is the same.
There is no offense if the matter is actually so, or if one does not intentionally cause vexation, but fears that the other person might later give rise to doubt.

[This is] a confession (*deśanā*). It is spoken for the sake of a beneficial mind; even [cases such as] speaking erroneously [are included]. (The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "If one acts with a mind of benefit, in accordance with the Vinaya teachings, and guides others through reasoning, there is no offense whatsoever.")
Precept 64: Concealing the Gross Offenses of Others.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a gross offense, conceals it, he commits a pāyattika.

The commentary states: The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Upananda repeatedly committed offenses and spoke of them to a bhikṣu with whom he was intimate, entrusting him not to tell anyone.
Later, Upananda quarreled with that bhikṣu, who immediately informed other bhikṣus of the offenses he had committed.
When the other bhikṣus questioned him, they learned that he had spoken of them only because of the subsequent quarrel. [He] reported this.
The Buddha established this precept: "One who knows" means either one knows by seeing it oneself or another person tells one that they know.
"Another bhikṣu" refers to a person who has received the full ordination within this Dharma. "Gross offense" refers to the four *pārājika* and thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.
"Concealing" means to hide one's transgression and not confess it. Regarding the offense herein: if one knows while eating a small meal...

If one speaks after having eaten, or knows [the offense] after having eaten, and speaks during the first watch of the night, or knows it during the first watch and speaks during the middle watch, in all such cases it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If one knows it during the middle watch and intends to speak during the last watch but has not yet spoken when the dawn appears, it is a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation).

If one conceals another’s offense, or conceals one’s own grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), or conceals the grave offense of a person who has not yet received full ordination, in all such cases it is an *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), if one perceives it as such, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). In all other cases, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). The same applies to the nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*). For the three lower assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
If a nun conceals another's grave offense, she incurs a *pārājika* (defeat). There is no offense if: she did not previously know it was a grave offense;

she did not perceive it as a grave offense; or there was no person toward whom she could confess it; or if, upon confessing it, there would have been danger to her life or danger to her holy life (*brahmacarya*).
It is said that there is no offense. If a bhikṣu possesses five internal qualities, he should expose the faults of others:
at the proper time, not at an improper time; truthfully, not untruthfully; beneficially, not to one's detriment; gently, not harshly.
With a mind of loving-kindness and free from ill-will, yet whose physical deportment is impure, whose speech is impure, and whose livelihood is impure;
who is of little learning and does not know the Sūtras; who is of little learning and does not recite the Vinaya; and whose eloquence is indistinct.

It is like a white sheep; one should not repeatedly point out the faults of others. If one possesses the necessary qualities, one should point out another's fault at the proper time and in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, this bhikṣu should point out a fault only if he has affection for me and respect for me;
or if he lacks affection but has respect; or if he lacks respect but has affection—he should point it out. If he lacks [these qualities], he should not.
Affection without reverence can cause one to abandon evil and resort to good; such a person should be exhorted.
If there is a bhikṣu whom they hold in high esteem, who they revere, trust, and delight in, and who can cause them to abandon evil and practice good, that person should be exhorted.
If there is no one at all [who can do so], the Saṃgha should immediately set him aside and expel him, saying: "Venerable sir, wherever you go, they shall act for your sake."

To cite: to cause [the offender] to remember; to cause [the offender] to speak for themselves; to obstruct the removal of guilt; to obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; to obstruct the *Pravāraṇā*. It is like a horse-tamer:
when a wicked horse is difficult to tame, he immediately joins it to the halter and tether and drives it away.

Such a bhikṣu should not first seek permission from him; this itself constitutes permission. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: there are three kinds of concealing another’s grave offense: first, concealing another’s *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which results in a *pāyattika*.)

If one conceals another’s act of shedding the Buddha’s blood or causing a schism in the Saṃgha, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one conceals three other offenses involving *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, because by hiding such sins and evils, one defiles the Buddha-Dharma.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Upon seeing another’s fault, one may speak of it to a single person and then stop; if one hears of it or suspects it, there is no need to speak. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When speaking, one must not go toward the person to speak; one should speak to a virtuous bhikṣu.

If they are one’s own *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, or if that offending bhikṣu is violent, or relies on the power of kings, ministers, or violent men, or if there arises a cause for taking his life or harming his practice of the *brahmacarya*, one should think: 'The retribution for that person’s sinful actions will surely come of its own accord; he should know this himself. It is like a fire breaking out."
One merely seeks to save oneself; how could one know of other matters? At such a time, it is sufficient to guard the sense faculties (which is without fault).
○ The sixth [offense] regarding conferring ordination upon one who is underage:

When fifty-five years have passed and one has reached twenty, one should receive the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa*). If a bhikṣu knows that a person is under twenty years of age, yet confers the full precepts upon them...
Regarding the precepts: this person does not obtain the precepts; that bhikṣu is to be censured for his folly.
This is a *pāyattika* offense. The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there were seventeen groups of youths in the city who had previously been close friends.
The eldest among them was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve. They went together to the monastery.
They requested to go forth from the household life. The bhikṣus immediately ordained them and conferred upon them the full precepts (upasampadā).

At that time, these youths had been accustomed to music since childhood; they could not endure eating only one meal a day. In the middle of the night, suffering from hunger, they cried out and wept loudly. The Buddha heard their voices; knowing the cause, he asked about it intentionally.
Ānanda reported the matter in detail, whereupon the Buddha established a precept: "One who has reached twenty years of age" refers to those born [into this world].
The age must already be twenty years. One who "should receive the Great Precepts" refers to one whose years have reached twenty and is thus capable of receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
"Full" means that by receiving the two hundred and fifty major precepts, one is able to fully possess the path to *parinirvāṇa*.
It is also called "complete possession" (*paripūrṇa*) and "near-perfection" (*upasaṃpadā*); these are all [synonyms for] the proximate [attainment].
This is the meaning of being close to *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the knowledge that one’s age is less than twenty:
it is known either by the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the community of monks themselves, or it is known through the words of the person receiving the precepts or others.

Because such a person is young and their disposition is frivolous and restless, they are unable to fully study the various precepts and rules of decorum (*vinaya*), nor can they advance in the cultivation of the path, nor can they endure [the hardships].
Harsh words, eating but one meal at midday, and the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat;

furthermore, because of their fickleness, such people are frequently rebuked by others and disparage the Buddha-dharma. If they were śrāmaṇeras, people would not have rebuked them. Regarding the conferring of the full precepts (mahā-śīla):
this is that which can be conferred and this is that which is received. "That which can confer" refers to the three masters and the rest of the monastic community.
"Those who receive" refers to persons seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*). If such a person does not obtain the precepts, it means that the recipient is not yet of full age;
although the Sangha may confer them through the ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, they do not achieve the nature of a bhikṣu and are thus termed "not fully ordained.
The Tathāgata deeply understands the distinctions in the karmic natures of sentient beings: if [the requirements] are not fulfilled, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is not realized.
Therefore, it is prescribed that those who have reached the age of twenty are permitted to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*). The Buddha is the King of Dharma and the Lord of all dharmas;
thus, the sons of the Buddha are born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma. Consequently, by relying on these regulations, the nature of a bhikṣu is fully realized;
yet if one violates the teachings, the dharma of the precepts will not be established. Those bhikṣus who are subject to censure are said to be not only...
The recipient does not obtain the precepts, and the one who bestows them also incurs an offense. Regarding "due to folly":
this means the person bestowing the precepts lacks wisdom and does not know the dharma of the precepts; therefore, they are called "foolish. The Buddha said:

"I allow bhikṣus who are ten years of age and possess wisdom to bestow full ordination upon others and to provide them with dependence (niśraya). They shall perform the duties of an upādhyāya and an ācārya."

Regarding the *upādhyāya*: one who has received from them the ten precepts or the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is an *upādhyāya*. Those who are equal to an *upādhyāya* are those who have been senior to oneself by more than ten years.
Regarding the *ācārya*, there are five types: first, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, upon whom one relies to receive the going-forth;
second, the *karmācārya*, who performs the *karma-vācanā* at the time of receiving the precepts; third, the *śikṣācārya*...
The *ācārya* is one who instructs in the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*). There are four types of *sūtra-ācāryas*:

those from whom one receives the sūtras, or from whom one receives the explanation of their meaning, even if only a single four-line verse. The fifth is the *niśraya-ācārya*, upon whom one relies for even a single night’s stay.
Regarding these *ācāryas* and others, they must be at least five years senior [to the disciple]. These five aforementioned persons all occupy the rank of teacher (*śāstṛ*).

Because they are able to produce a model of conduct, they are collectively called *ācārya* (軌範師). [Regarding the *upādhyāya*: this is translated as "Preceptor" (*qīn jiào shī*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Only after ten years have been fulfilled may one occupy the rank of a teacher. Furthermore, one must accomplish five qualities, including precepts, views, and extensive learning; benefiting both oneself and others; and having no deficiency or transgression in the methods of majestic deportment and practice.

Possessing such virtues, one is called a Preceptor. This is because he is personally able to teach the Dharma of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa-dharma*). There are five things that, if not accomplished, prevent one from conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another: namely, the precepts...

Concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—furthermore, one who cannot teach others to firmly abide in these five dharmas is ineligible to confer the full ordination upon others.
There are five dharmas by the accomplishment of which one may not grant the full precepts: namely, lack of faith, lack of shame, and lack of dread.
Laziness and forgetfulness. Furthermore, there are five qualities that destroy superior ethical discipline: [wrong] views, improper deportment, little learning, and lack of wisdom.
Again, there are five: not tending to sick disciples; when disciples are unhappy with their dwelling, not skillfully arranging for them to move;
being unable to teach according to the Dharma and Vinaya to eliminate their doubts; and being unable to instruct them to abandon evil views and abide in right views.

There are five further [qualifications] lacking for one less than ten years: not knowing what constitutes an offense, what does not constitute an offense, what is light, or what is heavy. There are another five lacking for one less than ten years:

not knowing how to instruct disciples in higher ethical conduct (*adhiśīla*), higher mental cultivation (*adhicitta*), higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), the *prātimokṣa*, and the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*).
Furthermore, there are five lacking: not knowing higher training in ethics, higher training in mind, and higher training in wisdom.

One who knows the *śukla* (the pure/white) but does not know the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure)—if he can reverse each of these [requirements]—may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, may provide formal dependence (*niśraya*) to others, and may keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).
However, he must not keep two novices unless he is able to instruct them in the observance of the precepts.
One should increase the mind, increase wisdom, engage in study, recitation, and listening. These should be sustained by two matters:

first, by the Dharma—meaning teaching the increase of morality up to recitation; second, by robes and food—meaning the four requisites and whatever else is needed, providing them according to one’s capacity.
If one does not comply with and respect [the teacher], one does not follow the dharma of a disciple.
One should reprimand [the student] by means of five matters. One should say to him: "Go away! Do not enter my room;

do not perform services for me; do not come to where I am; I will not speak with you. [In the case of an *ācārya*, one should instead change "do not come to where I am" to "do not dwell under my dependence"]. There are these five matters.
The teacher should reprove him for being shameless, lacking a sense of moral dread, refusing to accept instruction, acting contrary to proper decorum, and being disrespectful.
Furthermore, there are five other matters: he is shameless; he lacks a sense of moral dread; he is difficult to speak with; he keeps company with those of ill repute;
and he frequents the houses of courtesans, as well as the homes of women, young girls, eunuchs, and bhikṣuṇīs who study the Dharma.
Regarding nuns and female novices: it is improper to go frequently to their vihāras to watch them catch turtles and tortoises; such matters should be censured.
One should not censure them for the remainder of their life or until the end of the *vassa* (rainy season retreat). One must not censure one who is ill.
One should not censure someone in their absence, nor without having pointed out their transgression. Once the censure has been administered, one must not continue to accept their offerings.

One who is employed as a servant should not be granted formal reliance (*niśraya*). At that time, there may be one who, having been rebuked, finds no one to support him, leading him to abandon the path and take no pleasure in the Buddha-dharma.

In such a case, one may listen to another person’s intention to accept [the novice] as their own preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), for the sake of causing him to repent and restore harmony. However, one must not entice him away by taking his disciples with them. If...
When about to depart, one should act according to the Dharma. If that preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) has broken the precepts, broken right view, or broken proper conduct;
or if they have been subject to formal censure, or have been expelled, or are subject to expulsion; and thus provide no benefit to the qualities of a śramaṇa—one should form this intention:
"I am inducing them to go forth because I desire them to achieve long-term growth and benefit in the qualities of a śramaṇa. If...
The disciple should humble his mind and comply, without opposition or seeking out faults.

The teacher should accept [the confession] (according to the *Vinayaviniścaya*, if one fails to reprimand when one ought to, reprimands when one ought not to, fails to forgive when one ought to, or forgives when one ought not to, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense). If the Saṃgha intends to perform a formal act (*kamma*) for the disciple...

Regarding what are called: formal reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*), formal banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), formal dependence (*niśraya-karman*), formal prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (*pratisedha-avasa-gamana-karman*), formal censure for not seeing an offense (*adarśana-utksepa-karman*), formal censure for not confessing an offense (*aprati-karmāṇa-utksepa-karman*), and formal censure for not relinquishing a wrong view (*apratinihsṛṣṭa-pāpaka-dṛṣṭi-utksepa-karman*):

the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should manage these matters in accordance with the Dharma so that the Sangha does not perform a formal act (*karman*) against the disciple. If such an act is performed, he should ensure it is done according to the Dharma, and he should cause the disciple—
The disciple should be compliant with the Saṃgha and not act in opposition. He should seek the removal of his offense so that the Saṃgha may quickly grant him the *karmavācanā* of release.
If a disciple commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it must be dealt with according to the Dharma: if he should be granted *parivāsa*, he should be granted it;

if he should be granted *mūlāpakarṣa*, he should be granted it; if he should be granted *mānāpya*, he should be granted it; if he should be granted *āvarhaṇa*, he should be granted it—each being given as appropriate, just as prescribed above.
Regarding the duties of a preceptor (*upādhyāya*): if one does not act in accordance with them, one incurs an offense for each instance.

At that time, while the preceptor was performing his duties toward the disciple, the disciple did not perform his duties toward the preceptor. The Buddha said: "One must perform the duties of a disciple.
If the preceptor is subject to formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) performed by the community of monks (*saṃgha*), the disciple should act in accordance with the Dharma therein."

Regarding the management of affairs: even if it involves expediting the lifting of a *karmavācanā* for the Saṃgha, if the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, the disciple must manage the matter according to the Dharma, even to the point of performing the rite for the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*). If the preceptor is ill, he must be attended to;
if he does not find pleasure in his dwelling, he should be moved. Furthermore, he must protect him through these two matters. Without informing the preceptor, one must not enter a village, nor...
When entering the homes of others, one must not follow other bhikṣus, nor take other bhikṣus as companions.
One must not give [alms], nor receive [alms]. One must not assist in communal affairs, nor accept assistance from others in communal affairs.
One must not shave another’s hair, nor cause another to shave one’s own hair. One must not enter a bathhouse, nor rub another’s body.
Furthermore, having had one's body massaged by another, one must not go to the daytime dwelling, nor go outside the boundary, nor travel to other regions.

(The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya states: "Except for five matters that do not require notification—namely, chewing tooth-sticks, drinking water, defecating, urinating, and circumambulating a stupa within a distance of forty-nine *krośas* inside the boundary—all other matters must be reported to the teacher one by one.
At dawn, one should enter the teacher’s room to receive the scriptures and inquire about their meaning; one should then depart.

Regarding the urinal: one should announce that the time has arrived. Having washed the hands clean with soap-nuts (*śamī-kṣāra*) and ash, if there is food available or if there is an offering (*lābha*) within the Saṃgha, one should fetch it for the teacher.
One should provide soap-nuts and *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) and assist the teacher in washing his hands and rinsing his mouth.
If there is food available, one should present it; if there is an offering within the Saṃgha, one should inform the teacher, saying: "I have obtained such [an item]."
"Objects are the portion of the Upādhyāya. You should ask him, 'Does the Upādhyāya wish to enter the village? If he says he will not enter, you should ask where he intends to obtain food;
you must go to fetch it as instructed. If he says he will enter the village, you should wash your hands and then slowly take up his robes, ensuring they are not inverted or mixed up.
Take the *antarvāsaka* (inner robe), spread it out, shake it, and examine it to ensure there is no [dirt or damage]."
[He should check for] poisonous insects. Next, he takes the waistband, the saṃkakṣikā, and the uttarāsaṅga, spreads them out and shakes them to inspect them, and then hands them to the upādhyāya.
He should fold the saṃghāṭī and place it upon his shoulder. Next, he takes the bowl, washes it, places it in its bag, and carries it away.
He should take the teacher’s undergarment, fold it, and lift it up. Furthermore, he takes the items for washing the feet and the bedding—mats and blankets—and lifts them up.
When the teacher goes out, the student should take up his walking sandals. When leaving the room, he should look back and close the door, pushing the leaf with his hand to check if it is secure.
If it is not secure, he should close it firmly. Having inspected the area to the left and right, he should take the door-latch and place it in a hidden spot.
If he fears someone might see it, or if it is not secure, he should take it away and leave it where the teacher can find it.
When traveling on the road and encountering acquaintances, one should engage them in kind conversation and maintain a virtuous mind. While walking, one should avoid the main thoroughfares.
When wishing to enter a village, one should step slightly off the path, set the bowl aside, and spread out the saṃghāṭī robe to inspect it before handing it to the teacher.
If there are guest houses, market stalls, or workshops outside the village, one should carry [the belongings] while traveling.
If you entrust your sandals to someone while traveling, you should ask the teacher, "May I follow after you? If he says, "It is permissible," you should immediately follow.
If he says, "There is no need," you should stay at a certain place and remain there as instructed. If the teacher enters a village and does not emerge at the usual time, you should form this thought:
"He has entered the village to beg for food; this portion belongs to the Upādhyāya, and this portion belongs to me."
Having left the village, he should take up his sandals, step off the path, place his bowl on the ground, fold his saṃghāṭī robe and place it over his shoulder.

If this is the place where his teacher dwells or eats, he should sweep it clean, spread out a sitting mat, prepare a vessel for pure water, bathing utensils, and food containers, and further arrange a bathing seat, a foot-stone, and a towel for wiping the feet. If he sees his teacher from afar...
When [the teacher] approaches, one should immediately rise to welcome him. Take the alms bowl from his hand and place it upon a bowl-stand or on a bowl-bench.

Take the *saṃghāṭī* robe and spread it out to examine it; do not let it become stained by grease or other impurities. If there are such stains, they should be removed. If it requires washing, wash it.
Once the teacher has finished washing his feet, one should dispose of the water, take the foot-stone, wipe the towel, and return them to their original places. Furthermore...
Having washed one's own hands clean, one should offer pure water to the teacher for washing his hands. One should take whatever food one has and present it to the teacher, saying:
"This is my portion of food; please eat. If the teacher requires it, he should take it. When the teacher is eating, [one should attend to him].
One should stand in attendance and provide whatever is required. If the time for the meal is about to pass, one should eat at the same time as the teacher.

Once the teacher has finished eating, one should take the bowl from his hand and provide water for washing and rinsing. If there is a remainder after one has finished eating oneself, it should be given to another person;
if there is no human recipient, it should be placed on clean ground where there is no grass, or placed in water that is free of insects. Then, one should take [the bowl].
Thoroughly wash the utensils for food and drink, and take the sitting mats and other items back to their original places. Furthermore, when entering the teacher’s room, one should inspect it;
if there is dust or dirt, one should take out the beds, bedding, pillows, and floor coverings to air them outside.
Clean away the filth and soil within the room, and when discarding it, one should inspect it; if there are needles, thread, or worn-out cloth, [one should place them] below...

Take one pill and place it in a visible location. If there is anyone who recognizes it as their own, they shall take it. Furthermore, one should sweep and wipe clean the area above, upon the pegs, and on the shelves.
If there are damaged areas in the room, such as holes made by insects or rats, one should repair them and ensure the place is perfectly clean.
If the original seating arrangements are not orderly, one should rearrange them to be so. As for the robes one wears, do not [wear them]... [if they are not clean].
The robes should each be placed in their own separate location. If there is dust or soil in the courtyard, it should be removed.

Having taken the water jar and washed it clean, one should refill it with pure water and place it back in its original spot. Furthermore, one should provide the teacher with a water jar, a rinsing vessel, and a drinking vessel.
If there is bathing taking place in the bathhouse, one should ask the teacher whether he wishes to bathe. If he says he will bathe, [one should prepare accordingly].
One should first go to the bathhouse and inspect it. One should sprinkle and sweep it until it is clean. If there is impure water, one should discard it. One should split firewood and do so.
One should prepare all the bathing requisites and inform the Elder (Upādhyāya). Only then should one kindle the fire. Once the fire is lit, one should announce that the time has arrived.
If the teacher is ill and weak, or if he is extremely old, one should support him by embracing him; or, having given him his robe, one should go to warm it.
Inside the room, having taken the robes and placed them on the rack, he should rub and massage the teacher’s body. He should stand behind the teacher while washing him.
Once he has finished washing himself, if the teacher is weak or old, he should support and carry him out of the bathhouse and even back into the room.
Having spread out bedding for him to lie upon and covered him with robes and blankets, he then left the room and closed the door.

Returning to the bathhouse, he inspected all the bathing requisites and returned them to their original places; he removed any impure water and extinguished the fire, then closed the door and departed.
During the morning, midday, and evening, he should inquire after his teacher’s well-being three times a day and should attend to his teacher in two ways.
One must not shrink from or feel weary of laborious tasks. These include: first, the repair of rooms and dwellings; second, the mending and washing of robes.
One must carry out all matters as instructed by the teacher according to the Dharma.

If sent on a mission to a particular region or to travel about, one must not shrink from or feel weary of it, nor should one remain there under the pretext of some excuse. If one has been rebuked, one should confess in this manner before the teacher.
With shoulders bared and sandals removed, kneeling on his haunches with palms joined, he said: "Venerable Upādhyāya, please bear me in mind.
I now repent; I shall not do it again. If you grant me absolution, that would be well. If you do not grant it, I shall repent at the three periods of the day."
Furthermore, if [the preceptor] does not listen, the disciple should immediately humble their mind and comply, employing skillful means to seek understanding regarding the offense committed.
If one does not act according to the instructions above, one incurs an offense for each instance. If the upādhyāya commits five kinds of unrighteous acts, the disciple should repent and then depart.
One should say to the teacher: "If I act according to the Dharma, you do not know it; if I do not act according to the Dharma, you do not know it.
If I transgress the precepts, you abandon me and do not instruct or admonish me; if I transgress, you do not know it; and even if I confess my transgression, you do not know it.
At that time, there were newly ordained bhikṣus whose upādhyāya had passed away; they had no one to instruct them and did not maintain proper decorum.
[The Buddha] said: "I permit bhikṣus who are ten years [of standing] and possess wisdom to provide dependence for others and to act as ācāryas.
The ācārya should regard the disciple as a son; the disciple should regard the ācārya as a father."
Regarding the successive instructions for the matter of teaching: within the Buddha-dharma, there is an increase in its propagation;
one should make this request as follows: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], now seek the Venerable sir to be my preceptor (niśraya).
May the Venerable sir grant me his preceptorship. I shall dwell in dependence upon the Venerable sir. (Thus, say this three times. He should reply: "So be it. I grant you my preceptorship. You..."

Do not be negligent (*mā pramādaḥ*). [The rules for an *ācārya* are the same as those for an *upādhyāya*. The rules for a disciple serving an *ācārya* are the same as those for serving an *upādhyāya*].

If a newly ordained bhikṣu desires a quiet place, he is permitted to rely upon another location; he may go and return on that very day. If this is not possible, he is permitted to dwell without relying upon anyone.
At that time, a newly ordained bhikṣu who has been residing there for some time suddenly abandons his dwelling and departs in search of [another teacher].

Regarding dependence and the ruin of a dwelling place: the Buddha said that for the sake of protecting the dwelling place, newly ordained bhikṣus who have long resided there are permitted to live without depending on a preceptor (niśraya). One should not send a messenger to receive dependence;

if one goes with a preceptor or an ācārya to grant dependence and does not return that same day, or if a disciple goes and does not return that same day, in all such cases, [the status of dependence] must be renewed.
Regarding the reception of dependence (*niśraya*): because one has stayed overnight apart from [the teacher], one immediately loses that dependence.

If one does not maintain dependence for even one night, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* offense. (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* permit being without dependence for up to six nights. The *Nidāna* states: "If there is the intention to seek a teacher of dependence, one may remain for five or six nights;

if there is no such intention, one may not remain for even one night. Regarding the consumption of food and drink belonging to the Saṃgha, it is in all cases improper to receive them. One must not receive dependence without making a careful selection.
Regarding the granting of dependence (*niśraya*): if one is ill, or if there is no one to provide dependence for the caregiver, one may remain without dependence.

Furthermore, if the Saṃgha performs acts such as the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the two teachers or their disciples, that does not constitute a loss of dependence; however, it does so if the act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) is performed against them.
One immediately loses the formal reliance (*niśraya*). It is permitted for a wise bhikṣu of five years' standing to receive formal reliance from a wise bhikṣu of ten years' standing.
If [the preceptor] is foolish and lacks wisdom, one must rely on him for as long as life lasts.

There are five ways of losing formal reliance: first, the teacher rebukes; second, he departs; third, he abandons the path; fourth, he does not grant formal reliance; fifth, he enters the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

On the platform, there are further cases of losing one's *niśraya* (dependence): if [the teacher] dies; if [the student] has reached five years [of training]; if [the student] has exceeded five years; if one sees one's original *upādhyāya*;
if both teachers have abandoned the path; or if [the teacher] dies. Or if one returns to dwell under the supervision of the *upādhyāya*.
There are five kinds of Vinaya-holders (*vinayadhara*) upon whom one should rely and dwell: first, those who recite from the introduction of the *Prātimokṣa* up to the thirty rules; second, ...
Reciting up to the ninety matters; third, extensively reciting the *Vinaya* of the precepts; fourth, extensively reciting the *Vinaya* of both divisions of the precepts;
fifth, reciting the entire *Vinaya*. During the spring and winter, one should rely on any of the first four; if one does not so abide, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should rely on the fifth, the holder of the *Vinaya*; if one does not so abide, one falls [into a grave offense].

Regarding the offense (*āpatti*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are four kinds of preceptors (*ācārya*). First, one who provides neither food nor the Dharma; one should depart without asking permission. Second, one who provides food but not the Dharma; one should depart after asking permission. Third, one who provides no food but possesses the Dharma; although it may be difficult [to stay], [one should remain]."

One must not depart for as long as one lives. There are four cases where, even if one is expelled, one must not depart for as long as one lives. If the two teachers have committed a fault, the disciple should admonish them; one must not use harsh language, but should speak with gentle words according to the rules of instruction.

If the teacher does not do so, it is well if the disciple follows [the teacher's advice]. If, on the contrary, the teacher scolds and reviles him, then if he is the *upādhyāya*, the disciple should abandon him and go far away. If he is the *ācārya*, the disciple should take his robes and bowl, leave the boundary, stay overnight elsewhere, and then seek reliance upon another person.

If that [other person] has authority, he should go far away, or rely upon a virtuous and eminent person. If one has completed five years and is well-versed in the Dharma and the Vinaya, one may become independent of reliance. If one is not well-versed in the Dharma and the Vinaya and cannot stand on one's own, one [remains dependent].

One who can establish others should remain in dependence for as long as life lasts. If one has completed ten years [of training] and is proficient in the *dharmavinaya*, being able to establish oneself and others, one may receive the dependence of others. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one accomplishes five qualities and has completed five years, one need not receive dependence: first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense;

third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy; fifth, reciting the *Prātimokṣa* with its extensive explanations of the trainings. Even if one has received the precepts many years ago, if one does not know these five qualities, one must remain in dependence on another for the rest of one's life. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"If one has not yet completed five years, even if one accomplishes the five qualities—even if one is thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka, possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), and has eliminated the three impurities—one must still remain in dependence. If one has completed five summer retreats, one is permitted to live apart [from a teacher]."

During the summer retreat, one must cease traveling. However, wherever one arrives, one must still rely upon a preceptor for dependence. Even if one has reached eighty years of age or completed sixty years of the summer retreat, if one has never recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and does not understand its meaning, one must likewise rely upon an elder.

As with one who is not old, a junior [monk] may also do so; however, with the exception of prostrating, all other duties should be performed. Such a person is called an "old-junior" bhikṣu. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In times of famine, one may go daily to where the upādhyāya resides and stay there.

One should come every day; if one cannot, one may go every five days. If one cannot come every five days, one should come at the time of the *poṣadha*. If one still cannot come, one should come to see the upādhyāya by the time of the *pravāraṇā*, even if it requires traveling two and a half *yojanas*.

The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: 'Having completed the reception of dependence (*niśraya*), one may request the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary. When the seven days are complete, one returns to the monastery; thus, the dependence is not lost. As explained above.
Regarding the dharma of teacher and disciple, the main text shall be explained below. As for the offenses herein:

if the *upādhyāya* knows or suspects that [the candidate] is less than twenty years of age, yet confers the precepts upon them—once the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense; once the second *karmavācanā* is completed, three *dukkaṭa* offenses;

once the first *karmavācanā* is completed, two *dukkaṭa* offenses; once the formal motion (*jñapti*) is completed, one *dukkaṭa* offense; and if the formal motion has not yet been made, [it is an offense] for performing the act.
Regarding the skillful means: if one has shaved the head, or intends to assemble the Saṃgha, or the Saṃgha has already assembled—there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) offense in all such cases.

If the Saṃgha knows or suspects [the deception], even if the number is not yet complete, all members of the Saṃgha incur an *dukkaṭa*. The same applies to the Bhikṣuṇīs. There is no offense if: one did not know beforehand;
if one accepted the words of a person who had received the precepts; if there was testimony from a bystander; if one trusted the words of one's parents; or if one had already received the precepts.
[The Buddha] said: "If there is doubt, one may count the months of the pregnancy, including intercalary months.

If one counts all the fourteen-day *poṣadha* observances as years, and thus reaches the full number, it is well. If it is not full, he must revert to being a *śrāmaṇera*, and only then be granted the precepts again.
If it is not done in this way, he is considered to be dwelling like a thief (*steyasaṃvāsika*). If there is no *upādhyāya*, or if [there are] two..."
If one has only a single preceptor, or even many preceptors, it is not called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

One must not ordain government officials (the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "Only after one's salary is exhausted may one leave the household life; if the king permits it, one may also leave the household life"). Those who lack robes and bowls may not receive full ordination.
One may not receive full ordination by borrowing robes and bowls. It is not permitted to ordain those who have violated the rules for bhikṣuṇīs or to grant them the great precepts.

If one has already received [the precepts], they should be expelled. One must not ordain those who enter the path with a thieving mind; if they have already left the home life, they should be expelled. (This refers to those who have themselves become monastics.

If they have not yet participated in the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) for the recitation of the precepts, and have not been ordained and left the home life, they should not be ordained. If they have already been ordained and left the home life, and have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), [they should be expelled].)

This is immediately termed "having received full ordination" (*upasampadā*). If one has previously participated in the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) or the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), they must be expelled. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one has never entered into the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, but later develops a virtuous mind, they may be granted the going forth and receive full ordination.

If one has previously entered them, this is called "staying by theft" (*caura-vāsa*); such a person is not permitted to go forth. The same applies to the sons of princes or ministers who don the *kāṣāya* robes to evade danger. If a *śrāmaṇera* listens to the recitation of the precepts with the intent to steal [the knowledge], and understands the words from beginning to end, he shall not receive full ordination hereafter.

However, if he is dull-witted, or if his mind is distracted by other matters such that he does not remember the words from beginning to end, he may receive the full ordination afterwards. One must not grant the going forth to those who have violated the Dharma or are outside the fold.

The Path. If one wishes to convert a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), one should first have their hair shaved and cause them to don the kāṣāya. They should then receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts.
They must then request from the Saṃgha a four-month period of probationary residence. The Saṃgha should grant this by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).

Provided that they do not adhere to the practices of non-Buddhists or laypeople, do not associate with non-Buddhists, do not recite non-Buddhist scriptures, and upon hearing the teachings of non-Buddhists [do not adopt them].
[If] he does not give rise to anger, follows along with the bhikṣu, and is able to cause the bhikṣu joy, then one may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon him.
If, after having received the precepts, he again enters among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and later returns to seek ordination, he should not be granted ordination;
this is called a "corrupter of the Dharma" non-Buddhist. One must not ordain slaves, thieves, or those who owe debts (even if someone has paid them off).

[Those who owe] debts [or have not yet received] ordination. One must not ordain the five kinds of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs), namely: those born so, those castrated (*kliba*), those envious, those transformed, and those partial.
If they have already been ordained, they should immediately be expelled. If an animal assumes a human form and comes, one must not ordain them or allow them to go forth.

One must not ordain those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or those who lack male organs. There are three types of persons who cannot receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Not...

One who addresses himself by his own name rather than the name of his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), or one who does not request the precepts, is further among the three types of persons who cannot obtain the precepts:

namely, those wearing secular clothing, those wearing the robes of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or those adorned with ornaments. One may not receive the precepts while sleeping, intoxicated, insane, or in a state of rage.
Likewise, this applies to those whose hands, feet, ears, or noses have been severed; those lacking their genitals, testicles, arms, elbows, or fingers; and those who suffer from chronic scabies.
Ulcerated; if signs of death appear; if the body is emaciated; if the body resembles that of a woman; if one possesses a registered name yet evades official taxes;

if the body is mottled; if the head is pointed; if the back is deformed; if one has saw-like teeth; if the body is infested with worms; if the head is infested with worms; or if the hair is disheveled, the limbs are paralyzed, or the fingers are bent.
Six fingers; webbed fingers; one testicle; no testicles; or epilepsy; inward curvature; outward curvature; upper respiratory disease; abdominal disease.
The disease of spitting phlegm; leprosy and abscesses; white leprosy; consumption; insanity; and various afflictions.

Blue eyes, yellow eyes, red eyes, inflamed eyes, bloodshot eyes, cataractous eyes, crystalline eyes, extremely deep-set eyes, triangular eyes, monkey-like eyes, wide-open eyes, protruding eyes, one-eyed, squinting eyes, oblique eyes, wrathful eyes, staring eyes, and ulcerated eyes.
Spotted eyes; a foul odor from the body; suffering from venereal sores; or being mute, deaf, lame, dragging one's feet, or having curled toes;
having only one hand, one foot, or one ear; being hairless, lacking body hair, or toothless; having blue hair, yellow hair, or white hair; hair that is excessively long or excessively short;
women with the heads of elephants, horses, oxen, pigs, sheep, deer, snakes, fish, or birds; having only one head, or even many.
All [afflictions] such as those of the head; all colors—blue, yellow, black, red, and white; diseases of wind (vāta), heat (pitta), and phlegm (kapha);

chronic abdominal tumors (gulma); hoarseness of the throat; cleft lips; absence of the tongue; protrusion of the chest; protrusion of the back; internal diseases; external diseases; and the inability to turn over while lying down.

Those who appear extremely aged, who have lost their dignified deportment, who do not distinguish between good and evil, and even those who bring disgrace upon the Saṃgha—none of these may be ordained.
If one receives full ordination from an *upādhyāya* who does not maintain the precepts, the candidate obtains the precepts if they were unaware [of this], but does not obtain them if they were aware.
If there are eight obstacles (*aṣṭāv antarāyikā dharmāḥ*) or other such circumstances, [the ordination requires] two or three...
When people listen to the *karmavācanā* for the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*), it must not exceed [the prescribed time];

if it exceeds it, the precept is not obtained because it is contrary to the Dharma, and the Saṃgha incurs an offense. Once one has received full ordination, even if it is only for a brief moment prior [to another], they are called an elder (*sthavira*).
If two or three people undergo the *karmavācanā* simultaneously, there is no distinction of seniority, and they do not exchange salutations with one another.

If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and those who constitute the quorum are not present—being out of sight or hearing, or outside the boundary (*sīmā*)—it is not called receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one receives the full precepts without having first received the śrāmaṇera precepts, the precepts are obtained, but the Saṃgha commits an offense.
If one is in a central land (*madhyadeśa*), the full precepts cannot be received with fewer than ten monks. If one is in a border region...

In this country, it is permitted for five persons who maintain the Vinaya to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*). If one's parents do not grant permission, one may not be received into the order and ordained.
If one has their hair shaved within a *saṃghārāma*, they must inform the entire Saṃgha; if the assembly cannot be gathered in harmony, [the shaving] shall not take place.

One should inform each individual in their respective quarters so that they may know. If one is less than twenty years of age, yet is over twelve, capable of scaring away crows, maintains the precepts, and observes the practice of eating only once a day, it is permitted to ordain them and allow them to leave the household life. In the presence of the two masters, the *ācārya* bestows the ten precepts;

such a person is called a *śrāmaṇera*. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha-śāstra* states: "At sixty years of age, one may not receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*). Even if the teachers and the *saṃgha* forcibly confer them, the precepts will not be obtained. Only the status of a *śrāmaṇera* is permitted. )

Furthermore, it is not permitted to ordain those under seven years of age. If one is ordained and receives the precepts [at such an age], both [the preceptor and the candidate] commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one has previously invited a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) to receive the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*), even if the preceptor is not present, one still obtains the ten precepts;

however, if the preceptor dies, one hears that the precepts were not obtained, whereas if one does not hear this, the precepts are obtained. If one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, if the preceptor is not present, the precepts are not obtained because the quorum of the Saṃgha is incomplete.

If the quorum of the Saṃgha is complete, even if the preceptor is not present, one may still receive the precepts. The *Vinaya-kaṅkṣā-viṭaraṇī* states: "Four persons may not receive full ordination simultaneously. Why? Because performing a *karman* for a group when it is not actually a group contradicts the principle. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Those who arrive first at the place of ordination..."

One should first confer the precepts upon [the candidate]. If two persons arrive together, the one who is older in years receives them first. If they are of the same age, the one whose *upādhyāya* is senior receives them first. If their *upādhyāyas* are also of equal seniority, they should undergo the *karmavācanā* simultaneously; whichever person’s name is called first shall receive the precepts first.

The same applies to three persons. For other matters, one may perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) with three persons; however, one may never perform a *karmavācanā* with four persons. If two preceptors have left the religious life and later come to their former disciples to seek ordination and full admission (*upasampadā*), the former disciples should provide them with robes and bowls to assist in their completion of the rite.

It is also permitted for [the disciples] to immediately act as their preceptors. Those who receive the precepts again must pay respect to their preceptors in accordance with the Dharma. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In the method of receiving the precepts, one first provides the Dharma teaching to guide and open the understanding [of the candidate]."

One should cause [the practitioner] to give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings; thus, they attain the *adhi-citta* (higher mind), and subsequently attain the *adhi-śīla* (higher precepts). The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states: Once the reception of the precepts is completed, the original teacher next points out the *śīla-mūla* (root of the precepts) so that the student may recognize the characteristics of transgressions, only then instructing them in the recitation of the precepts.

Once this is mastered, they recite the *Vinaya-piṭaka*; they must recite it every day and be tested daily. Only after the recitation of the *Vinaya-piṭaka* is finished does one study the Sūtras and Śāstras. How could there be such extreme exhaustion at the time of receiving the precepts, yet once obtained, have no concern for the precepts? To have a beginning but no end is truly most regrettable.

There are those who seek to receive the precepts on a single occasion, yet after receiving them, do not visit their teacher again, do not recite the *Śīla-sūtra*, and do not consult the Vinaya texts; they vainly occupy a position within the Dharma, and for themselves— [The text continues: ...it is a great pity. From the very beginning, there was a gathering where people sought to receive [the precepts], but having received them, they did not rejoin their teachers, did not recite the *Śīla-sūtra*, and did not open the Vinaya scriptures; they merely superficially defiled the rank of the Dharma. For themselves—

To harm others is to cause their ruin. For those of such a nature who have become subject to the law of extinction, the Vinaya text states: "It would be better to be a butcher than to bestow the full precepts upon another; rather, one should abandon them and not instruct them. This is the tradition inherited from the Western Regions regarding the etiquette of serving a teacher:

during both the first and last watches of the night, one goes to the teacher's dwelling, where the teacher then directs the disciple to sit down.
