Among the Tripiṭaka, he provides instruction at all times regarding both phenomena and principles, ensuring that no time is spent in vain. He examines the disciple’s observance of the precepts so as not to allow any deficiency or transgression; should he know of an offense committed, [he must address it].

He would immediately order that the repentance rituals be performed. Only then would the disciple massage the master’s body, fold his robes, sweep and wipe the rooms and courtyards, observe for insects before pouring water, or perform any other minor task—all doing these things on his behalf.

This was the ritual of honoring one’s superior. If a disciple fell ill, he would personally attend to them, carrying them and providing whatever medicinal decoctions were required, caring for them with the same concern as for an infant. However, the fundamental principle of the Buddha-dharma is that instruction and admonition come first.

Just as the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is not neglected in his upbringing, the Vinaya contains explicit statements; how could one possibly allow such negligence? The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Even those such as Caṇḍālas or butchers, though they may engage in evil deeds, cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata; they will not necessarily fall into the three [evil realms]."

Within the evil realms, if one acts as a teacher but fails to instruct and admonish their disciples, they will destroy the Buddha-dharma and will inevitably fall into hell. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "It would be better to accept evil precepts and, within a single day, sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings, than to harbor and support wicked disciples who cannot be disciplined.

Why is this? Such evil discipline (evil vows) brings calamity only upon oneself; however, by harboring wicked disciples whom one cannot instruct, one causes immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil, enables them to slander immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas, destroys the harmony of the Saṃgha, and causes many beings to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution. Therefore, this is more grievous than the offense of evil discipline."
Precept 66: On Initiating a Dispute.
If a bhikṣu knows that a dispute has already been settled according to the Dharma through confession, yet he initiates it again, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: While the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the six groups of monks had settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, yet they later re-ignited it, saying:
"Your observation was not skillful; your observation is not accomplished. Your understanding was not skillful; your understanding is not accomplished. Your settling was not skillful."
It does not lead to the cessation [of disputes]. It causes disputes to arise where none existed before, and once disputes have arisen, it prevents their resolution.
The bhikṣus, having investigated and understood the cause of this, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
"Knowing" means knowing by oneself or knowing through the words of others. "Dispute" (adhikaraṇa) refers to that matter on account of which contention arises; thus, dispute [occurs].

There are four kinds: namely, disputes over speech (*vāda-vivāda*), disputes over searching (*anveṣaṇa-vivāda*), disputes over offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), and disputes over matters (*kicca-vivāda*). These are explained in detail as follows in the subsequent commentary.

"In accordance with the Dharma" means according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to what was taught by the Buddha. "Having already repented" means that the matter has been properly eliminated and extinguished.
"To raise it again later" means that once the dispute has already been settled, one raises it once more with an unwholesome mind.

This means not allowing it to cease. Regarding the offense herein: if one knows that a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, yet further instigates it by saying, "It was not well-observed," "The observation was not established," or even "Extinction was not achieved," then if these words are clearly articulated, one falls into an *āpatti* (offense);

if they are not clearly articulated, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). This applies whether it concerns other quarrels or insults, one's own disputes, or disputes with those who have not received full ordination (*anupasampanna*).

Regarding disputes: if one further incites them, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). If the dispute is settled according to the Dharma, and one perceives it as being settled according to the Dharma, there is an offense of falling (*pācittiya*).

If one has doubt [regarding the settlement], it is an *dukkaṭa*. If the dispute is not settled according to the Dharma, yet one perceives it as being settled according to the Dharma, or if one has doubt [regarding the lack of settlement], in all such cases it is an *dukkaṭa*.

A nun commits the same offense. For the three lower groups of disciples, it is an *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one did not previously know that it was settled according to the Dharma, or if it was actually not settled according to the Dharma.
The sixty-seventh precept on traveling with bandits:
If a bhikṣu, knowing he is with bandits who have made a pact to travel together along the same road, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks traveled from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī.

They secretly crossed the frontier with a caravan of merchants and traveled together with them on a palanquin. They were all seized by the frontier guards, and the Buddha established a precept on their account.
"Thieves' companions" refers to those who commit theft, robbery, or evade customs duties, whether returning or departing.
"Making a pact" refers to a mutual agreement to go to a city or a village.
"Traveling together on the same path" means acting as companions, traveling together through villages and along various roads. "Even as far as a single village" refers to...

Even if one travels as little as the distance between two villages, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). Regarding the degrees of gravity for these transgressions, they are explained as in the precept concerning traveling with a woman.
The offenses incurred by the other four assemblies (*catasraḥ parṣadaḥ*) are the same as above.

One is not guilty of an offense if one was unaware, did not travel as a companion, or was held fast by force or restraint. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one realizes on the way that the person is a thief, at that time one must not immediately abandon them; rather...")

Follow along. Upon reaching a nearby village, employ skillful means to leave them behind. If the bandits become aware of this, you should say: "Long-lived ones, I have merely arrived here. If one travels with rebels or persons in debt, it is an offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one makes an appointment to travel with an evil bhikṣu, it is an offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). However, there is no offense if one travels by appointment due to various circumstances of danger. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one takes a bandit as a protector or a guide; or if one has lost the way and they come to point it out—even if traveling together in such cases, there is no offense."
The Ninth Fascicle of the Commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* in Four Parts:

The Fourth Part of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra: Commentary, Scroll Ten.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Zaiqiu.
Section on the Sixty-eighth Precept: Not Abandoning Wrong Views.
If a bhikṣu should speak thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣu should be admonished by the others, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not speak such words. Do not slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not say such a thing.
By means of countless skillful means, the Blessed One has declared that the commission of sexual misconduct is an obstacle."

These are factors that obstruct the path. When that bhikṣu admonishes this bhikṣu, if the latter persists and does not relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣu may admonish him up to three times so that he might relinquish it.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished two or three times, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting for the Buddha is as before. At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to such a wrong view.

Although the other bhikṣus admonished him, he did not relinquish it. They went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) of reprimand against him so that he might abandon this matter;
it was for this reason that the precept was established. "To speak thus" means to erroneously cite the World-Honored One.

He spoke these words to corroborate his own view. Furthermore, because he saw that laypeople, despite having wives and households, were able to realize the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), he gave rise to such a wrong view.
"I know" means that he perceives and understands this for himself. Regarding "the Dharma taught by the Buddha," the Buddha is the Tathāgata.
That which is spoken by the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the teaching that reveals the meaning. There are two kinds of such Dharma: first, that which was personally taught by the Buddha;
second, that which was taught by his disciples. Although it is taught by disciples, because it is received from the Buddha’s teaching, it is also called the Dharma.
To engage in sexual desire is a base and evil matter. Regarding "it is not a factor that obstructs the Path," this refers to practicing it...

Matter. It cannot obstruct the fruits of the noble paths. When that bhikṣu admonishes this bhikṣu, it refers to the following specific words of admonition: "Venerable One" is the term used to address him.
"Do not speak such words" means that one must not utter such speech of evil views. "Do not slander the World-Honored One" refers to the Buddha.

The Dharma taught is free from desire and is tranquil and pure. If one were to say that desire is not an obstacle to the Path, this would contradict the Buddha’s teaching and constitute a slander against the World-Honored One.
"Slander" means uttering unreasonable words. "Unwholesome" means that it will certainly bring about an evil retribution in the future.
To say "the World-Honored One did not speak thus" means that the Buddha did not teach that sexual misconduct is not [an obstacle].
These are the dharmas that obstruct the path. Regarding the phrase "innumerable skillful means," etc., it means that the Buddha, through various expressions, taught that sensual desire is impure;
it is a dharma with outflows (*sāsrava*) and a dharma that constitutes an obstruction.

When that bhikṣu exhorts this bhikṣu and the latter persists in not relinquishing [the view], meaning he maintains his refusal to abandon such a specific admonition regarding a wrong view, one should say to him: "You..."
Now you should abandon this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit further offenses. If you accept this instruction, it is well.

If you do not follow this instruction, then a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) shall be made and three admonitions given. Regarding the offense herein: it is committed when the third proclamation of the *karman* has been completed.
A *pāyattika* offense. If one relinquishes [the object] after the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made and two *karmavācanas* have been completed, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one relinquishes it after one *karmavācana* has been completed, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses. If one relinquishes it after the formal motion has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one relinquishes it before the formal motion is completed, or if, prior to the formal motion, one makes such an illegal statement as "Do not stop him from relinquishing it," there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for each instance. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, the offense is the same.

For the three lower groups of disciples, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). There is no offense if one performs an illegal *kamma* and so forth; in such a case, one does not incur a *pācittiya* (offense involving confession), but only incurs an *dukkaṭa*.
(The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "One should confess this within the great assembly and instruct them regarding the *pācittiya* offense.")
Precept 69: Not Abandoning One with Evil Views.

If a bhikṣu knows that a person who speaks in such a manner has not had the formal act performed, and yet does not abandon such wrong views, and provides them with their necessities, shares in formal legal acts (karmavācanā) with them, stays overnight with them, or converses with them, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: At that time, Āḷavaka was admonished by the community of monks, yet he still did not relinquish [his position].

The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) of suspension for not relinquishing wrong views against him. At that time, the group of six monks provided him with his necessities, participated in religious rites together with him, stayed overnight with him, and conversed with him.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept: "Regarding such a person" refers to one who speaks [in this manner].

A bhikṣu who engages in sexual misconduct is one for whom the path is obstructed. One who has not had the formal act performed refers to one who has been suspended because he stubbornly clings to wrong views and lacks the intention to repent;
thus, the Saṃgha has not yet performed for him the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of rehabilitation.
"One who holds such wrong views" refers to one who professes a malicious view that what is not an obstacle to the Path is indeed an obstacle.

"Does not relinquish them" means that despite the admonitions and exhortations of the Saṃgha, they persist in their stubborn adherence to those wrong views. "Providing with necessities" is of two kinds.
First is the Dharma, which refers to teaching and practicing the training in higher virtue, mind, and wisdom, as well as studying and reciting the scriptures.
Second is material wealth, which refers to providing clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.
"Common *karmavācanā*" means reciting the *Poṣadha* together and performing various ritual acts. "Dwelling together" means staying overnight in the same room. There are four types of rooms.
There are various types [of dwellings]: some have four walls and are entirely roofed over; some are entirely roofed over but not entirely enclosed;
some are entirely enclosed but not entirely roofed over; and some are neither entirely roofed over nor entirely enclosed.
Regarding "speech," this refers to instruction as well as the discussion of matters such as good and evil. Within this context, as for the offense: if a bhikṣu enters a house first... [and so forth].

If a person with evil views comes, or if he enters first and the bhikṣu enters later, or if both enter together to stay the night, then whichever side they lean against the ground constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, the offense is the same; for the three lower groups of disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If a bhikṣuṇī complies with a bhikṣu who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and does not relinquish her position after being admonished three times, she commits a *pārājika* offense. There is no offense if she was unaware that such words had been spoken.

If a person stays overnight with one [who has committed an offense], whether the dwelling is not fully covered and enclosed, or it is in the open air, or the person is lying down due to illness, or due to various difficult circumstances—according to the Vinaya text, regarding the four matters of providing supplies, performing *karmavācanā*, staying overnight, and conversing—if one acts in accordance with any of these, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each instance. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Whether teaching the Dharma to another, receiving the Dharma from another, giving property to another, taking property from another, or staying overnight together—all constitute a *pāyattika* offense. Sitting through the entire night without lying down constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense. The *Mūla-vinaya* states: "If that person is ill, there is no offense in attending to them. Or, if one dwells together with them in order to cause them to abandon wrong views, this is likewise permitted."
(There is also no offense).
○ The Seventieth Precept: Regarding the Keeping of a Sāmanera Who Has Been Expelled.
If a bhikṣu knows that a sāmanera has spoken thus: "I have heard from the Buddha that if one engages in sexual intercourse, it is not [a transgression]," [and yet he keeps him], [it is an offense].
Regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path: that bhikṣu should admonish this śrāmaṇera, saying, "Do not slander the Blessed One.

To slander the Blessed One is unwholesome; the Blessed One does not speak such words. Śrāmaṇera, the Blessed One has taught through countless skillful means that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path.
When that bhikṣu admonishes this śrāmaṇera, if he persists firmly and does not relinquish his position... [the bhikṣu] should [address him as follows].
The Bhikṣu should then admonish and rebuke him two or three times, so that he may abandon this matter.
If, after being admonished up to three times, he abandons it, that is well. If he does not abandon it, that Bhikṣu should say to this Śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you must not say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One,' nor must you follow after other Bhikṣus as other Śrāmaṇeras do."
"I have stayed for two or three nights; you do not have such a privilege now. Get out! Be gone! You should not remain here.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled from such a community, should entice him away, keep him as his attendant, or stay overnight with him, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, the two śrāmaṇeras of Upananda conceived such evil views.
The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to place these śrāmaṇeras before the assembly of monks, standing in a place where they could be seen with their eyes but not heard with their ears.

The formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) was carried out to admonish him with reproof; yet he still did not relinquish [his conduct]. Consequently, the Saṃgha established him as previously described and performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (the act of banishment).
At that time, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks, knowing that the Saṃgha had performed the act of banishment, enticed him away, kept him as their attendant, and stayed together with him overnight.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. In this text, the passage begins from the first sentence and extends up to the words "sexual desire."

These are the dharmas that obstruct the Path; these constitute the words of formal admonition. If one persists and does not relinquish [the offense], then the *karmavācanā* (formal act) of threefold admonition is performed.

If one does not relinquish it after the third admonition, then the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) is carried out. "From this day forward, you must not remain here"—this is the text for the *karman* of banishment.
What follows below consists entirely of the texts for the formulation of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). As for what is called "banishment" (*pravāsanīya*), it means to exclude...
"Expelled" means that one may no longer dwell together with the bhikṣus. "In the assembly" means within the *saṃgha*.

"One who has been expelled" refers to one who has already been subjected to the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion and three proclamations) by the *saṃgha* for the purpose of expulsion. "Śrāmaṇera" refers to one who has received the ten precepts.
And those who give rise to evil views. "To entice and lead away" means to exhort and move another by means of wealth or the Dharma, luring and calling them away.
Whether one entices them oneself or instructs another to entice them, one incurs guilt in both cases. "To keep and nourish" means: either to keep them oneself or to cause others to keep them.
"Keeping" refers to receiving them under one's care and providing them with a place of reliance; "nourishing" refers to supplying them with food and clothing, as well as instruction.

This refers to studying the sūtras and the Dharma. "Staying overnight together" means lodging in the same room. As for the remaining meanings, as well as what constitutes an offense and what does not, all are explained as previously stated.
(The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a śrāmaṇera is disliked by his two teachers, a bhikṣu must not entice him to live with him, saying, 'I shall give you robes, a bowl, and medicine;

I shall teach you the sūtras. If he knows that this śrāmaṇera will return to lay life because of this, he may use gentle words to entice him away. Once he has been enticed away, he should say: 'The kindness of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya is profound and difficult to repay; you should return to them. )

[The text] "dwells below" [refers to the following]. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If they are kinsmen, or if they are afflicted by illness, or if one intends to cause them to abandon wrong views—even if one provisionally accepts them under such circumstances—there is no offense in any case.

The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states: "In all cases where one partakes in the use of things with a person who has been suspended (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*) for not seeing their transgression and so forth, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrong-doing). Regarding *śrāmaṇeras*: from as young as seven years of age, if they are able to protect the monastery's grain and wheat by driving away crows and birds, it is appropriate to grant them ordination.

They should receive the Three Refuges along with the ten precepts (*śikṣāpada*). If an eight-year-old is incapable, one should grant [ordination] to a seven-year-old; if a six-year-old is capable, one should not refuse to ordain a seven-year-old. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Those who are too small—if they are less than seven years old, or even if they have reached seven but do not know good from evil—none of these are [to be ordained]."

One should grant ordination [only to those who are capable]. Those who are too old—if they are over seventy and still able to perform tasks, it is permissible; however, if they are under seventy yet incapable of managing affairs, requiring assistance for rising and reclining, they are not permitted to leave the household life.

If one has reached seventy years of age and is healthy, capable of practicing various disciplines, then ordination is granted. Furthermore, there are three grades of *śrāmaṇera*: first, from seven to thirteen years of age, called the "crow-driving *śrāmaṇera*"; second, from fourteen to nineteen, called the "dharma-conforming *śrāmaṇera*";

and third, from twenty to seventy, called the "nominal *śrāmaṇera*. These three grades are all termed *śrāmaṇeras*. The commentary states: Since those who have left the household life are young and not yet capable of other duties, they are instead assigned to the monastic kitchen or to meditation.
...in such places, one should drive away crows and birds to perform this small service and simultaneously generate merit and goodness).
○ Precept 71: Prohibiting Contrary Admonition and Difficult Questioning.
If a bhikṣu, when other bhikṣus admonish him in accordance with the Dharma, speaks thus: "I will not train in this precept now. When...
To interrogate other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya constitutes a *pāyattika*. However, one may interrogate them for the purpose of gaining knowledge or for study.
The commentary states:
When the Buddha was in the Udena Grove, other bhikṣus admonished Chanda in accordance with the Dharma; at that time, Chanda...
He then said, "I will not train in this precept now; I shall instead question other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha and he established the rule: "Other bhikṣus" refers to those within this Dharma.

"In accordance with the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught. "At the time of admonishing" means precisely admonishing with sincere words.
This is the time [for such speech]. To speak thus means to utter words of defiance.
To say, "I do not train in this precept now," means not to practice the *prātimokṣa*. It is not that one truly does not practice;
rather, it is merely an attempt to reject the words of admonition with such a statement. To "interrogate" means to cross-examine another with clever words.
Furthermore, regarding "wisdom" (*jñāna*): wisdom is the union of knowledge and insight. To explain them analytically: knowledge is that which cognizes, while insight is that which perceives.

Moreover, definitive and critical investigation is called knowledge, whereas the mental differentiation of phenomena is called insight. Regarding "one who upholds the Vinaya": this refers to one who maintains the *Vinayapiṭaka*.

"For the sake of knowing" means desiring to thoroughly understand what is light or heavy, what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes observance or transgression. This is for the purpose of study.
"Those who" refers to those who wish to extensively master the meaning of the texts. "Should question and inquire" means desiring to know and desiring to learn;

questioning and inquiring in this manner constitutes no offense. Regarding offenses herein: when one is being admonished according to the Dharma, if they respond with words of resistance and defiance, they incur a *pāyattika* (offense of falling) if the speech is intelligible;

if it is not intelligible, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). The same applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*. For the three lower groups of followers, it is an *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in the following cases: [if one is] not at fault.
...that person who offers such admonition is truly deluded, even to the point of speaking erroneously, and so forth.
○ The seventy-second precept concerning the light derision of the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of the Precepts):
If a bhikṣu, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, speaks these words: "Venerable sirs, what is the use of reciting these trivial and fragmented rules? and so forth.
Regarding this precept: if one causes others to feel vexed, ashamed, or doubtful by disparaging the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a large number of bhikṣus gathered in one place to recite the True Dharma and the Vinaya.
Fearing that they would master them through repeated study, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) frequently raised charges against their offenses and went to speak to them, saying: "Elders..."
"Old man, what is the use of these trivial precepts? If you must recite them, you should recite only the four matters and the thirteen matters;

the rest should not be recited, as they cause people to harbor doubts and suffer from anxiety. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha of this, and he established a rule: "Regarding 'the time for the recitation of the precepts' (*poṣadha-kāla*):

'precepts' refers to the rules beginning from the four *pārājika* offenses down to the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptadharmāḥ saṃgha-vivāda-samatha*). 'Time' refers to the proclamation..."

This refers to the time of speaking. "One who speaks thus" means one who utters words of contemptuous reproach. "Venerable One" (Bhadanta) is a title used to address the other person while expressing one's own feelings.
"Of what use? is precisely the manifestation of such contemptuous reproach, arising from the fact that [the other] has repeatedly committed offenses.
When hearing the recitation of the precepts, his mind felt uneasy, and he consequently spoke with contempt and reproach. "Minor precepts" refers to the lower three categories [of the Vinaya].
"Causing others to be so" means using another person as a pretext to reveal one's own self.

"Distressed, ashamed, and harboring doubts" means that when one has committed an offense oneself, upon hearing the recitation of the precepts by others, one does not feel joy; because of this lack of joy, agitation and distress cross over the chest.
This is called "affliction" (*daurmanasya*). To regret what one has transgressed is termed "shame" (*hrī*). Being unable to resolve what one has transgressed constitutes "doubt.

To "despise the precepts" means to utter words of censure. Regarding the offense herein: if one despises the precepts and speaks so as to be clearly understood, one falls into a formal offense (*āpatti*);
if not clearly understood, it is a transgression of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If one censures the *Abhidharma*...
Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* and other sūtras, all constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above.
There is no offense if one tells them to first recite the Abhidharma and the sūtras, and only then recite the Vinaya; or if they are ill, telling them to recite after they have recovered;

or if one tells them to diligently seek the realization of the fruits [of the path] before reciting. (The *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya* states: "If one wishes to cause others to distance themselves from the Vinaya so that they neither read nor recite it, but instead disparage it...")

To revile [the Prātimokṣa] is an offense of falling (pāyattika). If one reviles it with the intent that the Prātimokṣa shall not endure for long, it is a grave offense (sthūlātyaya). To revile the Sūtras is likewise. If one reviles the precepts of the other four assemblies or the two assemblies of lay followers, it is in all cases an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

If a nun reviles the precepts of both assemblies, it is an offense of falling; to revile the precepts of the other five assemblies is an offense of wrongdoing. If, fearing that a newly ordained person might develop doubt or a mind of despondency and withdrawal, one teaches them that they may not yet recite the precepts, there is no offense.

The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Whenever a sūtra that accords with the Vinaya is being recited, one who reviles it commits an offense of falling; when other sūtras are being recited, one who reviles them commits an offense of wrongdoing. Why is the offense heavier for reviling sūtras that accord with the Vinaya, while the offense for other sūtras is lighter?"

Precepts are the level ground of the Buddha-dharma; from them all myriad virtues arise. Furthermore, all disciples of the Buddha rely upon them for their abiding. Without precepts, there is no support. Moreover, they are the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma.

If one lacks the precepts, there is no means by which one may enter the city of Nirvana. Furthermore, they are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma, adorning the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, the offense is grave. In the *Five Hundred Questions*, Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha: "After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa..."

"Who upholds such a Vinaya? The Buddha said, "One who contemplates and studies the Vinaya—know that such a person is able to practice this Vinaya. After my parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who slander such a Vinaya, know that these people are companions of Māra and not my disciples.

Such individuals will fail to achieve the Way throughout their successive lives and shall not escape the three realms. The *Śariputra-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* (Shanjian lü) states: "If one studies the Vinaya, there are five virtues: first, protecting the precepts oneself; second, being able to sever the doubts of others;

third, entering the assembly without fear; fourth, being able to subdue enemies; and fifth, causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time. At the very least, there must be five bhikṣus who understand the Vinaya present."

World-Honored One, one can cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time. If the Buddha-dharma is extinguished in Central India, yet there are five persons in a border region who have received the precepts, and when they reach ten, they may go to Central India and bestow the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others;

this is called causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time. Furthermore, a master of the Vinaya possesses six virtues: first, he maintains and leads the *Prātimokṣa*; second, he knows the *Poṣadha* ceremony; third, he knows the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony; fourth, he knows the method for bestowing the full ordination upon others;

fifth, he accepts others as his dependents (*niśraya*); and sixth, he is permitted to maintain *śrāmaṇeras*. If one does not understand the Vinaya but only knows the Sūtras and Śāstras, he may not ordain *śrāmaṇeras* or accept others as his dependents. Because the masters of the Vinaya uphold the Vinaya, the Buddha-dharma shall remain in the world for five thousand years.
73. The Precept on Falsely Claiming to Have Only Now Learned the Rules:
If a bhikṣu, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, speaks these words: "I have only now come to know this rule as it is contained in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."

Every half-month, the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra is recited. If other monks know that this monk has sat through two or three such recitations of the precepts—and how much more so if it were many—yet he remains ignorant and lacks understanding, then if he commits an offense, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, this increases the offense of ignorance. He says, "Elder, you have gained no benefit; you have not attained what is wholesome.
When the precepts were being recited, you did not apply your mind, nor did you listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus. Because of that ignorance, it is a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The setting for the Buddha is as before. Among the group of six monks, one committed an offense.

When it was time for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, he realized his own transgression and, fearing that a pure monk might expose him, went first to speak, saying, "I have only now come to know this rule," and so on, up to, "the *Śīlaskandha* has arrived.
The monks, having discerned the reason for this, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. Thus it was spoken.
"Precepts" refers to the sequence from the four *pārājika* rules down to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), which sequentially elucidate their essential meanings.
To speak in such a manner is to feign the words of one who has only now begun to know, saying, "I have only now come to know this dharma."

This refers to having repeatedly listened to the precepts together, yet now falsely claiming to have only recently learned them. The "Dharma" consists of the four *pārājikas* up to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
These are the texts contained within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is the source scripture.
The statement that "the *Sīla-sūtra* is recited every half-month" means that it is produced from the *Poṣadha* (confession) ceremony held during both the waxing and waning phases of the moon.
This is not recorded in other sūtras. If this applies to those who sit during two or three recitations of the *Prātimokṣa*, how much more so for those who sit more than that?

This means they have already twice or thrice participated together in the *Poṣadha* and heard the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*; how much more so, then, for those exceeding two or three times? Regarding "ignorant and without understanding":
not recognizing the characteristics of offenses is called ignorance; not distinguishing the meaning of offenses is called [lack of understanding].

[The Buddha] explained: "Regarding the phrase 'if one commits an offense, it should be dealt with according to the law,' etc., this means that one cannot escape punishment on the grounds of ignorance;
rather, one must be punished for the offense committed as prescribed. Furthermore, an additional *pāyattika* (offense of falling) for ignorance shall be imposed.
As for the term 'Venerable Ones' (*sthavira*), this is a word of exhortation. To not apply the mind [to mindfulness] is an unwholesome mode of mental attention (*manasikāra*)."
One does not listen to the Dharma with a one-pointed mind. This is because of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*);
due to this lack of one-pointedness of mind, the ear attends to other objects. Because it attends to other objects, one is unable to listen to the Dharma.
"Because of that ignorance" means: by reason of that ignorance, one incurs the offense. Regarding the transgression herein:

if one speaks such words while the precepts are being recited either by oneself or by another, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika). If one does not grant the offense [to the offender], it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For a nun, the offense is the same; for the three lower assemblies, it is an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense if it is actually the case that [the teaching] has never been received before.
"I have heard it said that the precepts were recited, yet now for the first time I hear them. Or, "I have not heard the detailed exposition;

now for the first time I hear it," and so on, including cases of joking or speaking erroneously. (*Vinaya-viniścaya* states: If, due to afflictions, or through forgetfulness, or while sleeping, or with a distracted mind, one fails to listen to any single precept, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one hears the *bhikṣuṇī*-specific precepts and speaks thus, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if it concerns the common precepts, one incurs the primary offense. If one is aged and infirm, lacking the capacity for discernment, there is no offense if one speaks according to the truth. At the time of the *poṣadha*, one should cause those who are proficient and skilled...)

Regarding the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra: it shall be recited for the assembly. When the *ghanṭī* (wooden gong) is first struck, all bhikṣus should reflect upon their own offenses and confess them according to the Dharma before proceeding to the gathering. The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya states: "Within the Saṃgha, one who is proficient in recitation should be appointed to speak."

Others must listen with single-minded attention; they must not practice meditation or engage in other activities. If one fails to listen at any point during the exposition of the four matters up to the seven rules for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*), one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*.

If one does not listen at all, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). This offense cannot be confessed privately to another person. One must confess before an assembly in the presence of a keeper of the precepts who possesses majestic virtue and is respected by others. That person should reprimand him, saying: "Venerable sir, you have lost a great benefit.

When the *Prātimokṣa* was recited every half-month, you did not show respect, you did not attend with a single-minded mind, and you did not listen to the Dharma with an attentive ear. Once he has been reprimanded, he must perform the *pāyattika* confession.
Offense of the 74th Pāyattika: Transgression regarding the Kamma.

If a bhikṣu, after a formal act (kamma) has been performed together with others, should speak thus: "The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to personal favoritism," it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain, the Venerable Trapusa (Ṭhapussa) was managing the affairs of the Saṃgha.

A donor had organized a feast and offered alms, but as he was unable to attend due to his robes being worn out and having no replacements, at another time the community of monks obtained a single robe and conferred it upon him through a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
At that time, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks likewise performed the *karman* after the fact.

He spoke with regret, slandering the Saṃgha. The Buddha established a precept for this: "Those who act together in a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) mean those who have mutually consented in their hearts to perform the same action.
To speak thus" means that after having participated in the Saṃgha’s *karmavācanā*, one acts contrary to one's own prior intention and utters such words of regret.
"The various bhikṣus" refers to those who performed the *karmavācanā* together. "Intimate friends" means...

This refers to one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*), an instructor (*ācārya*), those who share the same preceptor or instructor, and other relatives or friends with whom one is harmonious in sitting, rising, and conversation.
"Property of the Saṃgha" is as explained previously. "Property" refers to the six requisites of a bhikṣu, down to the drinking vessel.
"To give" means to divert property belonging to the Saṃgha and bestow it upon an individual. Regarding the offense herein: if first...
When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) with the Saṃgha has been completed, if one later utters words of regret, the offense is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) if the speech was clear;

it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) if it was not clear. For the other four assemblies (*catur-vidha-saṃgha*), the acquisition of offenses is the same as above. There is no offense if the matter is actually so. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states:

"In general, among the Saṃgha, if there are those who perform laborious service, those of great virtue, or those who are impoverished—if the Saṃgha is in harmony, one may give [possessions] to them all. However, if one says they should not be given, one commits an offense in every case.")
Precept 75: On Not Granting Consent.
If a bhikṣu departs while rising from his seat before the Saṃgha has finished its formal legal proceedings, and he has not granted his consent (*chanda*), it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. A group of bhikṣus gathered in one place to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya.

The group of six bhikṣus, suspecting the Saṃgha, had a formal ritual (karmavācanā) performed against them; they immediately rose from their seats and departed. The assembly of monks attempted to stop them, but they would not stay.
The Buddha established this precept: "The Sangha" refers to those who share the same recitation of the *pātimokkha* and the same *kamma*. "To decide" means to deliberate.

"Matters" refers to the eighteen matters that cause schism in the Sangha, from what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what is spoken and what is not spoken, as well as other various matters concerning *kamma* and ritual procedures.
"Not having given one's consent (*chanda*)" means that when a matter arises for oneself, one does not entrust it to another.
“Monks,” [if one] speaks to other bhikṣus so that they understand, yet remains silent and departs; “departs” means to rise from one’s seat and go outside the assembly.
Regarding the offense herein: if one rises and goes outside the door, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one foot is outside the door; or if one makes an effort to leave but does not go; or if one intends to leave at a later time but does not go—all these constitute *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
For the other four assemblies (*parṣad*), the offenses are the same as above. There is no offense if it is for the sake of temple affairs, monastic affairs, or nursing the sick;
or if one has given consent (*chanda*) before leaving; or if one’s mouth is so clenched that one cannot give consent; or if [the assembly] is acting contrary to the Dharma.

This is not a formal act (kamma) contrary to the Vinaya. If one wishes to go to a stupa, or to attend to two teachers, or to visit a relative or friend, and departs without granting consent (*chanda*) for a matter that would cause harm or lack benefit to the Sangha, there is no offense.
(The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one intends to go for the sake of defecating or urinating and returns immediately without neglecting the affairs of the Sangha, there is no fault.")
The Seventy-sixth Precept: Regretting a Grant of Consent.
If a bhikṣu, having granted consent, subsequently regrets it, it is a pāyattika.

The commentary states: The setting is as before. At that time, among the group of six, there was one who had committed an offense and, fearing that the Saṃgha would censure him, [granted his consent].
At all times, these six people followed one another so closely that they could not be separated, thereby preventing the Saṃgha from performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*) against them.
Later, when the group of six was making robes, the Saṃgha, seeing an opportunity, sent someone to summon them. They replied, "We cannot go because we are making robes.
The Saṃgha said, "If you cannot come, you must have at least one or two bhikṣus bring your consent (*chanda*). They...
He immediately ordered one bhikṣu to come and receive the *chanda* (consent). The Saṃgha then performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against this bhikṣu.
When this bhikṣu returned and informed the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*), the group of six then expressed regret, saying:
"The ritual performed by them was not a valid ritual; the ritual was not accomplished. We gave our consent for that matter, not for this matter. The bhikṣus [reported this].
He informed the Buddha and the precept was established: "Regarding one who has already given their consent (*chandadāna*"):

this refers to when the Saṃgha has a formal matter (*dharmakarma*) and one has previously, with a willing mind, expressed their approval; "to regret afterwards" means that after having given consent, a sense of remorse arises in the mind.

This precept is largely identical to the previous *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) precept regarding violations; there is only a slight difference therein: whereas the former involved knowing the matter in advance and collectively granting permission.
Regarding the *karmavācanā*: if one later regrets it and slanders the Saṃgha, this is based on ignorance. Later regretting it constitutes an obstruction to the *chanda* (consent).
In both cases, the precepts are intended to be violated, which causes the ritual procedure (*karmavastu*) to fail. As for the offense herein:

if one has already given consent to another and later utters words of regret, if the speech is clear and distinct, one falls into a *pāyattika* offense; if it is not clear, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The other four assemblies also incur offenses.

The same as above. There is no offense in the following cases: if he actually performed a non-quorum *karmavācanā* (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If the Saṃgha has already settled a matter through a collective act, and later regrets it and censures it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;

if the Saṃgha has performed all *karmas* according to the Dharma, and one later censures them saying they are 'unacceptable,' it is a *pāyattika* offense; however, if the Saṃgha performs an *adharma* *karman*, and at that time one lacks the power to change it and thus remains silent without censuring it, but later says it is 'unacceptable,' there is no offense).
The Seventy-seventh Precept: Regarding Listening in Secret and Relaying Words During Quarrels.
If a bhikṣu, after bhikṣus have engaged in a quarrel, listens to what is said here and reports it to those there, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The setting for the Buddha is as before. At that time, the bhikṣus were quarreling.

The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) listened to these words and repeated them to others, causing disputes to arise where none had existed before, and preventing those already present from being extinguished.

The bhikṣus, having investigated and understood the cause, informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. There are four kinds of disputes: namely, disputes concerning speech, up to disputes concerning matters.

Furthermore, regarding "listening to these words and speaking them to others": this refers to secretly eavesdropping on the speech of others in a secluded or hidden place, seeking out their faults, and then passing the information back and forth to one another, thereby inciting anger and contention. Thus, a minor matter begins and develops into a great dispute;
once a great dispute has arisen, it cannot be pacified. As for the offense herein: if one intends to listen to the contentious speech of others...
One who goes and hears it incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*); one who does not hear it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If one intends to go but does not go, or if one has made an appointment with another but does not go, in all such cases there is an offense of wrong-doing. If two persons are conversing together in a dark place or in a secluded spot...

Or if one is walking ahead and speaking; thus it should be understood that whenever a bhikṣu unexpectedly encounters anyone engaged in private conversation in a secluded place, he must snap his fingers or make a coughing sound. If he does not do so, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
The same offense applies to the other four assemblies. There is no offense if the conversation concerns an illegal or un-disciplinary *kamma* performed for the sake of the stūpa or the Saṃgha.
If the two teachers or their close friends perform acts that are harmful and unbeneficial, and one wishes to know of them, going to listen does not constitute an offense.

(The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śūtra* states: "In this case, whether the disputing parties or other non-disputing persons come to listen, and whether one speaks to others or not, all constitute an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 'If one goes to listen for the sake of reconciliation, there is no offense. The *Sudarśana-vinaya* states:

'If one goes to listen with the desire to reform oneself, there is no offense. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: 'Listening silently to the speech of the other four assemblies constitutes a duṣkṛta offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: 'If two bhikṣus are conversing privately inside a hall, and a bhikṣu wishes to enter, he should snap his fingers or make a movement [to signal his presence].')"

If one makes a sound with one's feet, and the person ahead remains silent, one should withdraw. If the person ahead continues speaking and does not stop, there is no offense in entering. If one bhikṣu is already sitting inside the hall and two bhikṣus come from outside whispering privately.
The bhikṣus within the hall should make a sound; if they remain silent, the bhikṣus within the hall should exit. This applies equally to those walking in front or behind.

If other bhikṣus are quarreling, harboring resentment, and uttering such insults as, "I must kill this wicked man," and a bhikṣu hears this, he may say to that person, "Venerable sir, be on your guard; I have heard an evil sound. If there are visiting bhikṣus who say, "We shall steal from such-and-such a storehouse" or "such-and-such property of a stūpa," [the same applies].

Regarding monastic property: when a *karmadāna* (administrator) hears that the robes and bowl of a certain bhikṣu have been lost, he should remain silent and say, "They should be returned. Once they have been returned, he should announce within the Saṃgha: "Venerable sirs, such-and-such a storehouse, and even the robes and bowl of such-and-such a bhikṣu, must be guarded.

I have heard an evil report and must let the person concerned know. If a bhikṣu has many disciples, and at dusk they come secretly to inspect the various rooms to see whether things are according to the Dharma, if he hears them engaged in worldly conversation, he must not immediately enter and reprimand them.

He should wait until they have come of their own accord, and only then instruct and rebuke them, saying: "You have left the home life out of faith and eat the offerings of the faithful; you ought to practice meditation and recite the sūtras. Why do you discuss worldly and unrighteous matters? This is not the way of one who has left the home life to follow the wholesome Dharma."

If you hear them discussing the sūtras, explaining their meaning, posing questions, or providing answers, do not immediately enter into praise. Wait until they come to you of their own accord, and only then offer words of commendation, saying: "You all are able to discuss the sūtras, explain their meaning, and discourse upon the matters of the Buddha-dharma, just as the World-Honored One has taught."
When the bhikṣus assemble, they should practice two things: first, noble silence; second, discourse on the meaning of the Dharma.
Pāyattika 78: The Precept Against Striking a Bhikṣu out of Anger.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The setting for the Buddha is as before. At that time, one bhikṣu from among the group of six struck a bhikṣu from the group of seventeen out of anger.
The person who was struck cried out loudly. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and he established the precept regarding those who are displeased. "Those who are displeased" means:

This refers to the mind being bound by anger and resentment, such that displeasure arises within one’s feelings. As for "striking," it means to strike a stūpa or another person with the hand, a stone, or a staff.
Regarding the offenses herein: if one strikes with the hand, a stone, or a staff, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one strikes with other items such as a door-bolt, a curved hook, a fly-whisk handle, or an incense burner handle, these are all *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Nuns commit the same offense. Below...

Three cases constitute *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). There is no offense if: it is necessary to strike due to illness; it is necessary to strike the spine because one is choking on food; or it is an accidental touch. The *Śariputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states:

"If one strikes a resident of a monastery, one who has received the fivefold dharma, or one who has committed the four grave offenses, it is all *duṣkṛta*. If one takes sand or beans and throws them at many bhikṣus, for each one that is hit, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling);

if none are hit, it is *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Whether they observe the precepts or have broken them, if they possess the appearance of a bhikṣu and one perceives them as such, or if one harbors doubt [regarding their status], striking them results in a *pāyattika* offense."

If one who is not a bhikṣu is struck while being perceived as a bhikṣu, or when one is in doubt, or if one strikes a pillar, a wall, or other objects with a distracted mind, in all such cases one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). There is no offense if it is done without a mind of anger for the sake of benefiting [the person].

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Striking any of the other four assemblies or animals constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Striking a bhikṣuṇī constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; striking those of the three lower assemblies constitutes a *vinayātikrama*; and down to striking a layperson, it is a *vinayātikrama* with mental repentance (*cittapratideśana*). Furthermore, if a ferocious beast approaches...

One must not strike [the ground]. One may, however, take up a staff, a stone, or similar object and strike the ground to create a terrifying appearance. If animals enter the monastery and damage property, one should likewise create a terrifying appearance to make them depart.
The Seventy-ninth Pāyattika: The Precept on Striking a Bhikṣu with Anger.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. "Brandishing" means to gesture with one's palm toward another without actually making contact with their body.
Since the Blessed One has already prohibited striking, yet one still brandishes the palm to instill fear, the offense incurred here is light;
its gravity is the same as before. However, in the previous precept, the original intention was to strike, and although the blow did not hit the body, the primary intent was not fulfilled.
Offense. This precept involves merely brandishing the palm. Brandishing it constitutes the full offense; this is the distinguishing characteristic.

There is no offense if the other person intends to strike and one raises the hand to ward them off, or in all cases where one does not intentionally strike (*bó*; *bó* is pronounced like *bó*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: [text continues].

If one directs the palms of the hands or feet toward [a person], it is an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*). If one raises other parts of the body toward them, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one raises a single hand toward many bhikṣus, the offense is incurred according to the number of persons, following the same standard as for individuals."
The Eightieth Precept: Slandering with Groundless Saṃghāvaśeṣa Charges.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger, slanders another with groundless charges of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. Since it was prohibited to strike or even to threaten to strike, one consequently slandered another with groundless charges.
While the previous prohibition forbade slandering with a *pārājika* offense, this refers to slandering by means of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharma.

"Ground" (*mūla*) refers to the three grounds of seeing, hearing, and suspecting, as explained in the section on the thirteen matters. Regarding the offense herein: it is [the case] when one uses groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* [charges].

If one slanders [a monk], if the meaning is clearly understood, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika); if not clearly understood, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). For the other four assemblies, the offenses incurred are the same as above.
There is no offense if one speaks based on factual evidence with the intent to cause reform and repentance, rather than out of malice.

(*The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states: Slandering a nun incurs a sthūlātyaya; slandering those in the three lower assemblies incurs a vyatikrama-vinaya offense; slandering a layperson incurs a vyatikrama-vinaya offense of mental regret. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: Slandering another person constitutes a grave sthūlātyaya and incurs an offense of wrongdoing. Even slandering toward a single individual constitutes an offense.)
The eighty-first precept on entering the threshold of a royal palace:
If a bhikṣu enters a palace belonging to a Kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkling lineage while the king has not yet emerged and the treasures have not yet been stored away,
and he crosses the threshold of the palace gate, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Queen Mallikā heard the Buddha preach the Dharma.
Having attained the realization of the fruit [of the path], she exhorted King Prasenajit to gain faith and joy, and obtained permission for the bhikṣus to enter and leave the palace gates.
Kāḷudāyin went for alms and entered the royal palace. At that time, the king and his consort were lying together during the day.
When the consort saw him approaching from afar, she rose to greet him; however, she lost her garment and fell to the ground, her body exposed. In her shame, she crouched down.
He returned to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus, "I have already seen the King’s foremost treasure. The bhikṣus...

They found it expensive and complained to the Buddha, who then established the precept. Regarding the "Kṣatriya water-sprinkled head royal lineage": *Kṣatriya* means "Lord of the Fields" (*kṣetra-pati*).
These were virtuous persons at the beginning of the eon whom the multitude established as rulers over the distribution of land.
Because they were noble and possessed sovereign power, their descendants inherited this as their clan name. "Water-sprinkled head" refers to the time when one is consecrated as a king.
Having taken the waters of the four great oceans and assembled the minor kings and great brahmins, they pour [the water] upon the crown of the king’s head.
If he is of the kṣatriya caste, he is thus established as a king; therefore, he is called a "kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkled lineage.

Even if he is not of this caste, once he has received the water-consecration, he is likewise called a "kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkled lineage. This is before the king has yet emerged [from his palace].
This refers to when the king has not yet departed from the palace chambers and the court ladies have not yet returned to their respective quarters. Regarding "not having hidden the treasures":
this refers to when the queen and the court ladies, while staying overnight with the king, have adorned their bodies with various precious necklaces and ornaments;

as long as these jewels have not been gathered and put away, it is called "not having hidden the treasures. Furthermore, that which is held in high esteem is termed a "treasure," and the court ladies are what the king holds in such esteem.
Because it was cherished and highly valued, it had not yet been put away; thus it is also called "unconcealed treasure. "Entering" refers to entering the royal palace.
"Passing over" means that the feet have crossed the threshold (*umbara*). A "threshold" is the crossbar at the bottom of a door, serving as the boundary between the interior and exterior.
Regarding the offense herein: to enter the royal palace and pass over the threshold constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

If one foot is outside [the boundary], or if one forms the intention to leave, or if one fails to go due to a prior appointment, or if one enters the home of another minor local ruler, a noble, or a wealthy householder—in all these cases, there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). For the other four assemblies, the offenses incurred are the same as above.

There is no offense in the following cases: when the king has already departed; when the court ladies have returned; when the necklaces and ornaments have already been removed; when there is a matter to be reported; when one is summoned;

or when one is held by force or authority. (The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "In entering a royal palace, there are ten faults: first, if a palace woman is pregnant, people will suspect that the bhikṣu has committed an act of impurity;

second, if something is lost within the palace; third, if secret words are leaked outside; fourth, if harm comes to a prince; fifth, if harm comes to the king's person; sixth, if a high minister is promoted; seventh, if the prime minister is dismissed; eighth, if the people of the country suffer oppression; ninth, [if the king] goes on a military expedition... )
In other countries, they frequently assemble military forces for such matters as these; because people everywhere suspect monks [of being involved], one should not go there.
The Eighty-second Precept: Regarding the Handling of Precious Objects.
If a bhikṣu takes hold of a precious object or an ornament made of precious materials, or instructs another to take hold of them—except within a saṃghārāma...

In a lodging, it is a *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣu, while in a monastery or in a lodging, should himself take hold of, or instruct another to take hold of, jewels or jewel-ornaments, he should form this intention: "If there is an owner who recognizes them, they shall be taken [by him]."
"This was due to these causes and conditions, and not others.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a householder who was a disciple of a non-Buddhist sect.
While traveling on the road, he stopped by the roadside and departed, having forgotten a bag containing a thousand pieces of gold. At that time, a group of bhikṣus came along later and saw it.
"Take this away and wait for its owner to be identified. Layman, remember it and return quickly; I shall immediately take the bag out and give it to him.

When he returned and claimed the amount was insufficient, he went to inform King Prasenajit. The king investigated and recognized his deceit, so he confiscated the man's household wealth along with the gold and brought them into the royal treasury.
Consequently, the Buddha established a precept. At that time, Viśākhā entered the Jetavana Monastery and removed her [jewelry].
He placed his necklace beneath a tree and went to see the World-Honored One. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; his mind remained fixed on the Dharma, and he forgot to take it back home.
A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who permitted [monks] within the monastery grounds to pick up and store items they see that have been left behind, so as not to let them be lost.
Furthermore, a group of bhikṣus arrived at a village without a permanent residence and stayed in the house of a goldsmith.
Staying overnight: A goldsmith placed gold and silver objects inside his lodging and departed. Because they were guarding them, the bhikṣus could not sleep throughout the night.

They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha permitted that when there are goods in a place where one is staying overnight, for the sake of preventing their loss, one should collect and secure them.
Therefore, with the exception of items within a monastery or in a lodging, one should take hold of them.
"To lift without transgressing" means not to violate the precepts. "Jewels" refers to the seven precious substances.
"Adorned with jewels" refers to copper, iron, lead, tin, and white pewter, which are used to inlay and fill the surface. "To hold it oneself" means to grasp it with one's own hand.
"To instruct another to hold it" means to send someone else to grasp it. "Saṃghārāma" translates as "monastic garden," meaning a place for the assembly of people.

The garden where they dwell is likewise regarded as a place for cultivation and growth; it is said to be the site where the disciples of the Buddha cultivate the sprouts of the Path and the fruits of holiness.
It is also translated as "zhòngyuàn" (monastic complex). "Yuàn" (complex) is a term following the conventions of this region, referring to the name of a residence, courtyard, or pavilion.
As for the current designation of a monastic dwelling as a "sì" (temple), "sì" is also a public term of this region.

Regarding the name of the monastery: it was originally the place where the feudal lords resided. In the past, when Western monks first arrived, they were temporarily housed in the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si).
Later, the White Horse Monastery (Baima Jingsha) was constructed, and they were invited to reside there. Although their dwelling place has since been moved, the original source is not forgotten.
It returns to the designation of "temple" (si). From this time forward, all were called "temples. To speak of a "vihāra" (jing-she) refers to its location:

it is not a place where the coarse and violent reside, but rather where refined practitioners dwell. To speak of a "lodging place" (ji-su chu) refers to staying overnight in the houses of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).
Regarding the phrase "one should form this intention," etc., it means [the intention] while in the temple or when lodging...
When staying overnight and seeing precious objects, one should form this thought: "If a master comes and recognizes them, I shall give them to him;

only then will I take them. This refers to the specific causal conditions and no others; that is to say, apart from these two permitted exceptions, there is no other means by which one may take hold of them.
What are the characteristics of an offense in this regard? If one takes them oneself, or instructs [another to do so]...

If one takes hold of it oneself, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*). If one sees precious objects within a temple or a dwelling, whether taking them up oneself or instructing another to take them up, one should note the characteristics of the bags or containers, as well as the manner of their wrapping and tying.
One should open the bags or containers and examine them to know how many [items] are strung together.
How many are unstrung? How many are square? How many are round? How many are old? How many are new? If there is anyone who comes seeking, one should ask: "What is your object like?
If it corresponds [to what is held], one should return it; if it does not correspond, one should say: "I have not seen such an object.
If two people come together to seek, one should likewise engage in the above questioning and answering. If two...
The human speech and the [other] sounds correspond. One should place the items to be kept before them and say: "These are your belongings; each of you take them and go.
If one does not perform the aforementioned act of identification, nor untie and examine the bag, there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for all.
The *bhikṣuṇīs* commit the same offense; for the three lower assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if these are ornaments for the worship of a stūpa or monastery.

To ensure it is secure, one should pick it up (the *Śariputra-vinaya* states: "To seize and pick up a counterfeit pearl constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, if there is gold, silver, precious ground, beds, or utensils in the human realm, a bhikṣu should not walk over them").

One should not sit upon it, nor should one use it. However, there is no offense if it is a treasure from the heavens. The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: If one sees another's property outside the monastery, one should cover it with leaves, grass, or the like to ensure it is hidden. One should not regard this as an act of neglect.

If the owner comes seeking it, one should take it back to the residence and keep it under private custody for seven or eight days. If no one comes to claim it, one should deposit it in the monastic storehouse (*saṃgha-kośa*). If after five or six months no one still claims it, it should be offered to the Saṃgha to purchase durable utensils.

If the original owner later comes to claim it, one should exhort them to donate it to the Saṃgha. If they refuse to donate it, one should repay them the original value. If they demand interest, one should tell them: "By the Buddha’s established precepts, I am returning your original item; do not seek further interest. This is the rule.

It is not appropriate [to do otherwise]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is no one who recognizes [the owner], one should wait for three months. If it is found within the precincts of a stūpa, it shall be used for the stūpa; if it is found within the precincts of the Saṃgha, it shall be used for the Saṃgha of the four quarters."

If someone comes to demand [the property], the response should be appropriate to the inquiry. One should assemble the people, bring forth the treasure, and show it, saying: "Long-lived one, is this your property or not? If he says, "It is," one should instruct him: "Take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

If the World-Honored One had not established the precepts, you could not have even seen this with your own eyes; how much less could you have obtained it. If he says there is some other property, one should say: "Long-lived one, I have obtained only this; I see nothing else. You are an evil person.

You have already received more than enough. Why do you use such expedients to falsely demand further property and slander others? If the World-Honored One had not established the precepts, you would not even be able to see this object, let alone obtain it. If, even after this, he still does not understand, one should lead him to an *upāsaka*.

Regarding the borderland dialect: "I originally obtained only these items; I have now returned them all in full. Yet now you falsely slander me. At that time, the upāsaka should scold him, saying: "Son, you already received more than enough of these items, yet now you turn around and slander a bhikṣu.

You may go; I shall act as your adversary to adjudicate this matter. If it is a precious object for which no one comes to claim it, after three years have passed, it should be used within the local boundary according to the place where it was found.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: If a lost treasure is found within a monastery, for the sake of its safekeeping, when one departs, it should be entrusted to someone who knows the Dharma and fears transgression, with the instruction: "If the owner comes to claim it, you must return it. If after a long time no owner comes to claim it, it may be used for the needs of the Sangha.

Should the owner later come to claim it, one should show them the monastic quarters and say, "This was the property of a donor. If they do not consent to relinquishing it and wish to have the original item returned, one should speak to a layperson of faith and extensively exhort them to restore it.
The Eighty-third Precept: Entering a Village at an Improper Time.
If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
The commentary states: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Udāyin entered the village at an improper time and played *chuppu* (a gambling game) with a householder.
The householder did not win; out of stinginess and malice, he said, "A bhikṣu enters the village in the early morning for the sake of begging for food;
for what purpose does he enter the village at an improper time? When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept: [It is not permitted].
"Time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the dawn light. "Village" is as explained above.
"Without informing a bhikṣu" means not making it known to other bhikṣus if there is business for the Saṃgha, business for a stūpa, or business regarding the care of the sick.
Having received the entrustment from another bhikṣu, one may depart. If one is staying alone in a single room, one should entrust oneself to a neighboring room.
One should make this entrustment by going to a bhikṣu, assuming the proper deportment, and saying: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a focused mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am entering a village at an improper time to go to the house of [Name] for a certain reason. I inform you, Venerable sir."

To cause [the layperson] to know [of one's departure] (this is called "one statement"). Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu enters a village gate without having entrusted his presence to a layperson, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one foot is inside the gate, or if he intends to leave but does not go, or if he has made a mutual agreement not to go, these all constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.
The offenses incurred by the other four assemblies are the same as above. There is no offense if the path passes through the village, or if there is something to be announced, or...

To summon. If one accepts an invitation, or due to various difficult circumstances (the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states: "If, after having made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one enters a village and returns to one's residence, and then immediately makes the same announcement and goes to the village again, one falls into an offense").

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If two bhikṣus are staying in an araṇya and wish to travel, they should announce their departure to one another. If one has announced it and departed, and the other later wishes to depart as well, he should announce it to another bhikṣu.

If there is no other bhikṣu, he should form this thought: 'Whether on the road, at a gate, in a village, or at a bhikṣuṇī-vihāra, when I see a bhikṣu, I shall announce it. Having announced it, he may then enter. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "If..."
If there is no bhikṣu, one should inform a bhikṣuṇī, or even a śrāmaṇerikā. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If there is no bhikṣu, there is no offense in entrusting [the matter] to another layperson."
Precept 84: Regarding the Making of Oversized Beds.
If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Tathāgata’s fingers, excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes.
[The rule concerning] cutting [cloth] is concluded. If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.

The commentary states: The setting is as before. At that time, Kāḷudāyin, knowing in advance that the Buddha would come by this path, prepared a high and fine bed and seat along the way. When the Buddha saw it, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "This foolish man..."
He prepared a high, wide, and large bed solely for his own use. Having rebuked him, he established the precept:

"Whoever makes one—whether making it oneself or having another make it—the 'bed' refers to the five types as explained previously. 'The Tathāgata’s eight finger-breadths' means that one finger of the Buddha is two *cun* wide.
'Excluding the portion entering the step-hole above' means excluding the part of the bed-leg that enters the wooden step; the height below [the step] is..."
"Eight finger-breadths" refers to the measurement. "Having cut it off" means that if the length exceeds eight finger-breadths, one must cut it down before the offense can be expiated.
"If it exceeds" means if it is higher than eight finger-breadths, one incurs the offense immediately. Regarding the offenses herein:

whether committed by oneself or instructed to be done by another, if completed, all constitute a *pāyattika* (offense of falling); if not completed, all constitute a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). This applies equally to acting on behalf of another, whether the act is completed or not.

This constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). The remaining four assemblies incur the same offense as above. There is no offense if [the height] is eight finger-breadths; if it exceeds eight finger-breadths, one should cut it down.

Or, if another has already offered a finished [bed], one may cut it to size and use it. (*Vinayaviniścaya* states: "The Buddha’s 'eight fingers' is equal to the length of one cubit for a person of average height, which corresponds to one chi and five cun on a *hu* ruler.

Anything exceeding this is the measure of a high bed; using such a bed constitutes an offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: 'The reason this does not fall under the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* is that it involves cutting. Once it has been cut to the proper measure, one should confess before the Saṃgha. If the ground is low and damp, its use is permitted.)
[The rule concerning] the eight-finger width for the legs of a bed.
(If they exceed eight fingers, one commits an offense. **The Eighty-Fifth Precept:
