Regarding Beds and Mattresses Stuffed with Cotton Wool.** If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed, a wooden bed, or a large or small mattress stuffed with cotton wool (*tūla*), and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

The commentary states: The setting is as before. The group of six monks made this bed and mattress storage unit. When the laypeople saw it, they felt resentment, saying, "They lack a heart of compassion;
they are taking the lives of living beings," just like the king’s ministers. The Buddha, for their sake, established the precept: "To make" means to do it oneself.
"To instruct another to make" refers to this. "Tūla-cotton" is a general term for the flowers of the white poplar (*śiṃśapā*), the willow (*vaṭa*), and the *pūtīka* tree.
"To store" means to accumulate or to fill. A "large mat" is used for sitting and reclining; a "small mat" is... [as above].
"To use as a seat. "When completed" means that at the moment of completion, one incurs the offense. Regarding the offenses herein:
whether one acts oneself or causes another to act, if it is completed, all constitute a *pāyattika* (offense of falling); if not completed, all are *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

If one acts for the sake of another, whether completed or not, it is entirely *dukkaṭa*. The offenses for the other four assemblies are the same as above. There is no offense if [one uses] grass or...
Wool, cotton, or tattered rags—if these are used to make shoulder-supports or pillows for a litter (*śibikā*)—the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "These are items kept by persons of high status;

furthermore, they are objects of public disdain, and because they readily breed insects. Moreover, if one lies upon something soft and warm, one will find it unbearable when later encountering cold or coarse, hard surfaces. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should tear them apart and discard them."
Thereafter, one must repent. (If it has not yet been broken, the Saṃgha should order it to be broken.
The Eighty-sixth Precept on Needle Cases Made of Bone, Ivory, or Horn:
If a bhikṣu makes a needle case out of bone, ivory, or horn, carving and hollowing it out, it is a pāyattika.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a faithful artisan who, for the sake of the bhikṣus, made needle-cases from bone, ivory, and horn without ceasing for even a moment.
Because of this, his work was neglected; his household affairs fell into poverty, and he no longer had sufficient food or clothing.

The people of the world mocked him, saying that he sought blessings but obtained calamity. The Buddha established a precept for this matter: "To make [an object]" means to make it oneself or to have another make it.
"Bone" refers to the bones of elephants, horses, oxen, dragons, and so forth. "Tusk" refers to the tusks of elephants, boars, large fish, and so forth.
"Horn" refers to the horns of oxen, rhinoceroses, deer, sheep, and so forth. "Needle-case" is of two kinds: either individual pieces or a combined case. If one uses [such items]...
Regarding the three types of objects mentioned above, both [methods of preparation] are prohibited. As for "carving and scraping": "carving" (kū) means to split open the interior to hollow it out;
"scraping" (ka) means to pare away the exterior to polish its surface. "When finished" refers to the moment when the object has first been completed.
One then incurs an offense. Regarding the gravity of the offenses within this category, they are as described above. For the other four assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
There is no offense if one uses iron, copper, lead, tin, pewter, bamboo, wood, reeds, sugarcane, or grass to make a needle case;
or if one makes a knob for a staff, a handle for an umbrella, a handle for a measuring scoop, a curved hook, a sweat-scraper, or a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) [staff].
A jade ring-fastener; a spoon; a ladle; a hook; a garment-clip; an eye-salve spatula; a tongue-scraper; a tooth-pick; an ear-cleaner.

**Needle Case.** Regarding the incense-burner for the nose (the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should break it and confess the offense. If one has not broken it, the Saṃgha should order it to be broken. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: 'Because this is a minor object, it is not included among the thirty [offenses].

Furthermore, because it must be broken, if it is returned to its owner and the owner does not accept it, or if it is given to another, it will cause distress; if it is offered to the Saṃgha, it is contrary to the Dharma. It should simply be discarded. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: 'One who keeps a needle case should store it securely.

If a shameless bhikṣu or an unordained person asks to borrow it, it should not be lent. It should be lent only to one who can protect it well. When storing needles or knives, fearing that the iron will rust, they should be wrapped in waxed cloth—meaning cloth treated with heated yellow beeswax.'"
[To wipe] wax from cloth or silk).
○ The Eighty-Seventh Precept: Regarding the Making of a Seat-Rug (Nisīdana) Exceeding the Proper Measure.
If a bhikṣu makes a seat-rug, he must make it according to the prescribed measure. Herein, the measure is: two spans (vitasti) of the Buddha’s hand in length.

The width is one span and a half; it may be increased by an additional half-span in both length and width. If it exceeds these measurements, it must be cut down, and [the offender] commits a *pāyattika* offense.
The commentary states: While the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, he inspected the monks' quarters and saw that impurities were defiling the bedding and sitting mats of the monks.
He then permitted the bhikṣus to make *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) for the purpose of protecting the body, the robes, and the bedding.
The group of six monks then made them wide and large. Because of this, the Buddha established a precept. At that time, Kālodāyin’s body was large while his sitting mat was small;
it could not accommodate him, so he pulled and stretched it with his hands, wishing to make it wider and longer.
When the Buddha saw this, he permitted an increase of half a *vitasti* (span) both in width and length. Regarding the term *vitasti*, some say that one of the Buddha’s *vitastis* is two feet long.
Some say it is two chi and four cun; however, this varies according to location and time, as the size of the *chi* is not fixed.
Now, taking the middle standard as the definitive measure: according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda*, one *vitasti* (span) of the Buddha is equal to three *vitastis* of an ordinary person.
One *vitasti* of an ordinary person is approximately six inches by the large *chi*. Regarding "making": making it oneself or instructing others to make it. *Nishi-cha*... [text ends]
The *tán* (altar/mat) refers to a sitting cloth (*niṣīdana*). It is that which is spread upon a bedding mat when one is sitting or reclining;

it should follow the body whether one lies down or sits, so as not to allow grease or filth to soil the bedding. Nowadays, people spread it on the ground for prostrations, which is a profound departure from the original ritual.
This corruption has persisted for a very long time. One ought to have it made according to the proper measurements, ensuring it conforms to the Buddha’s regulations.

This refers to measurement. Regarding the measurement therein: "exactly as measured" means as prescribed below. "A length of two *vitasti*s of the Buddha" corresponds to six *vitasti*s of a person of medium height.
"A width of one and a half *vitasti*s" corresponds to four *vitasti*s and an additional six finger-widths (*aṅgula*) of a person of medium height.
"Increasing the width and length by an additional half *vitasti* each" refers to the width and length [being increased respectively].
In the middle [section], each side is further increased by one span (vitasti) and six finger-breadths (aṅgula).

In total, the length should be approximately four chi and five cun, and the width should be approximately three chi and six cun. If it exceeds these measurements after being cut, this is called making it without relying on the prescribed dimensions;
one must cut it away until it conforms to the measure, and the offense should be confessed. Regarding the offenses herein: if the length exceeds the limit...

If the width does not exceed the prescribed measure, even if the length exceeds it; or if both the width and length exceed the measure, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for its completion, but not a *dukkaṭa*.
If one causes another to construct it, whether the construction is completed or not, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
The remaining four groups incur *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if: the measurement is reduced; or if one receives from another what is already completed and cuts it down to the proper measure;

or if it is folded double (according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-daśādhyāya-vinaya*, both require that the length be increased by one span [vitasti], while the width is not mentioned; according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it requires that the square be extended by one hand-span).

This means that it should be cut into three parts; the long section is joined together, while the remaining one part is used to patch the four corners, though it may be omitted if not desired. Tripitaka Master Yijing states: "The original intent behind the regulation for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) was to serve as a protective layer beneath bedding, fearing that it might be damaged;

If its size were smaller, it would be unfit to replace the bedding. As for spreading the sitting mat during prostrations, this practice is not observed in the Five Indic Regions.

What is required is solely for the purpose of protecting another’s woolen rug or mat during sleep. If using another's property, whether new or old, a protective layer must be provided. If it is one's own property, a new one is not required; if it is old, one need not provide a layer, provided it does not become soiled."

[If one] dyes [it], it degrades the offerings of the faithful and does not constitute a formal act of worship. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The new [cotton] should be double-layered; the old [woolen] should be four-layered. One should not accept a single-layered *niṣīdana*.

What was previously accepted should not be discarded. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "In making a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one should make it double-layered and dye it to a discolored hue (*kāsāya*). Fold it into three parts; the bottom part should be cut into strips (*pattra*) identical to the strips of the three robes (*tricīvara*). A border should be attached to all four sides. At that time, the bhikṣus did not carry their sitting mats with them.

If one stays overnight in another location, it constitutes the offense of being separated from one's robes. The Buddha said: "I have ordained that bhikṣus must not stay overnight having separated themselves from their three robes; this does not include the sitting mat (niṣīdana). Nevertheless, bhikṣus should not intentionally fail to take it with them.

There is no offense for those who forget it. Furthermore, a bhikṣu should not go outside without his sitting mat. One who violates this incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the rule). If he intends to return immediately but encounters other circumstances and is unable to return, he may stay overnight at that place.

He must not travel by night. He should borrow a substitute from a fellow practitioner of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*). If he obtains one, that is well. If none is available, he should take his seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*), fold it four times, and use it as a seat or mat. He should sleep little and remain awake much."

The *Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one stays overnight [with the robe], it need not be relinquished; one merely commits a *duṣkṛta* offense and must repent. My analysis is as follows: Since the Dharma has already fallen into corruption, it cannot be restored in a single day. If one enters a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) and cannot avoid conforming to the masses, one must recognize that this is not the original regulation.

One should use the robe with a sense of shame and reverence, maintaining the thought that it is the Tathāgata’s dharma-cīvara. In this way, one may perhaps barely avoid the transgression of violating the teachings. However, during times when the tradition is rare, one should follow the original regulations according to the fundamental rites.

Prostration. The intention is for one to wrap oneself [with the cloth]. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have made this *niṣīdana* according to the prescribed measurements. I now accept and maintain it. (Recite this three times. Precept 88: Regarding the Making of a Sore-Covering Cloth Exceeding the Proper Measure.
If a bhikṣu makes a sore-covering cloth, he must make it according to the prescribed measure. Herein, the measure is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length.
If it exceeds two spans in width after being cut, it is a *pāyattika*.
The commentary states: The setting is as before. At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from various kinds of sores; pus and blood defiled their bodies, as well as their robes and bedding.
The Buddha permitted them to keep a "sore-covering robe. However, because the robe was coarse and hairy, it caused pain when applied to the sores or when the robe was lifted.
The Buddha permitted the use of fine, soft cloth to cover a wound, followed by wearing a skirt.

If one was invited to sit in the home of a layperson, one should say, "I am afflicted with an ailment. If the host says, "Please sit," one should lift up the skirt and sit while covering the wound with the cloth.
At that time, the group of six monks made many large and wide cloths for covering wounds. Consequently, the Buddha established this precept.
Regarding the "wound-covering cloth": this refers to having various types of sores or diseases and using [the cloth] to cover the body.

A length of four *tala*-hands of the Buddha’s measure is equivalent to twelve *tala*-hands of a person of medium height; a width of two *tala*-hands is equivalent to six *tala*-hands of a person of medium height.

Within this, as for what constitutes an offense and what does not, including the offenses incurred by the other four assemblies, all are identical to the aforementioned precept (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*).

The Vinaya states: "This wound-covering cloth is a personal garment; it must not be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*), nor may it be subject to formal dedication (*pariṣkāra-dāna*), nor used for miscellaneous purposes. Once the wound has healed, it may be made into one of the three robes, formally dedicated, or used for other purposes. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Up until ten days after the wound has healed, if one keeps it beyond that time, it constitutes an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*). One should cut it off and perform confession (*deśanā*). If it has not been cut, the Saṃgha should order it to be cut. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one should perform the ritual of formal acceptance (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for it. Once it has been formally accepted, there is no further offense of keeping an extra robe.

Regarding the faults concerning robes, one should accept and maintain them in this manner: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], am now accepting and maintaining this wound-covering robe, which has been made according to the prescribed measurements. This is to be recited three times. The other person should reply: "So be it. According to the Sanskrit original, it should be said as follows:

*Oṣṭhika*. This is translated as "yes" (*er*), and is also called "good. It also carries the meaning of "skillful means" (*upāya*). Because this sacred teaching serves as a skillful means, it leads one toward *nirvāṇa* and reaches the place of peace and security. One should respond by saying *sādhu*; this is translated as "well done" (*shan*) or "excellent" (*shanzai*).

Whenever a ritual action is completed or when reporting on matters according to the day, one should always respond in this manner. If one does not speak thus, one incurs the offense of transgressing the Dharma (*vyatikrama-āpatti*). If one wishes to decline [the invitation], it should be understood that the wording is reversed from what was received.
Precept 89: Regarding Making a Rain-Bathing Robe Exceeding the Proper Measure.
If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, he must make it according to the proper measure. Herein, the measure is: six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length.
The width shall be two and a half spans (*vitasti*). If it exceeds this, once the cutting is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.

The commentary states: The setting is as before. When the group of six monks heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to make rain-bathing robes (*vassikasāṭikā*), they themselves made many large rain-bathing robes.
The Buddha then established this precept. A "rain-bathing robe" refers to that which is worn...

This refers to bathing during heavy rain. The remaining meanings are as explained previously. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not within this context, as well as the offenses incurred by the other four assemblies, they should be understood as stated above.
(The *bhikṣuṇīs* do not possess rain-bathing robes; they are permitted to keep bathing robes. If one makes them exceeding the prescribed measure, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense.)
Pāyattika Rule 90: On Making Robes Equal to the Buddha’s Measure.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to that of the Tathāgata, or makes one exceeding that measure, it is a pāyattika offense.
Herein, the measure of the Tathāgata’s robe is ten spans (vitasti) in length and six spans in width; this is called the measure of the Tathāgata’s robe.

The commentary states: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of the Śākyas at the Nyagrodha Park, the Venerable Nanda—who was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha—was seen from afar by the bhikṣus.
Thinking it was the Buddha who was coming, they rose to welcome him. Only upon his arrival did they realize it was Nanda.
Both felt ashamed. The Buddha then had Nanda wear black robes to distinguish him from others (meaning they were dyed with black clay to produce a discolored, monastic hue).
At that time, the group of six monks made robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata, or even larger than them. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
Regarding the term "Tathāgata": this is the foremost of the ten epithets of the World-Honored One, as explained in the section on the ten titles.

The Sūtra commentary explains: This means that just as the Buddhas of the past practiced the six pāramitās and attained the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena to arrive at the Buddha-way, so too does the present Buddha arrive by this same path. Because he comes in the same manner as the Buddhas, he is called the *Tathāgata*.
If explained according to the three bodies (*trikāya*), it is as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "He has nowhere from which he comes, nor anywhere to which he goes. Therefore...
"Tathāgata" (Thus-Come-One) is the name. This is an explanation based on the *dharmakāya*. The *Tattvārthasaṃgraha-śāstra* states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is called 'thus' (*tathā*);
perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) is called 'come' (*āgata*). This is an explanation based on the *saṃbhogakāya*. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Because one comes by means of the path of reality as it is (*yathābhūtamārga*) and attains perfect awakening, one is named 'Tathāgata'. This is an explanation based on the *nirmāṇakāya*. These are explained in detail elsewhere.
A length of ten *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha corresponds to fifteen cubits (*hasta*) of an ordinary person;

a width of six *vitasti* corresponds to nine cubits of an ordinary person (one ordinary cubit being one chi and two cun). Regarding the remaining meanings, as well as what constitutes an offense and what does not, and the transgressions incurred by the fourfold assembly, all are explained as above.

○ The First Precept: Receiving Food from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.

If a bhikṣu enters a village and, being free from illness, takes food with his own hand and eats it from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable offense."
"This was not something that should have been done. I now repent before the Venerable One. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).

The commentary states: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at a time when grain was expensive and alms were difficult to obtain, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā took the food she had obtained from begging on the first day and gave it to a bhikṣu; she did the same on the second and third days.
Again, carrying her alms-bowl, she entered the city. On the road, she encountered an elder riding in a carriage to pay his respects to the king.

The nun, in order to yield the path, fell into deep mud and lay there covered by it. The elder took pity on her and ordered his attendants to help her out. Upon questioning, he learned the reason for her fall;

he then reproached the bhikṣus for their lack of courtesy and yielding spirit. He immediately invited the nun back to his home, where he had her wash her robes, provided her with food, and [honored] the other bhikṣus.
The Bhikṣu Qiu addressed the Buddha regarding the precept: "Entering a village" refers to being within a settlement; if one takes food from a bhikṣuṇī there, it constitutes an offense.

Outside the settlement, there is no offense. "One who is not a relative" means that if she is indeed a relative, one may know for certain whether she has food or not, and thus receiving food from her does not constitute an offense. "Bhikṣuṇī" refers to [a member] of the two-fold Saṃgha.
A person who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and is not ill means one whose body is free from affliction or suffering.

"Taking with one's own hand" refers to receiving food directly from another using either the hand or a vessel. If the food is placed on the ground for one to take, or if someone else is sent to give it, these do not constitute an offense.
Regarding "food," there are two kinds: namely, substantial food (*bhojana*) and non-substantial food (*abhojana*). Furthermore, "eating" refers to swallowing.
Furthermore, "this bhikṣu" refers to one who has committed an offense; "other bhikṣus" refers to those who have properly received full ordination and are pure.
"Repenting of the offense" means declaring and exposing the name, category, and characteristics of the transgression committed.
"A matter subject to censure" means that what was done was not wholesome and was prohibited by the Buddha; since it violates the established precepts, it is fit for reprimand.
Furthermore, that which "should not be done" refers to actions that are not the proper conduct for a bhikṣu.

To now repent before the Venerable One is to clear away one's transgressions. As for this rule being called the "Rule of Repentance," it means that this is precisely the category of the offense committed.
Regarding the offense herein: if one is not ill and receives such food with one's own hands...
Regarding eating: for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika* offense; for the other four assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if one gives [the food] while in a monastery of monks, or if one gives it within a nunnery.

**The Second Precept on Receiving Food Directed by a Bhikṣuṇī:** If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson to eat and there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who directs that "soup be given to so-and-so" or "rice be given to so-and-so," the bhikṣu should speak to that bhikṣuṇī as follows: "Sister, please stop for a moment."
It must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating. If not even a single bhikṣu says to that bhikṣuṇī, "Sister, please stop for a moment;
wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating," then that bhikṣu should confess his transgression, saying: "Venerable sirs, I have committed a censurable act which ought not to have been done.
I now confess this transgression before the venerable ones. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).

The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. While the bhikṣus were eating at the home of a layperson together with the group of six, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs requested soup and rice for the group of six, saying, "Give this soup; give this rice.
They skipped those in the middle and did not give them anything, instead serving out of order so that the bhikṣus in the middle could not eat. The Buddha, on account of this, established the precept.
"Directing" means assigning the task. "Giving" means not giving equally. "Soup and rice" indicates that it is not coarse food.
"Cease for now" is a word used to issue a reprimand and stop [the action]; it means to stop for a short while and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.
"If there is not even one bhikṣu" means that among the assembly, there is not even a single [bhikṣu].
If people rebuke and stop that nun, the bhikṣu who ate [with her] immediately incurs the original offense (*mūlāpatti*).
Regarding "confessing one's transgression before the venerable ones": this refers to the bhikṣu who ate; he must confess his offense in the presence of the assembly of bhikṣus.
This is not like the other three precepts, where the offense is extinguished by confessing before a single person. Among these, as for the offender: if there is none...
If a single bhikṣu rebukes [the donor] while they eat, for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika* offense. For the other four assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense.
There is no offense if the nun herself acts as the patron (*dānapati*), or if the patron directs the nun to manage the distribution, or if it is not done intentionally that she gives preferentially.

(According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda*, the *Mahāsāṃghika*, and others: if there is not even one bhikṣu among the assembly who rebukes [the donor], all the bhikṣus incur an offense upon eating; however, the *Mahāsāṃghika* prescribes [confession] only toward...)

Confession before one person. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If another nun instructs a nun to give more food to a bhikṣu and does not tell her to step back slightly, it is an *dukkaṭa*. If a bhikṣu instructs [another] bhikṣu to give more food and eats it unequally, it is an *dukkaṭa*."
**The Third Precept on Receiving Food from a Family Under Discipline:** If a *kula-kamma* (formal act) has been performed regarding a family under discipline, and a bhikṣu, at such a family,

receives food with his own hands and eats it without having been previously invited and without being ill, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying: "I have committed a censurable offense."
This is a dharma that one should not have committed; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable One. This dharma is called the *deśanā-dharma* (the rite of confession).
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was the house of a lay devotee where both husband and wife had attained faith and joy.
Now, it is the constant rule for the disciples of the Buddhas who have realized the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*) that they cherish nothing among the bhikṣus, even unto their own flesh and blood.
He constantly provided offerings until he eventually fell into poverty; his food and clothing were exhausted, and his neighbors reviled him.

The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for him as a "family-in-training" (*śaikṣa-kula*), and thus established this precept. Regarding the term "family-in-training": "training" refers to the first fruit [of the path].
Regarding the second and third fruits: because their afflictions (*kleśa*) and outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted, they must still train in order to sever them;

therefore, they are called "trainers" (*śaikṣa*). "Householder" refers to the families of the four castes. Since these trainees still reside within the household, they are called "householder-trainees. This is not the case for an Arhat.
Those whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and who have accomplished what was to be done are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the *kamma* (formal act):

it refers to a case where a husband and wife have both realized the fruit of holiness (*āryaphala*) and possess no stinginess or attachment toward the Triple Gem. Yet, their household affairs have become impoverished;

therefore, the Saṃgha performs for them the "protective rite" (*parihāradharma*), whereby they do not go to that house to receive food and drink. Such is the "family under training" (*sekha-kula*), which refers to the Saṃgha.

This refers to a family for whom the *karmavācanā* has already been performed. "Without having been previously invited" means that even if the *karmavācanā* has been performed for them, there is no offense in accepting an invitation.
"Not being ill" means that if one is ill, there is no offense. Regarding the offense herein:
if, without having been previously invited and not being ill, one receives food or drink with one's own hands from such a family, there is an offense of *pāyattika* for every swallow.
This is a *pratideśanīya* offense; for the other four assemblies, it is an *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense if one gives by placing it on the ground, or if one receives it from another person, or if the wealth subsequently increases and that person requests the Sangha to revoke the *śikṣādattaka-karman*.

The Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) to release [the householder from the restriction]. Once released, he may receive food without offense. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If the wife is an *āryā* and the husband is not an *ārya*, or if the husband is an *ārya* and the wife is not an *ārya*, the *karman* should not be performed for them. Only if both husband and wife are *āryas*, possess no heart of stinginess or greed, and their wealth and goods are completely exhausted, should the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the karman for a family under training) be performed for them.

If the Saṃgha possesses gardens or fields, they should be granted [to the household] so that they may be made known; this shall ensure the fulfillment of regular obligations, while the remainder is used for their own support. If there are no gardens or fields, when the monastery receives offerings from different sources, they should be directed to prepare [food] at their home so that there is a surplus left over. If even this is not available, they may obtain it by begging. )

Having done so, one should go to that family’s home and eat there, giving them what remains. If one cannot do this, one should bring [the food] to the monastery and provide them with lodging, clothing, and food. The same should be arranged for the women of that learned family by the bhikṣuṇīs as well.

If a bhikṣu resides in an araṇya—a remote and isolated place where there is suspicion and fear—and if that bhikṣu dwelling in such an araṇya does not first inform the donor, nor receive food outside the monastery grounds, [he commits an offense]. In the saṃgha...

"Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy act that should not have been done. I now confess this to you, Venerable sir. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).
The commentary states: When the Buddha was at the Nyagrodha Park, the women of the city of Śrāvastī brought food and drink to the monastery to make offerings.
On the road, they were harassed and molested by bandits. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, the bhikṣus should tell the women not to go out, for there are bandits on the road who cause terror. If...
Once they have left the city, one should tell them: "Do not go into the monastery; there are thieves on the road who cause fear.

This was then established as a precept for *āraṇyakas* and those in places of suspected danger, both of which are explained in detail in the section on the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture). Regarding the term *dānapati* (donor):
*dāna* is a Western [Sanskrit] sound, which here means "to give away" (*tyāga*); *pati* is a word from this region [of India], meaning that he is able to break through stinginess and envy.
By practicing the giving of alms, one may personally cross over the ocean of poverty and later attain great wealth;

this is because it draws forth and generates the provisions of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*). It is also called *dāna*; explained in detail, it is *dānapati*, which is translated here as "donor" (*shizhu*).
Regarding the phrase "within the saṃghārāma," it means that while in the monastery, being free from illness, one receives food with one's own hands. Thus...
One incurs the offense. The first three precepts involve the arising of transgressions within a village or a household; this precept involves the arising of the offense while in a monastery.
The characteristics of the offense herein should be understood as previously explained. As for those who do not incur the offense: they have first informed the donor; or there is illness;

or the gift is placed on the ground and given; or one instructs another to give it. (According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, both require that a formal act of double proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) be performed to appoint [a person].)
A certain bhikṣu was observing and guarding those traveling on dangerous paths. Consequently, he explained the rules for dwelling in an araṇya.
When an araṇya bhikṣu enters a village for alms, he should wash his hands clean at dawn, take up his robes, shake them out, and inspect them before putting them on in the proper order.
He should pin the saṃghāṭī robe over his shoulder, wash his bowl, place it in its carrying net, take up his leather sandals, his rattan staff, and his keys.
Upon leaving the room, one should close the door and push it to see if it is secure. If it is not secure, one should remain in retreat for another period of *anāgārika* (dwelling).
One should look around in all four directions; if no one sees you, you may hide the door-bolt. If someone sees you, you should hide it further, or perhaps take it with you.
While traveling on the road, you should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas. If you see someone, you should first greet them, saying, "Welcome. If...

When intending to go to a village, one should set down the bowl on the ground, put on the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), and entrust one’s sandals and staff to a shop or dwelling at the edge of the village.
Upon entering the village, one should observe the characteristics of the streets, as well as the characteristics of vacant places, marketplaces, gates, and heaps of refuse.
When entering the house of a layperson, one should observe the characteristics of the first gate through to the seventh gate. If one wishes to adjust one’s robes, one should turn toward—

[He should] have a wall [behind him]. With his right hand he holds a staff, and with his left hand he holds an alms bowl. He should not stand in the middle of the road, nor should he stand in a secluded place.

He should not go out to meet [a donor] to receive food. If he is called, he should go to receive it. If he receives boiled rice, dry rice, or the like, he should not place them all together in one spot;
if they are in a single bowl, he should separate them with an object. He should not select only large families to beg from, nor should he be forceful.

One should beg for what is necessary. If one knows that it will be obtained, one should wait. Having begged and when departing, one should observe the signs at the gate, even up to the signs at the heap of refuse.
Once out of the village, one should take up the staff and sandals, place the bowl on the ground, and fasten the great robe over the shoulder.

While traveling, he should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas. Upon returning to his usual place for eating, he should sweep and sprinkle it clean, prepare water, wash the vessels, and set out the vessel for leftovers, a seat, a foot-washing stone, a water vessel, and a towel for wiping the feet.
If he sees another forest-dwelling bhikṣu arriving, he should rise to meet him from afar, take up his bowl and robes, provide a seat, offer a water vessel, and wash his feet.
Regarding such items: once they have been washed, all objects should be returned to their original places.
Having cleansed one's hands with soap powder (*śāṇa*), one should set aside a portion of the remaining food in a clean manner. To any who arrive carrying *śāṇa*, it should be given.
Next, water and food should be offered to that forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu. While he is eating, one should watch over him and provide whatever is required. If during the day...
When the time for the meal has passed, they should eat together. Having finished eating, one should take their bowls and wash them.
If there is leftover food, it should be given to humans; if not, it should be placed on ground where no grass grows or into water that is free of insects.
One should then wash the vessels, return them to their original place, and sweep the dining area. If a *śramaṇa* comes by, one should say to them: "This is water; this is for washing."
These provisions are food; for your sake, I have set aside this pure and clean portion.

If you wish to eat, you may do so, but you should well understand the divisions of the night and its seasons, well understand the directions and signs, and well understand the constellations. You should not spread out fine bedding to sleep soundly;
rather, during the first and last watches of the night, you should remain vigilant and engage in contemplation. A bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya should act thus.
One should conform to the *āraṇyaka* dharma. If one does not conform, one incurs an offense for each instance (*Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"A person who is not foolish is fit to dwell in an *āraṇya* location. Even if they are not widely learned, if they clearly understand the characteristics of the precepts, they may still dwell there. In whatever region they reside, they should have thorough knowledge of the terrain, the constellations, and the roads. They should provide for those who come and go according to their means. They should store dry parched grain and water, measuring the quantity according to the time.

If they see a guest arrive, they should cry out 'Welcome! with a smile and speak first; they should not frown. If a woman comes, they should regard her as a mother, a daughter, or a sister according to her age. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 'The *āraṇyaka'..."*

If a bhikṣu should possess fire, a fire-drill, food, and utensils for eating; he should always keep a water jar filled with water; he should even recite and understand the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; he should know the four dhyānas and the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], and if he has not yet attained them, he should know how to study and recite them.
He should not possess sun-crystals or moon-crystals. He should not dwell in uninhabited deep mountains or in places that are fearsome.
△ Finally, the formal inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have recited the four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times. "Venerable sirs, we are pure in this matter, because of our silence. Thus it shall be held."
The commentary states: The concluding phrasing is as explained previously. If one wishes to repent for this offense, one should first invite a presiding master of confession (*karmavācanā-ācārya*).
Having done so, one should then make the following confession: "Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], being free from illness, accepted food directly from the hands of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative within a village and ate it (the remainder follows...)"
[This refers to] the specific designation of the various types of offenses). Venerable Sir, I have committed so many *pāyattika* (or *pratideśanīya*) offenses.
These are blameworthy matters that I ought not to have done; I now confess them to the Venerable One. I dare not conceal them. To confess is peace;
not to confess is not peace. Recalling my transgression, I disclose it; knowing it, I do not conceal it. May the Venerable One [accept this].

"Virtuous one, remember my pure body of precepts. Having fulfilled the pure *poṣadha* (the single recitation), you should esteem your own mind and give rise to world-weariness. [He] replied, "So be it."
The Tenth Fascicle of the Commentary on the *Sifen jieben*, Phonetic Glossary:
The character 閾 (yǔ) has the phonetic value yù.
*Chūpú*: the first character is pronounced *kōu*; the second is pronounced *pú*. It refers to the game of dice.
*Hù*: pronounced *hū*. *Suōnà*: this word means "thief."
The Commentary on the *Caturvarga-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, Fascicle Eleven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Jiqi. Section Seven:
The Training Rules for the Seven Classes of Disciples (Opening in three parts). First, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration; third, the concluding inquiry.
△ First, a general heading for the various Venerable Ones: These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharmas), recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
The commentary states: In Sanskrit, they are called *śikṣākaraṇī*, also known as *śikṣāpada-nī*. This is translated as [the rules of training].
"One should train" refers to the matters that ought to be studied. The Hu (Central Asian) monks translated this as "guarding the precepts" (*śīla-rakṣā*).
This is because these offenses are subtle and extremely difficult to maintain; thus, the name was established based on training in and guarding them accordingly.
This is a translation based on the meaning rather than a literal translation. The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "In other sections, it does not say 'one should train,' yet..."
This precept alone is thus. The answer is: the other sections are easy to maintain, yet their offenses are grave;
if one commits them, the offense is established, and one must repent either before the assembly or face-to-face with another. This precept is difficult to maintain, yet its offense is light;

even if one should happen to commit it, provided one feels remorse and resolves to train, no formal offense is incurred—it is simply stated that "one should train. Nevertheless, although this method of training does not go beyond...

Regarding their names: should any transgressions occur, they are all to be confessed as *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅). Furthermore, there are two categories of offenses—intentional and unintentional—and the stages of confession are likewise twofold.

For intentional offenses, one must confess and repent before another; for unintentional ones, they are removed through self-reproach and mental purification. This is stated in various Vinayas and treatises.
In all cases, intentional acts constitute two types of offenses. As stated in the Vinaya-mūla: "Regarding an intentional act, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession;
because it was done intentionally, one also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*). If it was not done intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: If a bhikṣu does not rely on the Buddha’s teaching and, disregarding shame, intends to act contrary to the Dharma, if he takes up his robe and spreads it out, he incurs an *āpatti* of mental censure (*kaukṛtya*).

If he puts it on his body, he incurs an *āpatti* of verbal confession (*pratideśanīya*). If a bhikṣu has a mind of compliance [with the rules] but wears the robe improperly—whether due to forgetfulness or...
At that time, those who were ignorant and attached to what is not the Dharma incurred only the offense of *pācittiya* (requiring confession) for mental misconduct (*duṣkṛta*).

According to various Vinayas and Śāstras, it is generally said that these are the *śaikṣa-dharmas* (rules of training). Although the Buddha established them first at the very beginning, those who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka placed them later in the sequence.
This is because, although the names of the offenses are identical, there are five degrees of gravity; the heavy precepts are placed first, while the light precepts follow.

This precept is the lightest among the five categories [of offenses]; therefore, it is placed last. Furthermore, one is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) while two are proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*);

since the natural offense is real, it is placed first, and the proscribed offense is placed last. Moreover, one is an offense without remainder (*anavaśeṣa*) while two are offenses with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*);
thus, the grave ones are placed first and the light ones are placed last. Nevertheless, among the hundred matters, this is not necessarily so.
All are contained within the first formulation. Because the primary precept is placed at the beginning, it is called "the first.

For example, when the Buddha first ordained the five bhikṣus, their attire was still that of laypeople. The Buddha then thought: "How did the Buddhas of the past instruct their disciples regarding clothing?
He then observed with his divine eye and perceived that they wore garments like those of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
He put them on and then addressed the five bhikṣus, saying: "From this day forward, you should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) as neatly and properly as the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: Among the five categories of precepts, why did the Buddha specifically regulate the wearing of the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* and the three robes by observing the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven? The answer is: The Buddha... [text continues]

The precepts of the five categories were established, and this [Prātimokṣa] was placed at the very beginning. Because it governs the beginning, the other categories do not need to be explained separately.
Furthermore, if this precept were treated as minor compared to the others, future disciples would not develop a sense of profound respect for it.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, having observed the Buddhas of the past and future, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities with his Buddha-eye, subsequently established it. This was so that future generations...
Sentient beings do not give rise to the sin of arrogance. Furthermore, among the precepts established by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, there are similarities and differences;

within the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), they are not necessarily identical in all respects. However, this practice of wearing the inner robe (*nivāsana*) and the monastic robe (*kāṣāya*) is entirely the same for all Buddhas of the three periods.

For this reason, when observing this precept, one contemplates the Buddhas and the Śuddhāvāsa devas, whereas other categories of offenses do not require such contemplation. (This is a real offense, that is, a natural transgression.)
(These are offenses).

△ Within this section, these rules of training (śikṣāpada) are listed individually; their wording is concise and their practical applications largely follow the same pattern. Therefore, there is no need for an elaborate enumeration of their specific titles.

Contemplate this with careful thought, and you will immediately grasp its essential meaning. Regarding the explanation of the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) of these offenses, whether the Vinaya texts contain them in full or not, an examination of the *Khandakas* reveals that they were mostly initiated by the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).

Since these are all offenses of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and are equally intended to protect one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), their distinction lies solely in the degree of gravity resulting from negligence;
no other distinct characteristics can be found. Nevertheless, as for the facts and principles of these matters, they are singular...
Furthermore, there is no fixed order. Now, the hundred dharmas are unified and categorized into ten matters, summarized into verses so that students may easily memorize them:
first, the matter of wearing robes; second, the matter of entering a village; third, the matter of sitting and rising; fourth, the matter of eating and chewing;

fifth, the matter of protecting the bowl; sixth, the matter of defecation and urination; seventh, the matter of preaching the Dharma; eighth, the matter of stupas and images; ninth, the matter of the path...
On Ritual Conduct: The Ten Matters Concerning Ascending a Tree. The Verse says:
Properly arranging the lower robe and the three robes, Entering villages and dwellings, sitting, eating, and chewing;
Guarding the bowl, relieving oneself, and the etiquette for preaching the Dharma; Venerating stupas, monasteries, images, walking on paths, and [ascending] trees.
One should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) neatly; this is how one should train.
(1) The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* either too low or too high;
some made them like an elephant’s trunk, some like a *tāla* leaf, and sometimes they made fine pleats. Householders criticized and disparaged them, saying they resembled royal ministers.
As well as those who engage in jesting and comedic discourse, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha and he established this precept: "The *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*—also called *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī*;
this refers to the lower garment (*śīrṣaka*)—should be worn in a neat and orderly manner. This means one should avoid the fault of wearing it in a disordered fashion.
What constitutes being disordered? It includes tying the belt below the navel, hitching it up so high that it reaches the knees, or letting the front hang down.
One corner [of the lower garment] is shaped like an elephant’s trunk; or the two front corners are allowed to hang down like the leaves of a *tāla* tree;

or they may be gathered around the waist with fine pleats (the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: this refers to taking the edge of the skirt, folding it finely into pleats, and pinching them all together at the waist; the shape is like a *tāla* leaf, with the upper part gathered and the lower part spreading out). Regarding the offense herein:
if one intentionally acts in contravention of the Buddha’s teaching, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*). This is because...
If committed intentionally, it is an offense of improper conduct (*duṣkṛta*). If not committed intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For all subsequent precepts, one should understand this accordingly; they will not be stated separately again. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. These constitute the hundred dharmas.
The nuns all study this together; there are one or two points that differ, which will be annotated below according to the specific circumstances.
As for non-offenses: if a sore develops at the navel, it may be worn low; if there is a sore on the calf, it may be worn high. This applies whether inside a monastery or outside a village.

And when putting it on, while walking on the road—[the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states that *nivāsana* means "skirt" in the language of Tang; the old term *nirvāṇa-saṃgha* is an error]. Since it has neither ties nor loops, when one is about to wear it, one gathers the cloth into pleats and secures them with a cord.

As for the pleats, each school has its own variation, and as for the colors, they differ between yellow and red. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* says: "As for the style of the skirt according to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is five cubits wide and two cubits long.

It may be made of silk, gauze, or cotton, whichever is available. In the Western Regions, all are made single-layered; in China, one may make them double-layered at will. The width and length are determined by preference. Once it is wrapped around the waist, lift it so that it passes above the navel. With the right hand, pull the upper corner of the left side inward."

Toward the right side of the waist, take the outer edge of the left upper hem and cover the left side. With both hands at the two sides, lift them to make them even and level; keep the center perfectly straight, which will form three pleats. Then, with both hands, gather each side toward the waist.

Fold the cloth three times and bring it behind to cover [the body]. Lift each of the two corners by three finger-widths and insert them both toward the spine, allowing them to enter the waist by about three finger-widths. Even if the sash has not yet been tied, this will keep the garment on the body and prevent it from falling. Next, take the waist-sash, approximately five cubits (*hasta*) in length, and hook it at its center.

Raise it below the navel and smooth it over the upper edge of the skirt, arranging the two ends together toward the back. Cross them over in front and pull them through; then, pulling them to the left and right, firmly press both sides with one hand each and wrap the two strands around three times.

If there is excess length, cut it off; if it is too short, add more. The head of the sash should not be embroidered or decorated. The width of the sash should be like the surface of a finger, such as those used for boots or socks; they may be either square or round.

Both [methods] are without fault. However, items such as hempen ropes are not permitted by the Vinaya texts. When sitting on a small stool or when picking things up, one should pull the skirt upward; the lower corner of the skirt should be tucked tightly under the edge of the skirt and pressed beneath the knees, merely covering both thighs.

It is permissible for the calves to be exposed. The upper limit must cover the navel, and the lower limit should reach four finger-widths above the ankles; this is the protocol for lay dwellings. If within a monastery, it is also acceptable for it to reach halfway down the calf.

These measurements were personally established by the Buddha and are not a matter of human opinion; one must not arbitrarily adjust them upward or downward. How could it be appropriate to willfully violate the intent of the teachings simply to follow worldly sentiments? As for the skirt one wears, if its length extends to the ground, first, it wastes the pure offerings of those with faith, and second, it shows contempt for the Great Master’s authoritative words. West... [text ends].

The national skirt-garment (*saṃkakṣikā*) is worn entirely horizontally. This is because in that region, the width of the self-woven cloth is two *hasta*. Regarding the ritual for wearing this garment, the regulations are fully contained within the Vinaya texts; however, I shall briefly present only the essential points here, as a detailed discussion cannot be conducted without face-to-face instruction. This is what is called "wearing the skirt in a rounded and neat manner.

Nevertheless, the four Nikāyas differ in their methods of wearing the skirt to distinguish themselves. In the Sarvāstivāda, both sides are folded outward in double pleats. In the Mahāsāṃghika, the right skirt is gathered at the left side and tucked inward so that it does not fall.

The methods of the Sthavira and Sammitīya schools are also similar to this, differing only in that they turn the skirt straight outward and tuck it to the side. The regulations for the waist-belt are likewise no different. For nuns, the rules follow those of their respective schools just as the monks do; there is absolutely no distinction.
[The body]. One should wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner; this is how one should train. (2) The commentary states:
The setting and circumstances are the same as before. "In a neat and orderly manner" means being free from disarray. What constitutes disarray?
It must be neat and orderly. It should not hang down past the elbows so as to expose the ribs; nor should it be raised so high that it goes above the ankles.
Nor should one corner hang down like an elephant's trunk, or should the two front corners hang down while the back is hitched up high to form fine pleats, even after the border has been fixed.

There is no offense if one wears it low because there are sores on the shoulders or arms; otherwise, all other rules are as stated above. (The *Neifa zhuan* states: "Regarding the method for wearing the dharma robes and the fashion for applying the fastenings and ties...")

According to the Vinaya, one should take a robe measuring five cubits (*hasta*) and fold it into three pleats. At the point where the shoulder is folded, four finger-widths from the edge, one should attach a square patch measuring five fingers on each side.

Sew around all four edges; in the center, pierce a small hole with an awl to secure the collar (*kaṇṭhaka*). This collar may be made of cord, silk, or cloth, with a thickness similar to the collar itself and a length of two fingers. Tie it firmly, pass the collar through the hole, pull it out toward the outside, and cross it in a "ten-character" (cross) pattern.

Fasten it so that it forms two loops; the inner ties are positioned in the center. At the pleated section of the chest, place ties along the edge, just like the ties on a shirt; this is the method. Approximately eight finger-widths from each corner, provide one loop and one tie for each.

This is required for the time of eating: fold it back across the chest and fasten the ties so they meet; this constitutes the essential rule. Whenever one is within the monastery, or at times when facing the assembly, one must never wear it with ties fastened, nor employ the method of draping it over the shoulders. However, if one is traveling outside [the monastery], [these rules do not apply].

When entering a lay residence, one must fasten the neck-loop (*kaṭhina*). At other times, it may simply be draped over the shoulder. When performing tasks in a private place, one may fold the robe across the back as one pleases. However, when facing a venerable image, it must be kept neat and orderly; the right corner of the robe should be draped wide over the left shoulder.

Let it hang behind your back; do not rest it upon your elbows. If you wish to fasten it with ties, you must first drape it over both shoulders, tuck the ties inside, and loop them back behind your shoulders so they do not slip off.

Rest the corners upon your shoulders so that the robe encircles your neck, with both sleeves hanging down and one corner draped forward. The image of King Aśoka is precisely according to this model; his appearance as he walks while holding a parasol is most graceful, for this is the proper way to wear the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) in accordance with the teachings.

Regarding the three robes (tricīvara), if you attach short ties and cut the long cords, you will avoid the fault of violating the instructions. When wearing the lower robe (antarvāsaka), remove the waistband so that the labor of sewing is brought to rest. As for the water flask and alms bowl, each should be hung from two shoulders, reaching only to the armpits; they must not be crossed over the chest.

The loops [of the robe] should not be long; they should merely be sufficient to pass over the shoulders. If they are crossed across the chest, it will cause one to feel short of breath, as this was not the original design and thus should not be practiced. If there is surplus cloth, let it drape over the shoulders before donning the robe fully to cover the bowl and robes.

When heading toward a monastery or visiting a layperson’s home, one must first go to the quarters to set down the umbrella and canopy, and only then untie the knots to hang the bowl and robes. Regarding those who make the *kāṣāya* from thin silk, the fabric is often too slippery to stay on the shoulder; during prostrations, it consequently falls to the ground.

One should therefore choose materials that do not slip, such as *śī* (fine silk), *chou* (silk gauze), or white woolen cloth (*pūrmaka*). As for the *saṃkakṣikā* (under-robe), it is simply a covering for the shoulders; adding one more *hasta* (cubit) to its length makes it conform to the original standard.

Regarding the ritual for donning [the upper robe]: one should expose the right shoulder and cross it over the left arm. This alone, together with the lower skirt (*nivasana*), is to be worn constantly within the dwelling. When going outside to pay respects to the Honored One, one may add other garments as appropriate. The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"When it is hot, a bhikṣu within his own room may wear only the lower skirt and the *saṃkakṣikā*; he may read, recite, preach the Dharma, or perform tasks such as making robes according to his inclination. In all four modes of deportment, there is no transgression. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "When performing acts of worship, one should bared the shoulder to facilitate the task.

When acting as a field of merit, one should cover both shoulders to manifest the marks of the field. What constitutes performing worship? It is like when seeing the Buddha, or when greeting teachers and elders; one should act according to the specific circumstances. Whether wiping the bed or sweeping..."

Whether folding his robes, or engaging in various forms of making offerings, whenever he acts as a field of merit— whether invited by a king for a meal, entering a village to beg for alms, sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, or walking in meditation beneath a tree— people see him as dignified and worthy of contemplation.
One must not enter the house of a layperson with one’s robe tucked up behind the back.

This is the third precept to be studied. The commentary states: The setting and circumstances are the same as before. “Tucking the robe up behind the back” means to fold the robe over both shoulders from left to right or right to left.

There is no offense if there is a wound or similar affliction on the side of the ribs (the *Vinayaviniścaya* states: regarding upper and lower garments, one must not fold them unevenly to one side so as to expose the body; they must be worn evenly).
One should fold both ends together and place them over the shoulder.
One must not sit in the house of a layperson with the robe folded back over the shoulders; this is how one should train (4).
The commentary states: The preceding precepts concern the deportment of walking; these precepts concern the deportment of sitting.

That is to say, when sitting in a layperson’s house, one should properly cover the body and not be disheveled, lest one lose the decorum of a bhikṣu. One should sit with the body upright and the mind composed, inspiring faith and respect in others.
If one were to indulge the sense faculties, pulling up one's robes to expose the body, one would incur the derision and slander of others, which is to one's own detriment.
It causes harm to others.
One must not enter the home of a layperson with a robe wrapped around the neck; this is how one should train (5).
The commentary states: The setting and circumstances are the same as before. "With a robe wrapped around the neck" means grasping both corners of the robe together and placing them upon the shoulder.
This is the highest [standard]. As for those who do not commit an offense:
if there are sores on the shoulders or arms and so forth, one must not enter the house of a layperson with the robe wrapped around the neck and sit down. This should be practiced (6).
The commentary says: This means that when one is in a layperson’s house, one should wear the robes neatly and sit while manifesting the appearance of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
One must not enter the house of a layperson with the head covered; this is how one should train. (7)
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. "Covering the head" means to cover the head with a garment, a tree leaf, or pieces of cloth.
There is no offense if one is suffering from cold, has a sore on the head, or faces a threat to life.

It is difficult to maintain the holy life [if one acts thus]. One must not run away with the head covered (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: if there is wind, cold, rain, or illness, one must not cover the head entirely; one should cover only half so that one ear remains visible.

If one sees the two teachers or a senior elder, one should withdraw. One must not enter the latrine with the head covered. However, if one is in a secluded private room and covers it, there is no offense).
One must not sit with one's head covered while entering the house of a layperson; this is a training rule (8).
The commentary states: the meaning is as explained previously. Furthermore, a bhikṣu must not wrap his head, for that is the custom of laypeople.
However, if the head is cold or painful, it is permitted to use wool, or to tie a turban, or to wear a cap.
One must not skip steps when entering the house of a layperson;

this is how one should train (9). The commentary states: The setting is as before. The group of six monks entered the homes of the laity skipping steps. A householder remarked with disdain, "They are just like birds.
The Buddha established this precept for them. "Skipping" refers to leaping with both feet together. There is no offense if—
If one has been beaten by others, or if there are thieves, wild beasts, or thorns;
or if one has crossed a ditch, a moat, or similar obstacles, one must not enter the house of a layperson by jumping and sit down. This is how one should train (10).
The commentary states: It refers to a bhikṣu that whatever manner of walking he performs which does not possess the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), he should abandon it all.

(The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not sit embracing the knees; one must not sit with legs crossed. To have legs crossed means: the thighs rest upon thighs, the knees rest upon knees, the calves rest upon the shins, and the feet rest upon the insteps. If one is ill, there is no offense.")
One must not squat while inside the house of a layperson;
this is how one should train. (11) The commentary states: The setting is as before. A householder invited the Saṃgha for a meal.

When the time arrived, the bhikṣus went to the house and sat down in their assigned seats. The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika monks) squatted. Their neighbors touched them with their hands, whereupon they fell over and were exposed.

The Buddha established this precept: regarding "squatting," whether on the ground or on a bed or seat, it means that the buttocks do not touch the ground, such that both feet are planted on the floor and both knees are held upright.

There is no offense in cases where there is a sore on the side of the buttocks, or when one is giving something away, performing a prostration, confessing a transgression, or receiving instruction and admonition. This is what is called *hukuei* (half-kneeling).
[This refers to] the *kai* (the coccyx; pronounced *kǎo* in the level tone; it refers to the end of the spinal column, which is the buttocks).
One must not walk into the house of a layperson with hands crossed over the waist; this is how one should train. (12)
The commentary states: The setting for the Buddha is as before. Because the group of six monks walked into lay households with their hands placed across their hips, this rule was established.
Regarding "placing the hands across the hips": this refers to crossing one’s arms over the waist, either with one hand or both hands, and tucking the elbows under the armpits.
There is no offense in cases where sores have developed under the armpits, or when inside a monastery, outside a village, while working, or while traveling on a road.
One must not sit in the house of a layperson with hands placed on the hips; this is how one should train (13).
The commentary states: this refers to placing the hands on the waist and elbows, thereby obstructing the neighboring seat.
Even if there is no neighboring seat, it is still contrary to proper decorum (the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states: "one must not sit supporting the cheek with the palm").
One must not enter the house of a layperson while swaying the body; this is how one should train. (14) The commentary states:
The setting is the same as before. "Swaying the body" means walking with the body twisting to the left and right.
A bhikṣuṇī incurs a *pāyattika* offense. There is no offense in cases such as when she is struck by someone and twists her body to avoid the blow, or when she avoids...

If one encounters a wild beast, or meets a person carrying thorns, one should twist the body to avoid it; or when crossing a ditch or canal, or at times while putting on clothes, one should turn the body around to check whether the garments are properly arranged.
One must not sway the body while entering the house of a layperson to sit; this is how one should train.
(15) The commentary states: This means that when inside the house of a layperson, one should maintain a dignified and composed demeanor and sit with the body upright.
One must not walk into the house of a layperson with arms swinging; this is how one should train.
(16) The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. "Swinging the arms" means swinging the arms back and forth while walking.
There is no offense if, for instance, one is being struck by someone, or if a wild beast approaches and one raises the hand to ward it off, or uses the hand to beckon a companion.
One must not walk into the house of a layperson with arms swinging and sit down; this is how one should train (17).

The commentary states that when in the house of a layperson, one should sit with hands folded in a respectful posture. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "One must not move the hands, move the feet, or wave the hands."
One should sit with feet still; one should dwell in tranquility and composure. If someone asks a question, one should first guard the precepts and answer in accordance with them.
One should train oneself to enter the houses of laypeople while properly covering the body (18).
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. If one does not properly cover the body, it will be exposed in various places.
There is no offense if one is bound, or if the wind blows the robe away from the body.
One should train oneself to enter the houses of laypeople and sit with the body properly covered (19).
The commentary states: when sitting in the houses of the laity, one’s bodily deportment must be properly covered; one should not wear only a single garment.
Except in the place for defecation and urination, one should not wear garments with tassels at the neck, nor embroidered garments;
one should not wear a padded jacket (a type of fur garment or a long robe); one should not wear leather garments; one should not wear pleated skirts;
one should not wear garments made of grass, tree bark, leaves, jeweled ornaments, wool, hair, or horse and ox tails—none of these should be worn.

One should not practice the ways of the white-robed householders or the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If one suffers from cold, it is permitted to wear double-layered robes (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"It is permitted to insert padding in all three robes; one should use dense material to make the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*). If the material is thin, it should be made in two or three layers. If the five-strip robe is thin, the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṣāya*) should be made with dense material.

If the seven-strip robe is thin, the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) should be made with dense material. If the great robe is thin, the seven-strip robe should be made with dense material"). When sitting, one should lift the robe with one hand and press down on the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) with the other, and then sit in a composed and dignified manner.
One must not look left and right while walking into the house of a layperson; this is a training rule (the twentieth).
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. "Looking left and right" means glancing about in various directions. There is no offense [in the following cases]:
If one looks up at the sun to observe the time and season, or if there is a danger to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one may seek out a path or means on either side to escape.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Regarding 'not looking upward,' one raises the eyes to look ahead for a distance of one *vyāma*; this is the measure of sight. A *vyāma* measures four cubits (*hasta*) in length. One should not look sideways, nor should one look back.

One should proceed with a composed posture, looking straight ahead and walking slowly. One should observe cattle, horses, dogs, and the like in advance; one should not approach them closely, for fear of injury. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should walk while looking attentively."

At that time, one must not walk with the head bowed like a horse; rather, one should walk with a level gaze to guard against wild elephants, horses, and oxen. One should walk as if carrying a palanquin, without looking toward the east or west. If one wishes to look, one should turn the entire body toward the place one intends to look.
One should train oneself not to look left or right while entering the house of a layperson and sitting there. (21) Commentary:
Whenever one is in the house of a layperson, one should maintain an upright mind and gaze straight ahead, sitting with mindfulness fixed before oneself.

One should not look at other people passing by, coming and going, or at performers singing and dancing. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "In the house of a layperson, one should not sit down abruptly unless invited to do so.")
One should not sit [in a layperson’s house] without careful observation.
One should train oneself to enter the house of a layperson in silence (22).
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. "Not being silent" means speaking loudly or calling out at the top of one's voice, whether giving instructions or shouting.

One should give food with a loud voice. There is no offense if one is deaf, or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life, or if one runs while shouting, or enters the house of a layperson in silence and sits down. This is how one should train. (23)
The commentary states: When sitting in a layperson’s house, one should remain tranquil, like the noble silence (*ārya-tūṣṇīmbhāva*). If questioned, one should answer accordingly.
If one wishes to say something, one should speak with moderation. If one wishes to call someone, one should snap one's fingers to alert them.
If the person in front does not hear, one should speak to a neighbor to convey the message.
One must not enter the house of a layperson while laughing or joking; this is a training rule (the twenty-fourth).
The commentary states: The setting and circumstances are the same as before. "Laughing or joking" refers to smiling with the teeth exposed.
There is no offense if one smiles out of joy while recollecting the Dharma.
One must not sit in the house of a layperson while laughing or joking; this is how one should train. (25) The commentary states:
When sitting in the house of a layperson, one should maintain a composed and solemn demeanor, like the bearing of a great man, and must not engage in childish playfulness.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "One must not sit laughing within the house of a layperson. Furthermore, when eating in a monastery, one must not laugh before the two teachers or the elder monks. If there is something truly laughable, one must not manifest it outwardly."

If you laugh with bared teeth, you should endure it. You should give rise to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and contemplate the thought of death. You should bite your own tongue. If you still cannot stop, you must not laugh with bared teeth; you should cover your mouth with your robe to restrain yourself.
One should learn to receive food with careful attention. (Twenty-sixth) The commentary states:
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a householder invited the Saṃgha to offer a meal. He personally served various kinds of food and drink.
The group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) did not receive the food with care; they threw away the soup and rice. The Buddha therefore established this precept. One must not...
Regarding "intentionally discarding food": this refers to throwing away soup or rice while eating.

There is no offense if, because the bowl is small, one discards rice while eating, or if it falls back onto the table (the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One who receives food with a single-minded focus holds the bowl with the left hand with single-minded focus, while the right hand supports its rim").
One should learn to receive food with a level bowl.
(27) The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. The group of six monks received food until their bowls overflowed, causing them to spill the soup and rice.

Therefore, this rule was established. "Not leveling the bowl" means receiving until it overflows. There is no offense if, at times, the bowl is small, or if the food falls back onto the table. At such times...
The bhikṣus accepted the invitations of donors and departed in a disordered manner: some had already left while others were just leaving;

some had already sat down while others were just sitting down; some had already eaten while others were just eating; some had already departed while others were just departing. The Buddha said: "If you wish to go and accept an invitation..."
One should go to the place where the Sangha regularly takes its meals and stand where one is visible.

When the donor announces that the time has arrived, the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) should take the lead and proceed in a formation like a flight of geese. If there are matters concerning the Three Jewels or matters regarding the care of the sick, one should inform the senior monk.
One should go ahead. If there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one is permitted to go without asking permission.

Upon arriving at that place of eating, one should not stay in a confused or crowded manner; rather, one should sit according to the proper order—whether as a senior, middle, or junior seat—and should look out for one another.
If there is anyone sitting improperly or who has not properly covered their body, one should snap one's fingers to alert them. If necessary, one may send someone to speak to them.
One should know this: out of a desire for respect, one must not go to the place where food is being served last and cause the other bhikṣus to rise.
If [a guest] has not yet arrived, one may permit a neighboring seat to open up space. If a donor gives fruit to the *upādhyāya* (senior monk), he should ask, "Is the fruit pure?
If he says it is not, he should tell him to purify it. If it is already pure, he should ask, "For whom was it sent? If...
