If it is said, "For the Elder," one may take as much as desired. If it is said, "For the Saṃgha," one should speak so that it is passed around until it reaches everyone.
The same applies to the serving of soup. If there is a bhikṣu who cannot eat, it is permitted for a neighboring seat to request food on his behalf.

If no one else is available, the neighbor should give him half of their own portion. One must not eat what has been obtained without first announcing, "It is distributed equally. Only after this should one eat.
While eating, one should not rest the elbows on the sides of the bowl. One should not cough or spit loudly; rather, one should discard saliva slowly.
After finishing the meal, one should not depart in silence. The *upādhyāya* (senior monk) should recite the *dakṣiṇā* (dedication of merit) for the donor, even if it is only a single verse.
If the *upādhyāya* is unable to recite it, he should instruct someone who can do so to speak. If the *upādhyāya* does not give such instruction...
If one speaks but does not explain [the teaching], it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). At the time of the great almsgiving (*mahādakṣiṇā*), other bhikṣus should not depart;

rather, four senior monks (*sthavira*) should remain to wait for them. If there is business for the Three Jewels or matters concerning the care of the sick, they should inform the assembly before departing.
If a donor wishes to hear various teachings, they should preach according to the individual's capacity, praising generosity and upholding [the precepts].

Regarding the precepts and the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha (the term "equal" [samam] means "equally" or "equitably"). The *Lekha-śāstra* states: "When the community of monks is serving food, the Elder (*sthavira*) should say to everyone, 'Give equally,' and have them chant 'saṃgha-bhadra.

Only then may they eat together. As for the term "saṃgha-bhadra," it signifies that the food of the entire community is equal. The *Mūlamadhyama-vinaya* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Whenever one serves as the Elder at the head of the assembly, whatever offerings are placed before the community..."

First, have one person hold the food and drink, or perhaps go ahead with the salt, before the *upādhyāya* (senior monk). With the body bent in reverence, he should chant "Three *pātrā-khādat*" (*tri-pātra-khāda*). Until this has been chanted, no one may receive the food. One should know that these words possess great power;

to receive food by willfully violating this rule constitutes an *duṣkṛta* offense. The commentary states: "*Tri-pātra-khāda*" is translated as "proper arrival," "arrival of the time," or "good arrival. Alternatively, it is a secret mantra capable of removing poison.

Its intended meaning is that the offerings have been well-prepared and the time for eating has arrived. According to the literal meaning of the characters, it should indeed be understood thus. However, in the past, when the Buddha and the great assembly were about to receive poisoned food from others, the Buddha instructed them to chant [this phrase] before they ate. Consequently, all the poisonous substances [were neutralized].

It is transformed into a delicious flavor. Judging by this, it is indeed a secret terminology; it does not necessarily refer to the arrival of goodness itself. Regarding the two sounds "Dong" and "Xi," one follows the Way according to the occasion. As for the division of the ground, there are many established precedents concerning the chanting of the time of arrival.

"Equally offering" (*děnggòng*) and "food being distributed" (*shìbiàn*) are not literal translations. "Eating at will after the meal" (*shíbà suíyì*) is likewise not the teaching of the Sage. What was formerly called *sēngbá* is a corruption. The Buddhist tradition requires the announcement [of the meal] before eating; now it is made afterward. "Food being distributed" is not authentic and loses the original intent.

Even the *upādhyāya* cannot avoid this error. This has been a corruption for a long time; let the wise apply themselves with careful scrutiny. Regarding what is called *dàchǐn* (or *dáchǐn*), its meaning corresponds to a verse of giving (*dakṣiṇā*). Some say that the method of repaying a gift is termed *dáchǐn*, which guides and leads forth merit.

*Di* (Dhī) is also called *dakṣiṇā*, which refers to the recitation of benedictions for the sake of a donor. Tripitaka Master Yijing stated: “During the lifetime of the World-Honored One, he personally offered such benedictions. However, once the meal was concluded, he invariably recited a *te-khi-na* (*dakṣiṇā*) verse.

This carries the meaning of making an offering of the gift. *Te-khi-ni-ye* (*dakṣiṇīya*) refers to those who are worthy of receiving offerings; therefore, the Sage established the rule that whenever one has finished eating, one must mentally recite one or two *dāna* verses to repay the kindness of the donor.”

The old term "daxin" (酬報) is an error. A verse states: "When the meal is finished, may all beings be filled with virtuous conduct and attain the ten powers. Whoever practices giving will surely obtain its benefit; if one gives for the sake of happiness..."

"One will certainly attain peace and happiness hereafter. Yi says: *Dāna* is translated here as "giving" (*shi*). *Gāthā*—what was formerly called *jiatuo*—is this very term. The Buddha said: "At the time of eating, whether it be a human or a non-human, one should give food, even if only a single morsel. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When first obtaining food, first offer it to the Triple Gem, and afterwards bestow it upon the four classes of living beings. The *Vinaya-kaṅkṣā-viṭaraṇī* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*) states: The Buddha said, "Whenever eating, for the sake of giving to animals, set aside a pinch of food to bestow universally upon all sentient beings; do not restrict it to a single class. This may be done with rice..."

First, moisten [the ground] with water. The cakes must be broken into small pieces and scattered upon the ground; one should eat them as desired and not be obstructed. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If there is a dwelling where one cannot provide food, that person belongs to the retinue of Māra and is not my disciple.

The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Inner Dharma Sent Back from the Southern Seas) says: Once the meal is finished, rinse the mouth with a little water, swallowing it rather than spitting it out. Place a small amount of water in a vessel, briefly cleanse the right hand, and only then rise. When about to rise, one must use the right hand.

Take a full handful of food and carry it outside. Do not discriminate between items belonging to the Buddha or the Sangha; as the Holy One has sent this to be bestowed universally upon all sentient beings, present it before eating. There is no established instruction in the Vinaya regarding this practice.

Furthermore, take one plate of food and offer it to deceased ancestors, other spirits, ghosts, and those who ought to eat. One should then kneel before the Elder (Upādhyāya). The Elder shall sprinkle a few drops of water over it and recite the following prayer of aspiration:

"By the merit now cultivated, may it universally reach the realm of hungry ghosts. Having eaten, may they be freed from extreme suffering and, casting off their bodies, be reborn in a place of bliss. The karmic reward of a Bodhisattva is inexhaustible like space. By bestowing such results, may [this merit] increase without ceasing."

Taking it with them, they go outside to a secluded place, beneath a thicket of trees, or within a river or pond, to offer it to their deceased ancestors. Thereafter, the donor provides a tooth-stick and pure water; once the monks have rinsed and cleansed themselves according to the Dharma, at the time of taking their leave, they say:

"We rejoice in all the meritorious deeds [performed]. Then they disperse. This is one method for attending an invitation and receiving offerings in the Western Regions (India), as detailed in those texts; it is not described here in full.
One should learn to receive soup in a level bowl (28). The commentary states:
The setting is the same as before. Because the group of six received rice in excessive amounts, leaving no room to receive the soup, this rule was established.
There is no offense if the bowl is small or if the food falls onto the dining table.
"One should train in [the proper manner regarding] soup, rice, and other foods" (29).

The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. A householder prepared an offering and invited the Saṃgha; he personally served the food with his own hands, and after the rice had been set down...
He went inside to fetch the soup. The group of six had already finished eating their rice. After the householder gave them the soup, he went back inside to fetch more rice.
When he returned with the rice, they had already finished the soup. The householder criticized and disparaged them. The Buddha established a precept for this:
"Unequal" refers to when the rice is finished before the soup arrives, or when the soup is finished before the rice arrives. There is no offense if it happens to be so at that time.
One may require rice but not soup; at other times, one may require soup but not rice. Or it may be that the time for eating is passing;
or there may be difficult circumstances requiring one to eat quickly.
[One] should learn to eat in proper sequence (30).
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. A householder invited the Saṃgha to provide a meal, but the group of six monks took food from various places within their bowls and ate it.
Therefore, this was prescribed. "Not in proper sequence" means taking food from here and there within the bowl to eat. There is no offense if one is ill.
When the rice is hot, one should take it from the cool parts. If the time for the meal is about to pass (the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"One must not select choice food from within the bowl"), one must not pick at the contents of the bowl while eating; this is how one should train. (31)

The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. When a householder provided food and the group of six monks received it, they began to scoop out the center of their bowls while eating so as to make the interior appear empty;
therefore, this was prohibited. "Scoop" means to place the food at the four edges and scoop out the center down to the bottom of the bowl.
There is no offense if, for instance, one suffers from hot rice and opens the center to let it cool, or if the time for the meal is about to pass.
If a bhikṣu, when not ill, does not seek out soup or rice for himself, he should train himself [to do so]. (32) The commentary says: The setting is the same as before.

A layperson was making offerings to the Saṃgha and personally distributing the food with his own hands. The group of six bhikṣus sought food for themselves just as they had done during the time of the famine, which led to criticism.
Therefore, this rule was established. There is no offense if one seeks it for oneself when ill, or if one seeks it for another, or if another seeks it for him.
One should not seek for oneself [more].
One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more; this is what one should train in (33).
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. After a householder had given a bowl of soup to a group of six bhikṣus, he recognized their turn and [offered] more.
He went inside to take the soup. Later, he covered the soup with rice. When the householder returned and questioned him, he remained silent. Consequently, the Buddha established this precept:

there is no offense if it is strictly necessary for the rice and so forth (the *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Soup and rice must not be used to cover one another" means that if one wishes to obtain more, it increases the mind of greed;

one should instead cultivate a sense of detachment toward food and drink, as this is what those who have left the household life ought to do; eating whatever is obtained as it comes, with few desires as one's constant mindfulness).
"One shall not look into the bowl of a neighboring seat; this is how one should train" (34). The commentary states:
The setting and circumstances are the same as before. A householder prepared a meal to offer to the Saṃgha.

One member of the group of six received a small portion of food, but seeing that his neighbor’s portion was large, he immediately told the householder that he was partial. The Buddha established this precept for such looking. "Looking" means...
This refers to observing who has received much and who has received little, thereby manifesting signs of greed; seeing that others have received much, one then gives rise to resentment and envy.

Therefore, such looking is not permitted. There is no offense if the fellow monk sitting nearby has poor eyesight, and one looks for the sake of determining whether he has obtained food or not, whether it is pure or impure, or whether he has accepted it or not.
"One should eat while maintaining the mental focus on the bowl;
this is how one should train" (35). The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. After the group of six had received the soup and rice, they looked around to the left and right.
Unbeknownst to them, their neighbor took the soup and hid it. The Buddha established this precept for them. "Maintaining the mental focus on the bowl" means not looking around to the left or right.
Regarding this observation, one should bind the mind to itself, mindful that food sustains the body for the sake of accomplishing the Path. As for what constitutes no offense:

perhaps a neighbor with poor eyesight receives [the food] on one's behalf, or one examines whether it is pure or impure. (The *Lekha-śāstra* states: "When eating each morsel of food, one should contemplate from where this food comes.")

It emerges from the granary; the granary emerges from the earth. The earth produces it through the combination of seeds. Now, once again, one sustains this body of excrement. When lifting a morsel of food, one should conceive of it as feces. With right mindfulness present before one, one does not eat with a distracted mind.

One should cultivate the perception of the food as being contrary [to one's true nature], the perception of it as originating from the earth, the perception of it as a disease, and so forth. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When contemplating this food, one realizes its labor is exceedingly heavy. If one calculates the sweat shed by the laborer to produce a single bowl of rice and measures it all together, the food is small while the sweat is vast."

This food is as bitter and pungent as this; upon entering the mouth, it immediately becomes impure. Within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine. Originally a delicious flavor, it is now loathsome even to look upon. The practitioner reflects thus on such wretched food: "If I were to eat and become attached to this..."
One will fall into the three miserable realms. Thus should one contemplate food. One should cultivate revulsion for the five desires.
One must not take large mouthfuls of rice when eating. This is how one should train. (36)

The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. Because the group of six monks took mouthfuls of food that were too large, such that the mouth could not accommodate them, this rule was established.

"A large mouthful" means one that cannot be received by the mouth. There is no offense in cases where the time for the meal is about to pass, or when a difficulty arises and one eats quickly (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"One must not take a large ball, nor a small one; one should eat like a courtesan, taking two or three grains at a time, eating what fits the mouth. The elder should eat slowly; one must not eat hastily").
One should remain standing and watch [the serving of food], ensuring that novices do not become distressed or fail to receive their full portion.
One must not open one’s mouth wide while waiting for the food; this is how one should train. (37)

The commentary states: "Opening the mouth wide" means opening the mouth wide in anticipation before the food has even arrived. The absence of offense is as explained above (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"When a bhikṣu eats, he should follow the manner of eating of the Elephant King of the Snowy Mountains. Once the food has entered the mouth, he uses his nose to mark the boundary of the subsequent mouthful. After the preceding morsel has been swallowed, he continues to place the subsequent ball of food inside.
If there is a sore in the mouth, one may open the mouth in advance; there is no offense").
One must not speak with food in the mouth; this is how one should train (38). The commentary states:

Because the group of six monks spoke with food in their mouths, this rule was established. This refers to the origin of the offense (*nidāna*) for the formulation of the precept; hence it says "with food in the mouth."
This is the underlying principle: whenever one has food in the mouth, one must not speak.

"Speaking with rice in the mouth" means that when rice remains in the mouth, speech is indistinct and difficult for others to understand; it is also the custom of laypeople and Brahmins, not the proper deportment of a bhikṣu.
Therefore, it is prohibited. There is no offense in cases such as when it is cloudy and one asks for water, or when [one's life] is at stake.

It is difficult. It is difficult to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Regarding the matter of making a sound while eating (the *Mahāsāṃghika* says: if, when the two teachers or the elder (*sthavira*) calls out during a meal, one can respond without changing the sound even before the food has been swallowed, one may do so;

if one cannot, one should swallow first and then respond. If the person in front objects, one should reply: "There was food in my mouth, therefore I did not respond immediately. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: When food is being served, it is permitted to say whether one needs more or not.
One must not take a lump of rice and throw it from a distance into the mouth; this is how one should train (39). The commentary states:
The group of six [monks] took lumps of rice and threw them from a distance into their mouths. A lay devotee expressed his disapproval, saying, "They are just like illusionists.
Therefore, the rule was established. "Throwing from a distance" means first opening the mouth and then throwing a lump of rice from afar into it. Not...
Regarding the transgressor: if one is bound in fetters, one must not let food fall [from the mouth]. This is how one should train (40).
The commentary states: Because the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) held morsels of rice in their hands and bit them while eating, this rule was established. "Letting food fall" refers to half [the morsel].
"Half in the mouth" means that half is in the hand; that is, one eats half while leaving half behind.

There is no offense in eating thin pancakes, scorched rice, fruits, melons, sugarcane, vegetables, and the like (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a ball of roasted flour is large, one should divide it with the hand so that it is of a suitable size to eat; the same applies to cakes").
One shall not eat stuffing the cheeks; this is how one should train (41). The commentary states:
The group of six monks ate stuffing their cheeks, and the laypeople spoke with disapproval, saying, "They are just like monkeys.

Therefore, it was regulated. "Stuffing the cheeks" means intentionally chewing so that both cheeks bulge out, appearing like a monkey. (*The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "One must not [eat] in the mouth...")
One should not turn food back into the mouth; that is, one should not take a morsel of rice from one cheek and move it to the other cheek while chewing on one side and swallowing from that same side.
One must not chew food making noise while eating; this is how one should train (42).
The commentary states: "Chewing" means eating by masticating. "Not committing an offense" refers to chewing dry rice, scorched rice, melons, fruits, and the like.

(The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: One must not eat making smacking sounds; one must not swallow food whole; nor should one make gurgling sounds. However, there is no offense if one has a disease of the throat. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: When drinking congee, one must not make sounds; when eating roots, stalks, and so forth, do not allow loud noises to be made.)
One must not gulp down food with a large mouthful; this is how one should train. (43) The commentary states:
"Gulping" (*xi*) is synonymous with "inhaling" (*xi*). Exhaling is "blowing" (*chui*); inhaling is "breathing in" (*xi*).
This refers to drawing food into the mouth. To "gulp down rice" means to open the mouth wide and reach out to take the rice from afar. There is no offense if the mouth is in pain.
If eating soup, curd, thin gruel, or similar foods, one must not lick them with the tongue; this is how one should train (44).
The commentary states: "Licking with the tongue" means extending the tongue far out to lick up the food, or scraping it from both sides.

This refers to the lips. There are cases where one does not commit an offense: for instance, if one is bound, or if there is mud or grease on the hands (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not lick the hands while eating; if there is ghee or oil...").

Regarding honey and rock sugar: if they adhere to the fingers, one should scrape them onto the rim of the bowl, gather them in one place, and then eat. One must not eat by licking the fingers. However, if honey or salt adheres to the tips of the fingers, it is permissible to lick them; there is no offense.
One must not flap one’s hands while eating; this is a training rule (45).
The commentary states: “To flap” means to raise and shake. There is no offense if one flaps them to remove grass, insects, or impurities from the food;
or if one flaps them because the hand has become soiled by touching food that has not yet been formally received.

(The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: When shaking one's hand, one must not shake it toward a neighboring seat. If food is stuck to the hand, one should shake it toward the front of oneself. If there is food in the bowl, one should shake it out.)
One must not eat with rice grains scattered in one's hands; this is how one should train (46). The commentary states:
"Scattered rice" refers to rice that has been dropped or discarded. There is no offense as described above (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

when receiving food, one must not allow even a single grain to fall to the ground. If a *kappiya-kāraka* [a person who makes things permissible] spills it and it falls to the ground, there is no offense. When placing food into the mouth, do not let it fall to the ground. If it accidentally falls, there is no offense. However, when eating melons, fruits, or sugarcane, one must not [discard] the rinds, seeds, or pulp].

One should not scatter food across the ground; rather, one should gather it at the edge of one’s feet. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If food falls upon grass or leaves that have been accepted for eating, it should be eaten. If there is soil adhering to it, one should blow away the soil and eat it. If much soil adheres, one may wash it off and then eat it."
One must not grasp a food vessel with soiled hands; this is how one should train (47).
The commentary states: "Soiled hands" refers to those stained by the grease of food or defiled by other impurities.
Whenever eating or drinking, one should wash the hands clean before grasping the vessel for food or drink. There is no offense if one receives [the food] upon grass or leaves.

The superior [disciple] receives it; he washes his hands and receives it (*The Five-Part Vinaya* says: without curling the fingers, he collects the bowl and eats; he does not sniff the food while eating; he does not disparage or criticize the food).
One must not discard bowl-washing water inside the residence of a layperson; this is how one should train (48).

The commentary states: After the group of six had finished eating, they washed their bowls and discarded the bowl-washing water along with leftover food, leaving them scattered in disarray upon the ground.
Therefore, it is prescribed: "The water used for washing the bowl is water mixed with rice. There is no offense [if one acts as follows]:

if one uses a basin to catch the water and discards it outside. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When eating, one should take only as much as the stomach requires; one must not receive too much. If a lay attendant (*upadhivārika*) suddenly gives too much, before eating, one should reduce the amount and give it to a neighbor-monk.

If the neighbor-monk does not take it, one should give it to a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) or a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*). When washing the bowl, one must not pour even a single grain onto the ground. If there are any [grains], they should be gathered and placed on a wooden board or upon leaves. If they are very small grains or flour (*cūrṇa*), it may be impossible to gather them.")

[In such cases,] there is no offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Question: If one discards [the bowl] for the sake of the host, there is no violation. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There were some laypeople who had newly built a house and wished to obtain water from a bhikṣu’s bowl to sprinkle upon the ground as an auspicious rite.

The Buddha permitted this, provided that water free of food was used to sprinkle the ground. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If someone comes to beg for bowl-water, one should wash the bowl clean, fill it with pure water, and recite a gāthā three times before giving it to that person.

Whether they wash with it or drink it, it can eliminate ten thousand ailments. It further states: "One must not place leftover food into the water in the bowl. Commentary: A *gāthā* is a verse spoken directly by the Buddha, as recorded in other locations.
One must not void excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva upon living grass or vegetables, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (forty-nine). The commentary states:
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks voided excrement, urine, nasal mucus, and saliva upon living grass and vegetables. The Buddha established this precept for them.
At that time, a sick monk became exhausted from avoiding such living grass and vegetables; therefore, the exception for those who are ill was made so that they do not commit an offense.

Furthermore, there is no offense if one defecates or urinates in a place devoid of grass or vegetables, and [the waste] falls onto grass or vegetables, or is blown there by the wind, or carried there by birds, and thus lands upon living grass or vegetables.
If a bhikṣuṇī defecates, urinates, spits, or expectorates upon living grass or vegetables, she incurs an offense.
(The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If in the summer months the grass grows so luxuriantly that there is no vacant space, one should [defecate] on a camel...")

In places frequented by oxen, horses, and the like, or upon bricks, tiles, stones, or dry grass and leaves—if such [clean] locations are not available in the aforementioned sequence—one should support oneself with a wooden branch so that the excrement first falls onto the wood and only afterwards onto the ground.

If one’s hands or feet become defiled by feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva, they may be wiped on living grass. The *Vinayaviniscaya* states: "There is no offense if it is in a thicket of thorns. If traveling through a great forest where branches and leaves are densely interlaced, one should avoid the paths used by people. If traversing a field of living grass where there is no open space, [one may wipe there]."
One should spread dry grass or leaves upon it for defecation and urination; if none can be obtained, there is no offense.
One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water, except in cases of illness. This is how one should train (the fiftieth).
The commentary states: The setting is the same as before. There is no offense in the following cases: if one relieves oneself on the bank and [the waste] falls into the water by the current;

or if it is blown away by the wind or carried off by birds (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If during rain the water suddenly overflows, one should do so upon a clod of earth, or upon tiles, stones, bamboo, or wood, causing it to first fall onto the wood and subsequently into the water");

or if hands or feet become soiled by excrement or urine, one may wash them in the water; or when entering the water to bathe, one must not spit into it; if the bank is far away, one should spit into one's hand and then discard it. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If the water..."

If it is water that people do not use, such as seawater, there is no offense. Even if water is usable, if it is in a remote location where no one uses it, there is no offense. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Whenever one expels mucus or spits, one must not make a loud noise, nor should one do so frequently.

If one is naturally prone to much mucus and spittle, one should go to a secluded place. The Buddha said: "I permit the construction of latrines. One should construct many separate locations, partitioned by screens or barriers.
If the elderly or the infirm fall down, I permit the installation of railings nearby. One should construct a separate place for urination and dig [a pit]."

One should dig a pit in the ground and place bricks or stones at the bottom. Place a jar upon it and open its base so that waste flows out through the leak. Place wooden boards on both sides of the pit.

[If there is] a foul odor, one may construct a lid to cover it. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "A latrine should be constructed in the northwest corner behind the monastery. Wooden sandals should be placed outside; when entering, one must wear them. If it becomes foul-smelling, it should be washed and wiped clean.

One should place leaves, soil, and the like [inside], taking care not to harm flying insects. When washing, use a broom to scrub; one must not use the hands. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A latrine building must not be located in the east or north; it should be in the south or west, with openings provided.")

Regarding the wind-path (wind-pipe): as for its construction, whether one makes a pit, relies upon a high bank, or is situated on the edge of a bank where water flows beneath, one should install a wooden board so that [the waste] falls onto the board first and only afterwards into the water.

One should make two or three holes; the holes should be one cubit wide when the hand is not fully extended, and one and a half cubits long. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When the latrine is full, it should be cleared out. If insects arise, one should make a pit to house them. If insects have not yet arisen, place flour of malt (*mukta*) in the latrine pit, and the insects will not arise.
Commentary: In the Western Regions, all gates face east; therefore, [a latrine] is not permitted to be located in the east.
One must not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is how one should train (51). The commentary states:

When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, the group of six monks stood while defecating and urinating. A lay follower expressed his displeasure, saying they were like oxen, horses, pigs, or sheep.
Consequently, the Buddha established this precept. Throughout the five regions of India, when performing minor acts such as these:
All people squat; this is also largely true for the various countries of the frontier barbarians. Only in the Eastern Land (China) is the custom different, as practices are not uniform.
Those who stand are many, while those who squat are few. If one squats in a land where standing is the norm, they mock him as being "not a man.
Conversely, if one stands in a land where squatting is the norm, seeing it there is not considered strange.
Based on these two paths, how should one practice protection? Following the *Sūtra of Brief Instruction*, one should determine for oneself what is open or obstructed.
As stated in the *Mūla-karman*: "At the time when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
'I have previously expounded the Vinaya teachings for you at great length, yet I have not spoken of them in brief. You should now listen to this summary.'"
Regarding the instruction: suppose there is a certain matter concerning which I have neither previously permitted nor prohibited.
If, with respect to this matter, it conforms to what is impure and contradicts what is pure, then this is impure and should not be practiced; however, if the matter conforms to what is pure...
That which contradicts the impure is itself pure; it should be practiced accordingly. Question:
For what purpose did the World-Honored One deliver this brief instruction when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa? Answer:

So that after the Great Teacher’s passing, until the holy teaching has not yet vanished, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) shall not raise such criticisms, saying: "The World-Honored One, though possessing all-encompassing wisdom..."
There are matters in the world that are neither permitted nor prohibited. Faced with such cases, how should the disciples act?

To prevent this difficulty, the Buddha, having foreseen the future and considering the benefit [of others], established these rules. Furthermore, he wished to ensure that his disciples would dwell in peace and happiness without being hindered by such matters;
therefore, these must be explained. As the World-Honored One said: "If a matter accords with impurity and contradicts..."
Regarding purity: there are things that accord with purity and those that oppose it. As for what should and should not be practiced, I do not yet understand the intended meaning of these words.

The answer is as follows: If there is a matter that was neither permitted nor prohibited by the Buddha, yet if one were to perform it now and it gives rise to public censure and debate, this is impure and should not be practiced. What are such examples? For instance, in the West...
In various regions, people of both high and low station all chew betel nut (*pūga-phala*), combined with betel vine leaves, white lime, and fragrant substances, regarding it as a delicious delicacy.
If a bhikṣu, for reasons of illness, eats it in the hope of removing bad breath—as prescribed by physicians—there is no fault in doing so.
However, if it is done for the purpose of coloring the mouth or making the lips red, it constitutes an improper act. It is like using red earth [for such purposes].

Dyeing one's robes was likewise neither prohibited nor permitted from the outset; however, wearing them now is identical to the attire of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which gives rise to secular derision and gossip.

This therefore ought to be prohibited, as it is logically improper to use them (the matter of the yellow robes in China is similar to this). Furthermore, there is another case: [The text continues with: "There is a certain matter..."
Nor is it a case of prohibiting what was permitted for use at the present time; since people do not criticize its use, employing it constitutes no offense.
This is like the waist-belt (*kaṭisūtra*), of which the Buddha spoke as being of three types; other types are neither permitted nor prohibited.

Furthermore, when using these various other belts to tie around the waist, if people do not feel shame upon seeing them, there is likewise no fault, and they are all pure. Moreover, as the Buddha said, there are three kinds of items that may be used...
These are used for washing the hands: first, salty saline earth; second, dried cow dung; third, cleansing powder (*śāṭī*). These are permitted.
Such things as the flowers of the *nyagrodha* tree, the *kiṃśuka* fruit, and soapberry pods are all suitable for washing and bathing.

Since these are neither prohibited nor specifically permitted, and they are non-toxic and free of insects, their use is not a transgression. Regarding such matters as these, one should reflect and act accordingly. [Note]
It is said: "The Buddha only permitted the spoon and never mentioned the chopsticks. As for their current use, this is a slight relaxation of the teachings.
Eating while seated cross-legged on high beds within the sutra hall is entirely contrary to what the relaxed teachings permit.

However, because these practices have been established for so long, they are indeed difficult to discuss. Furthermore, the prohibition against standing to urinate was already enjoined by the Buddha; yet nowadays..."

If one practices this, the common people will give rise to criticism and debate. Although this is not permitted by the Buddha, it is done to conform to local customs and to protect against popular censure;
it is thought that this does not contradict the Sage’s intention. Nevertheless, all wise persons must reflect upon this deeply; do not be hasty in accepting such a teaching upon merely hearing it.
They then take other established prohibitions and falsely claim they accord with the holy teachings. This is to impose what was not prohibited and to relax what was prohibited.
Who shall bear the sin of abandoning the teachings? The brief explanation of the main text is concluded. Regarding the practical matters, I shall now set them forth. The Buddha said:
"One should not endure the urge to defecate or urinate for long. When going to relieve oneself, one should hold grass for wiping. If...
Those who go before should walk ahead. Upon reaching the latrine, one should place one's robes on a peg, a rack, a tree, or a stone.
Having reached the exterior of the latrine, one should snap one's fingers or cough to alert both humans and non-humans.
One should hold the robe firmly so that it does not touch either side of the latrine. One should plant one's feet firmly and first look for snakes or insects.
One should drive [the previous occupant] out. One should not lift the cloth before squatting; rather, one should squat together and gradually lift the cloth.
Having squatted, one should look [at the opening] so as not to let it move forward or backward or toward the two sides, thereby defiling the toilet hole with feces, urine, mucus, or spittle.

One should not make loud noises or great clamor. The toilet grass should be at most one span (*vitasti*) long and at least four fingers (*catur-aṅgula*) long. Once the grass has been used... [it should be discarded]. The unused grass... [should be kept aside].
One should use grass and place it in a separate spot. Then, having risen slowly and gradually lowered one's garments, one should proceed to the washing area.

Upon arrival, one should snap one’s fingers so that humans and non-humans may be aware of one’s presence. One should first look for venomous insects, then gradually lift the hem of the garment and squat down.
One should not wash directly in the water vessel. When washing, do not make any noise. Once finished, one should wipe oneself with the hand, a leaf, or a piece of worn-out cloth.
To remove the water from one's body, one should use salt earth, ash, mud, cow dung, earth from a trench, or bathing powder (*śāṭī*) to wash the hands.
Having washed them, one should gradually lower the robes and rise. If one sees impurity upon the toilet seat, one should sweep it away. (The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"One should enter the latrine carrying a cleaning stick (*śalākā*), three lumps of earth, and [other implements]. The stick is used to wipe the body; one lump of earth for washing clean; one lump of earth for washing the urinary area; and one lump of earth for washing the left hand. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* says: "One should...")

Wash [the anus] using the tips of two fingers—namely, the ring finger and the little finger. Tripitaka Master Yijing, following the Sarvāstivāda school, compiled the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Ritual for Defecation and Urination), which briefly sets forth its procedures:

For the matter of defecation and urination, the ritual is as follows: Put on a bathing skirt below and don a saṃkakṣikā (undergarment) above. Next, take the *spraśana-ghaṭa* (touch-pitcher), fill it with water until full, and carry it to the latrine.

Close the door and shield your body. You must have fourteen lumps of earth; place them outside the latrine upon a brick, a stone, or a small wooden board. Crush the earth into powder and arrange it in two rows, piling each lump separately. Set aside one lump. Then, take three lumps into the latrine and place them to one side. Use one to wipe.

The Body. First, wash the body. As for the method of washing the body: one must first take the left hand and wash it with water, followed by cleansing it with earth. When one remaining pellet remains, use it roughly once to wash the left hand. If there are wooden scrapes (*śalākā*), it is also good to bring them inside.

Once they have been used, they must be thrown outside the toilet; if old paper is used, it may be discarded inside the toilet. Having finished the cleansing, pull down the garment with the right hand and set the vessel to one side. Push aside those sitting nearby with the right hand, then take the vessel in the right hand and exit.

Alternatively, one may hold the vessel under the left arm, clench the left hand into a fist, and use the right hand to open the door before departing. At the place where the earth is kept, squat to one side. If a seat is required, adjust the position according to the circumstances.

Place the flask upon your left thigh and press it down with your left arm. If you have a three-pronged wooden stand, it is essential to place it on top. First, take seven lumps of earth from near your body and wash your left hand separately with each one; afterwards, use the remaining seven lumps, washing both hands thoroughly with each.

You must wash the flask and the wooden stand until they are clean. Once there is one lump of earth remaining, use it to wash the vessel. Next, wash your arms, calves, and feet until they are also perfectly clean. Only then may you set aside your worldly concerns and depart. This water from the flask must not enter your mouth or lips.

Upon returning to your room, rinse your mouth two or three times with the pure water from the flask. If you happen to touch this flask while attending to other matters, you must again wash your hands and rinse your mouth before handling any other utensils. This is the great [rule].

The general protocol for this has been roughly explained as such. For urination, one should use one or two handfuls of earth; this may be used to wash the hands and the body, which constitutes the very first step of purification and serves as the foundation of respect.

Some people regard this as a minor matter, yet the Vinaya teachings severely rebuke such negligence. If one does not perform this cleansing, it is improper to sit upon a monastic bed, nor should one pay homage to the Triple Gem. To practice this is to honor the Vinaya and generate merit; to neglect it is to violate the teachings and incur transgression. This practice was not transmitted to the Land of the East (China) long ago;

even if it had been introduced, people would have given rise to feelings of aversion, claiming that the Mahāyāna is all-encompassing and transcendent, asking what is pure and what is defiled, and asserting that the interior of the belly is always full, so what benefit could external washing possibly provide? How could they know they were slighting and mocking the disciplinary regulations, and deceiving the holy intent of the Sages, while still receiving offerings and paying homage?

Both [actions] incur transgressions. To wear robes and consume food [without cleaning] is detested by the devas; if one does not wash them clean, the people of the Five Indias will all laugh. Wherever one goes, everyone will see and mock it. For those who propagate and transmit [the Dharma], it is especially appropriate to spread these teachings.

Having grown weary of the mundane and departed from the dust of the world, leaving the household for the homeless life, one must diligently follow the words of the Father of Śākyas (the Buddha). How can one harbor resentment toward the explanations of the Vinaya? If you do not believe this, I hope you will rely on this [method] to wash [the robes] for five or six days.

One will then understand the fault of not washing. However, during the months of deep winter, one must prepare warm water; at other times, matters may be handled according to convenience. In all monasteries, the latrine area must first be thoroughly cleaned. If one lacks the personal means to do so, one should exhort others to act on one's behalf.

Providing for the monks of the ten directions applies equally to both ordinary and saintly beings, and it does not entail great expense; this is the essential point. This is the practice of purification, which is certainly not in vain. One should reasonably provide a large trough filled with soil and place it beside the latrine.

Since the assembly has no private rooms where such items could be stored, if a water pitcher is suddenly unavailable, the use of ceramic or earthenware bowls to carry water is permitted. One should stand to one side and wash with the right hand; there is nothing wrong with this. In the regions of Jianghuai, where the ground is low, there are "jar latrines" (weng-ce).

[It is] much. One must not perform the cleansing right here; one should instead prepare a separate place for washing. It is best if the water flows out. The *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "You should know this:
this is a constant practice that must always be kept in mind. Cleansing in this manner brings great benefit; it makes the body clean and pure, and the devas will pay you honor.

Therefore, from this day forward, whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have taken refuge in me and regard me as their teacher, all should perform this cleansing. If one does not cleanse in this way, one should not circumambulate the stūpa or walk its paths, nor is it appropriate to prostrate before the Buddha."

When reciting the scriptures, one should neither prostrate to others nor accept prostrations from them; one should not consume food, sit upon monastic beds, nor enter the assembly, because such physical impurity and lack of accordance with the Dharma cause the devas to see one without joy.

Any dhāraṇī practices maintained under such conditions will be entirely without efficacy. If one violates these rules, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. Furthermore, if one performs offerings for a fast, copies scriptures, or fashions images without having purified oneself, the merit obtained will be meager due to such negligence and disrespect.

You all should follow my instructions and must not deceive yourselves by performing impure rites, being indolent or heedless, and acting as those of inferior conduct, which will lead you to fall into the evil realms. When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s exhortation, they were all greatly rejoiced and practiced accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
One must not preach the Dharma to a person who is disrespectful and has their upper robe slung over one shoulder, except in cases of illness. This is the fifty-second precept to be studied.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, the group of six monks preached the Dharma to people who were disrespectful and had their upper robes slung over one shoulder.
Therefore, the regulations have been established; the text is easy to understand and requires no further commentary. As for those who do not commit an offense:

if it is due to illness, or if one speaks for the sake of a king or a high minister—though these are kings and ministers, they should be treated with special gravity—if arrogance arises, the rain of Dharma will not fall upon them;
even if they hear it, what benefit would there be? For the sake of the Dharma, one forgets the body; this is true for all those of the highest virtue, let alone those at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Because they were entrusted by their parents, they ought to be especially revered. Those who preach the Dharma should all the more esteem themselves in accordance with the Dharma.

If both parties lack mutual respect, both will suffer loss. As for the skillful means of encouraging or subduing others, these must be applied according to the individual's capacity and circumstances;
there is no single fixed rule. One must not act impulsively, as doing so would incur the fault of showing contempt for the Dharma. Thus, [the Ten...]

In the recitation of the Vinaya, it is stated that in all cases one is not permitted to preach for them. One should understand that the subsequent precepts follow this same principle (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"It is the constant law of the Buddhas not to preach the Dharma to sentient beings who do not possess a single-minded focus").
One must not preach the Dharma to someone who has wrapped their robe around their neck, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (fifty-three).
The commentary states: When the robe is wrapped around the neck, one’s deportment is not upright, which manifests a lack of respect; therefore, one should not preach to such a person.
One must not preach the Dharma to someone whose head is covered, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train (54).
The commentary states: "Covered head" refers to having the head covered with clothing or other materials.
One must not preach the Dharma to those who have wrapped their heads, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (55).
The commentary states: "Wrapping" refers to being enveloped or bound; it is distinct in meaning from "covering."
One must not preach the Dharma to one who has their hands crossed behind the waist, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (56).
The commentary states: whether with both hands crossed or with one hand crossed, one should in neither case preach the Dharma to them.
One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing leather sandals, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (57). The commentary states:
In the Western Regions (India), it is considered respectful to go bareheaded and barefoot, whereas in this land (China), it is considered reverent to be fully equipped with headgear and footwear.
However, as ritual forms are not fixed, one follows local customs; thus, doing so constitutes a gesture of devotion. If one does not...

Regarding the purification of difficult points: one must further eliminate other meanings concerning what is permitted or obstructed. This should be considered in accordance with the *Sūtra of Brief Teaching*. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If many people are wearing leather sandals and they cannot be made to remove them, one may preach to those who are not wearing them; there is no offense.")
One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (58). The commentary states:
those made of grass are called *fei*; those made of leather are called *li*; those made of hemp are called *jiao*; and those made of wood are called *ji*.
There are also silk clogs, which are made of silk. In the Western Regions, there are precious clogs made of gold, silver, and other such materials.

In accordance with this principle, one should not preach the Dharma to them at all. However, if one employs skillful means to guide them according to their capacities, it should be understood as explained above. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu goes to the presence of a king or a landowner for the sake of the stūpa or the Saṃgha, and that person says, 'Preach the Dharma to me,' he should not tell him to remove his shoes, for fear of giving rise to suspicion. If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (an attendant) nearby, he should direct his attention to preaching to the *kappiya-kāraka*.
If the king listens [to the *kappiya-kāraka*], there is no offense."
One must not preach the Dharma to those who are riding vehicles, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (fifty-nine).
The commentary states: "Vehicles" refers to mounts such as elephants, horses, oxen, and carriages.
One must not stay overnight in a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it; this is how one should train (60). The commentary states:
When the Buddha was at Jetavana, the group of six monks stayed overnight in a stūpa. Therefore, this rule was established.

There is no offense if it is for the purpose of guarding [the stūpa], or if one is being detained, or if there is a threat to life, and so forth. Regarding the character "stūpa" (塔), it is a corruption and abbreviation of the Sanskrit sound.
Formerly called *tāpa*, it was also termed *fútú*; in the new terminology, it is called *stūpa* or *caitya*, with the specific name *cetiya*.
This is translated as "accumulation of characteristics," meaning that the manifold virtues of the Tathāgata are all gathered here, making it an object of veneration for both humans and devas;
it refers specifically to the place where the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) were enshrined. It also includes places where the Buddha preached the Dharma or performed walking meditations (*caṅkrama*).
A stūpa may be erected therein; although it lacks relics, it is still called a Buddha-stūpa.
The term "Buddha-stūpa" used here is intended to distinguish it from the stūpas of bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.

Even if they are not Buddha-stūpas, they should all be revered and respected, and one should not use them for purposes such as lodging. However, the regulations governing them differ according to each case. If one follows the [Daśabhūmika-]sūtra...
In the *Dvayanidāna-sūtra*, it is stated that the exposed canopy of a Buddha-stūpa has eight tiers; that of a Bodhisattva, seven tiers; that of a Pratyekabuddha, six tiers;

that of the four [noble] lineages, five tiers; that of one who has attained the third fruit, four tiers; that of one who has attained the second fruit, three tiers; that of one who has attained the first fruit, two tiers; and that of a Wheel-turning King, one tier.
Those with eight tiers or more are all Buddhist stupas (*stūpa*). Ordinary monks possess only the *tāla-leaf* and *fire-jewel* [ornaments].
Although a Wheel-turning King’s stupa has only a single tier, a bhikṣu must not pay homage to it because it is not a sacred stupa. Ordinary monks, however, should pay homage according to their rank.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a Buddha-stupa is thirteen stories high and topped with a wheel-mark made of various jewels.
It is adorned. The Pratyekabuddha [stūpa] has eleven tiers; the Arhat [stūpa] has four tiers, both likewise embellished with various jewels.
Although the Cakravartin’s [stūpa] is also made of jewels, it lacks tiered levels, because he has not yet escaped the suffering of the three realms of existence.
In the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, this is largely the same; they may be square, circular, or octagonal, all according to one's preference (from the *Vinayaksudraka*).

The Vinaya states: Construct a double-layered foundation; next, install the body of the stūpa (*stūpakāya*); above that, place the inverted bowl (*pātrākṛti*), which may be made high or low according to one’s preference. Install a flat top (*samaśīrṣa*) measuring one or two feet in height and two or three feet in square, proportionate to the size [of the stūpa].

In its center, install the shaft for the wheel (*cakradhara*). Next, apply the wheel-marks (*cakralakṣaṇa*). These wheel-marks are layered, either one, two, three, four, or even up to thirteen. Next, install the precious vase (*ratnaghaṭa*). If it is constructed for the Tathāgata, it should be made complete as described before. If it is for a Pratyekabuddha, do not install the precious vase.

For an Arhat, the wheel-marks are fourfold; for a Non-returner (*Anāgāmin*), threefold; for a Once-returner (*Sakṛdāgāmin*), twofold; and for a Stream-enterer (*Srotāpanna*), onefold. For a bhikṣu who is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of pure virtue, there should be only the flat top, without wheels or canopies; this is called the "flat top" (*samaśīrṣa*).

Regarding *caityas*: whenever one approaches any incense hall, a flagpole *caitya*, or an image or shadow of the Tathāgata, one must recite a *gāthā* before stepping upon them with one's feet. If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*)."
One must not conceal or store wealth and goods within a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of ensuring its security; this is a training rule (61).
The commentary states: "Wealth and goods" refers to items intended for the offering of stūpas and images, or the property of the Saṃgha.
There is no offense in cases where it is done for the sake of security, or when the items have been seized by powerful persons, and so forth.
One must not wear leather sandals when entering a Buddhist stūpa; this is how one should train (62). The commentary states:
"Leather sandals" refers to footwear made of hide. This precept was established based on a specific origin story (*nidāna*);

however, according to the underlying principle, any object worn on the feet is prohibited from being brought into a Buddhist stūpa. There is no offense if, for instance, one is forcibly seized and compelled to enter the stūpa.

It is permitted [to wear leather footwear] for the purpose of protecting the body, protecting the robes, and protecting the sitting mat. Within the monastery, one may wear single-layered leather sandals.
If they become worn through use, it is permitted to repair them with tree bark, or with leather, using thread made of sinew, hair, or leather fibers.
One should sew it. If one is in a border country where leather is used for bedding, its possession is permitted.

Likewise, in places that are largely composed of clay, stones, or rugged terrain, it is permitted to wear double-layered leather sandals. If one obtains untreated leather, it is permitted to soften and treat it.
It is permitted to possess knives, scrapers, awls, boards, stones, and so forth. One should not sit upon new clothes or leather sandals; nor should one sit upon raw leather. If...
In border regions such as the country of Aparāntaka, it is permitted. However, it is not permitted to hold a sandal and a bowl in one hand.
One must not keep any large skins, namely those of lions, tigers, leopards, otters, wild cats, wild foxes, or black-skinned animals.
One should not sit on high or large beds, ivory beds, or upon mats spread with horse or elephant skins, brocades, multicolored bedding, or woolen rugs (*kūṭāgāra*).

One may make a pillow or a mat from *jū* fur. If one is in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*) and there is no separate bed or mat—except for a jeweled bed—one is permitted to sit on other types.
One should not beg for raw hides. It is permitted to carry a life-preserving float (*uḍupaka*) and to cross water by means of a hide boat.
It is not permitted to keep leather sandals with reinforced heels, sandals with curled horns, sandals with antelope horns, sandals with elephant-hair borders, or sandals made of variegated skins.
Sandals; silk-cloth sandals; sandals with woven leather borders; sandals that are blue, yellow, red, or white; sandals of brocade color; sandals stuffed with wool; sandals stuffed with cotton;

and all sandals stuffed with grass—if one’s eyes are impaired, it is permitted to wear leather sandals with padded heels and padded toes for the sake of protecting the body and protecting the sitting mat.
Within the monastery, it is permitted to wear reed sandals, and it is permitted to keep sandals of discolored (muddha-vaṇṇa) material.
Regarding footwear: one should not keep fur sandals, jeweled sandals, or any sandals made of leather. However, it is permitted to wear sandals when defecating, urinating, or washing one's feet.
When in the presence of one’s *upādhyāya* or other *ācāryas*, one should bared the right shoulder and remove one’s leather sandals.

There are instances of taking and giving, except when in the homes of laypeople or while traveling on a road. If it is dark at night and one fears venomous insects, wearing [leather footwear] is permitted.
If one obtains a palanquin or a cart, the leather covering may be removed and accepted. If one is old or infirm, riding in a carriage or a palanquin is permitted.
The attendants, upāsakas, and śrāmaṇeras should carry or pull them. It is permitted to use leather to make water-drawing ropes and door-ropes.
One should not make a bowl bag, a sandal bag, a needle-and-thread bag, a cap, a waistband, or a meditation belt out of leather.
Furthermore, one should not keep any impure or loathsome hides, nor any objects made of leather. In snowy countries, it is permitted to wear *puṭa*, *āṇḍika*, and socks.
The dwelling place should be swept and sprinkled with water; if there is dust, it should be sprinkled with a mixture of mud and water. Moreover...
Dust. One should listen to the rule regarding floor coverings. One must not make them from leather. One should wash one’s feet, wipe them dry, and then step onto the floor covering.
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in one's hand. This is how one should train. (63)
The commentary states: Since it was previously forbidden to enter while wearing [footwear], they nevertheless persisted in carrying them as they proceeded; therefore, this rule was established.
Leather sandals are objects for treading upon and are defiled by impurities; thus, it is not permitted to carry them into the stūpa.
One must not wear leather sandals while circumambulating a Buddha-stūpa; this is a training rule (64). The commentary states: there are two kinds of circumambulation:
first, circumambulating by way of passing along the side of the stūpa; second, circumambulating as an expression of reverence.
Here, "circumambulating" refers to passing along the side by way of the path. Originally, according to the etiquette for paying respect in the Western Regions, there was...
There are many varieties. Some take prostration as reverence, while others take circumambulation as respect. As for prostration, it is categorized into nine grades;
as for circumambulation, one distinguishes between the right and the left. Circumambulating to the right is called auspicious, while circling to the left is considered inauspicious.

Regarding the number of circuits, they range from one, two, or three, up to hundreds or thousands, each according to what it symbolizes. For instance, the common practice of performing three circuits symbolizes—
Make offerings to the Three Honored Ones. Cease the three poisons. Purify the three karmas. Eliminate rebirth in the three evil realms. Attain the fortune of encountering the Triple Gem.

The rest may be understood by reflection; it need not be discussed at length here. Regarding the "nine [grades of] respect," they are: first, speaking words of greeting; second, bowing the head to show reverence;
third, raising the hands in a high salutation; fourth, joining the palms in a formal gesture; fifth, bending the knees; sixth, kneeling for a long duration; seventh, [raising] the hands...
Kneeling with the knees on the ground; eighth, bending all five limbs; ninth, prostrating the entire body—these nine grades constitute the ultimate single prostration.
To kneel and praise the virtues is called the height of reverence. At a distance, one bows the head to the ground and clasps the hands; nearby, one licks the feet and rubs the heels.
Whenever presenting a petition or receiving a command, one draws up the robes and kneels for a long time. When honoring the worthy or receiving their prostrations, there must necessarily be...
Regarding consolatory words: one may either stroke the crown of the head or pat the back, using kind words to instruct and guide them as a sign of affection.
Once a renunciant śramaṇa has received a prostration, one should merely offer virtuous wishes rather than stopping at kneeling or bowing.

In this region, ritual propriety has long been inconsistent; the wise should follow the teachings and not conform to mere human sentiment, thereby failing the sacred regulations. (From the *Neifa zhuan*)

The Buddha said: "There are two kinds of persons who deserve to receive prostrations: first, the Tathāgata; second, elder bhikṣus. This is the sincere teaching from the Golden Mouth. Why labor over such matters by following the customs of the ignorant? When a junior sees a senior, he must respectfully extend his homage, chanting 'vandate' as he bows.

When a senior receives the prostration of a junior, he may simply sit with hands folded and say 'Gloruḍi. This is a benediction, meaning merely 'may you be free from illness. If one does not speak thus, both parties incur fault. [One should] rise when the other stands and sit when the other sits."

One must not alter the established custom. Since it is appropriate for [the superior] to receive [veneration], it cannot be that [the inferior] instead shows reverence [to the superior]. This is the standard practice between teacher and disciple throughout the Five Indias. How could there be such a thing as a junior wishing to pay homage to a senior, first hoping for the senior to initiate it, while the senior accepts the junior’s respect?

I fear the junior might harbor resentment. For this reason, one is hurried and anxious; though the honored person holds up their hands [in refusal] and will not permit a prostration, it is truly a hardship—a hardship—to seek respect while being unable to touch the ground. If one does not act in this way, it fundamentally violates the rules of propriety. Alas! The Holy Teaching takes this [as its measure].

Human sentiment dictates that receiving [offerings] with a lack of reverence violates proper ritual; this is truly something that must be deeply examined. Since these practices have spread for so long, who indeed could now suppress them? As for those who perform prostrations, their intent lies in showing respect to superiors through the ritual of self-humbling.

When wishing to pay homage or when making a formal request, one first adjusts the dharma robe, draping it over the shoulder and tucking its edge under the left armpit so that it remains against the body. Then, with the left hand facing downward, one gathers and covers the left side of the robe; the right hand follows the hem of the skirt as it is covered, and once it reaches the lower edge, it is rolled up.

The robe should reach down to the knees, covering both knees so that the body is not exposed. The hem of the robe at the back must be drawn tightly against the body; gather and hold the garments so they do not trail on the ground. With both heels raised and the spine held straight, place the ten fingers upon the earth before beginning to prostrate.

Since there is no clothing beneath the knees, one should again join the palms and once more touch the ground, paying respectful homage with earnest devotion. This is repeated three times. However, if it is merely an ordinary salutation, one may stop after a single bow;

there is no further requirement to rise between them. When people in the Western Regions see this triple prostration, they all find it strange. If one fears there is dust on the forehead, one must first rub the hands to clean them and then wipe the face. Next, one should brush away the dust from both knees and adjust one’s robes. In...

One should either sit to one side or stand for a short while; it would be appropriate for the Venerable One to grant a seat, yet there will surely be a reprimand. Even standing is not improper; this has been the tradition passed down from teacher to disciple since the time of the Buddha until the present day, without interruption.
*Pantei* means to pay homage (the old term *huanan* is an error).
One must not wear *pūras* (short boots) when entering a Buddhist stūpa; this is a training rule (65). The commentary explains:

*pūra* is translated here as "short-ankled boots" (*wùfēn* states: "The leather lining should not be made too deep; it is permitted to reach up to the ankle. One must not have the lining like a boot; the front should be open"). The *Nanhai Jiguī Zhuan* says:

"In accordance with the Buddha's teaching, when facing an image or in the presence of a venerable teacher, except in cases of illness, it is the proper etiquette to go barefoot. One must not rashly wear shoes or sandals. [One should] expose the right shoulder, cover the left shoulder with the robe, and [lower] the head...

There were no towels or cloths; from then on, they traveled directly [to their destination], with those remaining proceeding separately. This was not an offense for those who had departed. If it is a cold country, wearing short boots is permitted. As for various other types of footwear, they should be used as appropriate according to the circumstances. Since distant lands and foreign regions differ in their climates—whether cold or hot—it is often the case that practices deviate from the holy teachings.

In principle, during the months of deep winter, one may temporarily wear such items to preserve the body; however, during the spring and summer, one must strictly follow the Vinaya regulations. The rule that footwear must not be turned toward a Buddha stupa has already been clearly established in the teachings. Furthermore, the prohibition against wearing leather boots (*pura*) while entering the incense hall has been promulgated for a long time.
Yet, there are those who willfully violate these rules; this is simply an act of arrogant defiance toward the golden words of the Buddha.
"One must not hold a *puṭa* (foot-wrapping cloth) inside a Buddha-stūpa; this is how one should train. (66) The commentary states:
The previous rule prohibited wearing it; this rule prohibits holding it. The remaining meaning should be understood accordingly.
One must not sit and eat beneath a stūpa, leaving grass or food to defile the ground; this is how one should train. (67) The commentary states:
When the Buddha was at Jetavana, the group of six monks sat and ate beneath a stūpa, and having finished, they left behind leftover food and grass, defiling the ground before departing.
The Buddha established this precept for them. At that time, the bhikṣus, having completed the construction of a stūpa, offered food and built a hall.
The meal was served. As the assembly gathered, the seating area was so narrow that they did not dare sit beneath the stūpa to eat.

The Buddha said, "I allow you to sit and eat. However, you must not leave grass or food-stained ground behind. At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who did not dare leave behind leftover food or grass to soil the ground.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to gather it and place it by your side; when you depart, take it away and discard it."
One must not carry a corpse past the base of a stūpa; this is a training rule (68). The commentary states:
The group of six monks carried a corpse past the base of a stūpa, and because the guardian deity of the stūpa became angry, [the Buddha] established this prohibition.
There is no offense if one must travel by this path, or if one is led there by force.
One must not bury a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is a rule to be studied (69).
The commentary states: "To bury" means to inter. Whenever a bhikṣu passes away, one should follow the Buddha’s teachings by employing four methods of disposal:
namely, cremation, immersion in water, burial in the earth, and abandonment in the forest. These four methods must necessarily depend upon the appropriate location. Not...

One may act immediately in this manner, yet it would still contravene the holy teaching. (The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "When a bhikṣu dies, he should be cremated. Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the Buddha has taught, there are eighty thousand families of worms within this body; how can it be burned? The Buddha said: "These various types of worms arise together with birth and perish together with death. If the body has sores, one should observe whether they are free of worms;

only then may one perform the cremation and burial. If firewood cannot be obtained, one may discard the body in a river. If there is no river, one may dig a pit and bury it. Since the ground abounds in insects and ants, one should place the body in a secluded thicket, with the head pointing north and the body lying on its right side, supporting the head with a bundle of grass.)

Whether it be grass or leaves, they should cover the body. The monks escorting the funeral should have a capable person recite the *Triśaraṇa-anityatā-sūtra* and chant verses (*gāthā*) to offer prayers for the deceased. Once the task is finished and they return to the monastery, they should wash their bodies;

those who have touched the corpse must wash themselves along with their robes, while those who did not touch it need only wash their hands and feet. Upon returning to the monastery, they should pay homage at the *caitya*. The *Nidāna* states: "When a monk passes away, his robes and bowl must not be discarded;

the community should share them. One must not carry the corpse out uncovered; rather, the body should be covered with a lower garment (*nivasana*) and an upper robe (*saṃghāṭī*). Do not use fine garments, nor cover it with tattered rags; one should use a garment that is neither fine nor poor, but of a middle quality."
One must not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is what one should learn (70). The commentary states:

The sūtra refers to it as *śarīra-dāha* (cremation) or *caitya-pūjā* (funeral rites); this is translated as "incineration. The meaning is as explained previously (*The Record of Sending Back the Relics* states:

"At the time of death and mourning, monks and nuns often perform elaborate rituals, or even grieve in the same manner as laypeople, considering themselves filial sons; or they set up spirit-tablets in their rooms to serve as offerings to the honored one; or they wear coarse, dark-colored cloth, which deviates from the norm").

Some retain their long hair as a mark of mourning; some lean on staffs of wailing; some sleep in huts of sorrow. None of these practices accord with the ritual protocols of the teachings. To do nothing is not a fault; rather, one ought to prepare a chamber for the deceased, adorned with purity, or perhaps temporarily provide a canopy according to the occasion.

One should recite the scriptures and chant the Buddha’s name, providing incense and flowers in full measure, hoping that the deceased soul may be reborn in a good realm. Only then does one become a filial son, and only then does one repay their kindness. How could weeping blood for three years be considered a way to honor virtue? How could abstaining from food for seven days be deemed a means to requite grace?

Such acts merely bind one further to the dust of worldly toil and entangle one more deeply in shackles. Moving from darkness into death, one fails to awaken to the three stages of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); passing from death to death, how could one ever realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Vehicle?

However, according to the Buddhist tradition, when a bhikṣu has passed away and it is confirmed that death has occurred, he should be taken on that very day to the cremation site and immediately cremated with fire. At the time of cremation, relatives and friends gather and sit to one side;

they may fashion seats by tying together grass, pile up earth to form a platform, or place bricks and stones to serve as seating. They should have a capable person recite the *Anityatā-sūtra* (Sutra on Impermanence) for half a page or a full page, ensuring it does not become too long or tiresome. Thereafter, each person should reflect upon impermanence and return to their respective dwellings.

Outside the temple, by the pond, they bathe together with their robes on; where there is no pond, they wash their bodies at the well, always using old clothes so as not to damage new garments, and only after putting on dry ones do they return to their quarters.

The floor is smeared clean with cow dung, and all other matters remain as before. Regarding the etiquette for clothing, there has never been even a slight deviation. Some collect the *śarīra* (relics) to build a stupa for the deceased, calling it a *kūṭāgāra*; its shape is like a small stupa, but it lacks the wheel and canopy.

How can one possibly discard the sacred teachings of the Buddha, the Father of Śākya, to follow the secular rites of the Duke of Zhou, wailing for several months and wearing plain cloth for three years? I, Yi, say: *Śarīra* means "body-bone. This is found in the *Anityatā-sūtra*, in the "Xiao" volume of the Northern Canon and the Southern Canon.
[This concludes] the section on the letter-case).
One must not burn a corpse facing a stūpa; this is how one should train (71).
The commentary states: this means that one must not cremate a corpse directly in front of a Buddha-stūpa.
One must not burn corpses on the four sides of a Buddha-stūpa, causing the stench to enter it; this is a training rule (72).

The commentary states: Previously, the direction [of the corpse] was restricted; now, all four sides are regulated. One should keep far away from the site of the stūpa and perform the cremation in a secluded, out-of-the-way place.
One must not pass beneath a stūpa carrying a corpse’s garment or bed, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed;
this is a training rule (72). The commentary states:
The group of six monks passed beneath a stūpa carrying a corpse’s garment and bed. Consequently, the deity who protects the stūpa became angry.
The Buddha established a rule: At that time, bhikṣus wearing paṃsukūla robes did not dare to pass beneath a stūpa carrying the clothes of a dead person.
The Buddha said: "If they have been washed clean, dyed, and perfumed with incense, I permit them. There are ten kinds of paṃsukūla robes permitted to be taken: first, clothes gnawed by cattle;
second, clothes gnawed by rats; third, clothes burned by fire; fourth, clothes worn during the rainy season; fifth, clothes from a woman who has recently given birth; sixth..."

1. Garments from a temple; 2. Garments from a funeral pyre; 3. Garments worn by a deity; 4. Garments found in a cemetery; 5. Garments worn by a bird that has carried them off and dropped them; 6. Garments blown about and mixed together by the wind;

7. Garments from among birds’ nests; 8. Garments sought through prayer; 9. Garments discarded when a king assumes office (the old garments cast aside at the time of his inauguration); 10. Garments for travel and return (when a layperson dies, they give these garments for the funeral;

upon returning, one takes these garments to offer as a gift to the Sangha).
