"So be it. If one wishes to confess in the presence of three bhikṣus, the one receiving the confession should ask the others.

Once the two bhikṣus have obtained permission, they shall accept the confession. If one wishes to perform the confession within the saṃgha, one should go before the saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove one's sandals, prostrate at the feet of the monks, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and say: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen."

"I, bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now repent before the Saṃgha" (three times). The one who receives the confession should first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*), and then receive the confession.
The announcement is as follows: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen. That bhikṣu [Name] has committed such-and-such an offense."
"I now repent before the Saṃgha. If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha grant me its consent.

I accept the repentance of the bhikṣu so-and-so. Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made the announcement, one accepts the repentance, and proceeds with the censure and the taking of the vow as described above.

Once a legal dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, should one reopen it, one falls into an offense. What is "before the eyes like covering the earth with grass"? It is as in the [second]...
It is taught among the seven categories of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). This is a dispute involving an offense, which is settled by means of the three types of discipline (*vinaya*).

As for a dispute concerning the matter itself (*vādādhikaraṇa*), it is settled by means of all forms of discipline according to the specific offense committed. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "One should recognize a person who adjudicates cases as being endowed with twenty-two qualities:
they maintain the two hundred and fifty precepts; they are widely learned; they are well-versed in the Abhidharma and the Vinaya..."

A bhikṣuṇī does not quarrel with others, nor does she stubbornly persist in this matter. She remains only after having rebuked those who deserve rebuke; she remains only after having instructed those who deserve instruction;
she remains only after having carried out the formal act of suspension for those who deserve suspension. She is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion.
She does not accept food or drink from this faction, nor does she accept food or drink from that faction. She does not accept [from this...]
Regarding robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases: one does not provide for this faction if they do not receive [these items] from that faction, nor does one provide for that faction.
One does not enter a village together with this faction, nor does one enter a village together with that faction.

One does not make an appointment or agreement with them, nor does one go to their location, arriving later or taking a seat later. (The Mūlakalpa states: "There were two bhikṣus who had fallen into mutual discord; in various ways...")

They speak disparagingly of one another and slander each other. Regarding these two people: if both are observed in the precepts, one should trust the one who is more learned; if both are learned, one should trust the one who has fewer desires;
if both have few desires, one should trust the one who has the very least desire. It is impossible that they would give rise to discord if both possess the very least desire.
● Conclusion: Exhortation to Dedication (divided into four parts): 1. Summary of the preceding characteristics; 2. Exhortation to study other dharmas; 3.
The Three Buddhas’ Sūtra on the Precepts; 4. Concluding verses for dedication.
○ First, a summary of the preceding characteristics:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have already recited the four *pārājika* dharmas;
I have already recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas; I have already recited the two *aniyata* dharmas; I have already recited the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas..."
The *Pāyattika* Dharmas. The ninety *pāyattika* dharmas have been explained. The four *pratideśanīya* dharmas have been explained.
The *śaikṣa* training rules have been explained. The seven methods for settling disputes have been explained. These were spoken by the Buddha;
they come from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* recited every half-month.
The commentary states: The intent here is to make known the sequence of the aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*).

Furthermore, it demonstrates that the speaker’s text is free from omissions, that the meaning of the phrases is complete, and that the eight aggregates have been fully encompassed. Thus, the two hundred and fifty rules are concluded.
By stating "this is what was spoken by the Buddha," it is certified as not being his own composition, nor the composition of anyone else. As for "others," it refers to those outside the Dharma.

They are the masters, the Vinaya-holders, the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas. That which comes from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra was neither spoken by anyone else nor derived from any other sūtra.
II. Exhortation to Study Other Dharmas.
"If there are further other Buddha-dharmas, one should study them all in harmony with these.
The commentary explains: "If there are further other Buddha-dharmas" refers to those established by the Tathāgata within the various *khandakas*.
The training rules (*śikṣāpada*), as well as all the *sūtras*, *abhidharma*, and the teachings on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
By means of these teachings, one is able to transcend the cycle of suffering and proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. Regarding "in this":

it means that one should not only practice in harmony according to the two hundred and fifty rules of the *dharma-vinaya*, but should also harmoniously train together in all these remaining teachings. "Harmony" means:
Rejoicing without contention, they study under the same teacher and do not give rise to divergent views; they are like water and milk blending together. This is what should be studied:
namely, the matters in which a bhikṣu ought to train. Do not be negligent; you should practice with diligence.
(The Sūtra is the Piṭaka of Discourses, belonging to the training in concentration; the Abhidharma is the Piṭaka of Treatises, belonging to the training in wisdom.)
The Brief Sūtra on the Precepts Spoken by the Thirty-Seven Buddhas:
Patience is the foremost path; the Buddha says that non-action is supreme. One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
"This is the precept scripture spoken by Vipaśyin Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. The commentary states:
"To be able to settle the inner mind and endure external objects of insult is called patience (*kṣānti*). This is of two kinds: first, patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*);
second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). Patience toward living beings has two aspects: the first is [patience] toward those who show respect and provide offerings..."
Regarding cultivation: within favorable conditions, if one can endure without attachment, then arrogance and negligence will not arise.

Second, regarding anger, verbal abuse, physical assault, and harm—within these adverse conditions, if one can endure, then fury, resentment, enmity, and affliction will not arise; this is called patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*). Patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) also has two aspects.
The first concerns non-mental phenomena (*acaitasika-dharma*), namely: cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
The second consists of mental phenomena (*caitasika-dharma*), namely: anger, sorrow, doubt, sensual desire, pride, and various false views.

If one can endure these two types of phenomena without being moved, this is called "patience regarding phenomena" (*dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, by observing with right wisdom, one realizes that the nature of arising phenomena is empty;

insult is unattainable, and they are characterized by suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Who, then, is the one who endures? Since both the insult and the endurance are empty, [there is no real agent].
When non-arising manifests before one, one immediately realizes parinirvāṇa.
Because this patience is the swift path to the parinirvāṇa of nirvana, it is called the foremost path. That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is precisely nirvana:

profoundly still and eternally tranquil, without any fabrication, transcending the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and crossing over the stream of birth and death. There is no dharma superior to this.

Regarding this, it is called "supreme" (*śramaṇa*). "Śramaṇa" has the meaning of "quiescent purity. It was translated in older versions as "diligent practice," meaning one who diligently practices to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, it is rendered as "diligent cessation": "diligence" refers to diligently cultivating the work of the Path, while "cessation" means ceasing evil conduct and practicing loving-kindness.
Thus, the *Āgama* Sūtra says: "Having abandoned affection and love, one leaves the home life to cultivate the Path. This is what is meant by "to gather."

One governs the sense faculties, remains unstained by external desires, maintains a heart of loving-kindness toward all, and refrains from harming anything. One does not rejoice in encountering pleasure nor feel dejection when meeting with suffering;
being able to endure like the earth, one is therefore called a śramaṇa. If one has left the household life but does not practice patience, [one is not a true śramaṇa].
To instead harbor resentment and retaliate against others violates the path of Nirvana and non-contention; how could this be called the practice of diligent cessation?
If one’s conduct does not accord with this, one is not a śramaṇa. Those who wish to attain the supreme path must not afflict others.
If you aspire to the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), you should fully embody the qualities of a śramaṇa. Patience is the cause for transcending the world;
the unconditioned is the fruit of transcending the world. Harassing others is the cause of birth and death; being no śramaṇa is the fruit of birth and death.
Thus, good and evil are both manifest, and purity and defilement are presented together. A person of wisdom should be able to act like one who selects milk.
O King of Geese, if one selects and takes only those who are virtuous, it does not contravene the conduct of a śramaṇa.
When such conduct is peerless, one will indeed transcend even the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, when the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world, many among his disciples as well as non-Buddhist false teachers delighted in ascetic practices to cultivate the body, falsely seeking [liberation].
Regarding the fruit of pleasure: at that time, in order to refute this view, the Buddha spoke this brief instruction for his disciples, saying: "Patience is the highest among forms of diligence;
it can attain the state of Nirvana. One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa."
This means that among all forms of diligent effort, patience is supreme. One does not attain the sublime nirvana by inflicting suffering upon one's own body.
Furthermore, through the patience of discerning the Dharma, one attains nirvana by understanding the Dharma; it cannot be realized through the mere mortification of the body.

Furthermore, this is to refute those who have left home as heterodox practitioners with false views, who falsely preach divergent doctrines to instruct others, causing them needlessly to afflict their bodies and leading them to conform to their own practices;
thus, both themselves and others suffer, ultimately yielding no fruit or benefit. Therefore it is said:

"One who leaves home and annoys others is not called a śramaṇa. (In the Western Regions, there are ninety-six kinds of heterodox practitioners who have left home, all of whom are called śramaṇas, except for the disciples of the Tathāgata...)
The name of the son is Śākya Śramaṇa. Regarding the term "Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha": it refers to the Tathāgata at the time he realized nirvāṇa;
having exhausted all afflictions (kleśas) and rendered his body, speech, and mind pure, he was untainted and unattached. Therefore, he is called "Unattached" (Arhat).
Because he awakens all sentient beings through the equality of all phenomena and achieves unsurpassed enlightenment, he is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha (Equally and Perfectly Awakened One).
Just as a person with clear vision can avoid dangerous and evil paths, so too there are wise people in the world who are able to distance themselves from all evils.
This is the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin.
The commentary states: It is like a person with clear vision who does not take a perilous path but ultimately reaches a place of safety.
If there is one in the world who is wise, discerning, and intelligent, they will immediately know the path and what is not the path; "not the path" refers to the six [non-virtuous actions].

The perilous path leads to rebirth; the Way is the level thoroughfare of the Eightfold Noble Path. The perilous path is brought about by unwholesome causes, while the level thoroughfare is reached through superior wisdom.

Therefore, one must distance oneself from all evil causes and diligently cultivate the essential means of deliverance, until finally arriving at the place of Nirvana—peaceful, secure, and eternally blissful.
Do not slander, nor be envious; you should practice the precepts with devotion. Know moderation in food and drink, and always delight in solitude.
With a concentrated mind, take joy in diligence—this is called the teaching of the Buddhas. This is the *Dharmapada* (Verse on the Dharma) spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
The commentary states: Slander is a fault of speech; envy is an action of the mind. To wish to be free from these two, one should practice the precepts.
When the precepts are pure, the three types of action are immediately abandoned; how then could speech and mind be found?
Because one wishes to accomplish pure precepts, one is made not to slander and not to envy. Food and drink belong to the mouth; habitual pleasure belongs to the mind. Contentment, however—
Cease the false pursuit of external objects; when in solitude, all discursive thoughts naturally subside. How could there then be any instability of mind?

To accomplish the dharma of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is made to dwell in seclusion with contentment; to give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*) and sever delusions, it is said that one should delight in diligence (*vīrya*).

"Secluded" refers to an araṇya, a place of tranquility. By relying on such a place and diligently practicing the gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one will certainly attain the realization of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have all followed this same track to instruct their disciples;
therefore, it is said, "This is the teaching of all Buddhas. *Vipula* is the same as *Viśvabhū*, as explained previously.
Just as a bee gathers from a flower, neither destroying its color nor its fragrance, but taking only its nectar and departing; so too should a bhikṣu enter a village.
He should not interfere with the affairs of others, nor observe what they do or do not do; he should only observe his own conduct, whether it be right or wrong.
"This is the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The commentary explains: It is like a bee gathering from a flower; it takes only the nectar and departs, without damaging the flower's color or fragrance.
When a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for food, he should likewise act in this manner. Therefore, it is said thus. This does not contradict [the teaching].

Regarding "not disturbing others": this means that when a bhikṣu goes for alms, he should seek only enough to sustain his body and complete his journey, accepting whatever is offered without seeking more than necessary to disturb others or destroy their faith and respect.
He should be just like a bee gathering nectar, without damaging the color or fragrance [of the flower].
Regarding "not observing whether others act or do not act": this means that since one does not disturb others, one should likewise not observe whether people gain or lose.
This disturbs the body and mind, obstructing one's own realization and awakening. Regarding the practice of observing the body for oneself alone: it means one should simply examine oneself.
If one is without fault, then the body will surely be upright; if there is a transgression, then one's conduct is not correct. Therefore, it is said: "Whether upright or not."
Do not let your mind be negligent; you should diligently train in the noble Dharma. In this way, there will be no sorrow, and with a concentrated mind, you shall enter nirvana.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni.
The commentary states: Through heedfulness (*apramāda*), one is able to diligently train in the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
By training in the Noble Path, the afflictions of sorrow and distress (*daurmanasya-kleśa*) can be eliminated. By eliminating these afflictions of sorrow, the mind attains concentration (*samādhi*).

By attaining concentration, one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* here is translated as "extinction" (*jimiè*). This is what is meant by abandoning the origin (*samudaya*), cultivating the path (*mārga*), and realizing cessation (*nirodha*). If the mind...
Heedlessness creates the causes for various evils, which then invite the bitter fruit of sorrow and grief.

If one does not cultivate the Path, see the Truths, and realize cessation, then even if one attains a concentrated mind, the afflictions have not been eliminated; thus, one continues to revolve through the three realms of existence.
How can the suffering of sorrow and grief be avoided?
Commit no evil whatsoever; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The commentary states: "All evils" refers to the seven branches of body and speech that constitute transgressions of both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*) natures.

As for "all virtues," although they do not contravene natural or proscribed natures, because they merely restrain the coarse evils of body and speech within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), subtle disturbances remain undispelled;
thus, one cannot transcend the sphere of the desire realm and has not yet attained true virtue. Since this is [merely] one's own *śīla*...

Pure and radiant, his resolve was set upon the gates of *dhyāna*. By single-mindedly practicing the five dharmas, the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm manifested within his own body.
Through this, he successively attained the fundamental four *dhyānas* and various sublime qualities of the branches and forests (*aṅga-vyūha*).
Thus, having transcended the net of desire as the cause, he came to dwell in the form realm as the fruit; therefore, it is called "wholesome. He purified himself...
"Will and intention" refers to generating true, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

This wisdom destroys all perverse delusions, realizes that afflictions are empty and false, and sweeps away the impurities of the mind. It purifies all blemishes and illuminates the fact that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are ultimately ungraspable;
therefore, it is said to "purify one's will and intention. Although the ocean of Dharma is vast, these three encompass it entirely. Thus have the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time taught.

Benefiting sentient beings according to their needs is no different from this; therefore it is said, "These are the teachings of all Buddhas. Regarding the factors (*aṅga*): the first dhyāna has five factors:

first, applied thought (*vitarka*); second, sustained thought (*vicāra*); third, joy (*prīti*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). The second dhyāna has four factors: first, internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*); second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind. The third dhyāna has five factors: first, equanimity (*upekṣā*); second, mindfulness (*smṛti*); third, wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors: first, neither-pain-nor-pleasure; second, equanimity; third, mindfulness; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind (as detailed elsewhere).
Guard well the words of speech, purify your own will and intention, and commit no evil with the body; thus these three paths of action are purified.

"To be able to practice in this way is the path of the Great Seer. This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* which the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni recited for the sake of the Saṅgha of those free from worldly affairs (*anavassutaka*) during the twelve years of his ministry.

From that time onward, it has been explained in detail. Those bhikṣus who delight in the Dharma, who delight in the life of a śramaṇa, and who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame [should uphold it]."
Regarding those who delight in training in the precepts, they should train therein.
The commentary states: When the Buddhas appear in the world, they observe the capacities of beings and establish their teachings; thus, the Dharma is not fixed.

The World-Honored One appeared during this age of the five turbidities and evil times, when people mostly delight in contention, fail to guard their speech, and possess turbid minds with heavy defilements, even if [they do not commit] transgressions...
When confronted with present objects, one recollects past experiences and gives rise to desire and volition, thereby committing unwholesome bodily actions.
For this reason, the Tathāgata admonishes [the practitioner] through sequential stages and guards them against even the slightest incipient thought.

Furthermore, since the Saṃgha prioritizes harmony in its practice, it is appropriate to first prohibit such conduct. If one can thus guard oneself well, remaining pure and refraining from such acts, then—
The three paths of action are purified. To attain this pure conduct is the way of the Tathāgata, the Great Seer (*maharṣi*).
Because the Tathāgata is the God among gods, the Seer among seers, and the Honored One among men, he is called the "Great Seer.

As for the "monks with nothing to do," they refer to the various Arhats whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, whose holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, and who have accomplished what was to be done; thus it is said.
Regarding the state of *anabhisaṃskāra* (the effortless): during the first twelve years after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, no further outflowing phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*) arose.

He taught this brief instruction solely for the sake of the community of Arhats who had attained the state of *anabhisaṃskāra*. As for those who had not yet realized that state of *anabhisaṃskāra*, [he taught them extensively].
By studying this teaching, one purifies the three paths of action and thereby attains realization.

Twelve years later, when out-flowing (āsrava) phenomena arose, he then extensively formulated the two hundred and fifty rules of discipline, distinguishing between their gravity and lightness, as well as the characteristics of what is permitted and what is prohibited.
Question: Why did the World-Honored One not simply establish the precepts directly, but instead wait until others had committed an offense before codifying them? Answer:
When the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, the two hundred and fifty rules of the Dharma were already established.

However, because the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings were not yet able to withstand immediate regulation, he codified them only as offenses occurred. Thus, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī...
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, in future ages there will be people of false views who shall slander the Buddha, speaking these words:
‘If the Tathāgata is omniscient, why did he wait until sentient beings had committed offenses before establishing the precepts?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, “This very [situation] is the mark of omniscience. If I were to [act] prematurely...”
"If I establish the precepts, people will surely slander me. Why? Because I have committed no offense; why then do they speak of it so forcefully?

This proves I am not omniscient. Why? Because I am without fault. It would mean the Tathāgata lacks compassion, does not benefit others, and does not embrace sentient beings—like a man who has no son yet claims he has one, saying that at some time a son shall be born, which is empty."
There is this statement: "How can it be trusted? For what reason? Because it is not true. If one truly sees the offense, then faith arises.
Thus, Mañjuśrī, regarding offenses not yet committed, which humans and devas do not see, how could they be prohibited in advance? One must first see the offense before it is then prohibited.
Furthermore, in the *Sūtra-vibhaṅga* (the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*), the Buddha said: "There are no outflows (*āsrava*) for those who have not [yet] committed them."
When the Tathāgata established the precepts, sentient beings conceived thoughts of slander, saying: "All these disciples are of noble lineage or former royalty.
Having renounced their wealth, palaces, wives, children, and retinues, they do not spare even their own lives;
they are all contented and have no worldly desires. Why, then, does Gautama instead [punish them] with the *prātimokṣa*..."
They were bound with their hands crossed behind their backs. This was because Gautama had not yet skillfully distinguished between worldly people.
Had he established a formal precept [at that time], worldly people would likewise have failed to give rise to a heart of reverence. It is like a physician who is not skilled in treating illness:

seeing a person whose abscess has only just begun to form—though it possesses the nature of an abscess and has not yet fully developed—he immediately lances it. Blood flows out in profusion, and the patient suffers.
There was great pain. He applied medicine to it, and the ulcer was immediately healed. The physician said, "I have treated your illness;
you must give me my fee. The patient replied, "This foolish physician! If it were my illness, you might treat it for me."
"I was originally free from illness; yet you forcibly tore my flesh and drew blood, causing me great agony, and instead you rebuke me for being straightforward—is this not madness?
The śrāvaka disciples are likewise so: if they first establish precepts and then give rise to slander.
"I am personally without fault, yet you have forcibly established this precept; therefore, the Tathāgata did not establish the precepts beforehand.
If there were those with outflows (āsrava), it was at that time that the Tathāgata would have established the precepts for his disciples and pointed out the Prātimokṣa."
For example, it is like a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the illness, enabling the patient to be cured;

he then receives great rewards and is praised, being called an excellent doctor who skillfully treats his ailment. The Tathāgata is also like this: he establishes precepts in accordance with the transgressions committed.
They joyfully accepted and upheld [the precepts] without uttering a single word of complaint. Thus, in the Vinaya-mūla, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the Great Sage, together with the bhikṣus, will establish the precepts and recite them, so that those who cultivate the holy life may do so and the Dharma may endure for a long time."
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra, stop. The Buddha himself knows the proper time. Why is this? Among the bhikṣus, there has as yet been no one who has committed an out-flowing (āsrava) offense.
Only when there is one who commits an out-flowing offense will I then establish a precept to sever that out-flowing offense.
Śāriputra, as long as the bhikṣus have not yet received gains, offerings, or a reputation among people..."

Venerable Sir, because of the accumulation of much learning and great wealth, if one gains gain, offerings, and fame, up to the point of possessing great wealth, then tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) arise.
Once these tainted phenomena have arisen, the Blessed One will subsequently establish a precept.

This is for the purpose of severing the dharmas of outflows (*āsrava*). A question is asked: How do the dharmas of outflows arise? For the most part, these are the six groups [of monks] who act intentionally;
is it only through unintentional transgression that they occur? The answer is: The six groups of bhikṣus were manifestations of great spiritual power (*mahopāya*) to propagate the Buddha’s teachings.
Internally, they served as the main pillars of the Dharma-gate; externally, they served as the great protectors of the Buddhist teachings. They were no ordinary beings.
How could it be conceivable? Yet today there are foolish people who are unacquainted with the teachings;

they recklessly commit transgressions without a sense of shame or remorse, claiming that since the Tathāgata was in the world, the six groups of monks all acted this way, and it is not just me alone who does so now.
How can they know that the sages of old were precisely establishing the teachings for those who would come later, yet they instead condemn those ancient sages as wrong? Alas, the Dharma!
It is the end. Many people are indolent; possessing meager merit and scant wisdom, they are unable to endure the Tathāgata’s Dharma teaching.
Instead, they give rise to slander and create all manner of karmic deeds. Thus, the *Śatapañcāśatkā* states:

"People of the world do not understand that the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, for the sake of sentient beings, employs various skillful means to manifest what appear to be shortcomings. They then give rise to defamation and imitate what is incorrect."
For this reason, within the Buddha-dharma, they have forever lost their goodness and fall into the three evil realms.
As the Mahāmegha Sūtra says: "Devadatta was able to provide instruction for and lead immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings."
Abiding securely in the roots of goodness, the entire sphere of Devadatta’s activity is truly not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The group of six bhikṣus are also great Bodhisattvas who practice together with Devadatta.
If one can clearly understand Devadatta’s merits without doubt, know that such a person is a true disciple of the Buddha and has attained the Buddha’s [wisdom].
He possesses one-half of the merit [of the Buddha], attains one eye of the Buddha, and attains half the body of the Buddha.
If it is said that the wicked Devadatta destroyed the Saṃgha, one should know that this was actually a skillful means.
For one who seeks joy in the Dharma for the sake of being a śramaṇa, the Dharma is the cause of the fruit of a śramaṇa; if the cause is not bestowed, the fruit cannot be established.
That people today do not study the Dharma of a śramaṇa yet claim to be śramaṇas is an extreme error.
Furthermore, those who wish to attain the fruits of a śramaṇa are far removed from them. Some say, "I am not acting for myself. Alas!

If one has not yet attained realization oneself yet wishes to lead others to it, it is like someone falling into a vast ocean while attempting to rescue another who is drowning; will they not both perish?

This is lamentable. Some say, "Since there is already the Mahāyāna, what is the use of the Hīnayāna? This is truly because they have not yet attained realization of the Mahāyāna, and thus they speak these words.
Just as those six groups [of monks] were originally great Bodhisattvas, why would they further manifest such minor practices?
How could they know that protecting oneself and protecting others is the true fundamental intention of a Bodhisattva? Not abandoning even a single good deed is the mark of a Great Being.

To broaden one's mind—how much more so when both the Great and Small Vehicles alike converge upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)? To adorn the body with the myriad virtues, what else could it be?
Upon a detailed examination of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, it is only the narrow-mindedness of the śrāvaka’s self-deliverance that is censured;

it is not the śrāvaka’s observance of precepts and conduct that is rebuked. Only by practicing both the Great and Small Vehicles together, and guarding equally against both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) transgressions, can one [attain this].
This accords with the root of liberation and does not contravene the instructions of the Compassionate Honored One.

Therefore, in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it was said that when bodhisattvas practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should skillfully know how to learn and cultivate all the dignified deportment and disciplinary conduct of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
If one observes that someone’s deportment does not accord with the assembly, one should immediately distance oneself from them. If there is...
One should draw near to those whose conduct and deportment accord with the precepts of a śramaṇa. In the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, it is said that if a bodhisattva thinks:
"This dharma is profound; this is not profound. This dharma is pure; this dharma is not pure," [he falls into conceptualization].
"These are the dharmas of the Buddhas; these are the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas; these are the dharmas of the Śrāvakas; this dharma should be practiced;
this should not be practiced; this is a profound dharma; this is not a profound dharma"—this is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a Bodhisattva holds such a view and speaks thus: 'A Bodhisattva should not listen to the Śrāvaka [teachings]...'"
The sūtra teachings should not be accepted, nor should they be studied. Of what use are the Śrāvaka teachings to a Bodhisattva? This is called a transgression of many offenses.
The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states: "If one pays homage to Bodhisattvas and reads Mahāyāna sūtras, this is termed 'Great';
if one does not perform these acts, it is termed 'Small'. What is called the Mahāyāna does not exceed two types; the first is...
There are two [schools]: Madhyamaka and Yogācāra. In Madhyamaka, conventional phenomena exist while their ultimate nature is emptiness; their essence is void, like an illusion.

In Yogācāra, there is nothing external and everything internal; all things are merely consciousness. Both of these strictly follow the sacred teachings of the Buddha; which is right and which is wrong?
Since both equally aspire to nirvana, what is true and what is false? The intent lies in severing the afflictions and delusions to rescue and deliver sentient beings;

how could one wish to extensively provoke confusion and further increase the weight of their submerged fetters? If one acts according to [the teachings], both shall ascend to the other shore; if one rejects and turns away from them, both shall drown in the flow of birth.
In the Western Land, these two practices coexist; in principle, there is no discord or rivalry. Since we lack the eye of wisdom, who can discern what is right?

No. One should practice it through long-term cultivation as one pleases; do not trouble yourself with self-denial. As explained above, you may reflect upon this for yourself; there is no need for further prolixity.
Those who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and who delight in training in the precepts, do not commit offenses themselves—this is called having a sense of shame.
They do not instruct others to commit them—this is called having dread of blame. Furthermore, they feel personal remorse for all evils.

That which is called *hrī* (shame) is the feeling of embarrassment before oneself regarding evil. That which is called *apatrāpya* (remorse) is the feeling of embarrassment before others regarding evil.
If these two qualities of shame and remorse did not exist in the world, all would transgress the pure path of the noble ones and head toward the perilous road of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Therefore, a Great Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly declare this: there are two white dharmas that can save sentient beings. The first is..."

There are two kinds of shame: first, self-respect (*hrī*); second, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Self-respect means not committing offenses oneself; dread of blame means not instructing others to commit them.
Self-respect is feeling inward shame; dread of blame is confessing one's faults to others. Furthermore, there are two kinds of wisdom: first, not creating various evils;
second, repenting after having committed them. There are two kinds of delusion: first, regarding what is not an offense as such; second, concealing [one's transgressions].
Treasury. Now, this Prātimokṣa precept cannot be joyfully practiced and studied by those who lack a sense of shame and dread of blame, nor by those who lack wisdom.

Those who should study within it are those who should diligently practice and learn these two hundred and fifty rules of the Pratimokṣa Vinaya, as well as the Sūtra of the Brief Precepts spoken by the Seven Buddhas, in order to transcend birth, old age, and sickness.
Regarding the peril of death: if one does not study, then what is upheld and what is transgressed will remain obscure; how can one avoid being called a "mute sheep"?
If non-action (*avijñapti*) is deficient, how can the very essence of a bhikṣu be established? Therefore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna equally establish the three trainings.
Furthermore, the precepts are the foremost exposition; by practicing the five aggregates [of dharma] together, the three trainings are first initiated.

Thus, through the function of training in these three dharmas, one realizes the fruit of the five aggregates. One should know that regarding the fivefold body of dharma (pañca-dharmakāya), the first three manifest virtue from the perspective of the cause, while the latter two demonstrate capability from the perspective of the fruit.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) correctly severs both the active defilements and their latent tendencies, it is called liberation (vimukti).
The body [is thus purified]. To clearly awaken to and illuminate through the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is called "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*).

Because Bodhisattvas are urgent in transforming others, they augment their practice of patience (*kṣānti*) and vigor (*vīrya*) to cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Śrāvakas, however, because they seek only their own liberation, cultivate only the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the six perfections are the dharmas for sentient beings, while the three trainings are the dharmas for nirvāṇa; such is the nature of all dharma-gates.

One proceeds by means of training. If the three trainings are not cultivated, there will be no path to nirvana. If one does not uphold the prātimokṣa, then concentration and wisdom will be severed of their causes.
How, then, could one transcend the four currents and ascend to the other shore?
IV. Summary Verses on the Dedication (There are fourteen verses in total; all were added by the compilers. They are now divided into six sections for explanation).
The wise who are able to protect the precepts Shall obtain three kinds of happiness:
Renown and material gain in this life, And upon death, rebirth in the heavens. One should contemplate such benefits And diligently protect the precepts with wisdom.
"Purity of precepts and wisdom / Then one attains the foremost path.
Commentary: The first verse concerns the causes and effects of the mundane world; the second verse concerns the causes and effects of the supramundane.
By citing the causes and effects of the mundane world, one demonstrates the causes and effects of the supramundane.

To be "clearly enlightened" means to thoroughly understand that the miserable realms of the three paths are produced by evil causes, while the joyful states of humans and devas are summoned by wholesome karma;
therefore, one abandons all evil causes and cultivates various virtues. Since the precepts are the foundation of all virtues, this is what it means to be a person of clear and penetrating wisdom.
It can be protected; it is not something that those who are ignorant and dark, and who cannot distinguish between good and evil karmic retributions, are capable of upholding.

As for the three kinds of happiness: reputation and gain are the happiness of the present, which is the "flower-retribution"; being reborn in the heavens is the happiness of the future, which is the "fruit-retribution.
"Name" refers to one's renown, and "reputation" refers to praise; "gain" refers to the four holy [requisites].

"Seed" refers to a person who is able to maintain the precepts; the fragrance of their virtuous discipline pervades the ten directions and is universally heard, such that humans and devas praise them and together offer them support.
As for "heaven" (*deva*), it means natural and spontaneous purity, being the most supreme and the most blissful.
If one does not possess the cause of pure and supreme conduct, how could one be born in a place of pure and supreme excellence? This is the cause of purity.

This refers to the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*). "One should contemplate such states" means that one should reflectively observe that the three kinds of worldly rewards of happiness all arise from guarding the precepts;
thus, one knows that the supreme supramundane path must be attained through the purity of the precepts.
Those of wisdom who diligently guard the precepts will be reborn among the luminous beings of the heavens and attain the supramundane state.
This is not something that can be accomplished by those who lack wisdom, nor is it attained by those who are indolent or devoid of precepts.

By guarding the pure precepts, the body and mind become radiant and clear, giving rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom. Through the power of this wisdom, one destroys all afflictions (*kleśa*) and attains the supreme path of *nirvāṇa*.

Just as the Buddhas of the past, And those of the future, And the World-Honored Ones of the present—who are able to overcome all sorrow— All together revere and honor the precepts; This is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
If there are those who act for their own sake And desire to seek the Buddha-way, They should respect and honor the True Dharma.
This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The commentary explains: the preceding one and a half verses cite the fact that all Buddhas together honored the precepts to achieve the Way, thereby providing proof.
The subsequent verse shows that those who seek Buddhahood should revere the True Dharma, thereby providing exhortation. [It concerns] all afflictions and delusions.
Because it binds sentient beings, it is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*). The Tathāgatas of the three periods all uphold the *prātimokṣa* to counteract all afflictions and thereby attain liberation;

thus, it is called "that which can conquer. "Acting for one's own sake" means being single-mindedly devoted to this very body, seeking the Buddha-way to transcend birth and death, rather than aspiring for worldly pleasures while merely expecting the fruit of Buddhahood. It says:
Those who seek the Buddha-way must distinguish themselves from the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

their resolve should lie in seeking Buddhahood and cultivating the prohibitive precepts, rather than merely observing the disciplinary codes for the sake of the two vehicles. The profound purport of the Vinaya truly lies herein.
May students take care not to mistake its fundamental aim, thereby falling into the pit of partiality and inferiority. Those who are deluded should quickly reflect upon themselves.
The offense of disparaging and reviling through slander is a minor transgression if it merely reveals one's tracks; its underlying intent was actually to entice others toward the Great Vehicle.
Moreover, the ocean of precepts is boundless, its capacity equal to the great void. It bestows benefits according to the capacities of beings, dispensing equally without distinction.

It is only that the faculties and vessels of beings naturally differ in size and smallness; the Dharma itself bears no fault of being broad or narrow. Those who wish to escape the abyss of the two deaths should...
One should early on cast one's mind into the ground of the precepts, so that one may act for oneself without transgression; this is the purport of seeking the Buddha:
the True Dharma is the dharma of the precepts. It is said that as long as there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts, the True Dharma has not yet perished from the world.
By means of this Dharma of precepts, it serves as the ladder and vessel for transcending birth and death, and the path to Nirvana.
It differs from the heterodox teachings of external paths and the worldly arts of the ten virtues of a Wheel-Turning King; therefore, it is specifically designated as the "True Dharma" (Saddharma).
The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have extinguished all fetters and defilements, have preached this Sūtra of the Seven Precepts;
through these, one attains liberation from all bonds and enters into Nirvāṇa. All frivolous play is forever extinguished.
This was spoken by the Honored One, the Great Sage; the precepts praised by the noble sages are that which the disciples practice.

Regarding the entry into quiescent *nirvāṇa*, the commentary states: The preceding one and a half verses refer to the disciples of the Buddhas who, having upheld the *śīla-sūtra* (the discourse on ethical discipline), attained liberation from all fetters and have already entered *nirvāṇa*;
thus, they are cited as proof. The subsequent verse refers to the present-day disciples of the Buddha, who revere the Buddha.
By practicing the precepts as they have been taught, one shall attain the realization of the fruit of Nirvana; therefore, this is shown to encourage them.

As for the "fettering afflictions" (saṃyojana-anuśaya), these refer to the various defilements that bind and drive the mind and spirit of a person, causing them to transmigrate through the three realms without attaining liberation.
Briefly stated, there are the three fetters and the ten afflictions; explained in detail, there are the eighty-eight afflictions, up to five hundred.
Regarding the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*): the Seven Buddhas, as teachers of the world, preached this *Śīla-sūtra* in order to eliminate the fetters of their disciples.
When the disciples practice it, they are thereby liberated from all afflictions, bonds, and fetters;

they realize the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda-phala*), enter *parinirvāṇa*, and all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) concerning existence and non-existence are forever and utterly extinguished. (7)
This is the sūtra spoken by the Buddha, the Great Sage; it is the precept praised by all the holy and wise ones.
If the disciples of the Buddha now honor and practice it, there will be none among them who does not realize entry into the quiescent nirvāṇa.
"Nirvāṇa" is the Western (Sanskrit) term, while "quiescent extinction" (寂滅) is the Chinese term. Since both the Indian and Chinese names are displayed, the two are mentioned together.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he gave rise to great compassion and assembled the community of bhikṣus, giving them this instruction:
"Do not say that because I have entered parinirvāṇa, those who practice purity have no protector.
I have now spoken the Sūtra of Precepts and have also well expounded the Vinaya; even though I have passed into parinirvāṇa..."
One should regard it as the World-Honored One; thus this sutra shall long abide in the world.
When the Buddha-dharma flourishes in such a manner, one attains entry into nirvana.
If one does not uphold these precepts as they should be observed during the poṣadha, it is like the time when the sun sets: the entire world falls into darkness.
The commentary states: The first verse introduces the Buddha’s exhortation; the following two and a half verses clarify the Buddha’s instructions;
and the final verse reiterates the admonitory parable. Thus, after forty-nine years of preaching the Dharma, the Tathāgata’s work of transformation was complete.
As he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he once again emphasized the precepts and, turning toward his disciples, charged them with earnest instructions, exhorting them repeatedly.
Thus we know that these precepts are truly the mainstay of the Buddha-dharma, the lifeblood of the *saṃgha*, the bridge across the ocean of suffering, and the essential gateway to *nirvāṇa*.
If one does not receive and uphold them with the reverence due to a crown jewel, how could one avoid sinking into the depths of rebirth?
Furthermore, do not fail the Tathāgata’s entrustment. All you, children of the Buddha, should reflect upon these compassionate instructions:
uphold the bequeathed Dharma even at the cost of your lives, and revere the Prātimokṣa for as long as you live, so that the True Dharma may endure forever.
To remain in the world with blazing vigor is what it means to know gratitude and repay kindness, and to contemplate virtue and repay virtue.
As for the *śīla-sūtra*, it refers to the two hundred and fifty rules of the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya*. *Vinaya* is the method for eliminating and extinguishing transgressions.
*Parinirvāṇa* is the Chinese term for "entering quiescent extinction," meaning that birth and death have been eternally extinguished.
It is also called "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*), meaning that the great affliction has been forever extinguished and one has transcended the four currents.

One should regard it as the World-Honored One himself; this means that as long as this *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra remains in the world, it is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, eternally abiding and never perishing.
Therefore, it is specifically to be revered as such. As the *Śāriputra-śāstra* (or *Yījiào jīng*) says: "The Tathāgata, at the Śāla..."
Between the twin trees, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"O bhikṣus, after my passing, you should revere, treasure, and honor the Prātimokṣa. It is like one who encounters light after darkness, or a poor man who finds a treasure."
You should know that these individuals are your very own teachers; while I remain in the world, they are no different from me.
Regarding the statement that this sutra shall abide long in the world and so forth: it means that as long as there is practice according to the precepts, this sutra abides in the world.
When this sutra abides in the world, the radiance of the True Dharma blazes forth and is not extinguished. By means of this light, one is able to perceive the principles of the Truths (satya).
Thus one proceeds toward Nirvana; this constitutes the teaching, practice, principle, and fruit, all of which are intensely radiant.

If one does not maintain the precepts and the poṣadha to eliminate transgressions, the defilements of sin will increase daily, the light of wisdom will be lost, and one will fail to behold the Noble Path, thereby falling into the three miserable realms.
It is like the setting sun; because of the darkness and inability to see, one falls into pits and ditches.
One should guard and uphold these precepts, just as a yak loves its tail. Sit together in harmony, as the Buddha has taught.
The commentary states: This verse exhorts one to guard the precepts and to follow the Buddha’s regulations.
This means that a practitioner who cherishes the guarding of the precepts would rather die than transgress them, just as a yak treasures its tail even at the cost of its own life.

As for those sitting together in harmony, it is to prevent the fault of being separated from the assembly. "As spoken by the Buddha" refers to the removal of what is not in accordance with the Dharma.
In brief, it means that practitioners, cherishing the precepts for themselves and aspiring to remain free from transgressions,
gather together in one place every half-month to perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts, just as the Buddha has taught.
I have finished reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, and the Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha ceremony.
Now, I dedicate all the merits spoken of in this Prātimokṣa Sūtra to all sentient beings, so that together they may all attain the Way of the Buddha.
*Commentary:* The first half of the verse clarifies that the tasks performed by oneself and others are complete. The latter verse dedicates the merit from these performed deeds.
Dedicate [the merit] to sentient beings so that they may together attain the Buddha-way. What is called "the work to be done" refers to all merits.
All merits refer to the merits produced by each and every precept. To bestow these upon all sentient beings—
It means that whereas previously one performed the *poṣadha* and recited the precepts solely for one's own benefit, now by bestowing [these] upon sentient beings, it becomes the benefit of others.
"Together attaining the Buddha-way" refers to not allowing anyone to attain *nirvāṇa* alone, but rather bringing all to *nirvāṇa* through the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata.
This is also the Bodhisattva’s initial arousal of the great mind (*mahācitta*), which is immediately joined with...
It is the great vow that all sentient beings together aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood and ultimate nirvana. A question is asked:
"In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, what need is there to dedicate [merit] toward the path of the Buddha? The answer is: "This is precisely what is meant by being a true Śrāvaka."
By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, let all hear that there is only the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), neither a second nor a third.
Furthermore, the precepts serve to prevent error and cease evil; they are not held by Śrāvakas alone. The substance of a bhikṣu encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles;
how could he be designated solely as an Arhat? Since Bodhisattvas are originally divided into lay and ordained, how could a bhikṣu be equated with the laity?
If one does not maintain this cultivation of the body, by what means could the Dharma of the Saṃgha be established? Therefore it is said:
a lay bodhisattva maintains the lay precepts, while an ordained bodhisattva maintains the monastic precepts. A lay bodhisattva is called an upāsaka (lay devotee).
The renunciant bodhisattva is called a bhikṣu; he is one who knows the precepts of a bhikṣu.
These are not restricted to a narrow-minded [śrāvaka] perspective. How could a renunciant bodhisattva fail to protect them? All Buddhas of the three periods of time share this same teaching;

it is not only the case for the present alone. Some may say: "If a śrāvaka maintains the precepts, it is called breaking the precepts for a bodhisattva; if a śrāvaka breaks the precepts, it is called..."
"Śākyamuni upholds the precepts. What is the meaning of this? For the Śrāvaka, self-deliverance is the priority; thus, the cessation [of unwholesome conduct] is termed "upholding.
For the Bodhisattva, benefiting sentient beings is the fundamental principle; failing to extensively perform various wholesome deeds is termed a "transgression.
This correctly criticizes the fault of a narrow mind focused on self-benefit, and does not refer to those who possess the great mind of benefiting others and together realize the Buddha-way.

It is listed here. Although it is said that [the precepts] are for one's own benefit, they truly encompass the salvation of others. Thus, within each and every precept, there is nothing that does not involve protecting others.
This is indeed the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), secretly placing a pearl inside the lining of a garment so that its great utility may eventually be obtained.
People today do not understand the Sage’s intention and instead harbor resentment toward the *Prātimokṣa*. If one were to awaken to the nature of all phenomena...
There is nothing that is not sublime conduct. Thus, mounting the white ox, he returns to the place of treasure.
End of Volume Twelve of the *Commentary on the Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra*.
Phonetic Glossary.
The three realms of existence consist of: first, sentient beings of the desire realm; second, sentient beings of the form realm; and third, sentient beings of the formless realm.
This is because the sentient beings of these three realms have outflows (*āsrava*) as their cause and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their fruit, and thus possess birth and death.
The four floods (*ogha*): the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*): first, the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*);

second, attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); third, doubt (*vicikitsā*). The ten proclivities (*anuśaya*): first, greed (*rāga*); second, hatred (*pratigha*); third, ignorance (*avidyā*); fourth, pride (*māna*); fifth, doubt (*vicikitsā*); sixth, the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); seventh, [the view of] extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*)...

[The ten fetters are: 1. Belief in a self; 2. Adherence to precepts and observances; 3. Doubt; 4. Grasping at views; 5. Grasping at views concerning the extremes; 6. Hatred; 7. Pride; 8. False view; 9. Adherence to precepts and observances; 10. Grasping at views.

Regarding the *mao* (pronounced as in "mao" or "miao"): it is a beast of the Southern tribes, shaped like an ox. Its tail is five-colored and long and white, which it loves so dearly that it disregards its own life for its sake.

The Arhat who has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) enters into the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa*). Therein exists only solitary liberation; because the body has become like ashes, there is no body;

because ignorance has been extinguished, there is no further cognition. Because it is a singular liberation, it is called "solitary. If one employs worldly wisdom (*laukikajñāna*) to sever the afflictions of volition (*saṃyojana*), it is termed the knowledge of exhaustion;

if it is the untainted severance (*anāsravaprahāṇa*), it is termed the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). When the volitional afflictions of the three realms are exhausted, one attains exhaustion.
The wisdom of non-arising is called the non-arising of afflictions. Realizing the eighty-first part of true emptiness is called the non-arising of principle.
Being fully endowed with true wisdom is called the non-arising of wisdom. Not undergoing birth and death is called the non-arising of retribution.
The *Abhidharma* states: "The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) means: 'I have known suffering,' up to 'I have known the path. The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) means:
'I have already known suffering,' up to 'I have already cultivated the path; I shall no longer cultivate it. Furthermore, it says: 'My outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted; I shall not be born again.
The wisdom and abandonment of the two vehicles are likewise identical in their realization of the truth; however, because they lack great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they are not [so] named.

Regarding the Bodhisattva, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The true nature and characteristics of all phenomena are attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles as well, yet they are not called Buddhas.
[The Bodhisattvas] exclusively cultivate five dharmas: first, desire; second, diligence; third, mindfulness; fourth, skillful wisdom; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind. As for "desire":
This refers to having a joyful aspiration, longing, and delight in practice without weariness. As for diligence, it means being unremitting day and night.

To give rise to *prajñā*, one must rely on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which requires great diligence. Only when body and mind are applied with urgency will it be accomplished. This is mindfulness (*smṛti*).
This means that from moment to moment in continuous succession, one constantly recollects the first dhyāna and does not recollect other matters.

"Wisdom" (prajñā) refers to discerning the first dhyāna as worthy of honor and esteem, while regarding the desire realm as deceptive and loathsome; to cultivate this with a mind free of outflows (anāsrava-citta) constitutes skillful wisdom.

One-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). This means that when practicing this dharma, one concentrates the mind with single-minded devotion, without any other objects of focus, being determined to seek the first *dhyāna* through to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) with a focused mind.
If these five dharmas are absent, even mundane meditation (*vastu-dhyāna*) is difficult to achieve, let alone the concentration on the ultimate principle (*tattva-samādhi*).
One should know that these five dharmas serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for both small and great matters and for the ultimate principle. "Great" refers to...

The three teachings are the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect. "Small" refers to the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching. "Phenomena" (*shi*) refers to mundane dhyāna; "principle" (*li*) refers to supramundane dhyāna.
Regarding the pure four great elements of the form realm, the *Zhi guan* states: "If the body is upright and the mind is collected, the breath will become harmonious."
When one awakens to this path of the mind, it becomes utterly clear and still, profoundly peaceful and secure, entering step by step.

When the mind remains upon its object without wandering or scattering, this is called "coarse abiding" (*audārikasthiti*). Following this state, when the profound peace surpasses what came before, it is called "subtle abiding" (*sūkṣmasthiti*).
Between these two states—before and after—there must necessarily be a method for sustaining the body. When this method arises, [the practitioner] spontaneously...
Nevertheless, the body remains upright, without fatigue or pain, as if some external force were supporting its strength.

If it is brought [into the body] through an evil method, it is urgent and intensely painful; when it departs, it is relaxed and accompanied by exhaustion. This is the coarse and wicked method of bringing forth.

If one skillfully maintains the Dharma, abiding in both coarse and subtle states without the faults of laxity or urgency, then after perhaps one or two sessions, one or two days, or one or two months, one will gradually perceive a depth and subtlety that suddenly opens up the mind-ground with clarity.

The body becomes like a cloud or a shadow, while the illumination of the Dharma is bright and pure; thus, one accords with the dharmas of meditative concentration, maintaining the mind immovably within the embrace [of samādhi].
It is purified and cleansed, becoming fresh, clear, and cool. Although it is empty and pure, one still perceives the signs of body and mind; yet, the various constituent merits have not yet arisen.
This is called the "unattained concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the desire realm. From this unattained concentration, one gradually realizes that body and mind are void and tranquil.
Internally, one does not see the body; externally, one does not see objects. This may continue for a single day, or even for months and years, in meditative absorption.
The mind does not deteriorate. Within meditative concentration, one immediately perceives that the body and mind are subtly vibrating and moving progressively.

There may arise eight types of tactile sensations—movement, lightness, heaviness, cold, heat, roughness, and smoothness—which constitute the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Movement and lightness belong to wind (*vāyu*).

Itchiness and warmth are fire; coldness and smoothness are water; heaviness and roughness are earth. When their essential nature and functions are combined, there are eight tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*).

The tactile sensation of movement possesses the qualities of the "branch-cluster" (*śākhā-vana*). If the eight tactile sensations arise within the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), they are all erroneous contacts;
they increase illness and hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and lack true merit. If one enters the concentration of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*), then the eight [sensations] move.
Contact possesses ten virtues: first, emptiness; second, clarity; third, concentration; fourth, wisdom; fifth, a wholesome mind; sixth, pliancy;
seventh, joy; eighth, bliss; ninth, liberation; and tenth, correspondence with the object. The remainder is as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Fuxing*.

○ Summary Verses for the Two Hundred and Fifty Precepts (While both the *Mahāsāṃghika* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda* possess summary verses, those of the *Dharmaguptaka* are incomplete. Now, following the sequence of the original text, they are set forth so that beginners may easily memorize them).

If one commits an act of impurity, takes five coins with a thieving mind, intentionally takes the life of a human being, or falsely claims superhuman attainments—these are the four *pārājika* offenses; one who commits them is not to live in community.
Fondling the genitals, touching the body of a woman, coarse speech, soliciting sexual favors, acting as a matchmaker, and building an oversized house.

Not disposing of a large dwelling, taking what is unfounded, slandering with partial evidence, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, its associates, defiling families, and opposing the formal act of suspension;

being of evil character and refusing to accept correction—of these nine, one commits the offense at the very first instance, while for the latter four, it occurs upon the third admonition. To extinguish these remaining rules, they are excluded from the assembly of twenty.
To sit in private with a woman, or to sit in public; these two or three offenses, according to their respective regulations, are called the *aniyata-dharmas* (undetermined rules).
Keeping an extra robe overnight; keeping a robe for more than one month once it has been fulfilled;
taking a robe from a nun who is not a relative; having a nun wash, dye, or beat a robe; and begging for robes from laypeople who are not relatives.
Accepting robes after the [proper] time; requesting robes for the sake of excellence; seeking an increased price; encouraging two families to join together;
begging for robes more than six times; making bedding from raw silk; using pure black wool or wool that is not mixed; failing to keep them for less than six years;
failing to patch an old sitting mat with new material; and keeping wool for more than thirty days.
Causing a nun to wash, dye, or tear [cloth]; accepting or grasping gold, silver, or coins;
buying, selling, or trafficking; keeping an extra bowl beyond the limit; mending a robe and seeking a better one;
having a non-relative weave a robe, approving of the price, or encouraging fine weaving; giving a robe and then angrily snatching it back; and keeping leftover medicine for more than seven days.
Previously seeking [cloth] for use as a rain-cloak; Keeping it past the time limit; accepting urgent gifts;
During the Kārttika month, diverting monastic property belonging to the Saṃgha toward oneself after six nights have passed— These are called the offenses involving forfeiture (Naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
Having committed these thirty matters, one must forfeit them before the Saṃgha; As for the remaining offenses involving transgression (Pāyattika), one must confess them before another person.
Speaking falsehoods and words of disparagement; Divisive speech that creates estrangement between others;

Staying for more than three nights in the same room as a woman who has not received full ordination; Reciting together with them; speaking of the faults of others; Proclaiming one's own realization of the Dharma;
speaking excessively to women; Digging the earth; destroying sacred groves; Speaking harshly and uttering insults.
Spreading monastic requisites on the open ground; failing to put away items from within a room;
forcibly seizing a dwelling place; dragging another out of a monastery; sitting cross-legged on a bed with detachable legs;
using water containing living beings; covering a room for more than three days; failing to be dispatched to provide instruction; and providing instruction until sunset.
Reproaching one who gives instruction; giving robes to a nun who is not a relative; sewing robes for a nun; sitting in a secluded place with a nun;
making an appointment to travel together; traveling by boat together; accepting food praised by a nun;
traveling on the same road as a woman; receiving more than one meal offering; and distributing [robes] in turn to a separate group.
Accepting invitations exceeding three bowls; Not performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite; Causing others to commit the offense of eating at improper times;
Eating food kept overnight or food not formally accepted; Soliciting choice delicacies when not ill and giving them with one's own hand to non-Buddhists;
Entering another house without having informed [the host]; Forcibly sitting in a secluded place within a household where a meal is being served.
Being alone with a woman in an open space; intentionally causing another to be unable to eat; accepting an excessive amount of medicine when invited;
going to view a military array; staying for more than three nights among an army; remaining to observe the strength and power of an army;
drinking alcohol; playing in the water; tickling; not heeding words; and frightening other bhikṣus.
Bathing without a valid reason; lighting a fire on open ground to warm oneself; playing by hiding others' clothing and belongings; wearing robes that have not been consecrated as pure gifts;
wearing new robes without dyeing them to change their color; killing animals; drinking water containing insects;
intentionally causing distress; concealing another's offense; conferring full ordination upon one who has not reached the required age; and rekindling a dispute that has already been settled.
Accompanying a bandit; not abandoning evil and wrong views; providing for one who holds such views; keeping a suspended *śrāmaṇera*;
interrogating and lightly reviling the precepts; falsely claiming "I only know this now" when violating the *karmavācanā*;
departing after giving consent (*chanda*); and later regretting having given consent.
Eavesdropping and relaying disputes; striking a bhikṣu; groundless accusation of saṃghāvaśeṣa; entering a palace and taking precious objects;
arriving in a village at an improper time; high beds and cushions stuffed with cotton;
ivory, bone, or horn needle-cases; oversized sitting mats; and bandages for sores as well as rain-cloaks.
Making [a robe] equal in measure to the Buddha’s robe is called a *pāyattika*. Thus, for one who commits any of these ninety rules, there should be confession and repentance.
To conceal [an offense] and not disclose it; to fall into the suffering of being boiled and burned;
to receive food personally from a nun who is not a relative; to take [food] on behalf of others without ceasing [the practice]; and eating at a house of study where fear exists.
These four are called the dharmas of regret: Wearing the lower robe with proper neatness, Entering the houses of the laity with full decorum;
One must know the rules for eating and chewing, Protecting purity by discarding bowl-water, And attending to the calls of nature according to the teachings.
When preaching the Dharma, one should not violate the proper decorum, And one should show reverence toward the Buddha’s stūpas; While on the road, one must not carry them along.
Climbing a tree no higher than a man’s height; carrying a net-bag without piercing it with a staff—these and such like hundred dharmas are called "matters to be trained in.

The presence [of the accused], recollection, being not insane, speaking for oneself, seeking [the truth], the majority verdict, and the covering over as with grass—thus there are four kinds of legal disputes.
These seven are able to eliminate [defilements]; furthermore, there are other qualities of the Buddha’s Dharma. One should train in harmony with these;
such a person is called a bhikṣu. This is a true son of the Buddha; by this, all bonds are loosened and the cause for nirvāṇa is attained.
The Summary Verses on the Two Hundred and Fifty Precepts (End).
