The *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Lightness and Heaviness of Offenses for Violating the Precepts* states: At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, during the late afternoon...
Awakening from his meditative concentration, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have a doubt; I now wish to inquire about it. I only pray that you will grant me your permission."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you.

Maudgalyāyana then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī lacks a sense of shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and violates the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma)."

“In this way, for committing a *pāyattika*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pārājika* offense, how many unwholesome transgressions (*anartha*) are incurred? I pray that you will explain this. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

Listen attentively, listen attentively! I shall now speak for you. If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī is shameless and lacks a sense of moral dread, and out of contempt for the Buddha’s words violates the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma), they will fall into hell with a lifespan equal to five hundred years as measured by the gods of the Four Great Kings.

In human reckoning, this is nine hundred thousand years. Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and dread of blame, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *pāyattika* offense, they will fall into hell for the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, which is one thousand years;
in human reckoning, this is three hundred and sixty million years. Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and...
If one lacks shame and, out of contempt for the Buddha’s words, commits a *pāyattika* offense, they will fall into hell with a lifespan of two thousand years according to the Yāma heaven;

by human reckoning, this is twenty-four billion and forty thousand years. Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and, out of contempt for the Buddha’s words, commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense, [the retribution] is like a lifespan of four thousand years in the Tuṣita heaven.
They fall into hell for fifty billion and sixty thousand years by human reckoning. Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana,
if one is shameless and lacks a sense of propriety, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,
they will fall into hell for eight thousand years as measured by the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati devas— two hundred thirty billion and forty [million] years by human reckoning.

"O thousand-year one! Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *pārājika* offense, they will fall into hell for a lifespan of sixteen thousand years as measured by the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.
In human reckoning, this amounts to nine hundred twenty-one *koṭis* and sixty thousand years. When the Venerable Maudgalyāyana heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced.
So it shall be practiced. At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses:

"Because of the causes and conditions of contempt, one falls into the evil realms at the end of life; But by the causes and conditions of practicing virtue, one is born in the heavens in this very life."

By virtue of this, one cultivates wholesome karma; Leaving evil behind, one attains liberation. One who does not contemplate the causes and conditions of the body will fall into the evil realms when the body perishes.
A bhikṣu delights in heedfulness; Heedlessness brings much sorrow and reproach. A small dispute can lead to great calamity.
Accumulated evil leads to entry into the fires of hell;
the merit of observing the precepts brings joy. One who breaks the precepts harbors fear; only by eternally severing the outflows (*āsrava*) of the three realms does one attain *nirvāṇa*.
The virtue of precepts is to be relied upon; The reward of merit constantly follows the mind. Seeing the Dharma, one becomes a leader among men;

Forever severed from the three evil realms, one is cautious through the precepts and removes all fear. With merit and virtue, one is honored throughout the three worlds; Ghosts, nāgas, and malevolent poisons cannot cause harm.
Those who do not transgress and uphold the precepts—
sages and seers possessing the five supernormal powers— who have mastered the various worldly incantations and arts, act as a source of shame for those lacking shame,
thereby severing all such lack of conscience.
The Tathāgata established the prohibitive precepts, Reciting them every half-month; Having explained the benefits of the precepts, I prostrate to all Buddhas.

According to the Tripiṭaka, both the methods of repentance and the principles are fully presented, with matters and theory mutually elucidated. Regarding the practice of repentance, it is called "Prostrating to the Buddha."

Regarding the Sūtras, the methods for empowered mantras, and the practice of the Vaipulya rituals, one must behold auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*). By verifying the mind according to the teachings, one can subdue the root of karma.

If one practices the ritual of repentance through principle (*li*), one contemplates the emptiness of the nature of offenses (*pāpa-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) to extinguish the source of karmic activity. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
If one can cultivate the precepts of body, speech, and mind, as well as wisdom, and is able to contemplate all phenomena as being like empty space,
then even if one has committed evil deeds, through such reflection and observation, one can transform heavy retributions in hell into light experiences in the present life.

However, if one cannot extricate oneself from minor offenses, lacks any initial intention to repent, fails to practice virtue, and conceals one's flaws— even if one possesses goodness— [one will not escape].
Karma, when defiled by the stains of transgression, transforms what would have been a light retribution in the present life into the extremely heavy and evil fruits of hell.

As stated in the sutras, one must practice rational repentance (*yili chan*) by contemplating the emptiness of the nature of sin. This requires the integration of bodily precepts, mental discipline, and wisdom;

furthermore, it is necessary to rely on specific ritual acts to openly confess and eliminate faults. Only then does one accord with the intent of the sutras and extinguish the source of karma. Although sin arises from the mind, [it must be addressed through both internal realization and external action].
Necessarily, karma is accomplished through phenomena; therefore, one eliminates it by relying back upon those very phenomena.

That is to say, offenses arise from causes and conditions, and they likewise cease from causes and conditions. Since that which arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature, it is said that "the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty.

Yet, cause and effect are not obscured; this is what is meant by "the retribution of results is never lost. If that which arises from conditions possessed intrinsic nature, then even contemplating it would not [eliminate it].

They can be liberated. Because they possess no substantial nature, they are able to cease once again through causes and conditions. How could one negate dependent origination while seeking the emptiness of nature?

It is not that sins will naturally be expiated without performing repentance (*pratikramana*). If one discards phenomena to discuss principle, one truly does not yet know the true characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that principle;
how then could one observe all dharmas as being like empty space? Even if one were to depart from conditions...
When observing all phenomena (*dharmas*), one realizes that deluded phenomena are not different from principle (*li*); how could one fail to awaken to the fact that their very substance is emptiness?
Yet today there are the狂愚 (mad and foolish) who, shameless regarding their own faults, constantly use the mouth to speak of principle while falsely claiming to "observe the mind" (*guanxin*).

They neglect phenomenal characteristics (*xiang*) and fail to repent; since they are deluded regarding both phenomenon and principle, how can their practice and understanding correspond? Furthermore, principle has no capacity for dual establishment, whereas phenomena...
There is the merit of embracing principle; therefore, even if one performs *kṣamā* (confession) without contemplating the mind, it can still resolve the flow of transgressions.

However, if one discusses principle without speaking of repentance, it will be difficult to clear the source of the offense. When practice and principle proceed together, offenses are extinguished like frost melting in the sun.
If a bhikṣu violates the monastic discipline (*vinaya*), he must rely on the Vinaya school to eradicate it; he must certainly understand...

Regarding the names, types, and natures of offenses, if they are specifically cited during the confession, the essence of the precepts is restored to purity. If one is doubtful or does not recognize the offense, it is improper to apply the ritual procedure;
thus, the offense is difficult to eliminate. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Although an offense within the Vinaya may be extremely subtle, it becomes pure through confession.
However, having violated the ten wholesome precepts, although one confesses, the karma for the three evil realms is not removed. This is like the case of a bhikṣu who commits an offense...

Regarding the various categories of natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and so forth, speaking from this perspective: when a bhikṣu confesses his transgressions, he merely extinguishes the six offenses that violate established regulations (*prajñapti-śīla*).

As for natural transgressions (*prakṛti-āpatti*), one must repent and eliminate them in accordance with the aforementioned principles and facts. If one relies merely on the facts and principles without confessing the offense of violating regulations to another person, the violation of the regulations will still remain;
how then could one avoid those six defeats (*pārājika*)? All three [methods] must be practiced together, such that both natural and proscribed offenses are simultaneously addressed.
[The Buddha] sent [them away]. Those who possess wisdom and desire to make their body and mind pure should cleanse themselves according to the Sūtras and Vinaya.
If one does not repent according to the Dharma as prescribed by the Vinaya, even a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition) cannot be extinguished. Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:

"There may be circumstances where there is no offense, yet one incurs an offense; for example, when a bhikṣu commits an act that is not an offense but performs a formal confession of an offense, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."

Regarding offenses under the Vinaya, there are circumstances where one who has committed an offense becomes free of offense, such as when constructing a small hut, a large dwelling, or in all matters up to the three formal admonitions.
There are also circumstances where an offense remains an offense until it is addressed within the Saṃgha;
at the time of the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, after the three inquiries, those with offenses must confess according to the Dharma, while those without offenses remain silent. At that time...

If one has committed an offense and does not repent according to the Dharma, nor informs others, nor forms the thought, "I shall wait for a pure and like-minded person to confess my offense according to the Dharma," then by remaining silent, one incurs a *vayinītikā* offense. However, there are circumstances where there is no offense;
that is, one who does not act and thus does not transgress. Furthermore, there are circumstances where what was heavy becomes light, as compared [to other cases].

If one commits a *pāyattika* offense, or toward one who holds evil and heterodox views, or toward one who has been subject to formal suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), and then confesses the transgression, one incurs a *vibhaṅga-vinaya* offense.
There are also circumstances where an offense may shift from light to heavy: if a bhikṣu commits a *vibhaṅga-vinaya* offense and confesses it to someone who slanders the sūtras.

If a person who has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) confesses their transgression, they incur a *pāyattika* offense. There are cases where the conditions range from grave to extremely grave:

if a bhikkhu commits a *pāyattika* offense and confesses it toward someone who recites the Sūtras while being under formal censure, and that person confesses their transgression, they incur a *pāyattika* offense. There are cases where the conditions range from light to extremely light:
if a bhikkhu commits an offense against the Vinaya (*vibhaṅga-vinīta*) and confesses it toward one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), this is not called a valid confession.
Transgression. Furthermore, one incurs the offense of *vyatikrama-vinaya*.
End of the Attached Verse Summary of the Characteristics of the Precepts.
